Taxes on fuel make consumers aware of hidden costs such as planet-warming gases and other pollution. Where signals are missing, behavior barely responds. Electricity users react little to price in the short run because they do not face the actual cost of production at each moment.

  <!-- nature-econ-408 -->

- **Market economies: letting prices guide production**

  In a market economy, strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production. That price system is the heart of the definition. A market economy is one in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand. Prices signal people to adjust what they produce and invest. Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones, where governments correct market failures and promote welfare. All of them need clearly defined, enforceable rules of ownership (Property rights: the rules of who owns what), though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also trade in markets. Governments have several tools. They can set maximum or minimum prices, such as a lowest legal wage, or use taxes on harmful side effects (Pigouvian tax) to deal with externalities. Joseph Stiglitz argues that markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures. A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax breaks, carbon trading and environmental rules.

  <!-- nature-econ-395 -->

- **Price controls: when governments set prices**

  Diocletian tried to cap the price of every commodity in the late 3rd century AD, with little success. Price controls are government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services, and they are ancient: the Code of Hammurabi set wages for shipbuilders. There are two main kinds. A ceiling (Price ceilings: a legal maximum price) sets the most that may be charged. A floor (Price floors: a legal minimum price) sets the least. Controls on rents and wages are well-known examples. Governments use them to keep goods affordable during shortages, to slow inflation, or to guarantee a minimum income to some providers. Controls are also one of the indirect ways governments subsidize energy. A cap set low tends to backfire. Keeping prices artificially low raises demand beyond what supply can meet, and shortages feed black markets with higher prices. During the 1973–74 Arab oil embargo, a US price cap below the market level led to long queues and gas stations running dry. Most Western economists say consumer price controls do not work, though since the 1990s wage floors have won strong support among some economists.

  <!-- nature-econ-402 -->

- **Shifts in supply and demand: when the whole curve moves**

  A cheaper way of growing wheat does something a change in the price of wheat cannot: it moves the entire supply curve. Shifts in supply and demand are changes in conditions other than a good's own price that move a whole curve, and so change the equilibrium price and quantity. Economists guard the language carefully. A movement along a curve is a "change in quantity demanded," while a shift of the whole curve is a "change in demand." Demand can rise because of changing tastes, higher incomes, price changes in substitutes and complements, expectations or more buyers. A rise in demand lifts both the equilibrium price and the quantity. Supply shifts work in either direction. The cheaper wheat-growing method shifts supply outward, lowering the price and raising the quantity sold. A rise in raw-material costs shifts supply to the left, so less is offered at every price.

  <!-- nature-econ-361 -->

- **The price mechanism: how prices share out resources**

  When the 1970s oil crisis drove oil prices up, several countries started producing their own oil. That response is the price mechanism at work: the way prices decide how resources are shared out and steer how much of each good is supplied and demanded. Prices match buyers and sellers in three ways: as an incentive, as a signal and as a way of rationing resources. The mechanism can be slow. Dearer fuel does not quickly cut demand, but over time it pushes firms to offer alternatives such as biodiesel and electric cars. Once competition settles into balance, the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it, an ideal explored in Allocative efficiency: making the goods people want. The mechanism takes many forms. In the form covered in Auctions: letting the highest bidder set the price, bidders compete and the highest bid wins. Cap-and-trade for planet-warming gases applies the idea to emissions, as the US did earlier with sulfur dioxide, cutting overall smog. Ludwig von Mises argued that planned economies reject the price mechanism and so cannot allocate resources rationally.

  <!-- nature-econ-407 -->

- **Total cost: the full bill for making output**

  Total cost is the lowest cost of producing a given amount of output. It is made up of costs that vary with output plus costs that do not. Labor and raw materials change with output; buildings and machinery do not, in the short term. In economics, total cost includes the opportunity cost of every input, the benefit of its next-best use. The extra total cost of one more unit gets its own entry, Marginal cost: the price of one more unit. Given time, the bill can shrink. Long-run total cost is generally lower than short-run, because the amount of capital can be chosen to suit the output.

  <!-- nature-econ-413 -->

- **Marginal cost: the price of one more unit**

  To make one more car, a carmaker needs more labor and parts, but not a new factory building. Marginal cost is that extra total cost of producing one more unit of output. It counts only costs that change with output. It differs from the cost per unit on average, which is total cost divided by the number of units made. Because costs that do not vary with output stay put, doubling them leaves marginal cost, and the profit-maximizing price and quantity, unchanged. Textbooks expect marginal cost to rise in the short run, as more labor and materials press against a fixed building and machinery. A competitive firm keeps producing as long as the sale price exceeds marginal cost, stopping where the two are equal. On a graph, the marginal cost curve crosses the average-cost curves at their lowest points. Where growing bigger cuts unit costs (Economies of scale: why bigger can be cheaper), pricing at marginal cost fails to cover total costs and so needs a subsidy. The textbook picture is disputed. In a survey of 200 executives, 11% said their marginal costs rose with output, 48% said they were constant and 41% said they fell. Many empirical studies likewise find marginal cost constant or falling for most firms.

  <!-- nature-econ-347 -->

- **Profit: what is left after every cost**

  Economists usually assume firms try to maximize profit, so they define it carefully. Profit is what a business has left from its revenue after paying the total costs of its inputs, counting both explicit and implicit costs. Accounting profit subtracts only the explicit costs on a firm's books. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so it is smaller. The break-even case (Normal profit: just enough to stay in business) is when revenue just equals total costs, so economic profit is zero: the least a firm needs to stay in a competitive industry. Competition erodes anything more. In a perfectly competitive market, economic profit draws in new firms until prices fall and the profit disappears in the long run. Profit lasts only in markets with one or a few dominant sellers. Barriers to entry protect it: patents, rights to land and rules on how land is used. Competition laws aim to stop powerful firms from building artificial barriers to protect their profits. Profit is greatest where the revenue from one more unit equals its marginal cost. A wider measure, social profit, adds or subtracts the externalities, such as pollution, and the gains to buyers that a firm's activity creates.

  <!-- nature-econ-409 -->

- **Monopoly: the market with one seller**

  The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses. A monopoly is a market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service. With no competition and no close substitutes, it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits. Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market. Its power comes from barriers to entry, which may be economic, legal or deliberate. A monopolist does not simply charge the highest price. It picks the output where the revenue from one more sale equals the cost of making it, aiming at the largest total profit. Compared with a market of many small competitors it sells less at a higher price. The trades it forgoes are a pure loss to society (Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets). Contestable-market theory adds that a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low. Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behavior.

  <!-- nature-econ-349 -->

- **Perfect competition: the textbook ideal market**

  Real markets come close to it mainly for farm products and raw materials sold by many sellers to many buyers. Perfect competition is the idealized version: a market with many buyers and sellers, identical products and full information, so that no one can influence the price. Each firm faces a perfectly elastic demand curve and must take the market price. Every profit-maximizing firm ends up charging a price equal to its marginal cost, which makes the market allocatively efficient. In the long run no firm earns economic profit, because any profit draws in new firms until the price falls to the cost per unit. Under these conditions a market reaches an equilibrium where supply equals demand for every product, including labor. Without externalities and Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few, such equilibria are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. This is the first of the theorems in The fundamental theorems of welfare economics. Critics say the model treats firms as passive. It ignores price-cutting, product design, advertising and innovation, and leaves unclear who actually sets prices. They dispute both the realism of its assumptions and whether a model of price-takers can describe a decentralized market at all.

  <!-- nature-econ-353 -->

- **Market power: the ability to set your own price**

  Some sellers can name their price. Market power is a firm's ability to raise its price above its marginal cost, by controlling supply or demand, without losing all its customers. Firms with none, as in perfect competition, are price takers; firms with it are price makers. How much power firms have depends on market structure. Perfect competition and a lone seller are the extremes. In between sit Monopolistic competition: many sellers, each a little different and markets run by a few firms. Power lasts only behind barriers to entry, such as control of scarce resources, advantages of size, better technology or government rules; OPEC's rests on oil. The less elastic the demand a firm faces, the more it can raise price above marginal cost. Economists measure it by markups or, more often, by the market shares of the biggest firms (Concentration ratios: how much the biggest firms hold and The Herfindahl index: weighing market concentration). Competition law, such as the US Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, uses these measures to judge whether a firm has abused its power. Jean Tirole won the 2014 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for analyzing market power and regulation.

  <!-- nature-econ-397 -->

- **Oligopoly: a market run by a few**

  Civil aviation, electricity supply, telecommunications, sugar refining, beer making, and pulp and paper have all been cited as oligopolies: markets in which a few sellers control pricing. A duopoly is the smallest case, an oligopoly of only two firms. In such markets each firm's actions affect the others and provoke reactions, so the firms are mutually interdependent. That makes cooperation tempting. Oligopolists often collude to maximize profits, by price-fixing or by forming price-fixing groups (Cartels: rivals who agree not to compete) that keep new firms out. Competition laws mostly catch formal agreements to collude, so firms can escape through tacit collusion, coordinating without any explicit deal.

  <!-- nature-econ-364 -->

- **Competitive equilibrium: economics' benchmark of efficiency**

  If Alice values her car at 10 and Bob at 20, any price between 10 and 20 is an equilibrium price at which Bob buys the car. That small trade captures a competitive equilibrium, also called Walrasian equilibrium. It describes a market with flexible prices and many traders, each too small to move prices. Every trader gets the best bundle they can afford, and supply equals demand. Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu introduced the concept in 1951, and it serves as economics' benchmark of efficiency. Their model shows such an equilibrium exists in any exchange economy with divisible goods when everyone's preferences are strictly convex. The welfare theorems add that every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient, and every efficient allocation can be reached by one. At this equilibrium marginal benefit equals marginal cost: the value society puts on a good equals the value of the resources used to make it. Efficiency, though, says nothing about fairness. An allocation in which one person has everything can still be efficient.

  <!-- nature-econ-365 -->

- **Imperfect competition: where real markets fall short**

  Some theorists hold that no real market has ever met the conditions of perfect competition. Imperfect competition covers every market that falls short of at least one of them. A market is imperfect if sellers can set their own prices, there is only one seller, entry is blocked, buyers and sellers know different things, or products differ. The broad imperfect structures include Monopolistic competition: many sellers, each a little different, where many firms sell slightly different products, and oligopoly, where a few firms each sway the others. A perfectly competitive firm faces a flat demand curve. A firm in an imperfect market faces one that slopes down. Imperfect competition makes markets inefficient and so leads to market failure. The more a firm can lift price above marginal cost, the greater the inefficiency; at the extreme, a monopoly overcharges and underproduces. Economists dispute whether economic policy should assume perfect or imperfect competition.

  <!-- nature-econ-383 -->

- **Marginal revenue: what one more sale brings in**

  A seller can sell 20 books at $50 each, bringing in $1000. To sell 21, it must cut the price to $49, which brings in $1029. The 21st book adds just $29. That $29 is marginal revenue: the extra revenue a firm earns by selling one more unit. In a perfectly competitive market a firm gets the same price for every unit. Its marginal revenue equals the price, and its marginal revenue curve is a flat line at the market price. A monopoly must cut its price on all units to sell one more, so its marginal revenue is always below the price. Its curve slopes down and lies below the demand curve. When demand is inelastic, selling more forces a price cut on every unit, and marginal revenue turns negative. The rule for profit follows. A firm maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; while marginal revenue is higher, extra units still make money.

  <!-- nature-econ-392 -->

- **Cost curves: drawing what production costs**

  A cost curve is a graph showing a firm's production costs against the total quantity it produces. Profit-maximizing firms use these curves to decide how much to produce. There are curves for total, average and marginal costs and for fixed and variable costs, some for the short run and some for the long run. Costs that do not vary with output draw a flat line, while the same cost spread per unit falls as output grows. Short-run marginal cost first falls and then rises, because of diminishing marginal returns. The long-run curve is shaped by Returns to scale: what happens when you double everything. One rule links the curves. When marginal cost is below the cost per unit, the cost per unit falls; when above, it rises; where they are equal, the cost per unit is lowest. That gives the textbook U-shape. Real firms may not follow it. In a 1952 survey of 334 companies, 95% of managers reported constant or falling costs rather than the textbook U-shape.

  <!-- nature-econ-367 -->

- **Natural monopoly: when one supplier is cheapest**

  In 1848 J.S. Mill first called some monopolies "natural," pointing to gas and water supply, roads, canals and railways. A natural monopoly is a firm whose cost per unit keeps falling across the whole range of market demand. One large supplier is then cheaper than several small ones. Left alone, such markets tend to turn into a monopoly, often after an early entrant expands fast and drives out rivals. Breaking them up is inefficient by definition, so governments mostly use regulation and public ownership. Regulators often impose average-cost pricing. It removes excess profit but weakens the incentive to cut costs.

  <!-- nature-econ-350 -->

- **The law of supply: higher price, more for sale**

  A job paying £20 an hour draws more interest than one paying £15. The same logic runs through every market: all else being equal, a higher price leads sellers to offer more of a good. This is the law of supply. Producers offer more at higher prices because producing more is a way to make more profit, which is why the supply curve slopes upward. Other things shift the whole curve: production costs, the number of suppliers, subsidies, taxes and, in farming, the weather. The law works together with demand. If buyers want more than sellers offer, the price rises, cutting demand and raising supply until the two match. Some heterodox economists, such as Steve Keen, dispute the law for mass-produced goods. Their unit prices may fall as output grows, so the supply curve often slopes downward.

  <!-- nature-econ-391 -->

- **Price elasticity of supply: how sellers react to price**

  No price will produce more Van Gogh paintings, and a country's gold output may be capped by availability. These are extreme cases of price elasticity of supply. It measures how strongly the quantity sellers offer responds to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity supplied for a 1% change in price. Supply is inelastic below 1, elastic above 1, unit-elastic at exactly 1, and fixed at zero, when quantity does not respond at all. Unlike demand elasticities, supply elasticities are usually positive, because a higher price encourages more production. Time matters. Supply is usually more elastic in the long run, when all inputs can be expanded, than in the short run. So does spare capacity: once capacity is full, more output needs new investment, so supply becomes less elastic. The stakes are real. The more elastic housing supply is, the smaller the rent rise needed to clear a shortage after demand grows. Land is the classic example of a factor whose supply is inelastic.

  <!-- nature-econ-404 -->

- **Cross elasticity of demand: how one price moves another good**

  A 1% rise in the price of margarine raises demand for butter by 0.81%. That figure, 0.81, is a cross elasticity of demand: a measure of how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another. A positive value means the goods are substitutes, a negative value means they are complements, and zero means they are unrelated. Fuel and new cars are complements, so dearer fuel lowers demand for cars. Governments use cross elasticities between drinks when setting alcohol taxes and minimum prices to reduce harmful drinking.

  <!-- nature-econ-368 -->

- **The inverse demand function: price from quantity**

  An inverse demand function flips the usual question. Instead of quantity from price, it gives price as a function of the quantity demanded, which is why it is also called a price function. Its value is the highest price that still sells that quantity. It is found by solving the demand function for price: if Q = 240 − 2P, then P = 120 − Q/2. For a straight-line demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is a − 2bQ: the same starting height and twice the slope. Firms use it to find the most profitable output and then the price to charge.

  <!-- nature-econ-386 -->

- **Market size: counting buyers or money**

  Market size measures how big a market is, either by its number of buyers and sellers or by the money exchanged in it, usually per year. Measured in money, it is often called market value. The same goods can have different market values at each stage, usually rising from production to wholesale to retail.

  <!-- nature-econ-343 -->

- **Negative prices: paying someone to take it**

  In April 2020, oil for May delivery fell to -$37.63 a barrel, a one-day drop of $55.90, because holders feared there was nowhere left to store it. A negative price is a price below zero, where the owner or producer pays the "buyer" to take an item away. Lending at below-zero interest is a similar idea.

  <!-- nature-econ-357 -->

- **Disequilibrium: when markets are out of balance**

  Markets are not always in balance. Disequilibrium is the condition of a market in which the amounts supplied and demanded do not match. It can last only a moment or persist for a long time. Many economists see labor markets as stuck for long periods with more workers offering labor than employers want. Some goods' prices adjust slowly, because of the cost of changing prices and because of long-term contracts. Even so, they do not stay out of balance forever.

  <!-- nature-econ-336 -->

- **Dynamic equilibrium: growing in step**

  An equilibrium need not stand still. In a dynamic equilibrium, several quantities keep growing at the same rate, so the ratios between them stay fixed. In the neoclassical growth model, output and capital grow at the same rate as the workforce, leaving output per worker unchanged. In that model, a permanently higher saving rate raises capital per worker but leaves the growth rate of output unchanged. Comparing two such equilibria is called comparative dynamics.

  <!-- nature-econ-337 -->

- **Government-granted monopolies: exclusive by law**

  A publisher can use its copyright monopoly to charge American students more than Ethiopian students for the same textbook. That is a government-granted monopoly at work: one created when a government gives one person or company the exclusive right to supply something. The grant can come directly from a law that excludes rivals, or indirectly through patents, trademarks and copyright. States grant such rights to reward risky investment or to enrich a domestic interest group.

  <!-- nature-econ-351 -->

- **The inverse elasticity rule: markups and sensitive buyers**

  The less buyers respond to price, the more a monopoly can mark up. The inverse elasticity rule states this exactly: a monopoly's markup, as a share of its price, is inversely proportional to the price elasticity of demand it faces. The markup is measured by The Lerner index: measuring the markup: price minus marginal cost, divided by price, equals minus one over the elasticity of demand. Perfectly competitive firms sit at the other end, with zero market power, simply taking the market price.

  <!-- nature-econ-352 -->

- **Normal profit: just enough to stay in business**

  A business can make money and still earn nothing an economist would call profit. Normal profit is the return that just makes running a business worthwhile, equal to what the owner's time and capital could earn in their next best use. Economists count it as a cost, not as part of business profit. It varies within and across industries, in line with how risky each kind of investment is. Under perfect competition only normal profits survive in the long run, so firms have no reason to enter or leave. Profits above normal persist only where barriers to entry keep new firms out, as in monopoly or oligopoly.

  <!-- nature-econ-354 -->

- **The shutdown point: when to stop producing**

  A loss-making firm faces a short-run question: keep going or stop? The shutdown point is the price below which it does better to stop, where price falls under the per-unit cost of inputs that change with output. Shutting down avoids the costs that vary with output, but not those that must be paid anyway, so those are ignored in the decision. A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve at and above the shutdown point.

  <!-- nature-econ-355 -->

- **Partial equilibrium: one market at a time**

  Alfred Marshall's supply and demand model is the classic partial equilibrium model. It analyzes equilibrium in a single market, holding everything constant except the one change being studied. The prices of substitutes and complements and buyers' incomes are treated as given, which makes it much simpler than general equilibrium. The cost is missed knock-on effects. A tariff on French wine raises its price. Partial equilibrium ignores the knock-on rise in demand for domestic wine, which feeds back and pushes the price higher still. Such knock-on effects usually change the size of a price change but not its direction.

  <!-- nature-econ-399 -->

- **General equilibrium theory: all markets at once**

  General equilibrium theory studies supply, demand and prices across a whole economy of many linked markets, seeking to show that together they reach an overall equilibrium. The theory goes back to Léon Walras's Elements of Pure Economics of 1874. It took its modern form in the 1950s with Arrow, Debreu and McKenzie. Its best-known results are the welfare theorems. The first says market equilibria are Pareto efficient: no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. It quietly assumes complete markets and perfect information. The second says any efficient outcome can be reached by redistributing starting endowments and then leaving the market alone. That suggests efficiency and fairness can be handled separately. From the 1970s, faster computers let economists solve such models for real economies. Models of this kind (Computable general equilibrium: modeling a whole economy) use real data to estimate how an economy might respond to changes in policy or technology. The theory sits at the center of a dispute between schools. Keynesian and Post-Keynesian economists reject it as misleading, arguing that real economies are not in equilibrium.

  <!-- nature-econ-382 -->

- **Laissez-faire: leave prices alone**

  Laissez-faire is the principle that prices and wages should be free of non-market pressure, such as government taxes, subsidies, tariffs, regulations or granted monopolies. Hayek argued that its point is to keep the unique information a price carries. Karl Popper called the idea of the free market paradoxical, since it needs interventions to prevent interventions.

  <!-- nature-econ-379 -->

- **Spontaneous order: order nobody designed**

  No one designed the networks that coordinate a market economy. Friedrich Hayek popularized this idea of spontaneous order: market economies create order through networks that arise from many separate individual decisions. He held that such order shares out a society's resources better than any design could. The idea builds on Adam Smith's invisible hand from The Wealth of Nations.

  <!-- nature-econ-380 -->

- **Residual demand: what is left for one firm**

  A single firm does not face the whole market's demand, only what other firms leave unmet. That leftover is its residual demand curve: market demand minus the supply of the other firms at each price. With many firms, each firm's residual demand is extremely elastic and nearly flat, though not perfectly flat as textbooks draw it.

  <!-- nature-econ-370 -->

- **How taxes and subsidies change prices**

  Put a $0.50 tax on a good that sells for $3.00, and buyers do not pay the full $0.50 extra. In one example the buyers' price rises to $3.30, sellers keep $2.80, and sales fall from 100 to 80. A tax moves the market to a new equilibrium where buyers pay more and sellers keep less. Who legally pays the tax does not matter: a tax on sellers is largely passed on to buyers through higher prices. Most of the burden falls on the less elastic side of the market, the side less able to change how much it buys or sells. Taxes come in two forms. A specific tax, a fixed amount per unit, shifts the supply curve up by that amount. An ad valorem tax, a percentage of price, also pivots it. Subsidies run the logic in reverse. They give the same lower buyer price and higher seller price whether paid to producers or to consumers. Real taxes behave as predicted. Tobacco taxes cut smoking: most studies find an elasticity of 0.4 to 0.5, so a 10% price rise reduces consumption by 4% to 5%.

  <!-- nature-econ-373 -->

- **Arc elasticity: measuring between two points**

  An ordinary elasticity gives different answers depending on which of two points is treated as the start. Arc elasticity removes that problem. It measures elasticity between two points on a demand curve. The base is the average of the two prices and of the two quantities, which gives an average elasticity over that arc of the curve. Hugh Dalton introduced it very early on. Point elasticity instead uses calculus to measure elasticity for a tiny price change at a single point, but it needs the demand formula to be known.

  <!-- nature-econ-359 -->

- **Concentration ratios: how much the biggest firms hold**

  Add up the market shares of the largest few firms in a market, such as the top four, and you have a concentration ratio. The four-firm ratio is 100 per cent for a monopoly and zero for perfect competition. Studies suggest a ratio between 40 and 70 percent points to an oligopoly. Concentration measures are the most common gauge of market power, because they need only revenue data, though they ignore costs and profits.

  <!-- nature-econ-398 -->

- **The Walrasian auction: finding prices by bidding**

  A Walrasian auction finds a competitive equilibrium by steadily raising prices. The auctioneer starts all prices at zero, and at each round buyers name their favorite bundle. Any item wanted by more than one buyer has its price raised, until each item is wanted by at most one buyer. Such mechanisms are also called Walrasian tâtonnement, or English versions of Auctions: letting the highest bidder set the price.

  <!-- nature-econ-366 -->

- **The Herfindahl index: weighing market concentration**

  Square every firm's market share and add them up: the result is the Herfindahl index, a measure of how concentrated a market is. Squaring gives big firms more weight than a simple concentration ratio does. The index runs from 1/N to 1, where N is the number of firms. The more concentrated the market, the higher the value.

  <!-- nature-econ-384 -->

- **Excess supply: more for sale than buyers want**

  If 1000 televisions are offered at $600 but buyers want only 300, the 700 left over push sellers to cut the price until the market balances. That leftover is excess supply, also called a market surplus or glut. Sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy, because the price sits above its equilibrium level. It is the opposite of a shortage, and the two are the two kinds of disequilibrium in a competitive market. Unemployment is excess supply in the labor market. Farmers face it after a good harvest, and governments may step in to buy up the perishable surplus.

  <!-- nature-econ-375 -->

- **Price floors: a legal minimum price**

  Before US airfares were deregulated in 1978, price floors kept flying so costly that in 1965 more than 80% of Americans had never flown on a jet. A price floor is a limit, set by government or another body, on the lowest price that may be charged for a product or service. It only bites if it is set above the equilibrium price; set below, it has no practical effect. Common examples are laws setting the lowest legal wage, supply management in Canadian farming, US airfares before 1978 and minimum prices for alcohol. A binding floor makes buyers buy less while sellers want to sell more, leaving a lasting surplus. It shifts some of the buyers' gains to producers and creates a pure loss to society (Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets). EU support buying to hold farm prices at an intervention price has sometimes left "butter mountains" of surplus in warehouses. Floors can also steady a market. Hybrid cap-and-trade schemes add floor and ceiling prices to steady the carbon price.

  <!-- nature-econ-405 -->

- **Factor markets: buying land, labor and capital**

  Firms sell what they make in product markets, but they buy their inputs in factor markets, where land, labor and capital are bought and sold. Both kinds of market work in much the same way. Factor markets share out land, labor and capital among firms and pay income to their owners as wages, rents and the like. A factor in scarce supply earns a high price and an abundant one a low price, so when a factor's supply falls, its equilibrium price rises. Firms hire at the margin. A firm takes on another worker when the extra revenue that worker brings in exceeds the extra cost.

  <!-- nature-econ-376 -->

- **Monopsony: the market with one buyer**

  A monopsony is the buying-side mirror of a monopoly: a market with a single dominant buyer. An oligopsony has a few. Instead of taking the price of an input from the market, a monopsonist sets it, choosing a point on the input's supply curve. Monopsonies are more common in factor markets than in product markets, and there is growing concern about them in some kinds of labor.

  <!-- nature-econ-377 -->

- **Derived demand: wanting inputs because people want products**

  If shoppers want more new cars, carmakers want more of the inputs used to build them. That is derived demand: demand for an input that comes from demand for the final product it helps make. The link is direct and positive. A good used to make another, final good is called an intermediate good. Labor works the same way, and a firm's demand for it slopes downward: when the wage rises, the quantity of labor wanted falls.

  <!-- nature-econ-372 -->

- **The Lerner index: measuring the markup**

  Named after the economist Abba Lerner, the Lerner index measures market power as the gap between price and marginal cost, taken as a share of price. It runs from zero in a perfectly competitive market to 1. The closer to 1, the bigger the gap. At the profit-maximizing point, (P − MC)/P equals minus one over the elasticity of demand, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.

  <!-- nature-econ-393 -->

- **Veblen goods: when a high price is the point**

  Diamonds, gold, precious stones, famous paintings and antiques can become more wanted as they get dearer. These are Veblen goods: luxuries whose demand rises with their price, because a high price signals status. Thorstein Veblen described such buying as paying for status and social position rather than for extra usefulness.

  <!-- nature-econ-390 -->

- **The minimum wage: a price floor for labor**

  A minimum wage is a price floor for labor: the lowest hourly rate an employer is allowed by law to pay. Standard theory predicts trouble if it is set above the market wage for low-skilled work. Employers hire fewer workers, for example by switching to self-service or machines. The higher wage also draws more people into the labor market, producing a surplus of labor. Yet since the credibility revolution of the 1990s, minimum wages have often won strong support among economists, so the question remains contested.

  <!-- nature-econ-406 -->

- **The market mechanism: prices doing the sharing**

  Buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tend to share out goods and services well. That is the market mechanism. Its quality depends on information: prices tell producers what people want, and the less accurate that information, the worse the coordination and the fewer wants are met. The mechanism has limits. It often cannot provide shared goods (Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few) well, because of problems such as the one in The tragedy of the commons: when shared means overused, so highways needed government planning. Free-market economies leave resources to the private sector, planned economies to the public sector, and mixed economies to both.

  <!-- nature-econ-396 -->

- **The zero-profit condition: competition erases profit**

  In gold rushes few prospectors got rich, but many people built successful businesses selling shovels. The zero-profit condition describes where competition leads: when firms can enter or leave an industry almost freely, each firm's economic profit is pushed to zero. If firms earn positive economic profit, newcomers join until it is gone. If they make losses, firms leave until profit rises back to zero. This settled state is called the industry's long run, and it is close to perfect competition. In neoclassical models, the condition also makes a market economy of profit-seeking firms compatible with zero growth.

  <!-- nature-econ-414 -->

- **Economic surplus: the gains from trading**

  Early writers used the idea of surplus to study food. Farming must feed everyone, so the rest of the economy is limited by the food farmers produce beyond their own needs. Today economic surplus means the total gain that buyers and sellers get from trading in a market. The engineer Jules Dupuit first put forward the idea in the mid-19th century, and the economist Alfred Marshall made it famous, so it is also called Marshallian surplus. It has two parts. The buyers' share, Consumer surplus: the bargain buyers get, is the area above the price and below the demand curve on a supply and demand diagram. The sellers' share, Producer surplus: the sellers' gain, is the area below the price and above the supply curve. Their sum is called social or total surplus, or total welfare. When inefficiency shrinks that total, the lost part is called Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets.

  <!-- nature-econ-338 -->

- **Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets**

  Suppose a cleaning deal would create $40 of total surplus, and a $50 tax is imposed on it. The trade never happens. The government collects nothing, and the $40 simply vanishes. That vanished value is deadweight loss. It is the loss of society's welfare when a good is produced or consumed at a quantity where its benefit to society does not equal its cost. Unlike most losses, which are someone else's gain, it is regained by no one. Either goods are made that cost more than they are worth, or worthwhile goods are not made. Monopoly pricing is one cause. Suppose nails cost $0.10 to make and a monopolist charges $0.60. Buyers who value a nail between those prices are shut out, and their lost benefit is deadweight loss. A subsidy can do the reverse. A $0.03 subsidy lowers the price to $0.07, so people who value a nail below its true $0.10 cost buy it, which wastes resources. Externalities, taxes, and binding caps and floors on prices, such as a minimum wage, cause it too. The more elastic supply and demand are, the bigger the loss from a tax. It also grows with the square of the tax: doubling the tax multiplies the loss by 4.

  <!-- nature-econ-345 -->

- **Gains from trade: why exchange pays**

  Gains from trade are the net benefits people or economies get when they can trade more freely with each other. David Ricardo first clearly stated and proved comparative advantage in 1817, and it remains the basic explanation for where they come from. Technically, they are the rise in buyers' and sellers' combined surplus that comes from lower tariffs or freer trade. They come from specialization, the larger total output it allows, and selling one kind of output for other goods valued more highly. Prices do the steering. They draw labor and other inputs toward activities where they have a comparative advantage, that is, a low opportunity cost. Freer trade is not always best for everyone. A large economy may use taxes and subsidies to gain at other economies' expense, and market power can let some traders block other mutually beneficial trades.

  <!-- nature-econ-381 -->

- **Consumer surplus: the bargain buyers get**

  Drinking water usually carries a large consumer surplus, because people would pay very high prices for it to survive. Consumer surplus is the gap between the most a buyer would be willing to pay for something and the price they actually pay. The first few liters of water are worth the most, since they prevent death, so they hold more surplus than later liters. That points to the general source of the surplus. Buyers value each extra unit less than the last, yet pay the same market price for every unit. On a graph, consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve and above the price; with a straight-line demand curve it is a triangle. A rise in consumer surplus after a price change is read as a gain in welfare, a fall as a loss. When supply grows and the price falls, existing buyers gain on the units they already bought, and new buyers enter and gain too.

  <!-- nature-econ-339 -->

- **Price discrimination: different buyers, different prices**

  Student and senior discounts are a form of price discrimination. The same seller charges different buyers different prices for the same or nearly the same good, according to which group they seem to belong to. It works by exploiting differences in buyers' willingness to pay and in how sensitive they are to price. The aim is to raise profit by shifting consumer surplus to the seller. It needs market power; otherwise buyers would switch sellers or resell cheap units to those charged more. Economists sort it into three degrees, a scheme attributed to Pigou. In first-degree, or perfect, price discrimination each buyer pays their maximum, so the seller captures all consumer surplus. Second-degree discrimination varies price with the quantity bought, and third-degree charges different groups different prices. Drug-makers charge more in wealthier countries, and antiretroviral drugs cost far less in Africa, where sales would otherwise be very limited.

  <!-- nature-econ-403 -->

- **Producer surplus: the sellers' gain**

  Every seller has a lowest price they would accept. Producer surplus is the gain sellers get when the market price is higher than that. It is roughly equal to profit, since producers will not normally sell at a loss. On a graph it is the area below the market price line and above the supply curve. Higher market prices raise it, while higher production costs or lower prices shrink it, and taxes, subsidies, new technology and competition can shift it. Economists use it to judge how taxes, subsidies, price controls and trade policies affect producers.

  <!-- nature-econ-340 -->

- **The rule of one-half: a shortcut for surplus**

  When supply changes a little and the demand curve stays put, how much do buyers gain? The rule of one-half gives a quick estimate of the change in consumer surplus. With straight-line demand, the change is a trapezoid. Its height is the price change, and its middle width is the average of the quantities before and after.

  <!-- nature-econ-341 -->

- **Harberger's triangle: the shape of lost surplus**

  On a supply and demand graph, the deadweight loss from government intervention in an otherwise perfect market appears as a triangle. It is generally credited to Arnold Harberger. The interventions include price floors, caps, taxes, tariffs and quotas. A tax, for example, drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, and the triangle's area is the surplus lost for good. The triangle also measures the loss when a government fails to step into a market with externalities. How much it matters is disputed. Martin Feldstein holds these losses can drag down long-run growth, while James Tobin argued their effect on the economy is small.

  <!-- nature-econ-346 -->

- **Market clearing: no surplus, no shortage**

  Shops discount leftover Christmas decorations after Christmas until shoppers buy the excess supply. That is market clearing in miniature. Market clearing is the process by which a price settles where the amount supplied equals the amount demanded, leaving neither a surplus nor a shortage. The price that does it is the market-clearing, or equilibrium, price. A price above it builds up unsold stock. A price below it leaves buyers short, sometimes unable to find the product at any price. Shocks set the process going. After an earthquake destroys homes, a housing shortage pushes prices up, builders build more, and supply rises until it meets the new demand. From about 1785 to 1935 most economists took market clearing for granted. Then the long mass unemployment of the Great Depression led Keynes and others to doubt it. Most economists now see continuous market clearing as unrealistic but useful for long-run analysis. They still disagree over whether prices adjust quickly enough for markets to clear. Some blame sticky prices; others blame unions or government policy.

  <!-- nature-econ-394 -->

- **Shortages: when buyers want more than there is**

  In the 1980s Soviet Union, prices fixed artificially low left people queuing for cars, apartments and clothing. That is a shortage: a situation in which people want to buy more of a product than is available at the going price, also called excess demand. It is the opposite of excess supply. In a simple market, excess demand pushes the price up until demand matches supply, so a shortage persists only when something stops the price rising. Then something other than price, such as first come first served or a lottery, decides who gets the good. Causes include legal caps on prices, bans on selling a product and suppliers choosing not to raise prices. Shortages bring black markets, queues and rationing, more demand for substitutes, and wasted time that lowers overall wealth. Economists and historians note that lasting shortages and famines have mostly been caused by war, price controls and repressive regimes rather than by having too many people.

  <!-- nature-econ-410 -->

- **Price ceilings: a legal maximum price**

  Venezuela's food price ceilings from 2003 caused shortages and hoarding. A price ceiling is a limit, set by government or another body, on the highest price that may be charged for a product or service. Governments set them to protect consumers from goods becoming too expensive. Set below the market equilibrium price, a ceiling leads to a shortage. It also misallocates what supply there is: ceilings on Helsinki's Hitas apartments cause queuing and mean flats do not go to those who value them most. Ceilings can even raise prices, by giving competing firms a shared target to collude on. US states with an 18 percent interest cap saw rates just below it. Economists generally agree that consumer price controls fail at their aims, and many advise against them. A minority disagree. Isabella Weber argues for price caps to fight sellers' inflation, and Paul Krugman became open to them.

  <!-- nature-econ-400 -->

- **Rent control: a ceiling on housing costs**

  Rent control is a price ceiling on housing rents. The US rent controls of the 1940s, brought in under Franklin D. Roosevelt's Office of Price Administration, played out as economic models predicted. They cut the supply of rental homes available to returning veterans. At the same time homeownership and homes for sale rose, likely because landlords turned rentals into homes for sale.

  <!-- nature-econ-401 -->

### Firms, costs and market structure

Every business faces the same puzzle: what price to charge, which inputs to use and how much to make. Economists call the answer profit maximization, the choice that gives the highest possible total profit. This chapter takes that puzzle apart, starting with the technical link between inputs and output and the extra output each added worker brings. It then sorts costs into overhead that stays put and costs that rise with every unit made, and shows how time decides which is which. Along the way it asks why firms exist at all, why some band together to stop competing, and how new technology keeps shifting what can be made.

- **Profit maximization: where the next unit stops paying**

  Every firm in a standard textbook wants one thing. Mainstream economics treats the firm as a rational agent that seeks the most profit, meaning total revenue minus total cost. Profit maximization is the process of choosing the price, inputs and output that reach that peak. The answer lies at the margin. Marginal revenue is the extra money from selling one more unit, and marginal cost is the extra cost of making it. As long as marginal revenue is larger, producing more adds profit. Profit peaks where the two are equal. Under perfect competition the firm's demand curve is its marginal revenue curve, a flat line at the market price. Some costs do not change the decision at all. In the short run, a change in overhead such as rent, explored in Fixed costs: the bills that arrive regardless, leaves the best output and price untouched, because those costs are treated as sunk. Where an extra customer costs almost nothing, as with a seat on a scheduled flight, maximizing profit simply means maximizing revenue. The pursuit has limits. Some profit-maximizing behavior harms consumers, and competition law regulates it. And the newer field of Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics replaces strict profit maximization with a more limited kind of rationality in its models.

  <!-- nature-econ-315 -->

- **The production function: from inputs to output**

  Give a workshop more workers and more machines, and how much more will it make? A production function answers that question. It is a technical relation showing how much output can be made from given quantities of physical inputs. It is usually read as the maximum output each combination of inputs can give, so it traces a frontier of the possible. Economists write it as Q = f(X1, ..., Xn), where Q is output and the Xs are inputs such as capital, labor, land or raw materials. No inputs means no output. Prices and costs play no part; the function links physical things to physical things. From it economists define the extra output from one more unit of an input, the subject of Marginal product: what one more worker adds. It also shows how output responds when every input grows together, which Returns to scale: what happens when you double everything explores. For whole economies, aggregate production functions split growth into the part that comes from more capital and the part that comes from better technology. The Cobb–Douglas form, first developed in 1927, was the first aggregate production function to be estimated and presented to economists. Not everyone accepts these tools. Some economists reject aggregate production functions outright. A debate from the 1950s to the 1970s, begun by Joan Robinson, questioned how capital can be measured at all. Economists have long argued over whether such functions are valid.

  <!-- nature-econ-312 -->

- **Fixed costs: the bills that arrive regardless**

  A bakery pays the same rent whether its ovens run all day or sit cold. That rent is a fixed cost, also called overhead: a business cost that does not change with how much the business produces. Fixed costs tend to recur, like monthly rent or interest, and are often capital costs. The bakery's phone line is another. Its wages are not, because more bread needs more workers. 'Fixed' has a time limit. Costs stay fixed only for the period a contract sets, and in the long run there are none, because every input can change. Some costs are mixed, such as a phone bill with a fixed charge plus calls. Fixed costs also act as a barrier that keeps new businesses out. Accounting and economics use the terms differently, and in recent years fixed costs have come to exceed the costs that rise with output at many companies.

  <!-- nature-econ-307 -->

- **The short run and the long run: time in economics**

  Time changes what a business can do. In economics the short run is a period when some inputs or prices cannot yet change, while the long run is long enough for everything to adjust fully. Alfred Marshall introduced the distinction in his 1890 Principles of Economics. There is still no hard rule for how long either period lasts. In the short run some inputs are fixed, so only variable inputs such as labor and raw materials can change output. All actual production happens here. A profit-maximizing firm expands output while marginal cost is below marginal revenue and cuts back when it is above. In the long run nothing is fixed. Firms can change their capital, resize their plants, or enter and leave industries in response to profits and losses. That movement pushes them toward the lowest possible cost per unit. Economists who study whole economies use the terms a little differently. For them the long run is when prices, contracted wages and expectations have fully adjusted. Keynes thought economists neglected the short run in favor of that distant horizon. 'In the long run,' he remarked, 'we are all dead.'

  <!-- nature-econ-309 -->

- **Returns to scale: what happens when you double everything**

  Double every worker and machine a firm uses, and what happens to output? Returns to scale is the answer: how much output rises, in proportion, when all inputs grow together in the long run. Constant returns mean output doubles too. Decreasing returns mean it less than doubles, mainly because management and coordination get harder as scale grows. Increasing returns mean it more than doubles, thanks to the efficiency gains of size. One firm can show all three, with increasing returns at low output, constant in between and decreasing at high output. Mainstream theory holds that technology alone sets the pattern, not market conditions. With fixed input prices, constant returns mean flat long-run costs per unit, decreasing returns mean rising ones and increasing returns mean falling ones. For a Cobb–Douglas function, returns are increasing if the exponents sum to more than 1, constant if they sum to 1, and decreasing if less. Increasing returns can also trap whole economies. Path-dependent increasing returns help lock industrial economies into fossil-fuel energy systems.

  <!-- nature-econ-317 -->

- **Monopolistic competition: many sellers, each a little different**

  A street of restaurants is a lesson in economics. Each offers something slightly different, yet each can stand in for the others. This is monopolistic competition: many producers selling products that differ, by brand or quality, so they are not perfect substitutes. Differences may be real or perceived, in style, reputation or location. Cereals, clothing, shoes and city service industries are other textbook cases. Each firm has a little market power. Its demand curve slopes down, so it can raise its price without losing every customer. Entry and exit are free, so any economic profit in the short run shrinks toward zero in the long run. The result is inefficient. Firms charge more than marginal cost and run with spare capacity, below the output where cost per unit is lowest. Variety can raise total utility by meeting people's wants better, while heavy advertising is a common concern. Edward Chamberlin pioneered the theory in his 1933 book, alongside Joan Robinson's work on imperfect competition.

  <!-- nature-econ-311 -->

- **Marginal product: what one more worker adds**

  Add workers to a kitchen of fixed size and output first climbs, then slows, and can finally fall. Each step measures the marginal product. It is the extra output gained by using one more unit of an input, such as one more worker, while other inputs stay the same. The rise-then-fall pattern is general. As more of one input is added to a fixed amount of another, marginal product first rises, then falls, and can turn negative. When total output reaches its peak, marginal product is zero. With inputs that can be divided finely, it is the derivative, or rate of change, of the production function. For labor it is the slope of the total product curve. Neoclassical theory says that in competitive markets the marginal product of labor equals the real wage. Output here is usually measured ignoring external costs and benefits. For capital the idea is disputed. The Cambridge capital controversy showed that capital's marginal product cannot generally equal its return once a model has more than one good.

  <!-- nature-econ-310 -->

- **The theory of the firm: why businesses exist**

  If markets coordinate so well, why do businesses exist at all? The theory of the firm is the set of economic theories that explain and predict the nature of firms such as businesses and corporations. It covers their origin, survival, behavior, structure and relation to the market. Its central puzzle is why not every transaction goes through the market, and where the boundary between firm and market lies. The field took shape around the First World War. Economists then shifted from studying whole industries to single firms, because perfect competition no longer described how firms behaved. Its main frameworks look at the costs of using markets, managerial economics, behavioral theory, the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities. Managerial theories by Baumol, Marris and Williamson suggest managers pursue their own goals, for example maximizing sales once profit satisfies shareholders. Agency theory explains the governance problems that arise when ownership and control are separated.

  <!-- nature-econ-322 -->

- **Cartels: rivals who agree not to compete**

  Rivals who agree to stop competing can make a lot of money, for a while. A cartel is a group of independent firms that agree not to compete so as to raise their profits and dominate a market. Cartels raise prices by creating artificial shortages, through low production quotas, stockpiling and marketing quotas. A survey of studies put the median cartel price increase over the last 200 years at about 23 percent. International cartels reached 28 percent and domestic ones 18 percent. Yet cartels are inherently unstable. Each member is tempted to cheat, selling below the agreed price or above its quota. Outsiders respond too, producing more, using the good more efficiently or investing in substitutes. Discovered 20th-century cartels lasted on average 5 to 8 years. Oligopolies may form cartels, and OPEC is one of the best-known international ones. Adam Smith thought cartels undesirable because they could limit production and the quality of goods. The US Sherman Act of 1890 was the first enforced law against them. Price fixing is now illegal in more than 140 countries.

  <!-- nature-econ-301 -->

- **Variable costs: the costs that grow with every unit**

  Every shirt a clothing maker produces needs its own cloth and its own labor. Those are variable costs: costs that change as the quantity a business produces changes. Sales commission, labor and raw materials are the common examples. Add up the marginal cost of every unit made and the total is the variable cost. Add fixed costs to that and the result is total cost. Some costs straddle the line. Electricity often comes as a fixed standing charge plus a charge for use, which makes it semi-variable. The time horizon matters too. Whether a cost is fixed or variable depends on how far ahead one looks, and over five years all costs can become variable. Nor is every variable cost a direct cost: variable manufacturing overhead is indirect.

  <!-- nature-econ-328 -->

- **Average cost: what each unit really costs**

  A factory built for a set output is cheapest to run at that output. Below it, equipment sits idle; above it, bottlenecks build. The measure behind that pattern is average cost, or unit cost: total cost divided by the number of units produced. It weighs heavily in how businesses decide what price to charge. A typical short-run average cost curve is shaped like a U. At first, fixed costs are spread over more units, so the average falls. Then diminishing returns push marginal costs up and drag the average with them. The rule linking the two is simple. When marginal cost is below average cost, the average falls; when it is above, the average rises. So the rising marginal cost curve crosses average cost at its lowest point. Average fixed cost keeps falling toward zero as output grows. Where fixed costs are high and marginal cost is constant, as in hydroelectric generation, average cost slopes down continuously toward marginal cost. Supplying goods at the lowest possible average total cost is the mark of Productive efficiency: no waste on the production line.

  <!-- nature-econ-299 -->

- **Technological change: how new ways of making things spread**

  Fuel cells get cheaper every year. That steady decline is technological change at work: the overall process of inventing, innovating and spreading new technologies or processes. It covers invention, commercialization, research and development, continual improvement and diffusion through industry or society. Economists put it more narrowly, as a change in the set of feasible production possibilities. The old picture was a straight line from laboratory to market. That linear model has largely given way to one with innovation at every stage of research, development, diffusion and use. Improvement is often modeled as a learning curve of falling costs. How models treat it has shifted too. Models of the climate and other systems once treated technological change as coming from outside; now they more often treat it as something policy can influence. Markets give it direction. In market economies profit is a powerful driver, so technologies that meet social needs but promise little profit may never reach the market. And efficiency does not always save resources. As Jevons paradox explains, efficiency improvements can raise rather than lower total use of a resource.

  <!-- nature-econ-318 -->

- **Cournot competition: rivals choosing how much to make**

  In 1838 Antoine Augustin Cournot described a market with just two suppliers of spring water. His model became Cournot competition: a model of an oligopoly in which firms compete by each choosing, at the same time, how much to produce. The firms sell an identical product, and each firm's output affects the price. Each takes its rivals' quantities as given, looks at the demand left over, and acts like a monopolist on that remainder. The price settles where demand equals the total quantity all firms produce. The resting point, where no firm wants to change its output, was the first use of an idea now known as Nash equilibrium: where no one gains by moving alone. Prices are lower and quantities higher with two firms than under monopoly. As the number of firms grows, the price keeps falling, approaching marginal cost when firms are infinitely many. Joseph Bertrand objected that rivals would instead undercut each other's prices.

  <!-- nature-econ-302 -->

- **Can machines replace nature? Resources in production functions**

  Standard production functions usually leave natural resources out. Labor and capital go in; the energy and materials that feed them often do not. This debate asks how, or whether, they should be included. Solow and Stiglitz added natural resources, but in a way that let man-made capital fully substitute for them. In that model, enough machines could always make up for lost resources. The economist Georgescu-Roegen called this a 'conjuring trick', because it ignored the physical limits described in Laws of thermodynamics. Neither Solow nor Stiglitz replied. Others have tried to put energy in directly. Treating energy as an independent input gives a form like Q = A L^β K^α E^χ, where L is labor, K is capital and E is energy. Later work says this misrepresents how energy affects production. An alternative makes labor and capital themselves depend on energy, written Q = f(L(E), K(E)). The point is physical. If a region cannot get the resources needed to build or maintain its machines, their output eventually falls to near zero. Whether man-made capital can fully replace natural resources remains disputed, with Georgescu-Roegen's challenge still at the heart of the argument.

  <!-- nature-econ-313 -->

- **Isoquants: many routes to the same output**

  A factory can make the same output with many workers and few machines, or few workers and many machines. An isoquant is the curve joining all the combinations of inputs that produce the same quantity of output. Drawn with two inputs such as labor and capital on its axes, it is a level set of the production function, a slice taken at one output. It is the producer's counterpart of an indifference curve, except that output can be measured exactly in physical units. Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution, the rate at which one input can replace the other. Because that rate diminishes, isoquants bow toward the origin. Perfect-substitute inputs give straight isoquants; perfect complements give L-shaped ones with a kink at the fixed ratio. The cheapest input mix lies where an isoquant touches an isocost line, a line of equal spending. There the ratio of marginal products equals the ratio of input prices. Two isoquants never cross.

  <!-- nature-econ-308 -->

- **Why firms exist: Coase's answer**

  In his 1937 essay 'The Nature of the Firm', Coase asked a deceptively simple question. Why is all production not carried on by one big firm? His answer was that firms exist because organizing some production inside a firm costs less than coordinating it through market exchange. The costs of using markets, explored in Transaction costs: the price of making a deal, set where a firm ends and the market begins. The essay was one of the first attempts to define the firm in relation to the market. It became the starting point for the economics of outsourcing. It also explains the firm in a way consistent with constant returns to scale, rather than relying on increasing returns. Later economists note that the line between dealings inside a firm and dealings between firms is blurred by in-between forms, such as cooperation between firms.

  <!-- nature-econ-323 -->

- **Long-run average cost: unit cost when everything can change**

  Given enough time, a firm can rebuild itself around any output it chooses. Long-run average cost is the unit cost of producing a given output when every input, including buildings and machinery, can be changed. The firm is assumed to pick the cheapest mix of inputs for each output level. The curve is most often U-shaped. It slopes down where growing bigger cuts unit costs and up where it raises them, effects explored in Economies of scale: why bigger can be cheaper. If input prices do not change with the firm's purchases, falling unit costs come exactly when the production function has increasing returns to scale. Under perfect competition, long-run equilibrium has every firm producing at the curve's lowest point. Sometimes the curve keeps falling indefinitely. Then the biggest firm has a cost advantage, and the industry tends to become a natural monopoly, as in water and electricity supply.

  <!-- nature-econ-300 -->

- **Economies of scale: why bigger can be cheaper**

  Make a vessel bigger and its surface grows with the square of its size, but its volume grows with the cube. That rule, the square–cube law, is one physical root of economies of scale. These are the cost advantages a business gains from operating on a larger scale, so that each unit of output costs less. Put simply, they occur when average costs fall as output increases. Most sources are not physical. Large firms buy in bulk, hire specialized managers, borrow more cheaply and spread advertising costs over more sales. Returns to scale in production add to the effect. Engineers even use a rough rule: capital cost changes with the 0.6 power of the capacity ratio, so a plant with more capacity costs proportionally less to build. The two ideas are easy to confuse. Economies of scale concern a firm's costs, while returns to scale describe how outputs respond to inputs in the production function. Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) gave the first systematic analysis, through the division of labor. Economies of scale help explain why firms grow large in some industries, and they shape patterns in international trade. They matter for the climate too. Together with learning by doing, they can lower the costs of climate technologies over time.

  <!-- nature-econ-303 -->

- **Cournot's dilemma: why scale does not always breed monopoly**

  If bigger always means cheaper, the first firm to get a good start should swallow its whole trade. Alfred Marshall saw that Cournot's premises implied exactly that. Yet many industries keep numerous firms of different sizes. The puzzle is Cournot's dilemma. Marshall named factors that limit the runaway, such as the deaths of founders. Morroni argues that once knowledge and the organization of transactions are counted, economies of scale do not always lead to monopoly.

  <!-- nature-econ-306 -->

- **External economies of scale: savings shared by an industry**

  Sometimes a firm gets cheaper because its whole industry grows. External economies of scale are cost savings that come from the growth of a whole industry and benefit most or all of its firms, not just one. When new firms enter, average cost falls for all of them, while internal economies help only the single firm that grows. External economies tend to be more common than internal ones. Sraffa disagreed: he argued such economies are rarely met with, and that under perfect competition economies of scale should be excluded.

  <!-- nature-econ-304 -->

- **Learning and growth economies: getting cheaper with experience**

  Experience cuts costs. Learning and growth economies are dynamic economies of scale that come from the process of growing and from practice, rather than from size itself. Learning by doing improves skills and brings small innovations that steadily lower average costs. These learning economies rise with cumulative production, a pattern called the experience curve. Growth economies are different. They arise when expanding lets a firm use resources or skills it had not fully used.

  <!-- nature-econ-305 -->

- **The marginal revenue product rule: when to hire one more**

  Should a firm hire one more worker? The marginal revenue product rule says yes, as long as that worker brings in at least what they cost. Formally, a firm maximizes profit by using more of an input until the extra revenue it brings equals the input's extra cost. The marginal revenue product is the change in total revenue for each unit change in the input. For labor the rule is written MRP_L = MC_L: the marginal revenue product of labor equals its marginal cost.

  <!-- nature-econ-316 -->

- **Stages of production: the phases of adding inputs**

  Adding more of one input to a fixed plant passes through distinct phases. Economists divide a production function into three stages, according to how output per unit of the variable input changes. In stage 1, output per unit of the variable input rises to a peak. A price-taking firm, one too small to move the market price, always produces beyond this stage. In stage 2 output still rises, but at a decreasing rate, with average and marginal product both falling.

  <!-- nature-econ-314 -->

- **Asset specificity: when assets are tied together**

  Some assets are valuable together and worth far less apart. Asset specificity is Oliver Williamson's idea that firms exist because some assets are tied to each other and worth much less in any other use. If such assets are owned by different firms, the parties get locked in and bargain at length over the gains from trade. Repeated or long transactions need renegotiating, which raises the costs of dealing further. Bringing the assets into one firm is the way out.

  <!-- nature-econ-325 -->

- **The behavioral theory of the firm: good enough, not best**

  Real managers rarely hunt for the single best answer. The behavioral theory of the firm, developed by Cyert and March, explains how decisions are actually made inside firms, going beyond neoclassical economics. It builds on Herbert Simon's idea that limited mental ability lets people be rational only within limits in complex, uncertain situations. People and groups therefore 'satisfice', aiming for realistic goals rather than maximum utility or profit. The neoclassical theory of the firm was not seriously challenged by such managerial and behavioral alternatives until the 1960s.

  <!-- nature-econ-324 -->

- **Ownership and the hold-up problem: who should own the assets**

  Grossman, Hart and Moore built an approach that explains firm boundaries through ownership of assets when contracts are incomplete, unable to spell out every future case. Its seminal works, Grossman and Hart (1986), Hart and Moore (1990) and Hart (1995), built the incomplete contracting paradigm. The logic runs through the hold-up problem. Since deals will be renegotiated, each party expects only part of the return on its investment, and so invests too little. It explains the pros and cons of merging firms, and has been applied to providing shared goods and to privatization.

  <!-- nature-econ-623 -->

- **The resource-based view: advantage from rare resources**

  In 1959 Edith Penrose described a firm as a collection of productive resources. Its growth, she argued, depends on managers finding new uses for resources lying idle. From that argument grew the resource-based view of the firm, developed by Wernerfelt (1984) and Barney (1991). It holds that a firm's lasting competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable.

  <!-- nature-econ-326 -->

- **The shutdown rule: when to keep losing money**

  A firm can lose money and still be right to stay open. The shutdown rule says that in the short run a firm should keep producing while its revenue covers its variable costs. If revenue falls short, it should shut down. Fixed costs drop out of the decision, because in the short run they must be paid even at zero output. So a firm earning more than its variable cost but less than its total cost keeps operating. It makes an economic loss, but a smaller one than closing would bring.

  <!-- nature-econ-329 -->

- **Induced technological change: steering invention with prices**

  Make fossil energy relatively more expensive, and invention may turn toward other kinds of energy. Induced technological change is the hypothesis that policymakers can steer the direction of technical progress by changing relative input prices. Climate policy is the standard example. Yet evidence that policy actually induces innovation is still lacking, partly because of long-term policy uncertainty. A related idea, directed technical change, stresses price-driven direction rather than policy-driven scale.

  <!-- nature-econ-319 -->

- **Neutral technical change: which input does progress favor**

  Progress does not lift every input equally. Economists classify technical change by which input's productivity it raises. Hicks-neutral change, named after John Hicks (1932), leaves the ratio of capital's and labor's marginal products unchanged at a given mix of capital and labor. Harrod-neutral change is labor-augmenting, making each worker effectively count for more. Solow-neutral change is capital-augmenting, doing the same for machines.

  <!-- nature-econ-321 -->

- **Technology diffusion: the S-curve of adoption**

  New technologies rarely spread at a steady pace. Technology diffusion is the spread of a technology through a society or industry. It usually follows an S-shaped curve: slow at first, then rapid, then leveling off as the market saturates. Everett Rogers named five attributes that speed acceptance: relative advantage, compatibility, low complexity, trialability and observability. Channels matter too. Mass media mostly build awareness, while face-to-face contact mostly reduces the uncertainty that blocks adoption.

  <!-- nature-econ-320 -->

### Efficiency and welfare

Is an economy doing well? Economists answer with two questions that sound alike but are not: is it efficient, and is it fair? An economy is efficient when it gets the most of what people want out of the resources it has, and Pareto efficient when no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. Welfare economics uses those ideas to judge how well off a society is as a whole, resting on two results that link competitive markets to efficiency. Fairness is harder, because deciding how output, income and wealth should be shared draws on ethics, from utilitarianism to theories of justice, and this chapter follows both threads.

- **Economic efficiency: getting the most from what we have**

  An economy can be efficient and still deeply unequal. Economic efficiency means getting the most of what people want, such as well-being, out of the resources available. Economists usually mean one of two things by it. The first asks whether any change could help one person without harming another; it is named after Vilfredo Pareto and explored in Allocative efficiency: making the goods people want. The second asks whether more of one good could be made without making less of another, at the lowest average cost, the subject of Productive efficiency: no waste on the production line. The two need not go together. A market can pass one test and fail the other. Both matter because productive resources are scarce. They must go to each industry in just the right amounts, or too much or too little gets made. Theory says a perfectly competitive equilibrium passes the first test, but only without market imperfections, and these are significant in real markets. Efficiency in this sense says nothing about equality or a society's overall well-being. Removing one distortion does not always help either: if another cannot be removed, efficiency may even fall. Economists also split over who distorts more. One school stresses the distortions governments create; another stresses those markets create and wants more government involvement to fix them. Many economists consider putting a price on carbon, explored in Carbon pricing: charging for the harm of greenhouse gases, the most efficient way to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

  <!-- nature-econ-158 -->

- **Pareto efficiency: when no one can gain without someone losing**

  Smith owns an apple but wants an orange. Jones owns an orange but wants an apple. A swap makes both better off, so the starting point was wasteful. That small scene captures Pareto efficiency. A situation is Pareto efficient when there is no longer any way to make one person better off without making someone else worse off.
