  In 2006 the Stern Review warned that world output risked a 20% cut unless 1% of world output was spent now to reduce global warming. Critics objected that its findings partly rested on an extremely low pure time preference rate of 0.1%. A common misconception holds that Stern used a zero discount rate. In fact its projections used many positive rates while taking time preference near zero. The choice of rate for the benefits of cutting emissions of heat-trapping gases is one of the most controversial questions in climate economics. Rates used in climate studies of costs and benefits range from zero to over 3%. The rate is usually positive because resources invested today can, on average, become more resources later. Its size matters enormously. Too high a rate means too little action to cut emissions; too low a rate means too much. A rival model, with a 3% rate declining to 1% over 300 years, found taxes on carbon necessary but much smaller than Stern recommended. US policy has swung as well. Under Obama, the official estimate of damage per ton of carbon emitted was $51/ton at a 3% discount rate; Biden proposed over $190/ton using lower rates. Some argue that giving future generations less weight is ethically indefensible. Others reply that equal weighting yields nonsensical results.

  <!-- nature-econ-755 -->

- **Real options: the value of waiting and changing course**

  Standard Net present value treats managers as passive once money is committed, ignoring their freedom to react as markets turn out. Real options valuation fixes that. It applies the methods used to price financial options, contracts giving a right to buy or sell, to decisions about real projects. A real option is the right, but not the duty, to defer, abandon, expand, stage or shrink a project. In one worked example, NPV says invest now for a gain of 1M, but waiting a year for information is worth 1.21M, so the firm should wait. A negative NPV need not rule out acting either. Opening one store and expanding later if demand is high can be worth 0.41M. A mining firm can likewise delay work on a deposit until markets turn favorable. Real options are most valuable when uncertainty is high and managers have room and willingness to change course. Stewart Myers of MIT coined the term 'real option' in 1977, after the Black–Scholes work of 1973 made financial options analyzable.

  <!-- nature-econ-834 -->

- **Climateflation: when a warming climate raises prices**

  Heat, droughts and floods hit farm output, and shoppers feel it at the checkout. Climateflation is inflation driven by Climate change: a warming world and why it matters, through its effects on food production and supply chains. Isabel Schnabel of the European Central Bank first used the term. In 2022–2023, climate-driven heat in Europe raised food prices by about 0.7%, adding about 0.3% to overall inflation. The same study found that warming expected by 2035 could raise these effects by 30–50%. A related term, fossilflation, describes inflation caused by fossil fuel prices, which push up transport, food and shipping costs.

  <!-- nature-econ-802 -->

- **Inflation targeting: steering prices toward a set goal**

  In 1990 New Zealand became the first country to adopt an official inflation target. Inflation targeting is a policy in which the Central banks: the bankers' bank keeps adjusting its interest rate to steer inflation toward that target. It has since spread to most developed countries, and in most OECD countries the target is about 2%. Why not aim for zero? Research suggests true inflation runs about one percentage point below the official figure. A 2% target keeps true inflation from nearing zero or tipping into deflation, a fall in prices.

  <!-- nature-econ-803 -->

- **What causes inflation: a centuries-old argument**

  Rival schools have disputed the causes of inflation for centuries, from the quantity theory of money against the real bills doctrine to Keynesians against monetarists. In 1936 Keynes argued that wages and prices are sticky in the short run but respond gradually to swings in demand. In the 1960s Milton Friedman's Monetarism: Milton Friedman's case for steady money challenged this view, holding that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. In the 1970s the link between inflation and joblessness broke down, which was eventually put down to changing expectations. Since about 2000, the common view gives roles to demand shocks, supply shocks and inflation expectations.

  <!-- nature-econ-804 -->

- **Risk neutrality: caring only about the average**

  A risk-neutral investor would put every dollar into the single holding with the highest expected yield. A risk-averse one spreads money around. Risk-neutral preferences are neither risk averse nor risk seeking: the person cares only about the expected payoff, not how uncertain it is. The utility function is a straight line in money, so maximizing expected utility is the same as maximizing expected money. Risk averters have concave utility, and risk lovers convex. The QALY model in health economics, which counts quality-adjusted years of life, assumes risk-neutral behavior, among other things.

  <!-- nature-econ-835 -->

- **The discount function: weighting rewards across time**

  How much is a reward next year worth next to one today? A discount function answers by giving the weights an economic model places on rewards received at different times. Often each period's enjoyment is assumed to count on its own, called time-separable utility. Total utility from a stream of things consumed over time is then the sum of each period's utility, weighted by the discount function. The two most common examples are Exponential discounting: the same shrinkage every period and Hyperbolic discounting: why tomorrow's self disagrees with today's.

  <!-- nature-econ-791 -->

- **Exponential discounting: the same shrinkage every period**

  In finance, discounting is normally modeled as exponential. Exponential discounting is a discount function in which value falls by the same proportion for each extra unit of delay. Total utility is the sum of each period's utility multiplied by a fixed weight, δ, raised to the power of the time period. So the trade-off between consuming at two dates depends only on how far apart they are. That makes it dynamically consistent: preferences do not change as time passes unless new information arrives. It is the most common assumption in economics because of its simplicity. Yet alternatives such as Hyperbolic discounting: why tomorrow's self disagrees with today's have more empirical support.

  <!-- nature-econ-794 -->

- **Hyperbolic discounting: why tomorrow's self disagrees with today's**

  Many people take $50 now over $100 in a year. Yet almost everyone picks $100 in six years over $50 in five years, though the trade-off is the same. Hyperbolic discounting explains the flip. It is a model of how people devalue delayed rewards in which their choices are not consistent over time. Value falls quickly over short early delays but more slowly over longer ones. In an early study, people were indifferent between $15 now and $30 in 3 months, $60 in 1 year or $100 in 3 years. The implied yearly discount rates fell from 277% to 139% to 63%. The hyperbolic formula is g(D) = 1/(1 + kD), where D is the delay and k sets how strongly rewards are discounted. Its key consequence is temporary preferences for smaller, sooner rewards over larger, later ones, so people make choices their future selves regret. Such reversals were first found in rats and pigeons, so they do not depend on human culture. It is a cornerstone of Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics, used to study retirement planning, credit-card borrowing, addiction and procrastination.

  <!-- nature-econ-748 -->

- **Radical uncertainty: what no research can resolve**

  Some uncertainty would yield to enough research. Radical uncertainty would not: it is uncertainty that no available means of gaining knowledge could resolve. John Kay and Mervyn King popularized the term in a book published in March 2020. That is the line between it and Knightian uncertainty. If research could remove the uncertainty, it is not radical.

  <!-- nature-econ-775 -->

- **Uncertainty in science: what scientists mean and what the public hears**

  Scientists and the public often hear the word uncertainty in very different ways. The public can misread scientific uncertainty as ignorance or a lack of consensus. Differences between studies caused by their methods can look like disagreement where agreement actually exists. That gap can be exploited. Deniers of Climate change: a warming world and why it matters followed Frank Luntz's advice to frame global warming as a matter of scientific uncertainty. Scientific uncertainty may also be managed deliberately to reach certain goals.

  <!-- nature-econ-776 -->

- **How central banks use interest rates**

  From 1954 to 2008, the US federal funds rate, the key US policy rate, varied between about 0.25% and 19%. Each Central banks: the bankers' bank sets target interest rates as a main tool for influencing spending, inflation and joblessness. They usually cut rates when they want more spending by firms and households. Very low rates carry risks, feeding bubbles in property and share markets. At the extreme, a zero interest-rate policy sets the target near zero. There conventional policy struggles, because market rates are hard to push below zero.

  <!-- nature-econ-759 -->

- **Liquidity preference: the pull of ready cash**

  Cash can be spent at once, while some holdings take time and money to turn back into cash. Liquidity preference is the tendency of people and firms to prefer holding cash, or holdings that are easily sold, over ones that are harder to convert. It shows up as a gap in yields between holdings with different maturities and conversion costs. It also explains why longer-lasting holdings usually have to offer higher yields.

  <!-- nature-econ-761 -->

- **Negative interest rates: paying to lend**

  In theory, no lender should accept less than 0%, since simply holding cash avoids a guaranteed loss. Yet the European Central Bank from 2014 and the Bank of Japan from early 2016 used negative rates, alongside Quantitative easing: when interest rates hit bottom. A negative interest rate charges savers for holding money and has been described as a tax on holding money. Silvio Gesell proposed the idea in the late 19th century. During the European debt crisis, some countries' government debt sold at negative yields, so lenders in effect paid governments to borrow.

  <!-- nature-econ-760 -->

- **Heuristics: mental shortcuts and their traps**

  After a run of tails, the gambler's fallacy expects heads to be 'due'. It is not: a fair coin's chance stays 0.5. The error shows the price of mental shortcuts, ways of making a decision without working out the consequences of every option. Such shortcuts cut the thinking needed, but they are more prone to fallacies and errors than step-by-step reasoning. Another example is the compromise effect, which leads people to favor moderate options over extreme ones.

  <!-- nature-econ-789 -->

- **Must rational choice rest on probability?**

  Should probability remain the foundation of decision theory, or can something else replace it? The question is highly controversial. Defenders of probability cite Cox's justification of its axioms, de Finetti's Dutch book arguments and the complete class theorems. Supporters of fuzzy logic, Dempster–Shafer theory and info-gap theory reply that probability is only one option among many. Rules built on probability can be sensitive to the probabilities assumed, while rules such as minimax make no such assumptions and are robust. The ludic fallacy critique goes further: models of a fixed set of possibilities ignore 'unknown unknowns' that may have outsized impact. The two camps still disagree.

  <!-- nature-econ-790 -->

- **How people should choose, and how they do**

  Decision theory asks two different questions. Its normative branch asks how an ideal rational decision-maker should choose. Its descriptive branch asks how people actually choose. Putting the normative approach to work is called decision analysis, which builds tools and software to help people decide better. Descriptive models include Tversky's elimination by aspects and Laibson's Quasi-hyperbolic discounting: a simpler model of impatience, a model of choices that are inconsistent over time. Behavioral decision theory has drawn growing interest in recent decades.

  <!-- nature-econ-788 -->

- **Perpetuity: payments that never end**

  Payments that run forever still have a price today. A perpetuity is a series of regular payments that continues indefinitely, an annuity with no end date. Few such instruments actually exist. Its present value is the limit of the annuity formula as the number of payments goes to infinity. A perpetuity immediate pays at the end of each period and a perpetuity due at the start. Their values differ by a factor of (1 + i), where i is the interest rate.

  <!-- nature-econ-763 -->

- **Years' purchase: pricing a stream of payments the old way**

  In the early 16th century, the English crown resold manors seized at the Dissolution of the Monasteries. It set the prices by years' purchase. This traditional method values a stream of payments by multiplying its average expected yearly cash flow by a fixed number. A lease paying $10,000 a year sold at 20 years' purchase is valued at $200,000. That equals discounting in perpetuity at 5%. Buyers of riskier payment streams pay fewer years' purchase.

  <!-- nature-econ-764 -->

- **What makes a risk insurable**

  Insurability is the set of features a risk must have for private companies to be able to cover it. An insurable loss should be definite in time, place and cause. It should be accidental rather than in the insured's control, and large enough to matter to the buyer. Both the probability of loss and its cost must be at least estimable, and the premium must stay affordable relative to the cover. Ideally losses are independent and not catastrophic, so they do not all strike at once and bankrupt the insurer. Limited capital therefore caps how much earthquake cover, and wind cover in hurricane zones, insurers can sell.

  <!-- nature-econ-807 -->

- **Insuring crops and homes against nature's hazards**

  Weather, hail, drought, frost, pests or disease can all cost a farmer a harvest. Insurance for crops helps farmers manage those losses. It is a special form of property insurance, which protects against risks to property such as fire, theft or weather, with versions for floods, earthquakes and crops. Another kind, Index-based insurance, pays farmers when a modeled climate trigger, linked to a high chance of large crop loss, is exceeded and harvest losses occur. Floods show the limits of private cover. Many US insurers do not offer cover against floods in some regions, so a federal program acts as insurer of last resort.

  <!-- nature-econ-810 -->

- **Premiums and float: how insurers really make money**

  In the five years ending 2003, US property and casualty insurers lost $142.3 billion on underwriting, the business of writing policies. Yet they made $68.4 billion overall. The difference came from float: money collected as premiums but not yet paid out in claims, which insurers invest until claims are paid. An insurance premium is the price charged for cover. It is set to cover expected claims, costs and profit, minus what the insurer earns by investing it. Setting premiums, called ratemaking, uses statistics and probability to estimate future claims. Insurers check their rates by comparing past losses, brought to present value, with premiums collected.

  <!-- nature-econ-808 -->

- **Reinsurance: insurance for insurers**

  Even insurers need insurance. Reinsurance is cover for insurance companies: another insurer agrees to carry part of a risk that the first finds too large. A single property worth more than any one insurer's capital limit is shared among several insurers or syndicated into the reinsurance market. That market is dominated by a few large companies with huge reserves.

  <!-- nature-econ-809 -->

- **Arrow–Pratt: measuring risk aversion by curvature**

  How risk-averse is a person? The Arrow–Pratt measures answer from the curvature of their utility function: the more curved it is, the higher the risk aversion. Absolute risk aversion, named after the economists Kenneth Arrow and John W. Pratt, is built from the slope of utility and how fast that slope changes. Relative risk aversion has no units, so it can be compared across settings. Logarithmic utility gives a constant relative risk aversion of 1. In choices across time, relative risk aversion often cannot be separated from the How willing people are to shift spending across time.

  <!-- nature-econ-766 -->

- **Isoelastic utility: one number for how fast satisfaction fades**

  Market prices and lab experiments disagree wildly about one small number, η. Isoelastic utility, also called power or CRRA utility, is a standard formula linking utility to Consumption: spending to meet today's needs, with η setting how strongly each extra unit is valued less. It is the only family of utility functions with constant relative risk aversion, hence the name CRRA. When risk is involved, η is the degree of relative risk aversion. Setting η = 0 means risk neutrality. With η = 1 the formula becomes ln c, known as logarithmic utility. Under constant relative risk aversion, the share of one's money put into a risky holding does not depend on how rich one is. The true value of η is much debated. Some models of market prices need values up to 50, but most experiments suggest values just above 1. Estimates include 1.5 for the United Kingdom (Groom and Maddison, 2019) and about 1.4 across 20 OECD countries (Evans, 2005). Using six surveys of Well-being: how well a life is going, Layard and colleagues (2008) found values between 1.19 and 1.34, with a combined estimate of 1.26.

  <!-- nature-econ-822 -->

- **Rabin's puzzle: small bets and expected utility**

  Someone refuses a 50–50 bet to lose $100 or gain $110. Suppose they always refuse it. Rabin's calibration theorem shows that expected utility theory then implies they would refuse a 50–50 bet to lose $1,000 or gain any sum. Rabin finds this implausible. If caution over small stakes came from diminishing marginal utility, it would imply extreme caution at large stakes. His theorem therefore challenges using expected utility to explain risk aversion in small decisions. Prospect theory: how people really weigh risk offers an alternative. It judges outcomes against a reference point, usually the status quo, rather than against everything a person owns.

  <!-- nature-econ-767 -->

- **When playing it safe has a cost**

  Risk-averse planning of schools and playgrounds often keeps children from activities they would otherwise benefit from. The pattern runs through government. Many agencies have risk-averse mandates that require risks to be minimized, sometimes at the cost of the benefits of the risky activity. Yet reducing a risk has an opportunity cost: the value lost by not taking the risky action. Laws focused on risk without weighing its benefits may misrepresent society's goals.

  <!-- nature-econ-768 -->

- **Preference reversal: pricing one bet higher, choosing the other**

  A 'p bet' offers a high chance of a small prize. A '$ bet' offers a small chance of a big prize. Asked to price them, people put the p bet below the $ bet. Asked to choose between them head to head, they usually pick the p bet. This is a preference reversal: valuing one lottery more when pricing it but choosing the other when comparing them directly. Studies starting with Lichtenstein and Slovic in 1971 found the effect. Later work suggests the behavior can fit neoclassical theory under specific assumptions.

  <!-- nature-econ-800 -->

- **The St. Petersburg paradox: an infinite prize nobody pays for**

  A coin is flipped until it lands tails, and the prize doubles each time it lands heads. The expected payoff of this game is infinite. So someone caring only about expected value should pay any finite amount to play. In reality few would pay more than $25. Nicolaus Bernoulli described this St. Petersburg paradox in 1713. In a 1738 paper, Daniel Bernoulli used it to argue that expected value theory must be normatively wrong, and the puzzle prompted expected utility theory as a solution.

  <!-- nature-econ-798 -->

- **Subjective expected utility: choosing with personal odds**

  What if no one knows the true odds? Leonard Savage's subjective expected utility shows that expected utility, built on personal probabilities, can still guide choice. From seven axioms, Savage proved that expected utility can be used to make an optimal choice among acts. His key method was a focus on observable choices: psychology matters only as far as it changes choices. Frank Ramsey's 1926 representation theorem was an earlier approach to subjective probability. Savage concluded that people are neutral toward uncertainty and that observation is enough to predict the probabilities of uncertain events.

  <!-- nature-econ-799 -->

- **The rule of 72: a shortcut to doubling time**

  At 6 percent a year, money doubles in about 72/6 = 12 years. That is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate in percent to estimate how many years money takes to double. It is a quick shortcut for compound interest, and it gives a good indication for interest rates up to 10%.

  <!-- nature-econ-813 -->

- **Simple interest: interest on the original sum only**

  A $2500 credit card balance at 12.99% a year, applied monthly, runs up $27.06 of simple interest in one month. Simple interest is worked out only on the original amount owed, without adding interest on earlier interest. It can be applied over periods other than a year, such as every month. Compound interest differs by also earning interest on interest already accumulated.

  <!-- nature-econ-812 -->

- **Why interest exists: rival explanations**

  Aristotle and the Scholastics held that money is by nature sterile, so it was unjust to charge for being parted from it. Later schools of thought offered other explanations for why interest exists and what sets its rate. In the classical theory of Mill and others, the rate adjusts to balance the demand for borrowing with the supply of lending. Wicksell's 1898 Interest and Prices distinguished natural from nominal interest rates. Ohlin and Robertson later refined this into the loanable funds theory. In Keynes's 1936 General Theory, interest is set by the demand for money, liquidity preference, against a given amount of money.

  <!-- nature-econ-815 -->

- **The Fisher equation: interest after inflation**

  Subtract inflation from an interest rate, and what remains is roughly what a lender really earns. The Fisher equation says the real interest rate is approximately the nominal rate minus the inflation rate. Looking back, the ex post real rate is roughly the historical nominal rate minus inflation. Looking ahead, the expected real rate is the nominal rate minus expected inflation. Turned around, nominal interest is made up of the real rate plus inflation, among other factors such as credit risk, the chance a borrower fails to repay.

  <!-- nature-econ-833 -->

- **Price indexes: tracking the cost of a basket of goods**

  If prices rise 5% from a 2010 base, a price index set to 100 in 2010 reads 105 in 2011. A price index tracks the cost of a fixed sample basket of goods, a commodity bundle, relative to its cost at a base date or place. It is usually set to 100 at the base date, so a one percent rise in the bundle's price in the first period takes it to 101. The inflation rate between two dates is the change in the price index divided by its earlier value. The The consumer price index: pricing a basket of shopping uses a bundle of goods bought by consumers, while Gross domestic product: an economy in one number uses a price index of its own.

  <!-- nature-econ-832 -->

- **Odd patterns in how people discount the future**

  A single constant discount rate cannot explain how people really choose. Their discounting shifts with framing and with the kind of decision. Richard Thaler found that gains are discounted more than losses, and small amounts more than large ones. Discounting also rises as a time interval is cut into smaller parts. Daniel Read argues that this sub-additivity makes discounting look hyperbolic. Temptation theories explain another oddity: people pay for commitment devices that remove tempting options from their future choices.

  <!-- nature-econ-840 -->

- **Why some people discount the future more than others**

  Men generally discount more steeply than women, choosing sooner rewards more often. Discount rates vary between people with factors such as age, earnings, gender, connection to one's future self and early life stress. Feeling more connected to one's future self may make it easier to delay gratification. A study combining many earlier studies found that early life stress makes people more present-focused. Cultural traits such as individualism, uncertainty avoidance and long-term orientation may shape national differences in time preference.

  <!-- nature-econ-843 -->

- **Measuring how much people discount the future**

  Energy-efficient air conditioners cost more up front but save money later. One hedonic pricing study of such purchases, which reads values from market prices, found a discount rate of 13.6%. That is one way to measure personal discount rates: infer them from real-world choices. The other is to ask people to choose between smaller-sooner and larger-later rewards. Researchers vary the amounts and delays to find the indifference point, where the two rewards are valued equally. There is still no consensus on the rate, partly because how a study asks its questions can change the result.

  <!-- nature-econ-841 -->

- **Money, health, food, climate: discounting differs by domain**

  People do not discount every kind of future outcome alike. The rate depends on what is at stake: money, health, consumable goods or the climate. Studies repeatedly find steeper discounting for rewards consumed directly, like food and alcohol, than for money, possibly because of temptation. Tabi's revealed-preference study found rates from 3% for lives saved in 100 years to 29% for measures to prevent flooding. Some studies find the climate is discounted differently from health and money.

  <!-- nature-econ-842 -->

- **Discounted utility: the future as it looks from today**

  People who choose 1 candy bar now over 2 tomorrow also choose 2 in 101 days over 1 in 100 days, as Tversky and Kahneman found. Discounted utility is how desirable a future event looks from the present rather than when it happens. It is the present discounted value of future utility, smaller than that utility for anyone who prefers sooner gratification. The The discount factor: the multiplier that brings money back to today, β, lies between 0 and 1 and is sometimes explained as a person's patience. Models of spending over time maximize the sum of discounted utilities, within a budget on the present value of spending.

  <!-- nature-econ-795 -->

- **The Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans model: how much should an economy save?**

  How much of its output should a whole economy set aside for the future? Frank Ramsey tackled the question in 1928, framing it as a social planner maximizing what people consume across generations. In the 1960s David Cass and Tjalling Koopmans recast it as a market economy with a representative agent, one household standing in for all. The result, the Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans or neoclassical growth model, is a foundational account of how an economy grows when saving is chosen to maximize welfare. Unlike the Solow–Swan model, with its fixed saving rate, it derives saving from a household's choices over time. Future utility is discounted exponentially at a rate ρ, which must exceed n, the growth rate of the number of people, for total welfare to be finite. Spending grows when the return on extra capital, net of wear and tear, exceeds ρ. The best path is a unique saddle path that converges on a stable long-run balance; other paths end with all saving or with capital used up. It aims to explain long-run growth, not short-run booms and slumps.

  <!-- nature-econ-829 -->

- **Spending and saving across a lifetime**

  Saving tends to peak in middle age, as people prepare for retirement. Irving Fisher and Roy Harrod first described this 'hump saving'. Theories of intertemporal consumption try to explain how people choose between spending and saving over the course of their lives. John Rae first conceived the idea in the 1830s, and Fisher expanded it in the 1930s. The basic model has two periods, such as youth and old age. In the 1950s Modigliani and Brumberg, Ando and Friedman treated lifetime spending as an optimization problem, producing the life-cycle model. It says spending follows average lifetime earnings: the young borrow, earners save more, and retirees live off what they put aside. Tests have had mixed success. People spend too little early and late in life and too much in their peak earning years. Proposed fixes include a wish to leave bequests, limits on borrowing, utility that changes over time, or particular expectations about future earnings.

  <!-- nature-econ-820 -->

- **The discount factor: the multiplier that brings money back to today**

  Multiply a future payment by the right number, and out comes its present value. That number is the discount factor. It is computed from a zero, or spot, rate taken from a yield curve and the time in years until the cash flow arrives. Banks usually discount cash flows with daily compounding, because accrued interest on their holdings can be re-lent every day. For hand calculation, compounding without any pause is sometimes a close enough stand-in. In dynamic decision models, impatience is represented by a discount factor between 0 and 1.

  <!-- nature-econ-747 -->

- **The growing perpetuity: endless payments that rise**

  Some payment streams are expected not just to last forever but to grow. A growing perpetuity is an endless stream of payments rising at a fixed rate. When the growth rate stays below the interest rate, a simple formula values it. That formula is the well-known Gordon growth model used to value shares. Few real securities grow at a fixed rate forever, but the approach is still used to value real estate, shares and other holdings.

  <!-- nature-econ-771 -->

- **How willing people are to shift spending across time**

  Some people want their spending smooth from year to year; others shift it around readily. The elasticity of intertemporal substitution measures how willing a person is to shift Consumption: spending to meet today's needs between periods. It reflects how much they want to smooth spending over time. Formally it is the inverse of relative risk aversion. High relative risk aversion means a low elasticity and a stronger wish to smooth spending. With logarithmic utility the elasticity is constant at 1.

  <!-- nature-econ-830 -->

- **Continuous compounding: interest added every instant**

  In 1683 Jacob Bernoulli discovered the constant e by studying a compound interest question. Continuous compounding is where that question leads: the limit reached when interest is compounded ever more often, with the compounding period shrinking toward zero. The yearly rate actually earned then approaches an upper limit of e^r − 1, where r is the stated rate. The continuously compounded rate is called the force of interest. It is often used because it is mathematically simpler, for example when valuing financial contracts such as options.

  <!-- nature-econ-782 -->

- **The effective annual rate: comparing loans on equal terms**

  Debt that pays interest twice a year has a yearly compounded rate higher than its quoted rate. The effective annual rate captures this. It is the total interest payable over one year divided by the principal, which puts rates with different compounding on a common footing. Many countries require lenders and banks to disclose this annual compound rate so consumers can compare products fairly. It goes by names such as annual equivalent rate (AER), effective annual percentage rate and annual percentage yield.

  <!-- nature-econ-783 -->

- **Doubts about hyperbolic discounting**

  Hyperbolic discounting is not the only explanation for choices that flip over time. Researchers have proposed several alternatives. Daniel Read's subadditive discounting holds that discounting over a delay grows when the delay is split into smaller intervals. Others point to a judgment of similarity between options. The most obvious objection is that many people learn to choose consistently over time in most situations. A 2014 paper criticized studies for relying mostly on university students and concluding too quickly that the hyperbolic model is correct. Human experiments also often show wide differences between subjects. Which account fits best remains disputed.

  <!-- nature-econ-751 -->

- **Quasi-hyperbolic discounting: a simpler model of impatience**

  In 1997 Laibson proposed a handier stand-in for hyperbolic discounting. Quasi-hyperbolic, or beta-delta, discounting counts time in whole periods and uses two constants, beta and delta, each between 0 and 1. Rewards taken now are not discounted at all. The model keeps much of the mathematical convenience of exponential discounting while capturing the main feature of hyperbolic discounting: a strong pull toward the present.

  <!-- nature-econ-750 -->

- **Hyperbolic discounting as a response to uncertain risk**

  Offer a restaurateur $100,000 in sixty years instead of $50 today. He would reasonably discount the distant sum, since the payer or payee may have died by then. One explanation of hyperbolic discounting builds on this. A future reward carries a risk of not arriving, and that risk is itself uncertain. Suppose the hazard rate, the chance per period of losing the reward, is unknown and given a prior distribution, a spread of starting beliefs. The expected chance that the reward survives then takes exactly the hyperbolic form. Whether discounting future gains is rational, and at what rate, depends greatly on circumstances.

  <!-- nature-econ-749 -->

- **Danger money: how wages price risk**

  Dangerous jobs pay more on average. Workers in riskier jobs earn a risk premium, so the labor market puts a price on risk through wage differences. The premium rises with the risk of injury. The risk need not be physical. A higher risk of losing work is also paid for, one reason fixed-term contracts tend to pay more.

  <!-- nature-econ-837 -->

- **Integrated Future Value: discounting that counts nature**

  Traditional discounted cash flow counts only financial costs and benefits. Integrated Future Value extends it, and Net present value, to count the long-term value and risks of natural capital and Social capital: the value of trust and networks. It lets companies value projects for their long-term environmental and social returns as well as financial ones. The Social cost of carbon can be included to capture the damage to society from a project's emissions of heat-trapping gases. The method supports Integrated Bottom Line decisions, which combine financial, environmental and social reporting in one balance sheet, going beyond the Triple bottom line.

  <!-- nature-econ-793 -->

- **The cost of equity: what shareholders expect**

  Shareholders expect to be paid for the risk they carry. The cost of equity is the return they require, inferred by comparing the shares with others of similar risk. It is commonly computed with the capital asset pricing model: the risk-free rate plus beta times the market's risk premium. Beta measures a security's sensitivity to movements in the market. The market risk premium has averaged around 5% in some developed countries during the twentieth century and up to 7% in emerging markets. The matching cost of debt takes the risk-free rate on government debt of the same term and adds a default premium.

  <!-- nature-econ-786 -->

- **WACC: blending the cost of debt and equity**

  The weighted average cost of capital, or WACC, blends the cost of debt and the cost of equity into a single cost of capital. It is the minimum return a firm must earn to satisfy its lenders, owners and other capital providers, or they will put their money elsewhere. It can serve as the discount rate for a project's free cash flows. For profitable firms, debt is cheaper than new equity because of tax advantages. Too much debt, though, raises default risk and borrowing costs. Management seeks the financing mix that minimizes the cost of capital and so maximizes the firm's value.

  <!-- nature-econ-785 -->

- **The Fisher model: consuming now or later**

  Fisher's model shows how a person with earnings now and later, able to lend or borrow at an interest rate, chooses between consuming now and consuming later. Call present earnings Y(t), future earnings Y(t+1) and the interest rate r. The most one can consume now is Y(t) + Y(t+1)/(1+r), borrowing against everything tomorrow will bring. The most one can consume in the future is (1+r)Y(t) + Y(t+1), lending everything today. The model assumes steady earnings and utility maximization.

  <!-- nature-econ-819 -->

- **The Ramsey formula: building a social discount rate**

  Frank Ramsey's formula builds the social discount rate from three inputs. One is pure time preference. The second is the growth rate of the economy. The third is the elasticity of marginal utility: how fast the value of an extra unit of Consumption: spending to meet today's needs falls as people grow richer. The logic is simple. If future generations will be richer, each extra dollar will matter less to them, so a positive discount rate reflects diminishing marginal utility. The Stern Review let its discount rate vary with outcomes, reflecting growth and the elasticity of marginal utility, in line with Ramsey's growth model.

  <!-- nature-econ-753 -->

- **Precautionary saving: a cushion against an uncertain future**

  People cannot insure against every bad turn the economy might take, because markets for insurance are incomplete. So they save. Precautionary saving is putting aside part of one's earnings because future earnings are uncertain. People spend less now to build a reserve they can draw on if earnings fall, keeping their spending smooth. Typical reasons include health risk, business risk, unavoidable expenses, possible loss of earnings, retirement and children's education. Saving is a flow, measured per unit of time, while savings are the pile of funds built up at a point in time. Numerical simulations put precautionary saving at 20 to 60 percent of all saving, though the evidence overall is mixed. In recessions the motive strengthens, raising total saving and cutting total spending. Countries behave similarly. Fast-growing emerging economies have built up savings, sending capital 'upstream' to rich countries.

  <!-- nature-econ-827 -->

- **Minimax against nature**

  Prospecting for minerals is a gamble against nature. The cost is wasted if nothing is found, but the rewards are large if something is. Minimax can guide such a lone decision maker facing unknown facts. It treats the choice as a game against nature and minimizes the worst-case loss. Unlike expected value or expected utility, it makes no assumptions about the probabilities of outcomes, so it is robust to changes in assumptions. Extensions of this non-probabilistic approach include minimax regret and info-gap decision theory.

  <!-- nature-econ-825 -->

- **Rawls's maximin: judging a society by its worst-off**

  In A Theory of Justice, John Rawls proposed a maximin rule for society, the difference principle. Social and economic inequalities should be arranged to benefit the least-advantaged most. It carries the minimax idea into questions of justice. John Harsanyi drew the opposite lesson from the same original position. He argued for utilitarianism, since rational agents weigh expected outcomes rather than worst cases.

  <!-- nature-econ-826 -->

- **Where the internal rate of return goes wrong**

  Academics strongly prefer Net present value, or NPV, yet surveys show executives prefer the internal rate of return. The gap matters, because ranking projects by IRR can disagree with ranking them by NPV. When the aim is to maximize total value, IRR should not be used to choose between mutually exclusive projects. A bigger project can have a lower IRR but a higher NPV. When cash flows change sign more than once, a project may have several IRRs, and it is unclear whether high or low is better. Sources even disagree on whether IRR quietly assumes that cash flows are reinvested at the IRR until the project ends.

  <!-- nature-econ-817 -->

- **Life annuities: payments for as long as you live**

  A pension paying a regular sum for life is a life annuity. It pays for as long as one or more named people stay alive, so the number of payments is uncertain. An annuity certain, by contrast, pays for a fixed period whatever happens to anyone's survival. Valuing a life annuity accounts for mortality as well as interest. Its actuarial present value is the expected value of the discounted payments. Halley's 1693 work showed how a life table built from mortality data could be used to price annuities.

  <!-- nature-econ-780 -->

- **Black swans: the events nobody saw coming**

  Some events matter enormously, could not have been predicted, and yet seem obvious afterward. Nassim Nicholas Taleb calls them black swan events: important and inherently unpredictable events that people explain with hindsight once they happen. Black swan theory holds that preparing for them is hindered by pretending to know all the risks. Taleb goes further, arguing that Knightian risk does not exist in the real world, which instead has gradations of computable risk.

  <!-- nature-econ-823 -->

- **Maxmin expected utility: planning for the worst plausible odds**

  Suppose someone thinks the chance of red in Ellsberg's unknown urn lies anywhere between 0.4 and 0.6. Maxmin expected utility tells them to bet on the known urn. In this model a decision-maker holds several possible probability beliefs and picks the option whose worst-case expected utility is highest. Gilboa and Schmeidler proposed it in 1989 as an axiomatic account of ambiguity aversion. Schmeidler's Choquet expected utility model, which allows non-additive probabilities, includes maxmin as a special case. For a whole society, a max-min social welfare function reflects extreme uncertainty aversion, caring only about the worst-off.

  <!-- nature-econ-778 -->

- **Prudence: the urge to save against risk**

  Risk aversion measures the desire for insurance. Prudence measures something related: the strength of a person's precautionary motive to save in the face of risk. Kimball defined it in 1990, writing absolute prudence as q = -U'''/U'' in terms of how utility curves. Earlier, Leland (1968) linked prudence to decreasing absolute risk aversion with convex marginal utility, U''' > 0. He showed that even small risks to earnings create precautionary saving.

  <!-- nature-econ-828 -->

- **Declining discount rates: counting the far future more**

  Should one discount rate apply for centuries? Declining discount rates start relatively high for the near future and fall over time, to reflect long-term uncertainty and ethical concerns. Recent work on the Social cost of carbon supports declining rather than constant rates. One model in the debate over the Stern Review used a 3% social discount rate that slowly declines to 1% over 300 years. People's own stated time preferences point the same way: over long periods they become extremely hyperbolic.

  <!-- nature-econ-846 -->

- **Future value: what money grows into**

  Invest an amount PV at time 0 at rate i per period, and after n periods it is worth PV(1 + i)^n. That is its future value: what an amount invested today will be worth after a given number of periods of earning interest. The factor (1 + i)^n is called the accumulation factor, and (1 + i)^−n is the matching discount factor. Present value usually sits below future value because money can earn interest.

  <!-- nature-econ-770 -->

- **Quasi-option value: the worth of keeping choices open**

  Quasi-option value is the extra value of keeping future choices open when a decision's consequences may be irreversible and uncertain. Arrow and Fischer (1974) and Epstein (1980) showed that possible irreversible consequences lead even a risk-neutral society to favor flexible decisions. The idea grew out of Option value: paying to keep choices open. That value depends on uncertain future need for something, irreversibility or a high cost of replacing it if it is lost, and its not being storable. Climate policy weighs both sides: possible irreversible damage to each Biomes: the great living regions of Earth and ecosystem against the irreversibility of spending on emission cuts. Economists have analyzed the Precautionary principle as the interaction of irreversibility and uncertainty.

  <!-- nature-econ-847 -->

- **Epstein–Zin preferences: separating risk from timing**

  Standard expected utility ties two attitudes together: how a person feels about risk, and how willing they are to shift spending across time. Epstein–Zin preferences pull them apart. They are a form of recursive utility, which combines a time aggregator for preferences without uncertainty with a risk aggregator that sets the certainty equivalent of future utility. A parameter β sets the rate of time preference, ρ sets the elasticity of intertemporal substitution, and α encodes risk aversion. Unlike in isoelastic utility, that elasticity can be set independently of risk aversion. Setting α equal to ρ gives back ordinary time-additive expected utility.

  <!-- nature-econ-796 -->

### Measuring an economy

Before anyone can say whether an economy is doing well, someone has to decide what to count. This chapter gathers the measuring tools. Some describe things that exist at one moment, like a nation's machines or the skills and health of its workers, while others describe things that happen over time, like a year's output. Some boil the movement of many prices down to a single number. And some reach past the economy to the environment, which supplies materials and absorbs the waste that comes back.

- **Human capital: the skills people carry to work**

  Adam Smith counted 'the acquired and useful abilities' of a society's members as capital, alongside its machines and buildings. Economists now call this human capital: the knowledge, skills, know-how, health and education people bring to producing goods and services. Irving Fisher may have first used the term, and Pigou wrote that people can build up human capital just as they build up material capital. Just as land came to be seen as natural capital, the human inputs among the Factors of production: land, labor and capital came to be seen as human capital. Unlike money capital, it tends to grow steadily over long periods, built on education and health. It also has an odd property for an asset. A firm cannot own it, so it leaves when employees leave. It strongly shapes what people earn, and spending on it pays high returns through childhood and young adulthood. Gary Becker's theory holds that education and training raise efficiency and growth, an argument often used to justify public subsidies for schooling and job training.

  <!-- nature-econ-531 -->

- **Stocks and flows: what you have versus what moves**

  Michał Kalecki once called economics 'the science of confusing stocks with flows'. The joke rests on a simple distinction. A stock is a quantity that exists at one point in time. A flow is a quantity measured per unit of time. Suppose a country has 20 machines on 1 January 2010 and 23 a year later. The machine count on each date is a stock. The change between them, 3 machines per year, is a flow, the country's net new equipment for 2010. A nation's whole capital stock works the same way: the flow of new machines and buildings adds to it, and the flow of wear and tear drains it. Capital itself is a stock that yields a periodic income, which is a flow. Because stocks and flows have different units, they cannot be added or compared directly. A nation's capital stock is measured in dollars, while its yearly output is measured in dollars per year. Their ratios still make sense. A country's debt divided by its yearly output gives a figure measured in years. Irving Fisher formalized the distinction in economics in 1896, and it runs through everything that follows in this chapter.

  <!-- nature-econ-594 -->

- **Productivity: getting more out of the same inputs**

  Simply piling on more workers and machines makes an economy bigger, but it does not raise income per unit of input. Productivity does. It measures how efficiently goods or services are produced, usually as output per unit of input over a period. The most common measure, Labour productivity: output per hour of work, divides output by the number of workers. Measures that use one kind of input, such as worker hours, materials or energy per unit of output, are called partial productivities. Rising productivity can lift living standards, because higher wages let people buy more, enjoy leisure, and improve their housing and education. The gains can also go to owners as profits, consumers as lower prices, governments as taxes, and the environment when less resource or pollution goes into each unit. Pollution works in reverse. Counting lost labour and welfare, the World Bank put the global cost of air pollution at over $8 trillion per year.

  <!-- nature-econ-580 -->

- **Social capital: the value of trust and networks**

  In 1916 Lyda Hanifan, writing about local support for rural schools, used a phrase that would not catch on for decades. Social capital means the networks of relationships, built on trust, shared norms and give-and-take, that help people and groups reach their goals. The term became widely used only in the late 1990s. Pierre Bourdieu set it beside two other forms of capital, economic and cultural. Francis Fukuyama argues it forms through repeated dealings over time, is critical for development, and is hard for public policy to create. Knack and Keefer (1996) found that trust and civic cooperation strongly affect a country's growth. Communities rich in social capital also appear to enjoy better health. Critics, though, say the concept is imprecisely defined. Like natural capital, it has grown a separate literature of its own as a modern type of capital.

  <!-- nature-econ-590 -->

- **Depreciation: the value an asset loses as it ages**

  Every machine wears out, and accountants have a word for the value it loses along the way. Depreciation is the fall in an asset's value as it is used and wears out, and the spreading of its original cost over the years it stays useful. Businesses depreciate long-term assets for both accounting and tax purposes. The charge lowers reported net income, yet no cash leaves the business when it is recorded. The idea has close cousins. For resources such as oil the matching idea is Depletion (accounting), and for intangible assets it is amortization. When an asset's value falls unexpectedly, the loss is recorded instead as an impairment charge.

  <!-- nature-econ-519 -->

- **Financial capital: the money that buys the machines**

  A tailor's sewing machine is capital you can touch. The money that bought it is capital of a different kind. Financial capital is money, and other resources measured in money, that businesses use to buy what they need to produce goods or services. It comes from a firm's retained earnings, the profits it keeps, or from lenders and investors. Lenders charge a price for it: interest. Firms spend it on real capital, the physical goods that help produce other goods. Fixed capital buys lasting assets, while working capital pays for stock, running expenses and credit. Some ecological economists want natural capital added to the usual analysis of land, labour and financial capital. The link already shows in commodity markets, which respond to anything that affects natural capital, such as weather that damages food crops.

  <!-- nature-econ-604 -->

- **The consumer price index: pricing a basket of shopping**

  Often every month, statisticians collect prices from a sample of shops and service businesses. The results feed the consumer price index, or CPI, a statistical estimate of the price level of the goods and services households buy. It is a Price indexes: tracking the cost of a basket of goods calculated as the weighted average price of a market basket. The annual percentage change in the CPI is a standard measure of inflation. Governments and employers use it to adjust wages, salaries and pensions for inflation, and to convert money amounts into real values. The items in the basket are updated from time to time to follow changing spending habits. When a product is replaced by one of different quality, its price may be adjusted so the CPI shows price change rather than quality change. A statistical technique, Hedonic regression, is used in building it. The CPI is not a perfect measure of inflation or the cost of living, but it is a useful tool for tracking both.

  <!-- nature-econ-506 -->

- **Index numbers: one figure that tracks many**

  If a commodity's price doubles between 1960 and 1970, its index with 1960 as the base reads 200. That is the whole trick of an index number. It compares a value with a base value, usually set at 100. A single number can then track how a group of related figures, such as prices or employment, changes over time. The consumer price index is one example. Others include cost-of-living indexes, stock market indices such as the S&P 500, and commodity indices. Some compare places rather than times, as Purchasing power parity: comparing what money can buy does for currencies. Either way, index numbers turn complex data into figures that are easy to compare.

  <!-- nature-econ-534 -->

- **Total factor productivity: the growth nobody can explain**

  Robert Solow (1957) called it 'technical change', shorthand for any shift in the production function. Total factor productivity, or TFP, is the ratio of total output to total inputs: how much output a given bundle of inputs yields. Nobody measures it directly. Its growth is whatever part of output growth is left after counting growth in measured labour and capital, so it is calculated as a residual. For small changes, TFP growth is roughly output growth minus the growth of labour and capital inputs, usually weighted 0.7 for labour and 0.3 for capital. The leftover is large. Easterly and Levine estimated in 2001 that it accounts for 60 percent of growth in output per worker in an average country. Official statisticians prefer the name multifactor productivity, because inputs such as energy are left out, as are costs like the using up of minerals and pollution. Some economists consider TFP invalid, or at least in need of careful interpretation. Critics say it lacks meaningful units and may be a modelling artefact.

  <!-- nature-econ-599 -->

- **Source and sink: the environment's two jobs**

  The environment does two jobs for the economy. As a source, it supplies materials and services. As a sink, it absorbs and neutralizes waste and pollution. Natural inputs flow into production, and once consumed they leave the economy as pollution and waste. Both jobs can be overloaded. The source runs down as resources are used up or polluted. When waste exceeds the sink's assimilative capacity, long-term damage follows. Some persistent pollutants, such as nuclear waste, are absorbed very slowly or not at all. This view changes the economist's basic picture. Ecological economics replaces the simple The circular flow: money and goods going round with a diagram in which solar energy sustains the natural inputs and services used in production.

  <!-- nature-econ-553 -->

- **Carbon in the air as a stock and flow problem**

  The carbon dioxide in the air is a stock, measured in tons. Emissions raise it and sequestration, the capture and storage of carbon, lowers it, both measured in tons per day. Mathematically, a stock is the accumulation of inflows minus outflows over time. Seen this way, Climate change mitigation is a stock-and-flow problem: to shrink the stock of heat-trapping gases in the air, cut emissions and pull more carbon dioxide back out. Earth system science is full of such problems, from the cycles of carbon, nitrogen and water to Earth's energy budget. Stocks and flows are also the building blocks of the models in System dynamics: why systems surprise their owners, where Jay Forrester called them levels and rates.

  <!-- nature-econ-595 -->

- **Ranking countries by their human capital**

  Years in a classroom are not the same as learning. The World Bank's Human Capital Index, launched in October 2018, ranks countries by how much they put into young people's education and health care. It harmonized learning data across 164 countries, measuring knowledge actually gained rather than years of schooling alone. The World Economic Forum has published a Global Human Capital Index annually since 2012. The gaps between countries are vast. One measure of expected human capital put Finland highest, at 28.4 adjusted years between ages 20 and 64, and Niger lowest, at under 1.6.

  <!-- nature-econ-532 -->

- **The productivity paradox: new technology, slow gains**

  New technology should make workers more productive. Yet in the United States, overall productivity growth stayed slow from the 1970s to the early 1990s, and again from the 2000s to the 2020s. This puzzle is the productivity paradox. Several causes have been proposed, but there is no consensus on why growth slowed. The debate has also shifted. It now asks not just whether computers raise productivity but whether the potential for productivity growth is running out.

  <!-- nature-econ-582 -->

- **Bonding and bridging: two kinds of social ties**

  A criminal gang and a choir both build social capital, but not the same kind. Bonding social capital is the ties within groups of similar people, as in a gang. Bridging social capital is the ties between socially different groups, like those formed in choirs and bowling clubs. The harmful effects of social capital are more often linked to bonding than to bridging. Daniel Aldrich adds a third type, linking capital: the relationship between a person and a government official or elected leader. He applies these ideas to disaster recovery, studying Japan after the 2011 Fukushima meltdown.

  <!-- nature-econ-591 -->

- **Measuring social capital: how do you count trust?**

  How do you count trust? Researchers try trust surveys, network name generators that ask people to list their contacts, and counts of group membership. None settles the matter. There is no widely held consensus on how to measure social capital, and the dispute has become a debate in itself. Part of the difficulty is that social capital emerges as individuals take part in groups, rather than being held by any one person. Since 2016 the UN Sustainable Development Group's World Social Capital Monitor has used anonymous surveys of trust, solidarity and willingness to fund public goods.

  <!-- nature-econ-593 -->

- **When strong ties do harm**

  Strong group ties are not always good news. Negative social capital is the harmful side, where tight bonds produce bad outcomes for society. Research has linked civic associations to the rise of fascist movements. Pierre Bourdieu showed how social connections can reproduce inequality by giving insiders access to powerful positions. Without bridging ties to outsiders, bonding groups can become cut off from the rest of society. Scholars disagree on how much weight this deserves: Putnam sees social capital as positive, while a sizable literature finds it can do harm.

  <!-- nature-econ-592 -->

- **Three ways to spread an asset's cost over time**

  Take a machine that costs $70,000, will fetch $10,000 at the end of its life, and is expected to make 6,000 units. That end value is its salvage value. Units-of-production depreciation charges $10 for each unit made, so years of heavy use carry heavy charges. Straight-line depreciation, the simplest and most common method, divides cost minus salvage value evenly across the years of useful life. Declining-balance and sum-of-years-digits methods write off more in early years, assuming assets are most productive when new. Some methods follow the calendar; others follow use.

  <!-- nature-econ-520 -->

- **Leverage: running a business on borrowed money**

  Borrowing can magnify a business's profits, and its dangers. Leverage is the ratio between a firm's borrowed capital, its debt, and its own capital, its equity. Own capital comes from the owners, for example from money they have put aside or inherited. Borrowed capital comes through debt and usually must be repaid with interest. High leverage can bring higher profit, but it also raises the risk of insolvency, of being unable to pay what is owed.

  <!-- nature-econ-605 -->

- **The law of one price**

  Without transport costs or trade barriers, a good should sell for the same price everywhere. That is the law of one price. Real markets bend it. Transport costs and trade restrictions weaken it by making goods expensive to move between countries. Firms that sell the same product at different prices in different markets break it too. The principle still earns its keep: it is the basis of Purchasing power parity: comparing what money can buy.

  <!-- nature-econ-584 -->

- **Why no price index is ever quite right**

  When prices rise, shoppers switch to cheaper goods. A fixed basket cannot see that switch, so the consumer price index misstates living costs. This substitution bias is one face of the index number problem. Statistical indices cannot perfectly measure economic change, because they rest on fixed assumptions such as a set basket of goods. The The GDP deflator: a price index for everything produced has its own version of the trouble, skewing real output by not fully adjusting for new products. There is no perfect fix. Statisticians update baskets and weights periodically, but long-term comparisons stay inexact.

  <!-- nature-econ-535 -->

- **Is productivity growth really about energy?**

  Over history, total factor productivity has risen and fallen in step with two things: energy use, and how efficiently energy is converted into useful work. Reiner Kümmel concluded that the unexplained leftover in growth, the residual that total factor productivity measures, can be explained very well by an economy's energy input. On this view, technical progress is the ability to absorb primary energy and turn it efficiently into useful energy for production. Much of what looks like ingenuity in the statistics may track the energy behind it.

  <!-- nature-econ-601 -->

- **Chained price indexes: updating the base every year**

  A price index anchored to one distant year slowly loses its grip. Unchained indices compare every period with a single fixed base, so their bias grows over time as the quantities people buy drift away from that base. A chained price index avoids this by updating its base every period and multiplying the period-to-period changes together. Each link compares only neighboring periods, and the chain carries the comparison across the years.

  <!-- nature-econ-579 -->

- **Elementary indices: the building blocks inside the CPI**

  Inside every large price index sit many small ones. Elementary price indices are unweighted indices that compare the prices of single items between periods, and they serve as building blocks for larger indices such as the CPI. The formula matters. The Carli index averages price ratios, and it is biased upward: a doubling and a halving average out to 1.25, not 1. The Jevons index, from 1863, takes the unweighted geometric mean of price relatives instead, the ratios of new prices to old.

  <!-- nature-econ-578 -->

- **The Laspeyres index: yesterday's basket at today's prices**

  In 1871 Étienne Laspeyres asked a simple question: what would the basket people bought in the base period cost at today's prices? His index measures exactly that. It is the easiest index to compute, because it needs only new price data, not new quantities. The simplicity has a price. By ignoring consumers who switch to cheaper goods when prices rise, it often overstates inflation.

  <!-- nature-econ-575 -->

- **The Paasche index: today's basket instead**

  Hermann Paasche flipped the approach in 1874. His index uses current-period quantities, the basket people buy now, rather than the basket of the base period. That makes it harder to compute than the Laspeyres index, since statisticians need fresh quantity data as well as prices. It also leans the other way. By assuming consumers adjust their purchases instantly to new prices, it understates inflation.

  <!-- nature-econ-576 -->

- **The Fisher index: splitting the difference**

  If one index runs high and another runs low, why not meet in the middle? The Fisher index is the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices. It balances the Laspeyres tendency to overstate inflation against the Paasche tendency to understate it. It belongs to a class called superlative indices, introduced by W. Erwin Diewert in 1976 and preferred for measuring inflation and national output in Gross domestic product: an economy in one number.

  <!-- nature-econ-577 -->

- **Gross domestic product: an economy in one number**

  William Petty wanted to know how heavy a tax burden England could bear during the Anglo-Dutch wars of 1652 to 1674. His answer was an early version of the most quoted number in economics. Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a set period, usually a year. Final goods are those bought by their last user, not parts that go into something else. GDP adds up four major components: spending by households, spending by government, investment in new capital, and exports minus imports. Simon Kuznets developed the modern concept for a 1934 report to the US Congress. After the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944, GDP became the main tool for measuring a country's economy, and today it is the usual way to compare countries. The international rulebook for measuring it is the 2008 edition of The System of National Accounts: one rulebook for the world, prepared by the IMF, EU, OECD, UN and World Bank. Kuznets himself warned against using GDP to measure welfare. It is not a measure of overall living standards or well-being, since it ignores how income is shared. Critics also fault it for leaving out resource extraction, environmental damage and unpaid domestic work.

  <!-- nature-econ-483 -->

- **Economic growth and the power of small percentages**

  Over long periods, even a small growth rate such as 2% a year has large effects. Economic growth is an increase in the amount and quality of the goods and services a society produces. It is usually measured as the rise in an economy's output over a year or longer. The figure is adjusted for inflation so that rising prices do not distort the picture. The rate is typically calculated from inflation-adjusted GDP, either in total or per person, or from measures such as national income per person or median income. Adam Smith pioneered modern growth theory in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. He named two main drivers: the division of labour and the accumulation of capital. Historically, the most important source of real growth per person has been rising output per unit of labour. Growth has a shadow, though. So far, economic growth and carbon dioxide emissions have been closely correlated across nations, although the carbon emitted per unit of GDP varies widely. Worries about this harm have led some to argue for slower growth, or for abandoning growth altogether.

  <!-- nature-econ-478 -->

- **Macroeconomics: studying the economy as a whole**

  When Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936, he gave economics a new branch. Macroeconomics studies how a whole economy, regional, national or global, performs and behaves. It differs from microeconomics, which studies smaller units such as single firms, consumers and markets. Macroeconomists study economy-wide totals: GDP, national income, unemployment, inflation, consumption, saving, investment and trade. Three variables sit at the center: output, unemployment and inflation. The topics divide by time frame. The short term brings the swings of the business cycle, the alternating booms and slumps. The medium term concerns the levels of variables such as unemployment, and the long term concerns growth. The field also analyses how governments and central banks manage money and public budgets, especially when they aim to stabilize the economy or its growth rate. One accounting fact underlies it all: everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, and total net output is usually measured as GDP. Since World War II, Keynesians, monetarists, new classical and new Keynesian economists have shaped mainstream research.

  <!-- nature-econ-541 -->

- **National accounts: double-entry books for a whole country**

  Colin Clark and Simon Kuznets made the first efforts in the late 1920s and 1930s, spurred by the Great Depression and the needs of Keynesian policy. What they began became national accounts: a complete and consistent set of accounts for measuring a nation's economic activity, built on double-entry bookkeeping. Double entry makes both sides of an account equal even though they measure different things, such as production and the income it generates. The accounts record the output, spending and income of households, corporations and government, their links with other countries, and their net worth. They present both flows over a period and stocks at its end, and reconcile the two. GDP, perhaps the most widely cited measure of economic activity, is one of their totals. Figures can be nominal, at the prices of the time, or real, with the effect of price changes removed. Growth rates are usually measured in real terms. National statistical offices or central banks compile the accounts, yearly and quarterly, from surveys, censuses and administrative data. The United States published the first formal national accounts in 1947, and the UN published its first international guide to them in 1952.

  <!-- nature-econ-566 -->

- **Fiscal policy: steering the economy with taxes and spending**

  Fiscal policy grew out of the Great Depression of the 1930s, when the earlier hands-off approach to managing the economy stopped working. It is a government's use of taxes and spending to influence the economy. It rests on Keynes's theory that changing taxes and government spending shifts aggregate demand, the total spending in an economy, and with it economic activity. Governments use it to steady the economy through the business cycle. Fiscal policy usually runs through a government department. Its partner, Monetary policy: steering the economy through interest rates, handles the amount of money and interest rates, usually through a central bank. Spending can be paid for by taxes, by printing money, called seigniorage, or by borrowing at home or abroad. A deficit is often funded by issuing bonds, and if revenue cannot cover the interest, a nation may default. Developing countries collect about half as much tax as a share of GDP as developed countries, which limits their fiscal policy.

  <!-- nature-econ-522 -->

- **The System of National Accounts: one rulebook for the world**

  Almost every country keeps its national accounts by the same rulebook. The System of National Accounts, called the United Nations System of National Accounts until 1993, is the international standard set of concepts and methods for compiling them. More than 200 countries, territories and areas have adopted it, often with local adaptations. Using it is voluntary, but following it improves data quality and makes figures comparable between countries and over time. The roots are old. William Petty made the first known attempt in England in 1665, aiming to estimate national income and wealth. A global standard was first proposed at the League of Nations in 1928, but World War 2 interrupted the work. The UN published the first standard in 1953, with revisions in 1960, 1964, 1968, 1993 and 2008, and SNA 2025 is due to be published in 2026. Its most common criticism is that its concepts and classifications do not adequately reflect real-world activities and relationships.

  <!-- nature-econ-596 -->

- **Purchasing power parity: comparing what money can buy**

  A computer costs 500 US dollars in New York and 2000 HK dollars in Hong Kong. If the same thing should cost the same everywhere, that implies 4 HK dollars per US dollar. This is purchasing power parity, or PPP. It compares currencies by what the same basket of goods costs in each country, giving an exchange rate based on purchasing power. It applies the law of one price to whole baskets. Economists use PPP to compare countries' GDP, output per worker, consumption and cost of living. The OECD's basket covers around 3,000 consumer goods and services, 30 government occupations, 200 types of equipment and about 15 construction projects. PPP suits comparisons of whole economies, where goods that are never traded matter, while market exchange rates suit single traded goods. The calculations are disputed, because comparable baskets are hard to find and people in different countries buy different things. The global poverty line is converted between currencies with PPP rates, though high-end goods that poor people rarely buy skew them.

  <!-- nature-econ-583 -->

- **GDP per capita: the average slice of the pie**

  Divide a country's GDP by its population and you get GDP per capita, its average production per person. Its great advantage as a gauge of living standards is practical: it is measured frequently, widely and consistently across countries. Adjusted for purchasing power parity, it helps compare living standards between nations. Its weakness lies in the word average. Like total GDP, it ignores how income is distributed, and it tends to overstate the income of a typical person. In some countries, growth in median income, the income of the person in the middle, has diverged from growth in GDP per capita.

  <!-- nature-econ-487 -->

- **Nominal and real GDP: stripping out inflation**

  Suppose GDP rises from $100 million to $300 million while inflation halves the value of money. On paper the economy has tripled. In fact real GDP grew 50 percent, not 200 percent. Nominal GDP is measured at the current market prices of the time, so it does not account for inflation. Real GDP adjusts for changes in the value of money so that years can be compared. The factor that converts GDP from current to constant values is called the The GDP deflator: a price index for everything produced. Real GDP is the basis of the GDP growth rate, usually expressed as a percentage change from the previous year.

  <!-- nature-econ-486 -->

- **Can growth and a healthy planet coexist?**

  In 2019, 11,000 scientists signed a warning that named economic growth as the driving force behind the overuse of ecosystems. Can an economy keep growing without wrecking the natural systems it rests on? The sources do not agree. Critics such as those in Club of Rome argue that a narrow focus on growth, together with globalization, risks a systemic collapse of the resources nature provides. A 2019 Global Assessment by IPBES warned that, given heavy losses of biodiversity, society should not focus solely on economic growth. A 2021 review for the British Treasury by Partha Dasgupta argued that human demands far exceed nature's capacity, and called for abandoning GDP as the measure of success. Academics have proposed responses from eco-taxes and green investment to the ideas in Uneconomic growth, Steady-state economy and Degrowth. Optimists see it differently. Julian Simon argued in 1981 that the large-scale ecological effects of growth are minor, and that human ingenuity would adapt to any that exist. Growth-oriented environmental economists instead propose government action to shift energy production toward wind, solar, hydroelectric and nuclear power. Whether growth's ecological effects are minor and manageable or are driving ecosystems toward collapse remains disputed.

  <!-- nature-econ-480 -->

- **Where growth comes from**

  Robert Solow estimated that technological progress accounted for 80 percent of the long-term rise in US income per person, and more capital investment for only 20 percent. Output per person can be broken into four parts. They are output per hour of labour, hours worked, the share of working-age people in work, and the share of people who are of working age. Capital helps, but only up to a point. More capital per worker raises output, yet it faces diminishing returns, partly because of the growing burden of depreciation. Many analyses give a major role to human capital, though it is hard to measure because it is built at home, at school and on the job. It helps growth only if the population is healthy and well nourished. History adds other forces. Moving workers from low-productivity farming to high-productivity manufacturing raised overall output, and laws protecting contracts and private property helped economies move toward capitalism.

  <!-- nature-econ-479 -->

- **Putting nature into models of the whole economy**

  In 1865, Jevons's book The Coal Question made an unsettling argument: in a growing economy, productivity gains could speed up resource scarcity. Economists have since tried to build nature into macroeconomic models, especially growth models, by adding resource scarcity and Climate change: a warming world and why it matters. During the oil crises of the 1970s, Stiglitz and Solow added resources that run out to growth models, asking whether living standards could keep rising. The 2006 Stern Review gave the first comprehensive analysis of global economic damage from projected changes in climate. Integrated assessment models, pioneered by William Nordhaus and covered in Integrated assessment modelling, are now widely used to estimate regional and global climate damages under different policies. Such models treat land, water and energy as inputs to production. Early work by Herman Daly replaced the familiar picture of money circling between households and firms with one driven by solar energy. How to count environmental goods and services in national accounts is still debated.

  <!-- nature-econ-552 -->

- **Inflation and deflation: when all prices move together**

  Inflation is a general rise in prices across a whole economy, and deflation is a general fall. Economists track both with price indexes.
