Inflation tends to rise when an economy overheats and grows too fast, while a shrinking economy can push it down or into deflation. Shocks to supply also move it, as in the oil crises of the 1970s and the 2021–2023 global energy crisis. High inflation and deflation both raise uncertainty, especially when they come unexpectedly. That is why most central banks aim for low, stable, positive inflation. An old idea, the quantity theory of money, says prices change because the amount of money changes. It has proved unreliable over short and medium horizons.

  <!-- nature-econ-542 -->

- **Real GDP: measuring output, not prices**

  Because of inflation, nominal GDP can rise even when an economy makes exactly the same physical output. Real GDP removes that illusion. It values output with the effect of price changes taken out, so it tracks the quantity produced. The method is to value every year's quantities at the prices of one base year, so that differences reflect only changes in volume. Dividing nominal GDP by real GDP gives the The GDP deflator: a price index for everything produced, which equals 100 in the base year and shows overall price change. Annual real GDP growth is nominal growth adjusted for inflation, usually given as a percentage. Real GDP is also called constant GDP, and organizations use different base years, such as UNCTAD's 2015 constant prices. It is one case of the general distinction between real and nominal values.

  <!-- nature-econ-586 -->

- **Unemployment: who counts as out of work**

  Not everyone without a job is unemployed. Retired people, students and discouraged job-seekers are outside the labour force, the people working or seeking work, so they are not counted. Unemployment covers people in the labour force who have no job but are actively looking for one, and the unemployment rate gives them as a percentage. Part of it is cyclical, rising and falling with the business cycle. Part is a lasting structural, or natural, level. Search, or frictional, unemployment arises because matching workers to vacancies takes time when information is imperfect. Minimum wages, trade unions and efficiency wages, pay set above the going rate to motivate staff, can hold wages above the level where supply equals demand. Okun's law ties unemployment to short-run GDP growth: in its original version, a 3% rise in output cuts unemployment by 1%.

  <!-- nature-econ-543 -->

- **Green national accounting: putting a value on nature**

  Ordinary measures of national wealth usually leave environmental assets out, partly because they are hard to value. In effect, they count them as worth zero. Green national accounting is the proposed alternative: a method of putting values on those assets. It also aims to show whether welfare can be sustained while the environment is being degraded. The methods are not settled. How to include environmental goods and services in national output is still under discussion.

  <!-- nature-econ-569 -->

- **Greening the national accounts: a half-century effort**

  For decades, the world's standard rulebook for national accounts left out the natural world that holds the economy up. Critics argued that the System of National Accounts ignored the environment that contains and supports the economy. It did not value resource stocks, their running down, or ecosystem services. Leaving out pollution costs meant the accounts overstated the net benefits of economic activity. Change came slowly. SNA 1993 first introduced environmental side accounts linked to the main ones, described in Satellite accounts: extra detail without touching the main figures. It also introduced a net domestic product adjusted for resources used up, though not formally within the framework. The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting, or SEEA, followed the Earth Summit in Rio in 1992, and its Central Framework became a UN standard in February 2012. SNA 2025 goes further. It formally recognizes natural capital and ecosystem services and treats the using up of resources as a cost of production. In early 2025 at least 94 countries had produced at least one SEEA account in the past five years, 67 of them regularly. The argument is not over. Environmentalists say the SNA still undervalues nature, while statisticians note that measurement methods remain unsettled.

  <!-- nature-econ-597 -->

- **The GDP deflator: a price index for everything produced**

  A GDP deflator of 200 means prices have doubled since the base year; one of 50 means they have halved. The deflator is a price index covering all new, domestically produced final goods and services, and it turns nominal GDP into real GDP. It equals nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100, so the base year's value is 100. Unlike the CPI, it has no fixed basket. Its basket changes each year with patterns of spending and investment. In practice it usually differs only slightly from the CPI, but even small gaps can shift budgets.

  <!-- nature-econ-526 -->

- **The AD–AS model: where demand meets supply for a whole economy**

  A common textbook model finds an economy's price level and real output where two curves cross. One is aggregate demand, the total spending on goods and services. The other is aggregate supply, the total output producers offer. The demand curve slopes down, so more output is demanded at lower price levels. Near potential output, the full-employment level, extra demand only raises prices, not output. Modern versions put inflation on the vertical axis, with an upward-sloping supply curve based on the Phillips curve, a link between inflation and unemployment.

  <!-- nature-econ-557 -->

- **Endogenous growth: explaining progress from the inside**

  Older growth models, such as the one in Solow–Swan model, left long-run growth to technical progress they could not explain. Endogenous growth theory arose in the mid-1980s to fill that gap. It explains growth from inside the economy, through increasing returns, the gains from experience in Learning-by-doing, or firms' research and development. Knowledge spillovers, a kind of positive externality, keep returns to capital from falling to zero. So the long-run growth rate depends on policy, such as subsidies for research or education. Critics dispute its explanatory power, and ecological economists fault its neglect of energy and materials.

  <!-- nature-econ-551 -->

- **The money supply: counting the money in an economy**

  How much money is there in an economy? Economists answer with measures of the money supply, most commonly M1 and M2. M1 is liquid money: cash, coins and checking deposits. A liquid asset is one that can be turned into cash quickly without much loss of value. M2 adds less liquid items, such as time deposits, savings accounts and money market funds. The money supply is a stock, counted at a moment in time. It affects interest rates and sits at the center of Monetary policy: steering the economy through interest rates.

  <!-- nature-econ-544 -->

- **Monetary policy: steering the economy through interest rates**

  When a central bank changes interest rates, the effects ripple outward. Investment, consumption, asset prices and exchange rates shift, and with them demand, employment and inflation. Economists call this chain the monetary transmission mechanism. Monetary policy is what a nation's monetary authority uses to influence money and financial conditions, in pursuit of goals such as high employment and low, stable inflation. Setting interest rates, directly or through Open market operations: creating money by buying bonds, is generally its main tool. Expansionary policy lowers rates to stimulate activity, and contractionary policy dampens activity and inflation. Most developed-country central banks target inflation, while most in developing countries target a fixed exchange rate. Unlike fiscal policy, monetary policy works through financial channels, and it is usually run by central banks independent of government. When rates are near zero, conventional policy cannot loosen further, so central banks may turn to Quantitative easing: when interest rates hit bottom.

  <!-- nature-econ-560 -->

- **Stabilization policy: smoothing out booms and slumps**

  Economies boom and slump, and stabilization policy tries to soften the harm. It is short-run policy by governments and central banks, using fiscal and monetary tools. In a recession, policy turns expansive. When the economy overheats, it turns contractive. Economists usually prefer monetary policy for moderate swings, since independent central banks face less political pressure and shorter delays. Fiscal policy matters more after a major shock, under a fixed exchange rate, or in a liquidity trap, when cutting interest rates no longer revives spending. Longer-run structural policies are a different matter. They target things like the structural unemployment rate, or how much people save, invest and study.

  <!-- nature-econ-554 -->

- **Automatic stabilizers: cushions built into the budget**

  When unemployment rises, spending on unemployment benefits rises and tax revenue falls, without politicians deciding anything. These automatic stabilizers are parts of the tax and benefit system that cushion a downturn on their own, protecting part of private income and consumption. Because no new decision is needed, they avoid the delays that slow discretionary fiscal policy, the deliberate kind.

  <!-- nature-econ-556 -->

- **Central banks: the bankers' bank**

  The Bank of England, created in 1694 with power to print gold-backed notes, began the idea of monetary policy run independently of the executive. A central bank is a national bank that issues currency and sets interest rates. It also acts as lender of last resort, lending to other banks when no one else will. Industrialized nations set up central banks between 1870 and 1920, and the Federal Reserve, in 1913, was among the last. There is strong consensus today that an independent central bank runs more credible monetary policy.

  <!-- nature-econ-561 -->

- **Open market operations: creating money by buying bonds**

  A central bank can create money by going shopping. When it buys a security such as a government bond, it in effect creates money, expanding the monetary base. Selling securities shrinks the base again. The monetary base is currency in circulation plus the reserves banks hold at the central bank. This buying and selling, called open market operations, lets the bank influence interest rates, the exchange rate or the money supply.

  <!-- nature-econ-563 -->

- **Quantitative easing: when interest rates hit bottom**

  When interest rates are already near zero, the usual lever is stuck. Conventional policy can fail in such a liquidity trap. Quantitative easing is one way around it: the central bank buys bonds and other assets to push down a wider range of interest rates. Its purchases can include government bonds, corporate bonds, stocks and other securities. It is one of several unconventional tools, alongside credit easing, forward guidance and signalling.

  <!-- nature-econ-564 -->

- **Green monetary policy: central banks confront climate change**

  Around 2017–2018, central banks began asking what Climate change: a warming world and why it matters means for their own frameworks. They argue it will add market volatility, inflation pressure from severe weather or a disorderly transition, and financial risks. Green monetary policy is central banks' adjustment of monetary and supervisory policy to account for these effects. The Network for Greening the Financial System, founded in 2017, has more than a hundred central banks and supervisors as members. Proposals include green macro-prudential rules, which guard the financial system as a whole, along with green quantitative easing, green collateral rules and green refinancing operations. In 2021 the European Central Bank said it would tilt its corporate bond purchases, a form of green QE. It has not adopted a green interest rate.

  <!-- nature-econ-565 -->

- **Generational accounting: who pays, and when**

  A budget deficit shows one year's taxes minus spending. It says nothing about who will pay later. Generational accounting tries to fill that gap. It measures how social insurance shifts lifetime tax burdens between generations. It has been proposed as a better guide than the deficit to whether fiscal policy is sustainable.

  <!-- nature-econ-570 -->

- **Neutral, expansionary, contractionary: three fiscal settings**

  Fiscal policy has three settings. Neutral policy keeps deficit spending about at its long-run average, typically when the economy is neither in recession nor boom. Expansionary policy, used in recessions, lets spending exceed tax revenue by more than usual, through public works or tax cuts. Contractionary policy raises taxes and cuts spending to cool growth that is causing excessive inflation. Judging the setting takes care, because tax revenue rises and falls with the business cycle on its own. Analysts therefore use cyclically adjusted figures, which remove that swing.

  <!-- nature-econ-523 -->

- **Monetary or fiscal policy: which works better?**

  Which tool steers an economy better? Monetary policy is quicker to change, since interest rates can be set monthly, and it is shielded from election politics. But it has a weak spot. In a liquidity trap, rate cuts fail to boost demand because banks will not lend and consumers will not spend. In a deep recession, monetary policy alone is not enough, and government spending can kick-start demand. Fiscal policy appears to have the greater long-run effect, while monetary policy tends to succeed in the short run. Economists still weigh the two tools differently and debate how well each works.

  <!-- nature-econ-524 -->

- **Satellite accounts: extra detail without touching the main figures**

  National accountants often want more detail on a topic like the environment without disturbing the main figures everyone relies on. Satellite accounts provide it. They are extra accounts linked to the main national accounts, giving detail without changing them. In principle they are optional, and countries produce them when there is demand and budget. SNA 2008 recognized environmental satellite accounts such as material flow, emission and energy accounts.

  <!-- nature-econ-598 -->

- **The Big Mac Index: currencies compared by burger**

  In 1986 The Economist created a currency gauge with a single item in its basket: a McDonald's Big Mac. The Big Mac Index is a simple version of purchasing power parity, meant to teach economics and to spot over- and under-valued currencies. It has an obvious flaw. A Big Mac is perishable and hard to transport, so the law of one price is unlikely to hold for it. Even so, one study found a correlation of 0.73 between Big Mac prices and the prices in the Penn World Tables.

  <!-- nature-econ-585 -->

- **Growth accounting: sorting growth into its sources**

  Growth accounting splits economic growth into two parts: the share due to more inputs, such as labour and capital, and the share due to technological change. It uses national accounts data over long periods to estimate where growth came from. Multi-factor productivity, the leftover share, is typically estimated this way. Like total factor productivity, the method is open to the Cambridge critique, so some economists doubt its validity.

  <!-- nature-econ-600 -->

- **Consumption: spending to meet today's needs**

  In most countries, consumption is the largest part of GDP, usually between 45% and 85% of it. Consumption is the use of resources to meet present needs and wants, as opposed to investing for future income. Mainstream economists count only final purchases of newly produced goods and services by individuals for immediate use. In macroeconomics, consumption equals income minus savings. Economists consider income the most important factor affecting it. In microeconomics, the view is individual: consumers are assumed to choose the goods that maximize their utility within their budget. Add up everyone's consumption and you get one component of aggregate demand, the total spending in an economy.

  <!-- nature-econ-509 -->

- **Income: what you gain over a period**

  Watching a sunset is a joy, but it is not income. Income is the ability to consume and save that a person, household or firm gains over a set period, usually counted in money. Because non-monetary joys are left out, reported income may misstate well-being. Income is also hard to define, and its meaning differs between fields. Economic income can differ from income as the law defines it. US tax law, for example, counts wages, salary, profit, interest, rent and other earnings received in a calendar year as household income. For a firm, gross income can be defined as all revenue minus the cost of goods sold. Some rules hold under every definition. Borrowing or repaying money is never income, but interest and forgiven debt are. Education raises income by increasing workers' skills and productivity. Economists conventionally write income as Y. Because it is measured over a period, income is a flow, in the sense of Stocks and flows: what you have versus what moves.

  <!-- nature-econ-491 -->

- **Wealth: what you own minus what you owe**

  For 2018 the World Bank valued the world's produced, natural and human capital at $1,152 trillion. That is wealth counted on the widest scale. In general, wealth means a plentiful store of valuable assets or possessions that can be turned into a form usable in exchange. In economics it is net worth: the value of all assets owned minus all liabilities owed, at a point in time, for a person, household or nation. Adam Smith described wealth as 'the annual produce of the land and labor of the society'. Scarcity is fundamental. A commodity freely available to everyone gives its owner no potential for wealth. Wealth falls into three main categories: personal property, monetary savings, and income-producing capital such as real estate, stocks and businesses. Global household wealth was estimated at US$418.3 trillion at the end of 2020, excluding human capital. The UN goes further with the measure described in Inclusive wealth, adding up natural, human and physical assets in money terms. Natural capital includes land, forests, energy resources and minerals. Human capital is people's education and skills, and physical capital is machinery, buildings and infrastructure.

  <!-- nature-econ-499 -->

- **Saving: income held back for later**

  In a simple farming economy, saving might mean holding back the best of the corn harvest as seed for next season. Saving is income not spent on immediate consumption; in economics, it is after-tax income minus consumption. The grammar matters. Saving is an activity over time, a flow, while savings is an amount held at one moment, a stock. Saving supplies the funds for investment. Income not spent on consumer goods can build factories and machinery, which supports growth. Capital markets balance personal saving, government surpluses and net exports against physical investment. Yet more saving does not always mean more investment. It can instead cause a shortfall of demand and a recession. In personal finance, saving means low-risk preservation of money, while investment carries a higher risk of loss.

  <!-- nature-econ-587 -->

- **Investment: putting resources to work for a return**

  Modern investing is usually dated to the 17th century, and the Amsterdam Stock Exchange began in 1602. To invest is to commit resources, often money, to something expected to gain value over time. In finance, the aim is to earn a return. The return can come as a capital gain or loss when the asset is sold, or as regular income such as dividends, interest or rent. Risk and reward travel together. Investors usually expect higher returns from riskier investments, and low-risk investments generally earn low returns. Spreading money across many investments reduces overall risk. Common investments include stocks, bonds, cash, real estate, private equity and commodities. Compared with savings, they carry more kinds of risk and greater uncertainty. Much investing runs through intermediaries such as pension funds, banks and insurance companies, which pool money from many investors.

  <!-- nature-econ-538 -->

- **Investment in the national economy: adding to the capital stock**

  In a national economy, investment has a specific meaning. It is spending in a year that adds to the country's stock of buildings, equipment, software and inventories. In classical theory, it means producing goods that are not consumed right away but used to make other goods. Investment is a flow measured over a period. Capital is the stock it builds: the net investment accumulated up to a point in time. Net investment is gross investment minus depreciation, and net fixed investment is the yearly net increase in the capital stock. Investment is often modelled as falling when interest rates rise, since interest is the cost of funds, and rising with income. Some research models it as rising with the gap between the profit-maximizing capital stock and the current one. It is closely related to saving, but it is not the same thing.

  <!-- nature-econ-539 -->

- **The family of national income measures**

  Systematic national accounts began only in the 1930s, in the United States and some European countries, spurred by the Great Depression and Keynes's ideas. Out of them came a family of statistics, such as GDP, Gross national income: counting by ownership, not location and Net national income: allowing for wear and tear, used to estimate the total economic activity of a country or region. All of them count the goods and services produced within an economy and its sectors. They count them at market value, the price they fetch, not their actual usefulness. Three methods give the market value of all output: the product, expenditure and income methods. Some measures count only goods and services exchanged for money, while others impute values for bartered goods. One variant, adjusted national income, corrects that net figure for the using up of resources taken from nature.

  <!-- nature-econ-495 -->

- **Adding up GDP by who does the spending**

  Economists write GDP as a sum: Y = C + I + G + (X − M). Consumption (C), households' private spending, is normally the largest part. Investment (I) means spending on things like new equipment, buildings and software. Buying shares or bonds does not count here; it counts as saving. Government spending (G) covers final goods and services such as public salaries, but not transfer payments like unemployment benefits. Exports (X) are added and imports (M) subtracted. Imports already appear inside C, I and G, and they must not be counted as domestic supply. Throughout, only spending on final goods counts. Intermediate goods used to make other products are left out.

  <!-- nature-econ-485 -->

- **Keynesian economics: when markets fail to clear**

  During the Great Depression, goods went unsold and workers stayed unemployed, and the economists of the day struggled to explain why. The older neoclassical view held that prices and wages would fall until all goods and labour were sold. Keynes's General Theory, published in 1936, began a new school of thought. Keynesian economics explains why markets might not clear, leaving goods and workers unused, and it stresses total demand as the driver of output. Keynes argued that a return to normal output would be slow at best, and he recommended active fiscal policy to stabilize demand and employment. His followers merged his ideas with neoclassical microeconomics into the neoclassical synthesis, which most economists accepted by the 1950s.

  <!-- nature-econ-545 -->

- **Keynes's consumption function: spending tied to today's income**

  In his 1936 General Theory, Keynes proposed a simple rule: consumer spending is a linear function of current disposable income, the income left after taxes. This consumption function is also called the absolute income hypothesis. Keynes held that real income is the most important influence on consumption in the short run. There is also a floor. Autonomous consumption is the minimum a household always consumes, by drawing down savings or borrowing. The rule has a blind spot: it ignores future income. Its critics developed The permanent income hypothesis: spending on long-run income and The life-cycle hypothesis: spending over a whole lifetime in response.

  <!-- nature-econ-510 -->

- **The circular flow: money and goods going round**

  In 1758 François Quesnay drew the economy as a circuit in the chart described in Tableau économique, picturing an idea Richard Cantillon had described in 1730. The circular flow of income is a model showing the main exchanges in an economy as flows of money, goods and services between economic actors. Money and goods travel around a closed circuit in matching amounts but opposite directions. In the simplest version, households supply labour to businesses and spend the income they earn on the goods and services businesses produce. The model shows how activities depend on one another: without consumption there is no demand, which limits production and income. Frank Knight drew the first modern circular flow diagram in 1933. Circular flow analysis is the basis of national accounts, and so of macroeconomics.

  <!-- nature-econ-502 -->

- **Wealth versus income: the orchard and its apples**

  Picture an orchard. Wealth is like the value of the orchard on December 31, minus the debt owed on it. Income is like the value of the apples it yields each year. The first is a stock, measured at a point in time. The second is a flow, measured per unit of time. For a nation's wealth in the national accounts, the liabilities that count are those owed to the rest of the world. The two are linked by behaviour. The wealth effect is the rise in total consumption that follows a rise in national wealth.

  <!-- nature-econ-500 -->

- **Economic depreciation: the shrinking value of capital**

  Accountants depreciate an asset by spreading out its cost. Economists ask a different question: how much less are the asset's future services worth today? Economic depreciation is the gradual loss in value of a firm's or nation's capital stock through physical wear, obsolescence, or falling demand for what the capital provides. Formally, it is the fall in the present value of the services an asset will provide in future. The bookkeeping is simple. Next period's capital stock equals this period's stock plus gross investment minus depreciation, and gross investment minus depreciation is net investment. In national accounts it is called Consumption of fixed capital: the cost of wear in national accounts. Value can also rise, for example if the price of an asset's services rises unexpectedly or the discount rate falls. In the growth model of Solow–Swan model, the capital stock stops changing when gross investment equals depreciation.

  <!-- nature-econ-521 -->

- **Consumption of fixed capital: the cost of wear in national accounts**

  A large cost hides inside every GDP figure. The UN manual says this cost, consumption of fixed capital, may account for 10 per cent or more of total GDP. It is the national-accounts term for depreciation: the fall in the current value of fixed assets over a period through wear, normal obsolescence and normal accidental damage. It is valued at current market prices rather than historic cost, which is why the System of National Accounts avoids the word depreciation. Subtracting it from GDP gives net domestic product, and subtracting it from Gross national income: counting by ownership, not location gives Net national income: allowing for wear and tear. That net figure shows the income actually available for consumption and new investment, which makes it a better gauge of economic welfare than GDP. Some losses are left out. It excludes the using up or degradation of non-produced assets such as land, mineral deposits, coal, oil and natural gas. It also excludes assets destroyed by war or rare major natural disasters. Critics note that its economic valuation yields figures that differ from standard accounting practice.

  <!-- nature-econ-517 -->

- **Income inequality: how unevenly income is shared**

  UN Sustainable Development Goal 10 aims to reduce inequality. Income inequality is the extent to which income is spread unevenly across a population. It can be measured with tools such as the Lorenz curve and the The Gini coefficient: inequality in a single number. Many economists argue that some inequality is necessary, but that excessive inequality causes efficiency problems and social injustice. Globalization complicates the picture. It tends to raise a country's average income, but unequally.

  <!-- nature-econ-494 -->

- **The Gini coefficient: inequality in a single number**

  Corrado Gini published his measure in 1912, building on the work of Max Lorenz. The Gini coefficient sums up how unequally income, wealth or consumption is spread across a nation or group, from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for perfect inequality. It is usually defined from the Lorenz curve, which plots the share of total income earned by the bottom share of the population. On that chart, a straight 45-degree line means perfect equality. The simplest case shows the logic. With just two income groups, if the high earners are a share u of people and earn a share f of income, the Gini is f − u. It can be calculated on market income, before taxes and transfers, or on disposable income. UNICEF put the net income Gini of Latin America and the Caribbean at 48.3 in 2008, the highest of any region. Ecologists borrow it too, measuring biodiversity by plotting the cumulative share of species against the cumulative share of individuals.

  <!-- nature-econ-527 -->

- **What GDP leaves out**

  Robert F. Kennedy said GNP, a close cousin of GDP, measures everything except that which makes life worthwhile. Critics of GDP have a long list of reasons. It ignores negative externalities: industrial output may raise GDP while the pollution it causes goes uncounted. It excludes non-market activity such as unpaid work at home, barter and volunteer work. Estimates of unpaid work's value range from about 15% of GDP in Canada to nearly 70% in the United Kingdom. GDP also counts spending that would shrink if problems were solved, such as medical care and crime-fighting. The parable of the broken window makes the point sharply: GDP treats spending on repairs as a net benefit and ignores the original destruction. The man who developed the modern measure saw its limits. Kuznets warned in 1937 that a nation's welfare can scarcely be inferred from national income.

  <!-- nature-econ-488 -->

- **Why GDP looks good when nature suffers**

  A traffic jam is good for GDP. Stuck cars burn extra fuel, which counts as economic activity, while the resulting air pollution goes uncounted. That is the heart of the criticism: GDP rewards activities that harm the environment and fails to show natural capital being used up. Clearing forests, strip mining and taking too many fish all count as activity despite their long-term harm. GDP may not show how much natural capital an economy is building or protecting. The UK's Natural Capital Committee put it plainly in 2013. GDP focuses on flows, not stocks, so an economy can run down its assets while recording high growth. Alternatives have followed. In 1989 John Cobb and Herman Daly introduced Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare, which subtracts environmental degradation and the depreciation of natural capital. In 2020 China launched Gross ecosystem product to measure ecosystems' contribution to the economy, including its role in steadying the climate.

  <!-- nature-econ-489 -->

- **The threshold hypothesis: when more growth stops helping**

  Does more growth always mean a better life? The threshold hypothesis says no. Growth improves quality of life only up to a threshold point, after which further growth can make it worse. Plotted, the idea forms an upside-down U, whose peak marks the level of growth to aim for. Happiness has been shown to rise with GDP per person at least up to $15,000 per person. Yet health, education and political freedoms sometimes fail to improve as an economy grows.

  <!-- nature-econ-481 -->

- **Crowding out: when public spending displaces private**

  Government spending does not always add to an economy. Sometimes it just takes the place of private activity, an effect called crowding out. Full crowding out happens when government spending simply replaces private output instead of adding to it. A subtler route runs through interest rates. Government spending that raises interest rates can cut private investment, limiting what fiscal policy achieves.

  <!-- nature-econ-555 -->

- **Heterodox macroeconomics: the dissenting schools**

  Not every economist accepts the mainstream story. Heterodox macroeconomics covers the branches that reject mainstream theory, including the Ecological economics tradition, modern monetary theory and Marxian economics. One dividing line is how prices behave. Heterodox economists see price flexibility, not price stickiness, as the source of instability, so they build models with different assumptions.

  <!-- nature-econ-559 -->

- **Monetarism: Milton Friedman's case for steady money**

  Milton Friedman updated an old idea, the quantity theory of money, and built a school of macroeconomics around it. Monetarism stresses money's role in the economy. Friedman argued that monetary policy was more effective than fiscal policy, but he favoured steady growth of the money supply over frequent intervention. With Edmund Phelps, he denied a stable long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, a view the 1970s oil shocks supported. Monetarism was influential in the early 1980s. It faded when central banks found money growth, inflation and real GDP growth too unstably linked to target money.

  <!-- nature-econ-547 -->

- **Rational expectations: people look ahead, not just back**

  Before Robert Lucas, economists mostly assumed adaptive expectations: people forecast by looking only at the recent past. Lucas brought in rational expectations, the assumption that people use all current information about policy and conditions. The consequences were large. In new classical models with rational expectations, monetary policy had only a limited effect. The Lucas critique added that models built on past statistical relationships fail when the underlying economy changes. It called for models with microeconomic foundations instead.

  <!-- nature-econ-548 -->

- **New Keynesian economics: sticky prices bring policy back**

  New Keynesian economics accepts rational expectations but finds a way back for policy. It traces sticky prices and wages to imperfect competition, so monetary policy changes real quantities rather than only prices. Stanley Fischer and John B. Taylor showed that monetary policy could work even under rational expectations, when contracts fix wages.

  <!-- nature-econ-549 -->

- **How consumption shapes the environment**

  What people eat and wear, the homes they live in and where they shop all affect the environment. Consumption patterns changed drastically with the Industrial Revolution, as cheap mass-produced goods met rising wages. Researchers have since found affluence to be the key driver of carbon emissions. The stakes reach beyond the climate. Consuming too much, along with pollution and Climate change: a warming world and why it matters, can devastate biodiversity.

  <!-- nature-econ-516 -->

- **Household production: the economy inside the home**

  Households do not only buy things; they also make them. The New Home Economics holds that market consumption must be studied alongside the goods and services households produce for themselves. Time is the hinge. The opportunity cost of time changes the cost of home-made substitutes, and so changes the demand for bought goods and services. This home production is largely invisible in the statistics, since GDP excludes it, including unpaid childcare.

  <!-- nature-econ-515 -->

- **The life-cycle hypothesis: spending over a whole lifetime**

  Franco Modigliani argued that people do not spend according to current income alone. In his life-cycle hypothesis, people plan consumption using past, current and expected future income, spreading it over their lifetime. The source dates his publication of it to 1966. The theory grew out of criticism that the Keynesian consumption function ignores future income.

  <!-- nature-econ-514 -->

- **The permanent income hypothesis: spending on long-run income**

  Milton Friedman set out a rival idea in the 1950s, in A Theory of the Consumption Function. The permanent income hypothesis says consumption depends on a person's long-run, permanent income rather than temporary swings. Income is split into transitory and permanent parts, and changes in each affect spending differently. A change in permanent income changes consumption by the marginal propensity to consume, the share of extra income that is spent, times that change.

  <!-- nature-econ-513 -->

- **The relative income hypothesis: keeping up with others**

  In 1949 James Duesenberry argued that spending is a social act. His relative income hypothesis says people's consumption depends on their income relative to others, not only on its level. It assumes people's consumption choices are not independent of one another. So two people with the same income, but different positions in the income distribution, will consume differently.

  <!-- nature-econ-511 -->

- **Does school build skills or just signal them?**

  Does school make people more productive, or does it just reveal who already was? Human capital theory says education creates skills. In Spence and Stiglitz's signaling theory, education instead lets able workers signal their ability to employers and earn higher wages. Some labour economists criticize the Chicago-school theory for trying to explain all wage differences by human capital. Studies find wages also vary with gender, nativity, workplace discrimination and socioeconomic status. The two theories remain rival explanations of why education raises wages.

  <!-- nature-econ-533 -->

- **The circular flow ignores the energy that drives it**

  The textbook circular flow has a hidden assumption. It implies the economy runs like a perpetual motion machine, something the Laws of thermodynamics rule out. No economy can recycle its own waste without new energy, so it must operate as a subsystem of a larger ecosystem. In this critique, the economy depends on a one-way Throughput of matter and energy from the environment. Concentrated, useful matter and energy enter from natural capital such as solar energy, oil wells, fisheries and mines. They leave as dispersed, useless waste, a change physicists describe with Entropy. Because these inputs and the capacity to absorb waste are finite, there is a sustainable limit to the economy's growth. For this reason, Ecological economics replaces the simple circular flow with a diagram that includes solar energy and the natural inputs and services it sustains.

  <!-- nature-econ-505 -->

- **Who owns the world's wealth**

  In 2013, 1% of adults were estimated to hold 46% of the world's wealth. In 2008 the estimate had been 40%, or 32% adjusted for purchasing power parity. The distribution of wealth describes how a society's or the world's total wealth is shared among people and regions. At the other end, some adults have negative net worth, with debts larger than their assets. The pattern described in Kuznets curve holds that inequality of wealth and income rises in early development, stabilizes, then falls.

  <!-- nature-econ-501 -->

- **Does inequality help or hurt growth?**

  Does inequality help an economy grow, or hold it back? Theories point in opposite directions. The classical view, from Adam Smith, held that inequality boosts saving by the wealthy and so speeds capital accumulation and growth. Galor and Zeira argued that where credit markets are imperfect, inequality harms investment in skills and slows growth, except in very poor economies. Galor and Moav suggest it helped early industrial growth but turned harmful once human capital replaced physical capital as the main engine. Thomas Piketty argued in 2013 that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of output, inequality rises.

  <!-- nature-econ-482 -->

- **Tobin's q: when buying new machines pays**

  Tobin's q compares two numbers: a physical asset's market value and the cost of replacing it. The ratio helps explain investment. When q is above 1, a machine can be bought for less than the output it generates is worth, so firms gain by investing.

  <!-- nature-econ-540 -->

- **Factor income: rent, wages, interest and profit**

  Each factor of production earns its own kind of income: rent from land, wages from labour, interest from capital and profit from enterprise. Together these make up factor income. National income is divided among the factors of production through the factor market. In consumer theory, income takes a narrower meaning: the budget a person can spend on different goods at their given prices.

  <!-- nature-econ-493 -->

- **Gross national income: counting by ownership, not location**

  Gross national income, formerly called gross national product or GNP, is the total factor income earned by a country's residents. It equals GDP plus factor income residents receive from abroad, minus factor income paid to non-residents. GDP defines its scope by location, GNI by ownership. For the whole world the two are the same. GNI is a concept of income rather than of Value added: what each producer contributes. It includes the wages of cross-border and seasonal workers abroad, but not the remittances they send home, which is why France's GNI exceeds its GDP. The 1993 revision of the System of National Accounts renamed GNP as GNI. The United States used GNP as its main measure until 1991, when it switched to GDP. Subtracting depreciation gives Net national income: allowing for wear and tear. The gap between the two measures can matter a great deal. Ireland's GDP became so distorted by multinational profit shifting that in 2017 its central bank adopted a modified GNI measure.

  <!-- nature-econ-530 -->

- **Net national income: allowing for wear and tear**

  Machines, buildings and roads wear out, and gross national income ignores that loss. Net national income subtracts it: it is gross national income minus depreciation. It covers the income of households, businesses and government. Put another way, it equals GDP plus net wages, salaries and property income from abroad, minus wear and tear of buildings, machinery, equipment and infrastructure. By the expenditure method, it is consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, plus net foreign factor income, minus indirect taxes and depreciation of manufactured capital.

  <!-- nature-econ-571 -->

- **Haig–Simons income: consumption plus change in net worth**

  A widely used economic definition of income dates from 1938. Haig–Simons income is consumption plus the change in a person's net worth: what is consumed plus the change in the value of property held. Tax law usually counts less. Taxable income is typically lower, because unrealized gains, such as a rise in share prices, are economic income but not taxable income. A broader idea, full income, adds non-monetary consumption ability to money income. It cannot be observed, so economists must rely on money income.

  <!-- nature-econ-492 -->

- **The unpaid work the national accounts ignore**

  An Australian study put the value of unpaid work, such as household work, at about 50% of GDP. None of it appears in the national accounts or in GDP, which may distort the picture they give. Unpaid housework falls outside the SNA production boundary, the line that decides what counts as production. Feminist economists such as Marilyn Waring and Nancy Folbre call this biased, noting that GDP still imputes a rent for owner-occupied homes. They say it hides how much market production depends on non-market labour. Statisticians question whether valuing such work is feasible.

  <!-- nature-econ-568 -->

- **The marginal propensity to save**

  Of each extra unit of income, a household spends some and saves the rest. The share saved is the marginal propensity to save. The share of total income saved, by contrast, is the average propensity to save. The general level of interest rates directly affects the saving rate.

  <!-- nature-econ-589 -->

- **The multiplier: how spending ripples through an economy**

  A government pays for a bridge. The bridge adds its own value to output, and the workers who built it can then spend and invest more. This is the multiplier effect: a change in spending is magnified as it passes through the economy, moving total output by more than the original change. Such spending can help close an output gap, the shortfall of output below its potential. Keynes showed that the logic also runs in reverse. A small fall in consumption or investment can be magnified into declines across the economy.

  <!-- nature-econ-546 -->

- **Does fiscal stimulus work?**

  When a government spends more or cuts taxes in a slump, what actually happens? Keynesians argue that expansionary fiscal policy in recessions builds the base for growth and full employment, with the deficits repaid by the later expansion. The models give a more mixed picture. In The IS–LM model: two markets in balance, fiscal expansion raises the price level and real interest rates in the long run. The AD–AS model lets the price level vary, which makes it better for long-run analysis. Economists still debate how effective fiscal stimulus is.

  <!-- nature-econ-525 -->

- **Do interest rates keep saving and investment equal?**

  Classical economists believed saving and investment would always match. If saving rose, interest rates would fall, and cheaper funds would stimulate investment. Keynes disagreed. He argued that both are insensitive to interest rates, so saving could exceed investment for long periods, causing a general glut and recession. Savings withheld from investment cut total spending, incomes and jobs, which in turn reduces savings again. The two camps remain divided on whether interest rates keep saving and investment equal.

  <!-- nature-econ-588 -->

- **The IS–LM model: two markets in balance**

  John Hicks invented the IS–LM model in 1936. It finds the interest rates and output levels at which two markets are in balance at once. In the goods market, investment must balance saving, which gives the IS part of the name. In the money market, money supply must balance money demand, which gives the LM part. The model underpins the idea of aggregate demand, by asking how much is demanded at a given price level.

  <!-- nature-econ-558 -->

- **Gross or net, domestic or national: decoding the names**

  A French-owned cotton factory in Senegal counts in Senegal's domestic figures but in France's national figures. That example captures half of a naming scheme. 'Domestic' counts everything produced inside a country's borders, while 'national' counts everything produced by its nationals anywhere. The other half is gross versus net. 'Gross' means the total product, while 'net' subtracts the amount needed to offset depreciation of fixed capital. So net domestic product is GDP minus depreciation of capital. Each measure can also be framed as product, income or expenditure.

  <!-- nature-econ-497 -->

- **Is national income a good measure of welfare?**

  Cleaning up an oil spill adds to GDP, while the lost well-being from fouled beaches goes unmeasured. A paid nanny's income counts in GDP, but a parent's unpaid childcare does not. Such cases raise the question of how well GDP per person reflects people's welfare. It is not useless: countries with higher GDP may also score higher on other welfare measures, such as life expectancy. Still, alternatives exist, including Human Development Index, indexes of sustainable economic welfare and genuine progress, and a sustainable version of national income.

  <!-- nature-econ-498 -->

- **Two centuries of global income inequality**

  From 1820 to 2002, the global income Gini rose steadily, with a sharp increase between 1980 and 2002. That measure tracks income inequality among all the world's people, not just within single countries. The trend appears to have peaked and started to reverse, as emerging economies such as the BRIC countries grew rapidly.

  <!-- nature-econ-529 -->

- **Where the Gini coefficient falls short**

  The Gini coefficient is a relative measure, so it can rise even while the number of people in absolute poverty falls. That is one of several weaknesses. It is not additive, and different income distributions can share the same value. A population can have a very low income Gini and a very high wealth Gini at once. Small populations with less varied economies also tend to report lower values.

  <!-- nature-econ-528 -->

- **Weighting the CPI: why housing counts most**

  In one example of a consumer price index, housing carries 41.4% of the weight, food and beverages 17.4% and transport 17.0%. Each weight reflects that item's share of consumer spending, so a price change in housing moves the index more than the same change in a smaller category. Ideally the weights would reflect current spending, but in practice they use the most recent past data. Updating the weights only now and then saves money, but it delays new kinds of spending, such as Internet subscriptions, from entering the index.

  <!-- nature-econ-507 -->

- **Adjusted net national income: subtracting nature's losses**

  Net national income allows for machines wearing out, but not for minerals dug up and gone. Adjusted net national income makes that further correction, subtracting the running down of resources taken from nature. Economists divide capital into categories, among them manufactured capital and two kinds of natural capital. The non-critical kind includes minerals, and that is what gets deducted. The critical kind, such as air and water, is not accounted for; Critical natural capital returns to it. The European Environment Agency has proposed using the consumption of ecosystem capital to create an adjusted net national income.

  <!-- nature-econ-572 -->

- **From two sectors to five: building up the circular flow**

  The simplest circular flow has just two sectors: households and firms, with households spending all their income on firms' output. Each added sector brings the model closer to a real economy. The three-sector model adds government. The four-sector model adds foreign trade and capital flows. The five-sector model adds banks and other intermediaries, which borrow household savings and lend for firms' investment.

  <!-- nature-econ-503 -->

- **Leakages and injections: money leaving and entering the flow**

  Not all income flows straight back into spending. Saved money is a leakage: it is not spent, so not all output gets bought. Taxes are a leakage too, and imports a third. Injections add money back in: investment, government spending on services and welfare payments, and exports. In the five-sector model, the economy is in equilibrium when total leakages equal total injections. Savings plus taxes plus imports must equal investment plus government spending plus exports.

  <!-- nature-econ-504 -->

- **The capital consumption allowance: running to stand still**

  Part of every year's GDP buys no growth at all. It simply keeps the country's productive capacity from shrinking. This is the capital consumption allowance, the part of GDP due to depreciation. It covers wear and tear on physical capital, plus the investment needed to maintain human capital, such as educating workers to replace retirees. GDP equals net domestic product plus the capital consumption allowance.

  <!-- nature-econ-518 -->

- **Net national product: output after depreciation**

  Net national product is gross national product minus depreciation, the loss in value of fixed capital through wear and tear in production. Net domestic product is, likewise, GDP minus depreciation. Economics research usually uses the gross measures instead, a choice that has long been disputed. The net measures matter for the environment. Net national product serves as an indicator of sustainability in environmental economics and appears in models of resources running out. Research has also studied it as a dynamic welfare indicator.

  <!-- nature-econ-573 -->

- **Value added: what each producer contributes**

  A firm buys in materials and services, works on them, and sells the result. The difference between the market value of what it sells and the value of what it used is its value added. A firm's total value added equals its revenue minus Intermediate consumption: inputs used up in production, the inputs it uses up. It roughly equals pay to employees, a return to labour, plus earnings before taxes, a return to capital. In macroeconomics, value added is the contribution of capital and labour to a product's value, so national value added is shared between them. In national accounts, gross value added is gross output minus those used-up inputs, which equals net output. Net value added deducts depreciation from it. Add up gross value added across the whole economy at market prices and you get GDP.

  <!-- nature-econ-602 -->

- **Intermediate consumption: inputs used up in production**

  In the US economy, intermediate consumption is about 45% of gross output. It is the total value of goods and services that businesses use up as inputs while producing, such as raw materials, services and other running costs. Some inputs change form, like bulk sugar; others are used up completely, like electric power. It equals the gap between gross output, roughly total sales value, and net output, which is gross value added or GDP. Because it is subtracted from gross output to get GDP, how it is defined and estimated strongly affects the size of the GDP figure. Ordinary maintenance, repairs and research and development spending count as intermediate consumption. Depreciation of fixed assets and major renovations that extend an asset's life do not. Some odd results follow. Buying a service from another firm instead of doing it in-house raises a firm's intermediate consumption and lowers its own value added. And when businesses buy physical assets GDP rises, while renting or leasing them lowers GDP, because lease payments count as intermediate consumption.

  <!-- nature-econ-536 -->

- **Three ways to measure GDP**

  GDP can be measured three ways, and in theory all three give the same total. The production approach, the most direct, adds up the output of every class of enterprise. It is also called the value-added approach, because it counts how much value is contributed at each stage of production. The income approach sums the primary incomes paid out by producers; measured this way, the total is called Gross domestic income: GDP counted from the income side. The expenditure approach adds up final uses of goods and services, leaving out intermediate consumption. Within each country, a national statistical agency normally does the measuring.

  <!-- nature-econ-484 -->

- **Labour productivity: output per hour of work**

  A country's ability to raise its living standards over time is said to depend almost entirely on raising output per worker. Labour productivity measures exactly that: output volume, such as GDP or gross value added, divided by labour input, such as total hours worked or total employment. Output is usually measured as value added, the value of outputs minus intermediate inputs, to avoid double counting. Total hours worked is generally preferred to a headcount, which can hide changes in average hours. Labour productivity is a key indicator of growth, competitiveness and living standards. Yet productivity and wages do not always move together. They can decouple.

  <!-- nature-econ-581 -->

- **Gross domestic income: GDP counted from the income side**

  Everything produced and sold generates an equal amount of income, so GDP can also be counted from the income side. Gross domestic income does exactly that, adding up the primary incomes paid out by producers in a country. It should give the same total as the expenditure method.

  <!-- nature-econ-490 -->

- **The linked accounts that make up a nation's books**

  A nation's accounts are not one ledger but a linked set: production, income, expenditure, capital and financial accounts, plus balance sheets. Each account has a balancing item. These include value added, which equals GDP for the whole economy, along with disposable income, saving, net lending or borrowing, and net worth. Balance sheets record the stock of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities at a point in time. Accounts can be shown gross or net of consumption of fixed capital, the national-accounts version of depreciation.

  <!-- nature-econ-567 -->

- **Avoiding double counting: the meat that is counted once**

  Meat is worth $10 at the farm, $30 at the butcher and $60 at the supermarket. Adding the three sales gives $100, but only $60 enters national output. The rule is to count only the final value of a good, or the value added at each stage, not every sale along the chain. Here the values added are $10, $20 and $30, which sum to the same final value. In general, GDP at market price equals the value of output minus intermediate consumption.

  <!-- nature-econ-496 -->

- **Value-added tax: taxing each stage of production**

  A value-added tax is a tax on sales that is charged at each stage of production, but only on the value that stage adds. It is assessed step by step on a product or service, so each stage is taxed on its own unit value added.

  <!-- nature-econ-603 -->

- **Imputed rent: the rent homeowners pay themselves**

  Homeowners who live in their own houses pay no rent, yet national accounts record one for them. The imputed rent of owner-occupied housing is the market rent owner-occupiers would receive if they rented their homes out. National accounts add it to value added, and so to GDP. The idea is that a dwelling provides its owner with a service, whether or not anyone pays for it. Critics call this addition largely fictitious, since nearly all owner-occupiers do not actually rent out their homes.

  <!-- nature-econ-537 -->

- **Owner-occupied housing: the CPI's long-running puzzle**

  What does it cost to live in a home you own? Statisticians and economists have long disagreed over how a consumer price index should count it. Many economists argue the index should include the opportunity cost of living in one's own home. A spending approach would count repairs, maintenance and also mortgage interest. A transaction-price approach would count only purchases of new dwellings, treating them like other durable goods. No single method has won agreement.

  <!-- nature-econ-508 -->

### Behavior and decisions

Economic models long pictured people as an 'economic man', always rational and narrowly self-interested, pursuing their goals in the best possible way. This chapter tests that picture against how people really decide. Their rationality is limited, so they lean on mental shortcuts, settle for an option that is good enough, and often grab a smaller reward now over a larger one later. Controlled experiments, from games of betrayal to a shared pot of tokens, show when people cooperate and when individual interest pulls against the group. Shared standards of behavior steer choices too, and that matters for every problem in which everyone would gain from acting together.

- **Game theory: treating choices as moves in a game**

  Game theory began with a single book: von Neumann and Morgenstern's Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, published in 1944. It is the branch of applied mathematics that treats interactions between several decision-makers as strategic games. A game spells out the choices open to each player and the payoffs that result. Players are usually assumed rational in the sense of the Rational choice: people as careful calculators. They have consistent preferences, unlimited capacity to calculate, and each tries to maximize their payoff. Games come in two families. In a cooperative game, players can make binding promises that someone outside enforces. In a non-cooperative game, any agreement has to enforce itself. A central idea is the Nash equilibrium: where no one gains by moving alone, a situation where each player's choice is the best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone. John Nash, John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten shared the 1994 Nobel prize in economics for pioneering the field. Game theory now describes, predicts and evaluates choices far beyond markets. It is a major method for modelling competing agents in economics. It is also used in biology, political science and the study of how people decide whether to be vaccinated.

  <!-- nature-econ-034 -->

- **Homo economicus, the perfectly rational 'economic man'**

  Adam Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the kindness of the butcher or the baker, but from their regard to their own interest. Economic models turned that remark into a character: homo economicus, or 'economic man'. This imagined person is always rational and narrowly self-interested. As a consumer he maximizes his satisfaction, or Utility: the economist's yardstick for satisfaction. As a producer he maximizes profit. And he can think through every possible outcome to pick the best. The name came from his critics, who used it in the late nineteenth century to attack John Stuart Mill's political economy. 'Rational' here has a narrow meaning. It only means reaching one's own goals at least cost, and says nothing about whether those goals are wise in an ethical or social sense. Nor must the goals be selfish: a person's utility can include the wellbeing of family members, which fits models that stress cooperation. Two later ideas push against the picture: Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics, which studies biases, and Bounded rationality: why people settle for good enough, which stresses limits of mind and time. Advanced theory now often uses modified agents, with limited rationality or even envy, to depict real decisions more realistically.

  <!-- nature-econ-059 -->

- **Bounded rationality: why people settle for good enough**

  Herbert A. Simon compared rationality to a pair of scissors. One blade is the limits of the human mind; the other is the structure of the environment the mind faces. Simon coined the term bounded rationality as an alternative to modelling people as perfectly rational, like Homo economicus, the perfectly rational 'economic man'. Three limits bind every decision: how hard the problem is, what the mind can work out, and how much time there is. So people skip the full weighing of costs and benefits. They take an option that meets their standard of adequacy, a habit explored in Satisficing: stopping at good enough, and they lean on rules of thumb instead of strict optimization. Gerd Gigerenzer later showed that simple rules often beat theoretically optimal procedures. Kahneman and Tversky extended Simon's ideas into a map of these limits. The idea is still debated across economics, psychology, law, philosophy and cognitive science.

  <!-- nature-econ-022 -->

- **Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics**

  In the early 1900s economists pushed psychology out of their discipline. From then on, models treated people as purely rational, self-interested decision makers, the Homo economicus, the perfectly rational 'economic man' of the textbooks. Behavioral economics brings the psychology back. It studies how psychological factors shape the decisions of people and institutions, and how those decisions differ from what traditional theory predicts. Its main concern is the limits on how rational economic choices really are. It looks for the places where the standard assumptions of rational, selfish people break down, cataloguing biases, tendencies and mental shortcuts. That work has a practical edge: it helps judge whether people choose well and whether they could be helped to choose better. Its models combine psychology, neuroscience and microeconomic theory. Some of its ideas are old. The notion that losses weigh more than gains appears as early as Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments. Yet the field only became distinct in the 1970s and 1980s, and it spread widely after the work of Kahneman and Tversky, through the 1990s and 2000s. Nobel prizes mark its rise: Herbert Simon in 1978, Daniel Kahneman and Vernon Smith in 2002, and Richard Thaler in 2017.

  <!-- nature-econ-021 -->

- **The prisoner's dilemma: when betrayal is rational**

  In 1950 Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, working at the RAND Corporation, designed a puzzle that still troubles economists. Two players can each cooperate for mutual benefit or betray the other for individual gain. Betrayal is the rational choice for each, yet both would get a higher payoff if both cooperated. This is the prisoner's dilemma, the basic game behind research on social dilemmas, where individual interest pulls against the group's. Climate change: a warming world and why it matters fits the pattern closely. Every country gains from a stable climate, but each hesitates to cut its own CO2 emissions. Real climate politics is worse than the textbook game, because its payoffs are uncertain, which suggests states will cooperate even less. Hardin's tragedy of the commons can be read as a many-player version, in which widespread betrayal destroys a shared resource. The game has been called the E. coli of social psychology, a standard test case for studying oligopoly and collective action.

  <!-- nature-econ-039 -->

- **Experimental economics takes theory into the laboratory**

  How do you test an economic theory? One answer is to run it as an experiment, with real people and real money. Experimental economics uses controlled experiments to study economic questions, and analyses the results with statistical and computational tools. The data are used to estimate the size of effects, to test theories and to shed light on how markets work. Subjects are usually paid in cash, so the incentives in the lab mimic those of the real world. Vernon L. Smith shared the 2002 Nobel prize for establishing laboratory experiments as a tool of economic analysis. The field sits close to Behavioral economics brings psychology back into economics. Leading researchers in the two tend to share techniques, though some see a schism between them.

  <!-- nature-econ-027 -->

- **Social norms: the unwritten rules a group shares**

  Many of the rules people live by were never designed by anyone. They evolved through repeated interactions between individuals. A social norm is a standard of acceptable behavior shared by a group. Some norms stay informal understandings; others are written into rules and laws, and institutions are built from many of them. Norms differ from private ideas, attitudes or values because they are shared beliefs about behavior, and they depend on context, group and history. Breaking an informal norm brings reprimands, warnings or exclusion rather than legal penalties, and the rule-breaker is labelled a deviant. A norm's life cycle runs from emergence, pushed by norm entrepreneurs, through a cascade of broad acceptance to internalization, when it is simply taken for granted. Norms also curb free riding on voluntarily provided public goods, an effect economic models often underestimate.

  <!-- nature-econ-073 -->

- **Collective action problems: when acting alone defeats everyone**

  In 1738 David Hume described a puzzle through neighbours agreeing to drain a meadow. Economists now call it a collective action problem, or social dilemma. Everyone would be better off cooperating, but people fail to, because their individual interests pull against joint action. Trouble comes when too many members chase immediate, personal gain instead of the group's long-term interest. The pattern explains things as different as the running down of resources and low voter turnout. It also describes the environmental crises at the center of this course: Climate change: a warming world and why it matters, Biodiversity loss: a decline far faster than nature's pace and the build-up of waste. Without regulation, people and firms tend to pick the easier, cheaper option rather than the one that cuts emissions or saves resources that cannot be replaced. In a 1965 book, Mancur Olson argued that rational individuals do not automatically add up to a rational group, a claim explored in Logic of collective action. For a pure Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few, he argued, each contributor tends to give less as others give more. The problem is analysed with Game theory: treating choices as moves in a game and through the The free-rider problem: benefiting without paying, which arises whenever public goods must be paid for.

  <!-- nature-econ-030 -->

- **Heuristics: the mind's shortcuts**

  Humans, animals, organizations and even machines share a trick: simple strategies that form judgments and solve complex problems fast. These mental shortcuts are called heuristics. When information is incomplete and a need is pressing, a heuristic gives an answer that is good enough. It is not always right, and it can differ from what logic and probability would say. Herbert A. Simon introduced the idea in the 1950s, and his rule of settling for the first adequate option was one of the first models of a heuristic. In the 1970s Tversky and Kahneman tied heuristics to cognitive bias. They first proposed three: availability, representativeness, and anchoring and adjustment. Theories still differ on whether heuristics are irrational. One view sees unavoidable shortcuts for a limited brain; another sees fast methods that do as well as complex ones on less information. In a computer test of ten simple decision rules, most picked the option with the highest expected value and almost never the lowest.

  <!-- nature-econ-054 -->

- **Satisficing: stopping at good enough**

  Of 628 used-car dealers studied, 97% priced their cars with a simple rule of thumb. Typically, if a car was unsold after 24 days, they cut its price by about 3%. This is satisficing, a word Herbert A. Simon coined in 1956 by blending 'satisfy' and 'suffice'. The idea first appeared in his 1947 book Administrative Behavior. A satisficer looks through options until one is good enough, rather than hunting for the very best. Simon meant it for problems where the best answer cannot be found, because the calculation is too hard or information is lacking. The method has three steps: set an aspiration level, take the first option that meets it, and lower the level if nothing meets it in time. The behavioral theory of the firm treats profit the same way, as a level to reach, after which firms pursue other goals. Oddly, maximizers search more options than satisficers, yet tend to be less happy and more regretful about their choices.

  <!-- nature-econ-071 -->

- **The public goods game: tokens in a shared pot**

  In the public goods game, each player secretly decides how many tokens to put into a shared pot. The pot is then multiplied and split among everyone. A player's payoff is what they kept plus their share of the pot, so the game measures altruism, cooperation and free riding. It tests a theory about a Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few, such as street lighting that no one can be kept from using. The theory says such goods are under-provided, because no one has a private motive to pay. If everyone were purely selfish, the stable outcome would be that nobody gives. Real players do give. In repeated rounds contributions usually slide as generous players see others hold back, but a stubborn group of givers keeps them above zero. Players will also punish non-contributors at a cost to themselves, and in most experiments this raises cooperation. Details matter. With 40 players, a multiplier of 1.03 makes almost everyone stop giving, while 1.3 keeps average contributions near 50%. Unequal starting endowments lower contributions, and presenting the game as a climate negotiation can change behavior.

  <!-- nature-econ-070 -->

- **Present bias: why now beats later**

  Present bias is the pull of a smaller reward now over a larger reward later. It means overvaluing what is immediate and giving too little weight to long-term consequences. Early models assumed people discount the future at a steady rate, a fixed form of Time preference: why sooner beats later. Research showed instead that people discount sharply over short delays and less over longer ones. Their preferences are time-inconsistent: what they plan for later is not what they choose when later arrives. Phelps and Pollak captured this in 1968 with the quasi-hyperbolic discounting model. The consequences are familiar. Present bias feeds procrastination, especially when acting brings immediate costs. It discourages dieting, quitting smoking and regular check-ups, whose benefits come only later. It is linked to strong urges to spend and to failed saving plans, and short-termism in general has been tied to it.

  <!-- nature-econ-065 -->

- **Anchoring: how an arbitrary number pulls a guess**

  People asked to estimate 1 x 2 x ... x 8 quickly gave a median answer of 512. People shown 8 x 7 x ... x 1 gave 2,250. The first numbers they saw set an anchor, a reference point that pulls judgment toward it even when it is irrelevant. Tversky and Kahneman described this anchoring effect in 1974 as one of the heuristics people use when estimating under uncertainty. The usual explanation is that people adjust away from the anchor too little. Scholars agree the effect is easy to demonstrate, but they still disagree about what causes it. It is also hard to escape. Even obviously wrong anchors about Gandhi's age at death shifted guesses, to averages of 50 versus 67. Anchoring appears in legal sentencing, shopping, salary negotiations and forecasting, and experts fall for it too. In a negotiation, the first price offer sets the anchor for everything that follows.

  <!-- nature-econ-041 -->

- **Choice architecture: designing how options are presented**

  Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term choice architecture in a 2008 book. It means the design of the ways choices are presented, and the effect that presentation has on what people decide. Its tools include defaults, planning for error, information about results, structuring complex choices and incentives. It can also translate metrics into what people care about, for instance turning energy use into the emissions it causes. Advocates use it to steer people toward saving for retirement, healthier food or organ donation, making up for the biases that come with Bounded rationality: why people settle for good enough. The idea led to the UK's Behavioural Insights Team and a similar unit at the White House. It is contested. Critics say it can limit choice, undermine autonomy, or lift firm profits at consumers' expense through 'dark patterns'. Advocates reply that no presentation is neutral. Responses also differ by person: liberals and conservatives react differently to information about the environmental effects of energy use.

  <!-- nature-econ-045 -->

- **Nudges: steering choices without forbidding any**

  A calorie count on a menu forbids nothing. It simply supplies missing information for healthier choices. That is a nudge: a change in how choices are presented, designed to steer decisions without restricting anyone's freedom to choose. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularised the idea in their 2008 book Nudge, building on Choice architecture: designing how options are presented. Nudges work with the limits of bounded rationality rather than against them. They can simplify complex decisions by presenting information clearly, cutting the mental effort required. Making organ donation the default, with an opt-out, has helped raise actual donation rates alongside other policies. Nudges have critics, who call them manipulative, a threat to autonomy or scientifically weak. Sunstein has defended them at length. The evidence on staying power is sobering: a 2024 review reported that fewer than half of nudging experiments keep a long-term effect when re-tested.

  <!-- nature-econ-024 -->

- **Field experiments: testing ideas in the real world**

  A field experiment takes the method of the laboratory out into a real-world setting. Researchers randomly assign people to a treatment group or a control group. Any later difference then reflects the treatment rather than differences that were already there. Unlike a Natural experiments: when the world assigns the treatment, a field experiment lets the researchers themselves control the randomization and how the treatment is delivered. The gain is realism. Field experiments have higher external validity, meaning their results carry over better to everyday life, and they can test people who do not know they are being studied. Economists use them to study discrimination, health programmes, charitable fundraising, education and microfinance. Behavioural economists turned to them partly in response to criticism of lab experiments. They have weaknesses too. Spillovers to untreated groups, people who do not comply and people who drop out can all bias results. Such studies can also be costly, hard to replicate and ethically fraught.

  <!-- nature-econ-052 -->

- **Motivation crowding: when paying people backfires**

  In Edward Deci's classic study, some people were paid for each puzzle they solved and others just for showing up. Later, in their free time, the per-puzzle group did fewer unpaid puzzles and reported less interest. This is motivation crowding: an outside reward, such as payment, can weaken the inner motivation to do a task. Against the predictions of standard economics, the drop in motivation can lower total performance. Richard Titmuss argued in 1970 that paying for some behaviors could reduce them, and Bruno Frey coined the term 'crowding out' in 1997. People paid a token amount to collect money for charity collected less than unpaid volunteers. Crowding out has turned up in teachers' performance pay, commission pay, charitable giving and student performance. It is stronger when the reward is publicly known, since people who care about looking altruistic avoid looking paid. The evidence is mixed. A 2020 review of over 100 tests found that paying for enjoyable tasks boosts performance. But removing an expected payment can leave people worse off than if they had never been paid.

  <!-- nature-econ-064 -->

- **The energy efficiency gap: savings left untaken**

  Society passes up investments that could cut energy use substantially and at low cost. The energy efficiency gap measures that shortfall: the difference between the cost-minimising level of energy efficiency and the level people and firms actually achieve. Eric Hirst and Marilyn Brown coined the term in a 1990 paper. They split its causes into two kinds.
