Carbon dioxide leaves the air mainly through photosynthesis, entering life on land and in the ocean. In 2024 the global average level of carbon dioxide in the air reached a record 422.7 parts per million. The steps of this cycle are key to making Earth able to support life. Antoine Lavoisier and Joseph Priestley first described it, and Humphry Davy popularised it.

  <!-- nature-eco-164 -->

- **The water cycle: one supply, endlessly moving**

  Earth's total mass of water stays fairly constant. What changes with the climate is how that water is split between ice, fresh water, salt water and air. The water cycle, or hydrologic cycle, is the continuous movement of water on, above and below the Earth's surface, as it changes between liquid, ice and vapour. Energy from the sun powers it. Water rises by evaporation and by transpiration from plants. It condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation, rain or snow. Some ice turns straight to vapour, which is called sublimation. On the ground, water soaks in, flows across the surface or moves underground. The ocean is the source of 86% of global evaporation. Most rain falls back into the ocean or onto land, where much of it flows over the ground as Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in. That moving water does heavy work. It carries almost all eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to rivers, lakes and seas, and together with groundwater it carries nitrogen too. The cycle is essential to life and plays a large role in the global climate and ocean circulation.

  <!-- nature-eco-196 -->

- **The nitrogen cycle: plenty in the air, scarce in the soil**

  Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere, yet many ecosystems are starved of it. The gas is hard for living things to use, so usable nitrogen is scarce. The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea. Its main steps are Nitrogen fixation: pulling plant food from the air, Ammonification: freeing nitrogen from the dead, Nitrification: turning ammonia into plant food and Denitrification: returning nitrogen to the air. Microbes carry out many of these steps, either harvesting energy or gathering nitrogen to grow. Plants take up two usable forms, nitrate and ammonium, from the soil through their root hairs. Because usable nitrogen is so scarce, its supply can set the pace of key ecosystem processes such as primary production and decomposition. People have changed this balance sharply. Growing legumes, making fertilizer with the The Haber process: fertilizer pulled from the air and burning fuels have more than doubled the yearly conversion of nitrogen into forms life can use.

  <!-- nature-eco-176 -->

- **Evapotranspiration: how land breathes water back to the sky**

  Most of the rain and snow that lands on the continents never reaches a river. Globally, between three-fifths and three-quarters of it returns to the air through evapotranspiration. That is the combined movement of water into the air from open water, ice, bare soil and plants. The word joins two processes. Evaporation moves water straight into the air from soil and water bodies. Transpiration moves water from a plant's roots, up through the plant and out of its stomata, the tiny pores in its leaves, as vapour. Evapotranspiration is measured in millimetres of water over a set time. Three things mainly set its level. One is how much water is available. Another is how much energy is in the air and soil. The third is how much moisture the air can take up. Global warming has increased evapotranspiration over land, one of the ways a changing climate is altering the water cycle. The numbers matter in practice, because measuring evapotranspiration is key to managing water supplies and planning irrigation.

  <!-- nature-eco-226 -->

- **Soil carbon: a store three times the size of the atmosphere's**

  Soils store about 2,700 Gt of carbon, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere and 240 times a year's fossil fuel emissions. This soil carbon is the solid carbon held in soils, both as organic matter from living things and as carbonate minerals. It does daily work. It helps soil hold water, retain nutrients and build its crumbly structure. Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition are the main processes that set how much carbon land stores. Because soil can take up carbon from the air, it matters for slowing global warming and for the computer models scientists use to project the climate. Human activities have caused a massive loss of organic carbon from soils, but people could also deliberately return carbon to them. Warming adds a risk of its own. It could change the activity of the soil microbes that break carbon down, possibly adding to the warming.

  <!-- nature-eco-259 -->

- **Infiltration: how rain soaks into the ground**

  Whether a storm waters a field or floods a street depends largely on one thing: how fast the ground can drink. Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface down into the soil. The fastest rate at which water can soak in is called the infiltration capacity, usually measured in meters per day. When rain falls faster than that, the extra water usually runs off over the surface. Texture matters. Soils with small pores, such as clay, take in water more slowly than soils with large pores, such as sand. Compaction squeezes the soil and lowers infiltration further. Wet soil soaks up water more slowly, and fully saturated soil cannot take in any more. Living things help. Plant roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed water downward, while bare ground can have very low rates, which leads to runoff and erosion. Steeper slopes shed water more readily. Pavement and other impermeable surfaces stop infiltration entirely and send more water across the ground.

  <!-- nature-eco-237 -->

- **Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in**

  A roof or a parking lot lets no rain soak in at all. Every drop that lands becomes surface runoff, or overland flow. This is water flowing freely over the ground when rain, snowmelt or other water cannot soak into the soil fast enough. On natural ground, runoff starts when the soil is already saturated or when rain arrives faster than infiltration can take it in. Runoff is a major part of the water cycle. It is also the main way water wears soil away, the process covered in Soil erosion: losing the ground under the crops. Its main environmental harm is what it carries. Running water picks up petroleum, herbicides and fertilizers and delivers them into surface water, groundwater and soil. More runoff also means less water seeping down to refill groundwater, so water tables drop and droughts hit harder for people who rely on wells. When a stream cannot carry all the runoff flowing downstream, it floods. The remedies follow from the causes. Limit paved surfaces, control erosion on farms and building sites, build the green networks described in Green infrastructure, and control how chemicals are used.

  <!-- nature-eco-275 -->

- **Soil erosion: losing the ground under the crops**

  About 75 billion tons of soil erode from the land each year, some 13–40 times the natural rate. Soil erosion is the wearing away of the top layer of soil by water, ice, snow, wind, plants and animals, including people. It can be slow and unnoticed, or so fast that it causes a serious loss of topsoil. Farming is the main accelerator. Unsustainable farming raises erosion by one to two orders of magnitude, each a factor of ten, above the natural rate. That is far faster than new soil forms. On farms, erosion shrinks cropland and its production potential, lowers water quality and damages drainage networks. Erosion by water and wind together causes 84% of degraded land, and about 40% of the world's agricultural land is seriously degraded. Some soils resist better than others. Clay-rich and organic-rich soils hold together, and plant cover and roots protect soil from both water and wind. Longer, steeper slopes erode much faster in heavy rain, especially without plants. The outlook is not reassuring: the more intense rainfall expected as the climate warms will raise erosion unless measures are taken.

  <!-- nature-eco-264 -->

- **Cellular respiration: the slow burn inside every cell**

  Cellular respiration is technically a kind of burning, but one that releases energy slowly and under control. It is the process by which cells break down food molecules, usually with oxygen, to make ATP, the energy carrier cells use. With oxygen it is called aerobic respiration. When cells pass their electrons to some other substance instead, it is anaerobic. Aerobic respiration consumes glucose, a simple sugar, and oxygen, and it produces carbon dioxide, water and energy. In effect it releases the energy that photosynthesis stored in sugar. The oxygen route pays well: aerobic metabolism is up to 15 times more efficient than anaerobic metabolism. Current estimates put the yield at around 29 to 30 ATP per glucose molecule, below the textbook figure of 38. Plants respire too. Although they take in carbon dioxide overall, plant respiration produces about half of the carbon dioxide released each year by land ecosystems. The energy left after plants' own respiration is what ecologists call net primary production.

  <!-- nature-eco-212 -->

- **The Haber process: fertilizer pulled from the air**

  In 1909 Fritz Haber showed in his laboratory that nitrogen from the air could be turned into ammonia. Carl Bosch then scaled the method up for the company BASF. The Haber process, or Haber–Bosch process, remains the main industrial method of making ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen. It combines the two gases over an iron catalyst, a material that speeds the reaction. In effect it is nitrogen fixation done in a factory. Most of the ammonia goes into nitrogen fertilizer. The timing mattered. Demand for fertilizer was rising, and the mined niter and guano, or bird droppings, then in use were thought too scarce for future needs. The process still leans on fossil fuel. Its hydrogen usually comes from natural gas by steam reforming, which made 72% of global ammonia as of 2012. Ammonia production uses 1–2% of global energy, causes 3% of global carbon emissions and uses 3% to 5% of natural gas. As of 2018 it produced 230 million tonnes of ammonia a year.

  <!-- nature-eco-230 -->

- **The phosphorus cycle: the slow loop that skips the sky**

  Most of the great element cycles pass through the air. Phosphorus almost never does, because it rarely becomes a gas. The phosphorus cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves phosphorus through rocks, water and living things. Life cannot do without it. Phosphorus is part of DNA, RNA and ATP, and in animals it also strengthens bones and teeth. The cycle has four main steps. Rock that contains phosphorus is lifted up, then weathers and erodes. Rivers carry the phosphorus to lakes and the ocean, where it is finally buried in sediments. Phosphates, the compounds in which phosphorus usually travels, move quickly through plants and animals but very slowly through soil and ocean. That makes this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles. On land, the slow release of phosphorus from weathering rock limits how much ecosystems can get. In water, phosphorus can limit the growth of aquatic life, so phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can pollute lakes and streams. Freshwater algal blooms, sudden mass growths of algae, are generally caused by excess phosphorus. Saltwater blooms tend to come from excess nitrogen.

  <!-- nature-eco-185 -->

- **Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing**

  Nitrogen and phosphorus feed crops, but in a lake or a bay they become pollutants. Nutrient pollution is water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually these two, entering water. It is a main cause of Eutrophication: when a lake is fed too well in lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where the extra nutrients feed algal growth. Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, raw sewage and emissions from burning fuels. Fertilizer that crops do not use is lost from fields and harms air and downstream water. In Europe, agriculture is usually the main source of nitrogen in water, while households and industry often dominate phosphorus. Excess nitrogen brings toxic algal blooms, oxygen-starved water, acidic rain, nitrogen-saturated forests and global warming. The costs are real: dearer water treatment, losses to commercial fishing, fishing for sport and shellfish, and less tourism income. Excess nitrate in drinking water can cause blue baby syndrome. Remedies include vegetated buffer strips, artificial wetlands, better wastewater treatment and permits that make the polluter pay.

  <!-- nature-eco-245 -->

- **Eutrophication: when a lake is fed too well**

  The word comes from the Greek eutrophos, meaning well-nourished, and that is exactly the trouble. Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, causing extra growth of algae and plants that can use up the water's oxygen. It is caused by too much of a nutrient, most often phosphates and nitrates. It can happen naturally, or it can be caused by sewage, industrial wastewater, runoff carrying fertilizer and other human sources. Most of these nutrients arrive as the Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing described earlier. The sequence is grimly simple. Extra nutrients feed a boom in phytoplankton. The resulting algal blooms and bacterial growth deplete the oxygen dissolved in the water, causing serious environmental damage. Fish die in larger numbers, and desirable species disappear. The problem is everywhere. Surveys found that 54% of lakes in Asia are eutrophic, along with 53% in Europe, 48% in North America, 41% in South America and 28% in Africa. Along the world's coasts, the World Resources Institute has identified 375 zones where the water runs dangerously short of oxygen.

  <!-- nature-eco-216 -->

- **Hypoxia: when water runs short of oxygen**

  Most fish cannot live once water falls below 30% of the oxygen it could hold. Environmental hypoxia means low-oxygen conditions like this, usually in natural waters or in the thin air at altitude. Water with 1 to 30% of its possible oxygen saturation is called hypoxic, and water with none at all is anoxic. A healthy water body should seldom fall below 80%. The usual cause is nutrient pollution. Algal blooms die and sink, and the bacteria decomposing them use up the oxygen as they respire. Hypoxia can also happen without pollution. In estuaries, lighter river water can layer over seawater and block oxygen from reaching the bottom. Low oxygen is not bad for everything. It harms air-breathing organisms but is essential for many anaerobic ones, which live without oxygen.

  <!-- nature-eco-235 -->

- **Dead zones: stretches of sea where life suffocates**

  In 2017 the summer dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico covered over 22,000 square kilometres. Fertilizer washing off the land of the Mississippi basin had stripped its water of oxygen. Dead zones are low-oxygen areas in the world's oceans and large lakes where most aquatic life cannot survive. Hypoxia sets in when dissolved oxygen falls to 2 mg per litre or less, and mass die-offs follow below 0.5 mg per litre. The usual driver is eutrophication: extra nitrogen and phosphorus fuel algal blooms whose decay uses up the oxygen. Marine dead zones were first noted in the 1970s in heavily used waters such as Chesapeake Bay, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea. A 2008 study counted 405 worldwide. Some are permanent, some last only hours or days, and many are seasonal, usually in summer and autumn. Warming makes them worse, because warmer water holds less oxygen, so dead zones are expanding. Recovery depends on how long and how severe the low oxygen was; after brief, mild events, life returns quickly.

  <!-- nature-eco-214 -->

- **Methane: a small gas with a big warming punch**

  Since about 1750, methane has made up just 3% of human heat-trapping gas emissions by mass, yet about 23% of their warming push on the climate. Atmospheric methane is the methane in Earth's air, a powerful heat-trapping gas whose rising level is driving the change described in Climate change: a warming world and why it matters. Its level has risen about 160% since 1750, almost entirely because of human activities. By 2025 the concentration had climbed from 722 parts per billion before industry to 1936 ppb, the highest in at least 800,000 years. Methane is potent but less persistent than carbon dioxide. Over 20 years it traps about 84 times as much heat as the same mass of carbon dioxide, but over 100 years only 28 times. It is the second largest contributor to human-caused warming. From 2010 to 2019, methane emissions caused 0.5 °C, about 30% of the warming seen. Wetlands are the largest natural source, providing roughly 20–30% of the methane in the air. Cutting methane by the end of the century could make a substantial difference to meeting the goals of the Paris climate agreement.

  <!-- nature-eco-201 -->

- **Cultural eutrophication: the human hand in green water**

  Cultural eutrophication is eutrophication caused by human activity. It became more visible in the mid-1900s, when the green revolution spread chemical fertilizers through farming. Phosphorus and nitrogen are its two main causes, letting algae grow fast and bloom densely. Laundry detergents were once a major phosphate source. They fed the problem until phosphate detergents were phased out in the 1970s, and since then sewage and agriculture have supplied most of the phosphate. Nitrogen comes mainly from farm runoff of fertilizer and animal waste, from sewage, and from nitrogen that settles out of the air. The label separates these cases from the slow enrichment that lakes undergo on their own, described in Natural eutrophication: lakes grow richer with age.

  <!-- nature-eco-217 -->

- **Carbon pools: where the planet keeps its carbon**

  Most of Earth's carbon is going nowhere. It sits inertly in the rocks of the lithosphere, the planet's rigid outer shell. Scientists usually split the global carbon cycle into major carbon pools, or reservoirs, linked by pathways of exchange. A pool is any part of the Earth system, such as the air, ocean or soil, where carbon is held in some form for a period of time. The pools include the ocean; sediments, including fossil fuels; living things on land and their soils; the atmosphere; and the rocks of the geosphere. The deep ocean is the largest pool of actively cycled carbon, holding 50 times more than the atmosphere. Yet it exchanges carbon with the surface only over hundreds of years. About a third of soil carbon is stored in inorganic forms such as calcium carbonate. Pool is the broader term: Carbon sinks: the places that soak up carbon is one particular kind of pool.

  <!-- nature-eco-165 -->

- **Carbon sinks: the places that soak up carbon**

  A forest or an ocean does something no machine yet does at large scale: it pulls carbon out of the sky faster than it lets carbon go. Such a store is a carbon sink, a carbon pool, natural or artificial, that takes up more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases. Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle. Globally, the two most important are vegetation and the ocean. Soils hold more carbon than all land plants and the atmosphere together, but heavy, industrial farming has severely depleted the carbon in many agricultural soils. For gases other than carbon dioxide, a sink need not store anything. It can break the gas down, as when nitrous oxide is reduced to harmless nitrogen gas. Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground. Still, no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the air on a large scale. Meanwhile, deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this change in land use is one cause of global warming. Public awareness of sinks grew after the 1997 treaty described in Kyoto Protocol promoted their use to offset emissions.

  <!-- nature-eco-169 -->

- **Helping forests, soils and seas store more carbon**

  Two of the most powerful tools for cutting emissions before 2030 are simple: restoring ecosystems and converting less land. Enhancing natural carbon sinks means managing forests, soils and other ecosystems so they remove more carbon dioxide from the air and store it durably. Preserving and strengthening sinks is an important way to slow global warming. It requires changes in farming and forestry, such as preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by replanting trees. The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based options AFOLU mitigation, short for agriculture, forestry and other land use. Ocean methods such as seaweed farming and fertilising the sea have been proposed, but none has yet been used at large scale.

  <!-- nature-eco-171 -->

- **Forests as carbon sinks, and why they may falter**

  Each year the world's forests take up about 25% of the carbon people emit. Through photosynthesis they draw carbon dioxide from the air and store it as wood, roots and leaves. That service is weakening. In 2019 forests absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of higher temperatures, droughts and deforestation. Forests can switch from sinks to sources of carbon, and the typical forest in the tropics may become a source by the 2060s. Storage is also conditional: carbon stays out of the air only if trees are not burned and do not rot when they die. New forests take several decades to match the carbon benefit of keeping mature forests standing. Clearing and later replanting also causes lasting losses of wildlife and damage to soil. So scientists call protecting natural forests the major climate solution. How much new tree cover could help is disputed. One estimate of 0.9 billion hectares of extra canopy has been criticised as too high, once the effect of trees on reflected sunlight is counted.

  <!-- nature-nbs-103 -->

- **Two speeds of carbon: years and millions of years**

  A carbon atom can pass through a plant and back into the air within years. Another can stay locked in rock for millions. Carbon moves in a fast cycle through living things and a slow cycle through rocks. The fast, biological cycle carries carbon from the air into living things and back again. The slow, geological cycle moves carbon through the crust between rocks, soil, ocean and air. It may even reach deep into the mantle, the hot layer beneath the crust. Each matters in its own way. How the fast cycle responds to human activity will decide many of the more immediate impacts of global warming. The slow cycle, for all its slowness, is one of the most important controls on how much carbon is in the air, and so on global temperatures.

  <!-- nature-eco-166 -->

- **How people knocked the carbon cycle off balance**

  As of 2020, people had extracted about 450 gigatons of fossil carbon from the ground, nearly as much as is held in all living things on land. Since the Industrial Revolution, human activity has greatly disturbed the carbon cycle by moving huge amounts of carbon out of the ground. Extracting and burning fossil fuels moves carbon straight from rock into the air. It is the largest human impact and one of the fastest growing. Cement adds more, because heating limestone to make clinker, cement's raw material, releases carbon dioxide. Clearing forests for farms or cities releases carbon from land ecosystems into the air. That clearing also cuts biodiversity, weakening ecosystems' resilience and their ability to pull carbon from the air. Small amounts of halocarbon gases caused about 10% of the direct warming effect of long-lived heat-trapping gases in 2019. For now, the rest of the Earth system cushions the blow. Carbon exchanges between the air and the land and sea act as negative feedbacks, changes that push back, dampening the climate effect of human emissions.

  <!-- nature-eco-168 -->

- **How cities, farms and clearing reshape the water cycle**

  Pave a meadow, and the rain that once soaked into it runs off instead. Changes in how land is used and what covers it, such as cities, farm expansion and deforestation, alter the water cycle locally and regionally. They affect rainfall, evaporation, flooding, groundwater and how much fresh water is available. Compacted soils and paved surfaces reduce how much water soaks in and increase surface runoff. Clearing forests reduces local soil moisture, evaporation, rain and snow, and across a region it can shift temperatures and rainfall patterns. Dams can change natural river flows, lower water quality and destroy habitat for aquatic species. The effect can run the other way too. Trees help regulate the water cycle, reduce soil erosion and prevent runoff, so planting new forests can improve water management.

  <!-- nature-eco-198 -->

- **A warmer world, a stronger water cycle**

  Since at least 1980, the water cycle has been running harder. Water cycle intensification is this strengthening of the cycle, caused by human-driven global warming. Human-caused warming has visibly changed the global water cycle since the mid-20th century. The reason is simple: a warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapour, and that changes both evaporation and rainfall. One result is that heavy rain events become even stronger. The effects spread widely. Intensification harms the availability of fresh water, and it affects the oceans, the ice sheets, the atmosphere and the moisture in soils. The IPCC's 2021 Sixth Assessment Report predicted that these changes will keep growing, both globally and region by region.

  <!-- nature-eco-199 -->

- **The ocean's carbon cycle: a source turned sink**

  Before the Industrial Revolution, the ocean released carbon dioxide to the air. Today it does the opposite, taking up a net 2.9 billion tonnes of carbon a year on average. The oceanic carbon cycle is the set of processes that move carbon among pools within the ocean, and between the ocean, the atmosphere, Earth's interior and the seafloor. It is central to the global carbon cycle and holds both inorganic carbon and organic carbon, the kind built by living things. Three main pumps carry carbon dioxide from the air into the ocean interior and spread it through the oceans. Altogether, the oceans take up around 25–31% of the carbon dioxide people emit. Temperature matters. Cold water dissolves more carbon dioxide, so warming seas take up less. Carbon also arrives by river: rivers deliver roughly equal amounts, about 0.4 gigatons of carbon a year each, of dissolved inorganic and organic carbon. Since 1970, dams have cut that delivery by an estimated 13%. The final exit is burial in sediments, the ocean's long-term carbon sink and its largest loss of carbon. About 90% of organic carbon burial happens on deltas, continental shelves and upper slopes.

  <!-- nature-eco-252 -->

- **Ocean acidification: the other carbon dioxide problem**

  Between 1950 and 2020, the average pH of the ocean surface fell from about 8.15 to 8.05. The pH scale measures acidity, and lower numbers mean more acidic. That small-looking drop means roughly 26% more hydrogen ions, the particles that make water acidic. Ocean acidification is this ongoing fall in the pH of Earth's ocean as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. Carbon dioxide from human activities is the main cause. Dissolved in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions that lower the pH. Seawater is still alkaline, the opposite of acidic, with a pH above 8. Acidification means it is becoming less so. The creatures most at risk build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate: mollusks, corals and others. Speed is the danger. Today's rate of change is far faster than in the geological past, too fast for organisms to adapt gradually. Acidification has happened before, during several mass extinctions, including the end-Permian and Cretaceous–Paleogene events. Combined with ocean warming, it harms marine life far more than either alone. Only cutting carbon dioxide emissions addresses the root cause, though removing carbon dioxide from the air would also help reverse it.

  <!-- nature-eco-248 -->

- **The biological pump: how plankton send carbon to the deep**

  Without the ocean's living pump, the air would hold about 400 parts per million more carbon dioxide than it does today. The biological pump is the ocean's living process of moving carbon from the air and from land runoff into the deep ocean and seafloor sediments. It starts in the sunlit surface layer, where phytoplankton build organic and inorganic carbon compounds. Their reach is enormous: marine phytoplankton perform half of all photosynthesis on Earth. Uneaten phytoplankton clump together and sink quickly out of the well-mixed surface layer. The faecal pellets of zooplankton, tiny drifting animals, sink with them. In this way the pump moves about 11 billion tonnes of carbon into the ocean interior each year. Large animals help. Whales and seals boost surface productivity by releasing nitrogen-rich fecal plumes, a role that was larger before industrial fishing cut their numbers. The pump may weaken in future. As the surface ocean warms and stratifies, separating into layers that mix less, nutrient supply and primary production may fall.

  <!-- nature-eco-204 -->

- **What ocean acidification could cost people**

  About one billion people depend wholly or partly on coral reefs for fishing, tourism and protection of their coasts. Ocean acidification threatens that, along with commercial fisheries, shellfish harvests and coastal tourism. Slower calcification, the building of shells and skeletons, means smaller, slower-growing reefs, and reefs support about 25% of marine life. Depending on how much carbon is emitted, future acidification may affect the livelihoods of some 470 to 870 million of the world's poorest people. Rich countries are exposed too. The US commercial fish catch in 2007 was worth $3.8 billion, and 73% of it came from shell-builders and their direct predators. In the United Kingdom, the direct potential loss is put at 14 to 28 percent of shellfish fishery output, about 23 to 88 million pounds. Arctic fisheries are at risk because acidification harms pteropods and brittle stars, creatures at the base of simple Arctic food webs.

  <!-- nature-eco-250 -->

- **The solubility pump: cold water drags carbon down**

  A cold sea holds more carbon dioxide than a warm one, and the ocean puts that fact to work. The solubility pump is a physical and chemical process that carries carbon, as dissolved inorganic carbon, from the ocean surface into its depths. It works because carbon dioxide dissolves better in cold water, and because deep water forms from cold, dense water at high latitudes, near the poles. That cold water sinks with its carbon. The return trip closes the loop. When deep water rises in warm equatorial seas, it releases carbon dioxide back to the air. About one third of human carbon dioxide emissions, approximately 2 gigatons of carbon per year, are believed to enter the ocean, driven mainly by this pump. That uptake slows global warming but causes ocean acidification. The pump may falter. Ocean warming, stronger layering of the water and slower thermohaline circulation could all weaken it. Thermohaline circulation is the slow, deep movement of ocean water driven by differences in temperature and saltiness. The pump's living counterpart is the biological pump.

  <!-- nature-eco-271 -->

- **Erosion control: keeping soil in place with plants**

  New Deal programs in the United States planted 18,000 miles of tree and shrub belts to break the wind, from North Dakota to Texas, to fight soil erosion. Erosion control is the set of practices that prevent or repair soil erosion, chiefly by keeping land covered with plants. Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent erosion by both wind and water. Terracing, cutting slopes into level steps, is a highly effective method practiced for thousands of years around the world. Such belts along fields also improve growing conditions around the crops, shelter birds and store carbon. Mixed cropping, Crop rotation and leaving crop residues on the field under Conservation tillage all reduce erosion. Agroforestry, which mixes crops with trees, works especially well in rainy tropical climates. On coasts, the roots of the trees covered in Mangroves: trees that live in the sea's edge slow water, trap sediment and bind soils. Good erosion control manages surface runoff and helps prevent water pollution, the loss of soil and habitat, and damage to property.

  <!-- nature-es-092 -->

- **Managing soil carbon: farming as a climate tool**

  In the Netherlands, East Anglia and Florida, drained and tilled peat soils have sunk severely as their carbon oxidized. Managing soil carbon means using land in ways that keep or add carbon to soil. It matters because the exchange of carbon between soil and atmosphere is a major part of the global carbon cycle. Humans and farming systems are now the biggest influence on how soil carbon varies. Deforestation, fire, tillage, meaning plowing and similar working of the soil, and drainage all cause losses. Adding carbon brings co-benefits: less erosion, higher productivity, cleaner waterways and soil that holds water better. Farming practices that store carbon in soils, covered in Carbon farming, are a land-based way to remove carbon dioxide from the air. Selling that storage is tricky, though. Soil carbon offsets can be hard to verify, because measurements depend on how deep the samples are taken.

  <!-- nature-eco-262 -->

- **Nutrient trading: paying the cheapest cleaner**

  Two polluters on the same river can face very different bills to cut the same pollutant. Nutrient trading puts that gap to work. It is one form of Water quality trading: cleaner rivers at the lowest cost, a market-based policy tool in which sources swap credits for cutting nutrient pollution. Sources that can cut pollution cheaply sell reduction credits voluntarily to sources for which control is expensive. The underlying principle is that the polluter pays, usually backed by a rule requiring participation. A 2013 Forest Trends report found three kinds of funders. Some benefit from protecting a watershed, some are polluters offsetting their impacts, and some are public good payers such as governments and NGOs, the non-governmental organizations. As of 2013, payments were overwhelmingly started by that last group.

  <!-- nature-eco-246 -->

- **The sulfur cycle: an element that trades electrons**

  Sulfur is found in many proteins, so every living thing needs it. The sulfur cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves sulfur between rocks, waterways and living things. It runs through changes in sulfur's oxidation state, a count of how many electrons an atom has given up or gained. That state ranges from +6 in sulfate to −2 in sulfides. The steps include breaking down organic sulfur to hydrogen sulfide, oxidizing sulfide to sulfate, and reducing sulfate back to sulfide. Microbes that oxidize sulfide often use the energy to fix carbon dioxide, building it into living matter. Sulfur compounds can also serve in cellular respiration. Earth's main sulfur sink is the sulfate dissolved in the oceans. In the seabed, sulfate is used to break down buried organic matter and methane. Deeper down, where the sulfate runs out, methane production takes over. Sulfur also takes part in forming fossil fuels and most metal ore deposits.

  <!-- nature-eco-273 -->

- **Permafrost: the Arctic's frozen carbon vault**

  Permafrost soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they store between 25 and 50% of the organic carbon in the world's soils. Permafrost is ground that stays below 0 °C for at least two years in a row. The permafrost, or Arctic, carbon cycle is the part of the global carbon cycle that moves carbon between frozen soils, plants and microbes, the atmosphere and back. The northern circumpolar permafrost region alone holds around 1,460–1,600 Pg, or petagrams, of organic carbon in its soils. That is more than double the carbon now in the atmosphere. The carbon is old: radiocarbon dating shows it is often thousands of years old. It got there slowly. Wind and rivers dropped sediment, peat built up, and as the ground surface rose, the buried layers froze into the permafrost with their carbon locked inside. Early research often overlooked this huge store, but attention has grown enormously since the 2000s. What happens when it thaws is the subject of The permafrost carbon feedback: thaw that feeds warming.

  <!-- nature-eco-256 -->

- **Net ecosystem production: the carbon an ecosystem keeps**

  Net ecosystem production is the carbon an ecosystem has left after every living thing in it has respired. Formally, it is gross primary production minus all the respiration in an ecosystem, by plants, animals and microbes. It is given as mass of carbon per area per time, such as grams of carbon per square meter per year. The leftover carbon can be stored as biomass, buried in sediments or soils, or exported to another system. It can also be burned, or broken down by sunlight, and so turned back into carbon dioxide. Net primary production is different: it subtracts only the plants' own respiration, not that of animals and microbes. The measure has practical uses. It is one of the main factors directly linked to methane emissions from wetlands.

  <!-- nature-eco-241 -->

- **The light-dependent reactions: catching sunlight**

  Photosynthesis begins when a molecule of chlorophyll, the green pigment of plants, absorbs a photon, a particle of light. These light-dependent reactions are the first stage of photosynthesis, making the energy carriers ATP and NADPH. In plants they take place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. The absorbed photon makes chlorophyll lose an electron. The electron travels down a chain of molecules and ends up turning NADP into NADPH. Chlorophyll regains its electron when water is split, which releases oxygen.

  <!-- nature-eco-191 -->

- **The Calvin cycle: building sugar from air**

  At Berkeley in the late 1940s, Melvin Calvin and colleagues worked out how plants build sugar from air. Calvin won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The Calvin cycle is the light-independent stage of photosynthesis. In it the enzyme RuBisCO, a protein that speeds the reaction, captures carbon dioxide from the air and builds it into sugars. The power comes from the ATP and NADPH made by the light-dependent reactions. The products are carbohydrates such as glucose. These simple sugars become cellulose, building blocks for fats and proteins, or fuel for respiration.

  <!-- nature-eco-192 -->

- **Carbon concentrating mechanisms: photosynthesis in the heat**

  On a hot, dry day a plant faces a dilemma. Closing its stomata saves water, but the carbon dioxide inside the leaf then falls and a wasteful process called photorespiration rises. Carbon concentrating mechanisms are ways some plants and algae raise the carbon dioxide level around RuBisCO so photosynthesis keeps working. C4 plants first fix carbon dioxide into a four-carbon acid using the enzyme PEP carboxylase. C4 and CAM plants avoid photorespiration this way, raising their yield in some high-energy environments. Cyanobacteria concentrate carbon dioxide inside structures called carboxysomes.

  <!-- nature-eco-193 -->

- **What holds photosynthesis back**

  Shade from neighbouring plants is a major brake on photosynthesis. Total photosynthesis is limited by environmental factors: light, leaf area, carbon dioxide supply, water and temperature. Carbon dioxide shows how the limits work. As its concentration rises, sugar production rises, until some other factor becomes the limit. Part of the story lies in RuBisCO, the enzyme that captures carbon. It binds both carbon dioxide and oxygen, and it fixes carbon dioxide when carbon dioxide concentration is high.

  <!-- nature-eco-195 -->

- **Photosynthetic efficiency: plants versus solar panels**

  A typical plant turns only 3–6% of the light it receives into chemical energy. That share is its photosynthetic efficiency. It varies with the colour and intensity of light, temperature and carbon dioxide level, ranging from 0.1% to 8%. Mass-produced solar panels do better, converting light to electricity at about 6–20%, and laboratory devices exceed 40%. Scientists study photosynthesis partly in the hope of breeding plants with higher yields.

  <!-- nature-eco-194 -->

- **Agricultural runoff: farm chemicals on the move**

  Spray a field just before heavy rain, and the chemicals may end up in the nearest stream. Agricultural runoff is water flowing off farmland that carries chemicals such as nitrates, phosphates, pesticides and herbicides. It happens when chemicals are overused or applied just before heavy rain. Either way, farm chemicals are wasted and downstream ecosystems are threatened. Nitrate fertilizer is especially easily lost, because it is highly soluble and is repelled by negatively charged clay. Concentrated runoff from farms can cause dead zones in large water bodies.

  <!-- nature-eco-278 -->

- **Two ways a storm sets water running**

  Surface runoff is generated in distinct ways. Infiltration excess, or Hortonian, overland flow starts when rain falls faster than the soil can soak it up. It is common in dry regions with intense rain and sealed soils, and in paved urban areas. Saturation excess, or Dunne, runoff happens when rain keeps falling on soil that is already full of water. The wetter the soil before a storm, the sooner it saturates and runoff begins. Some water takes a hidden route. It soaks in upslope, flows sideways through the soil and re-emerges near a channel, which is called subsurface return flow, or throughflow.

  <!-- nature-eco-276 -->

- **Taming runoff, from medieval fields to city drains**

  Since medieval times, farmers have protected their soil by contour farming, plowing across slopes rather than down them. Runoff mitigation combines controls on how land is used, erosion controls, flood control and chemical handling rules to reduce the harm runoff causes. Construction sites use straw bales, silt fences and work scheduled for drier months to slow runoff. Holding ponds, also called detention basins, buffer peak river flows. In the United States, the federal law described in Clean Water Act requires urban local governments to run programs for managing storm runoff, under discharge permits.

  <!-- nature-eco-279 -->

- **Urban runoff: rain that never meets the soil**

  Rain that falls on a road, a parking lot or a roof cannot soak in. Urban runoff is the surface runoff that hard surfaces like these create, from rain, landscape watering and car washing. Instead of filtering through soil, polluted rainwater flows to storm drains. Most municipal storm sewers then discharge it untreated into streams, rivers and bays. Because more water stays on the surface, the water table drops and floods become more common. Many towns respond with building codes, such as narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth, that let more water soak in.

  <!-- nature-eco-277 -->

- **Timber buildings: storing forest carbon in cities**

  A wooden building can keep hold of carbon a tree once pulled from the air. Buildings made of mass timber, large structural pieces of solid wood, can therefore act as artificial carbon sinks. Replacing steel and concrete with timber could store between 10 million and close to 700 million tons of carbon a year, depending on the scenario. The benefit has conditions. The forests must be sustainably managed, and the wood must be reused or preserved when buildings are demolished. Fast-growing plant materials such as bamboo, straw or hempcrete can add further storage.

  <!-- nature-eco-172 -->

- **Coastal eutrophication: why nitrogen rules the sea**

  Over the last century, rivers' yearly delivery to the oceans rose from 19 to 37 megatonnes of nitrogen and from 2 to 4 megatonnes of phosphorus. Coastal eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of coastal seas, where nitrogen is usually the main culprit. In fresh water, phosphorus is often the limiting nutrient, the one in shortest supply that caps growth. In coastal waters, nitrogen usually is. So nitrogen levels matter more than phosphorus for controlling eutrophication in salt water. The pressure on each coast varies with land activities in its catchment, the land that drains into it. It also depends on how well the setting dilutes nutrients and exchanges oxygen.

  <!-- nature-eco-546 -->

- **Harmful algal blooms: when green water turns toxic**

  Some algal blooms do more than starve a lake of oxygen. Harmful algal blooms are dense growths of algae, often caused by eutrophication, that are toxic to plants and animals. When the algae die or are eaten, they release nerve and liver toxins that can kill animals and may threaten humans. The toxins can reach people through shellfish, causing shellfish poisoning. In fresh water, the culprits are commonly cyanobacteria that fix their own nitrogen. They are favoured when nitrogen runs short but phosphorus keeps pouring in.

  <!-- nature-eco-219 -->

- **The economic bill for murky, smelly water**

  Murky water costs money to clean. Eutrophication and harmful algal blooms impose economic costs through dearer water treatment, lost fishing and shellfish harvests, and lower tourism income. Drinking water plants must also deal with colour and smell problems. Tourism suffers because the water looks less attractive and is less safe, thanks to bacteria from decomposition. Could a little extra fertility pay? In principle, controlled eutrophication could raise fishery output and community income. It is not currently recommended, because damage can set in quickly.

  <!-- nature-eco-220 -->

- **Natural eutrophication: lakes grow richer with age**

  Lakes naturally grow more productive as they age. Natural eutrophication is this slow enrichment of waters by the gradual build-up of sediment and nutrients. It usually comes from dissolved phosphate minerals and dead plant matter collecting in the water. Climate, geology and other outside influences also regulate how productive a lake naturally is.

  <!-- nature-eco-218 -->

- **Nutrient bioextraction: oysters and kelp as water cleaners**

  Several studies show that oysters and mussels can greatly lower nitrogen levels in estuaries. Nutrient bioextraction is farming and harvesting shellfish and seaweed to remove nitrogen and other nutrients from natural waters. Seaweeds such as kelp absorb both phosphorus and nitrogen, helping clean polluted waters. The idea has an economic angle. If oysters keep nitrogen below legal thresholds, they spare polluters the compliance costs they would otherwise face. So nitrogen removal by reefs of oysters could benefit polluters facing nitrogen limits, much as nutrient trading does.

  <!-- nature-eco-224 -->

- **Preventing eutrophication at the source**

  The surest way to stop a lake being overfed is to stop feeding it. Eutrophication is prevented mainly by cutting nutrient pollution from sewage and from farming. Sewage treatment plants can be upgraded for biological nutrient removal, so they discharge much less nitrogen and phosphorus. That matters because even good standard treatment leaves substantial nitrogen in the treated water most sewage plants release. Farmers are advised to apply fertilizer in the right amount, at the right time, with the right method and placement. The UN's goal for the oceans, described in Sustainable Development Goal 14, targets a significant cut in marine nutrient pollution from land by 2025.

  <!-- nature-eco-223 -->

- **Reversing eutrophication: why lakes recover slowly**

  Stopping the flow of nutrients into a lake does not clean it overnight. Reversing eutrophication starts with reducing nutrient inputs, but recovery can take a long time, mainly because nutrients stored in sediments keep being released. Cutting inputs may not be enough. A water body can have several stable but very different states, so restoration may need more. One option is adding phosphate-binding materials such as alum to lock up phosphorus. Removal at the source can be thorough: Finnish phosphorus removal from the mid-1970s reached 90% removal efficiency.

  <!-- nature-eco-225 -->

- **Ocean alkalinity enhancement: making seawater less acidic**

  One proposed answer to an acidifying ocean is to add the chemical opposite of acid. Ocean alkalinity enhancement is a proposed way of removing carbon dioxide from the air that adds alkaline minerals, or products made from them, to the ocean surface. Adding alkalinity buffers pH change immediately, which may help sea life where it is added. Electrochemical methods that strip carbon dioxide from seawater are a related form. Such ocean-based methods are still under study, with low technology readiness and many risks.

  <!-- nature-eco-251 -->

- **The deep carbon cycle: carbon's trip into the mantle**

  In 2011 a study of rare super-deep diamonds from Brazil showed that carbon cycling reaches all the way to Earth's lower mantle. The deep carbon cycle is the slow movement of carbon between Earth's surface and its deep interior. Carbon mainly enters the mantle in carbonate-rich sediments riding on ocean plates, which sink beneath other plates. This return matters for life. Without it, carbon would build up in the atmosphere to extremely high levels, so the deep cycle helps keep conditions fit for life.

  <!-- nature-eco-167 -->

- **Bernard Palissy and the discovery of the water cycle**

  In ancient times many people believed the land floated on water and that river water came from under the earth. By roughly 500 BCE, Greek scholars were suggesting that much river water comes from rain. The modern theory, that rainfall alone keeps rivers flowing, was first published by Bernard Palissy in 1580. It was first tested scientifically in 1674, in a study usually credited to Pierre Perrault. Even so, the idea did not become mainstream until the early nineteenth century.

  <!-- nature-eco-200 -->

- **Mud in the water: sediment as a pollutant**

  Soil eroded mainly from farmland is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution, the kind that comes from many scattered sources rather than one pipe. The problem is the excess sediment it sends into waterways. Sediment is a pollutant in itself, and it also carries others, such as pesticides and heavy metals. Silt can smother fish spawning beds by filling the gaps between gravel on stream beds. Runoff from roads and urban areas adds sediment contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals.

  <!-- nature-eco-268 -->

- **Tillage erosion: when the plow moves the soil**

  On many hilly fields, the plow moves more soil than rain or wind does. Tillage erosion is the movement of soil down a field caused by plowing and other tillage. In many fields, especially on hilly land, it is a bigger cause of soil loss than erosion by water or wind. Its signature is the eroded hilltop. Water erosion removes soil mainly from middle and lower slopes, so worn-down hilltops point to tillage instead. The damage is costly, because degraded soil can sharply cut crop yields and cause economic losses for farms.

  <!-- nature-eco-267 -->

- **Splash, sheet, rill and gully: how rain carves soil**

  A single raindrop can throw soil particles up to 0.6 m into the air and 1.5 m sideways on level ground. That is splash erosion, the first and mildest of four main kinds of erosion caused by rain and the runoff it creates. Next comes sheet erosion, soil carried off by overland flow. Then come rills, small, short-lived channels only a few centimeters deep. Gully erosion is the most severe. It happens when runoff rushes through narrow channels after heavy rain or snowmelt, removing soil to a considerable depth.

  <!-- nature-eco-265 -->

- **The Universal Soil Loss Equation: predicting erosion**

  How much soil will a field lose to rain each year? The Universal Soil Loss Equation, or USLE, is the most widely used model for predicting average yearly soil loss from water erosion on a plot. It multiplies together factors for rainfall erosivity, the eroding power of rain; soil erodibility; slope length and steepness; cover and management; and support practices. Developed in the 1960s and 1970s, it is still the basis of global studies. It has blind spots. It cannot simulate gully erosion, which can make up 10–80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land. And all erosion models only roughly match real measured erosion rates.

  <!-- nature-es-079 -->

- **Wind erosion: soil carried off on the air**

  Dust blown off distant land has been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida. Wind erosion is the removal of soil by wind, a major force in arid and semi-arid regions. Wind works in two ways. It lifts and carries loose particles, called deflation, and it wears surfaces down with airborne particles, called abrasion. Wind erosion is a major source of degraded land, spreading desert, harmful dust and crop damage, especially where deforestation, urbanization and farming make it worse. Its dust is a major air pollutant.

  <!-- nature-eco-266 -->

- **Potential evapotranspiration: the air's thirst**

  Potential evapotranspiration is the amount of water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if enough water were available. It measures the air's demand for moisture. Actual evapotranspiration also depends on how much water the surface can supply. So the actual figure can never exceed the potential, though it can fall below it when water is short. The potential is higher in summer, on clear and windy days, and nearer the equator. It also defines a dry region: a place where yearly potential evaporation exceeds yearly precipitation.

  <!-- nature-eco-228 -->

- **How scientists estimate evapotranspiration**

  Water vapour rising from a landscape is hard to measure directly, so evapotranspiration is usually estimated indirectly. One approach is a catchment water balance. It relates the change in stored water to precipitation, evapotranspiration, streamflow and the water seeping down to refill groundwater, so evapotranspiration can be solved for. Energy balance methods, including the satellite-based SEBAL and METRIC algorithms, map it pixel by pixel. The Penman–Monteith equation, recommended by the FAO, calculates a reference value from weather data. Weighing lysimeters, tanks of soil that are weighed, measure it directly, but only over small areas.

  <!-- nature-eco-229 -->

- **How plants change the water a landscape yields**

  A dense forest may actually reduce the water that flows out of a landscape. The type and density of vegetation strongly shape evapotranspiration, and so how much water a landscape yields. Dense vegetation such as forest may raise evapotranspiration, sending more water back to the air and less downstream. Rainforests are an exception. While they stand, they raise humidity, cool the ground and slow winds, increasing stream flows and groundwater. Clearing them often turns land toward desert as soils dry out and erode. Deforestation also lowers evapotranspiration and so the moisture in the air, which can reduce rain downwind.

  <!-- nature-eco-227 -->

- **Legumes: plants that host their own fertilizer makers**

  Clover, soybean, alfalfa and peanut all carry their own fertilizer factories underground. These legumes house rhizobia bacteria in root nodules, small swellings on their roots, and the bacteria make nitrogen compounds for the plant. It is a mutualism, a partnership in which both sides gain. When a legume dies, its fixed nitrogen is released to other plants, fertilizing the soil. Many traditional farming systems put this to work by rotating fields through crops that include one mainly of clover. Farms that mix trees with crops can also use legumes to restore soil nitrogen.

  <!-- nature-eco-243 -->

- **Lightning: nitrogen fixed by a bolt from the sky**

  A lightning bolt carries enough energy to break nitrogen gas apart, something most living things cannot do. The freed nitrogen reacts with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides. These form nitrogen dioxide and then, in water, nitrous or nitric acid. In soil they yield nitrate that plants can use. Industry once copied the trick. Fixation with electric arcs, first described by Henry Cavendish in 1784, closely resembles fixation by lightning.

  <!-- nature-eco-244 -->

- **The microbial loop: bacteria recycle the sea's leftovers**

  In 1983 Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop to cover bacteria's role in cycling the ocean's carbon and nutrients. The loop is a pathway in which dissolved organic carbon in the sea is taken up by bacteria and returned to the food chain. That dissolved carbon leaks from many places: bursting bacteria, phytoplankton, sloppy feeding by zooplankton, and animal wastes.

  <!-- nature-eco-208 -->

- **Counting soil carbon for climate reporting**

  One model puts the organic carbon in the topsoil of EU farmland at 17.63 Gt. Under the UN climate convention, countries must estimate and report changes in stored carbon from land use and forestry, soil carbon included. Five pools are reported: above-ground and below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil carbon. Reliable soil carbon estimates are also needed for schemes that pay to cut emissions from the clearing and degrading of forests.

  <!-- nature-eco-263 -->

- **Soil inorganic carbon: carbon stored as minerals**

  In arid and semi-arid places, most soil carbon is not in decaying plants but in carbonate minerals such as calcite and dolomite. Soil inorganic carbon is carbon held in minerals. It comes either from weathered parent rock, the rock a soil forms from, or from soil minerals reacting with carbon dioxide in the air. These carbonates can come from the bedrock, or form in the soil itself, when they are called pedogenic carbonate.

  <!-- nature-eco-261 -->

- **Soil organic carbon: the carbon in decaying life**

  Soil organic matter is about 50% carbon by dry weight. Soil organic carbon is that carbon, and in humid climates it is the dominant form of soil carbon. Its main source is dead plant material: roots, fallen leaves and crop residue. Substances that roots release, called root exudates, add more. Some of it vanishes fast. Cellulose, starches and proteins break down quickly, while lignin, humus and charcoal persist for a long time. It also boosts fertility: in sandy soils, soil organic carbon raised cation exchange capacity, a measure of fertility.

  <!-- nature-eco-260 -->

- **The permafrost carbon feedback: thaw that feeds warming**

  For every 1 °C of global warming, the permafrost in the upper 3 m of ground is expected to shrink by about 25%. As it thaws, long-stored carbon escapes as carbon dioxide and methane, adding to the warming that caused the thaw. That loop is the permafrost carbon feedback. Carbon dioxide from microbes respiring with oxygen makes up the overwhelming majority of the emissions. Methane forms in waterlogged, oxygen-free places, such as thermokarst lakes left by thawing ice-rich ground. There is a brake. Thawed ground grows more vegetation, which takes up more carbon, and this is the main counteracting feedback. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates releases of 14–175 billion tonnes per 1 °C of warming, counted in the common yardstick of Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases. For comparison, human carbon dioxide emissions were about 40 billion tonnes in 2019. A 2021 assessment estimated that permafrost emissions would raise the Social cost of carbon by about 8.4%, though its methods were criticized. Researchers also debate where the rising emissions come from: ancient carbon, or faster breakdown of modern plant litter. Thawing permafrost is listed among the Climate tipping points: thresholds with no easy way back.

  <!-- nature-eco-257 -->

- **Tracing nutrient pollution back to its sources**

  Before a polluted river can be managed fairly, someone has to work out who put the nutrients there. Nutrient source apportionment estimates how much of the nutrient load reaching a water body comes from each sector, after treatment or natural losses. There are two approaches. Load-oriented methods work back from monitoring data collected in the stream. Source-oriented methods model emissions using export coefficients, typical losses measured in similar catchments. By identifying the sources, these models support proportional and practical management of polluted waters.

  <!-- nature-eco-247 -->

- **Ammonification: freeing nitrogen from the dead**

  When a plant or animal dies, or an animal excretes waste, its nitrogen starts out in organic forms such as amino acids and DNA. Ammonification, or mineralization, is the conversion of that nitrogen by bacteria and fungi into ammonia or ammonium. It is the last step of the nitrogen cycle that involves organic compounds. It runs faster where soils hold more organic nitrogen and more microbes, and where average yearly rainfall is higher.

  <!-- nature-eco-178 -->

- **Anammox: turning nitrogen compounds straight into gas**

  The bacteria behind anammox were identified only in 1999, to the great surprise of scientists. Anammox, short for anaerobic ammonium oxidation, is a microbial process that turns nitrite and ammonium directly into nitrogen gas and water, without oxygen. Despite its late discovery, it accounts for a major share of nitrogen conversion in the oceans.

  <!-- nature-eco-181 -->

- **The marine nitrogen cycle: feeding the ocean's plankton**

  Without new supplies, the ocean's fixed nitrogen would be used up in about 2000 years. The marine nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen through the ocean. Overall it resembles the cycle on land, but with different organisms and pathways. Nitrogen enters seawater through rain, runoff or as gas from the air. It must be fixed, mostly by cyanobacteria, before phytoplankton can use it. Nitrogen reaching the sunlit layer from fixation, or from deep water welling up, is called new nitrogen. Nitrogen recycled there from eaten or respired matter supports regenerated production. Ocean acidification may cut nitrification and denitrification, letting fixed nitrogen build up and possibly causing eutrophication.

  <!-- nature-eco-182 -->

- **Reservoirs and residence time: how long elements stay put**

  A coal deposit can hold carbon for a long time. That makes it a reservoir: a place where a chemical is held for a long time. Residence time is how long a chemical stays in one place, and it also goes by turnover time, renewal time or exit age. Places that hold a chemical only briefly, such as plants and animals, are called exchange pools. The pattern is broad. Reservoirs are generally non-living parts of the environment, while exchange pools are generally living things.

  <!-- nature-eco-174 -->

- **Where Earth's water sits, and for how long**

  Of the world's 1,386,000,000 km3 of water, about 1,338,000,000 km3, or about 97%, is in the oceans. Ice caps, glaciers and permanent snow hold only 1.7% of all water but 68.7% of all fresh water. A water reservoir's residence time is the average time a water molecule spends in it, a measure of the water's average age. Those times vary enormously. Soil moisture turns over in 1 to 2 months, and shallow groundwater stays 100 to 200 years. Deep groundwater stays about 10,000 years. At any moment, much more water sits in storage than is moving through the cycle.

  <!-- nature-eco-197 -->

- **Box models: a cycle drawn as boxes and flows**

  A box model simplifies a complex system into boxes, or storage reservoirs, for a material, linked by flows of that material. Each box is assumed to be evenly mixed. That lets simple formulas describe how the amount of a chemical changes and where it settles. In a one-box model, a source Q flows into the reservoir and a sink S flows out. When Q equals S, the reservoir is in steady state, and its contents do not change over time. Box models are widely used to model biogeochemical systems.

  <!-- nature-eco-175 -->

- **Equations for how fast water soaks in**

  Infiltration calculation methods are equations that estimate how much water soaks into soil, and how fast, as one term in a watershed's water budget. The rigorous standard is Richards' equation. It is strongly nonlinear, costly to compute and not guaranteed to converge on an answer. Other methods are simpler. The Green-Ampt method depends on soil suction head, porosity, hydraulic conductivity and time. Horton's equation is empirical: infiltration starts at an initial rate and falls exponentially to a steady rate once the soil is saturated. The Kostiakov equation lets the intake rate decline as a power function, and a modified version adds a steady intake term.

  <!-- nature-eco-238 -->

- **Anaerobic respiration: breathing without oxygen**

  In oxygen-free wetland mud, at hydrothermal vents and inside digestive tracts, some microbes respire without oxygen. Anaerobic respiration is respiration by bacteria or archaea, another group of single-celled microbes, without oxygen. Instead they pass electrons to an inorganic substance such as sulfate, nitrate or sulfur. Fermentation is different. It also works without oxygen, but it passes electrons to organic molecules, so it does not count as respiration.

  <!-- nature-eco-213 -->

- **Seasonal fish kills: when lake bottoms run out of oxygen**

  Seasonal fish kills are mass deaths of fish when the oxygen in a lake's deep water is used up, in summer or in winter. Each season sets its own trap. In summer, the lake settles into layers, and extra organic matter speeds respiration in the deep water. In winter, ice and snow cut the light for photosynthesis and block oxygen exchange with the air, while respiration carries on.

  <!-- nature-eco-236 -->

- **What dead zones cost fisheries and tourism**

  The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is reported to cost US seafood and tourism industries about $82 million a year. Dead zones harm fisheries and other sea-based businesses, to a degree that depends on how long they last and where they occur. They cut biodiversity and bottom-dwelling populations. Oddly, extra nutrients can briefly raise catches of some species, such as anchovies. Studies estimate that gains in surrounding waters do not offset the net loss of productivity in the dead zone itself. Still, scientists do not all agree on the balance. Some argue that nutrient loading has enhanced some Gulf fisheries, such as red snapper.

  <!-- nature-eco-215 -->

- **The carbonate pump: carbon sunk in seashells**

  Coccolithophores, foraminifera and molluscs build protective shells of calcium carbonate, and those shells carry carbon into the deep. This is the carbonate pump, the hard-tissue part of the biological pump. It is one of three pumps, with the solubility and biological pumps, that carry carbon dioxide from the air into the ocean interior. Ocean acidification may weaken it. Because carbonate also helps sinking organic matter sink, a weaker carbonate pump could weaken the soft-tissue pump too.

  <!-- nature-eco-205 -->

- **The continental shelf pump: shallow seas feeding the deep**

  Shallow water over a continental shelf can cool more than open-ocean water, because its shallowness limits convection, the stirring of water as it rises and sinks. The continental shelf pump is a proposed mechanism that carries carbon from these shallow shelf waters into the neighbouring deep ocean. It is thought to occur where the solubility pump meets cool, dense water on the shelf floor, which then flows down the continental slope.

  <!-- nature-eco-206 -->

- **Marine snow: the slow shower that feeds the deep sea**

  A constant shower falls through the ocean: dead and dying organisms, faecal matter and mineral particles, sinking from the upper ocean to the deep. This is marine snow. It sinks at approximately 100 meters per day, and only about 1 to 3% of surface production reaches the seabed. Even so, the deep ocean gets most of its nutrients from it, and many deep-sea organisms survive by feeding on it. As clumps of this material form and sink, they drive the biological pump, exporting organic matter to the deep ocean and its sediments.

  <!-- nature-eco-517 -->

- **Remineralisation: breaking life back down to basics**

  Every dead leaf and sinking scrap of plankton eventually comes apart into simple chemicals. Remineralisation is this breakdown of organic matter into its simplest inorganic forms. It frees the energy stored in organic molecules and recycles their matter as nutrients for other organisms. How much sinking matter escapes remineralisation varies from place to place.

  <!-- nature-eco-211 -->

- **Vertical migration: animals that ferry carbon downward**

  Krill, salps and fish feed near the surface at night and go deep by day, and on each trip down they actively carry carbon to depth. Without this vertical migration, the biological pump would be far less efficient. A seasonal version is the lipid pump. Zooplankton that migrate down to spend the winter at depth carry carbon there in their fat reserves.

  <!-- nature-eco-210 -->

- **The viral shunt: how sea viruses recycle microbes**

  Viruses contribute on average 8.6% to Earth's ecosystem carbon cycle: 1.4% in the sea, 6.7% on land and 17.8% in fresh water. In the sea, one of their routes is the viral shunt. Marine viruses turn microbial particles into dissolved organic matter that microbes can readily take up again. As much as 25% of phytoplankton primary production may be recycled within the microbial loop this way.

  <!-- nature-eco-209 -->

- **Dust storms: nutrients carried across oceans**

  Phosphorus blown from northern Africa is thought to help support the rich biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest. Dust storms carry phosphorus and other nutrients in weathered rock particles over long distances. Large dust events can supply phosphorus to areas where its lack would otherwise limit growth. Dust also carries potassium, calcium and magnesium, so storms matter for the cycling of nutrients.

  <!-- nature-eco-188 -->

- **Mining phosphorus faster than rocks can replace it**

  Global phosphorus mining rose 72-fold from 1900 to 2022, and it is expected to keep rising by 4% a year. Humans have greatly changed the phosphorus cycle, mainly by mining phosphate rock for fertilizer. Since the 1840s, about 110 teragrams of phosphorus, units of a million tonnes each, have been added to the environment. At this pace, slow geological processes cannot replace what is lost. Humans have raised the net storage of phosphorus in soil and ocean systems by an estimated 75%, increasing eutrophication in the ocean.

  <!-- nature-eco-186 -->

- **The nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio drifts out of balance**

  Over the last 40 years, the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio has risen from 19:1 to 30:1. This N:P ratio compares the amounts of these two plant nutrients, both widely used in farm fertilizers. Human activity has pushed it out of its normal balance, leaving phosphorus less available to ecosystems. There are two causes: extra nitrogen pollution, and phosphorus being trapped during water treatment. The shift matters, because as the ratio rises, organisms find it harder to grow.

  <!-- nature-eco-187 -->

- **Wetlands as natural nutrient filters**

  Wetlands are often used to strip excess nitrogen and phosphorus from water and so ease eutrophication. They handle the two nutrients differently. Nitrate is turned into nitrogen gas and released to the air. Phosphorus is held by wetland soils and taken up by plants. That second route has a limit. Wetland soils can hold only so much phosphorus, so continued removal needs new soil, built up from plant and microbial debris.

  <!-- nature-eco-189 -->

- **Methane sinks: what clears methane from the air**

  An average methane molecule lasts about 9.6 years in the air before it is removed. Methane sinks are the processes that destroy or remove methane from the air. The most effective is chemical breakdown as methane rises through the atmosphere, which removes 90% of it. Soil bacteria called methanotrophs are another major sink, using methane for energy and producing carbon dioxide and water. Forest soils are good sinks, but wetland soils with high water tables are often sources instead. One subtlety: a single emission affects the atmosphere for about twelve years.

  <!-- nature-eco-202 -->

- **Removing methane already in the air**

  Atmospheric methane removal is a set of approaches, still under research, to speed up the breakdown of methane already in the air. The appeal is leverage. Because methane is a stronger heat-trapping gas, removing a smaller amount of it than of carbon dioxide would have a similar climate effect. The catch is scarcity. Methane's background level is about 1.92 ppm, against about 420 ppm for carbon dioxide, which makes it harder to capture.

  <!-- nature-eco-203 -->

- **Reactive nitrogen: every form but the inert gas**

  In the past century, the world's generation of reactive nitrogen has risen more than 10-fold with industrialisation. Reactive nitrogen, or fixed nitrogen, is every form of nitrogen in the environment other than nitrogen gas, N2. Common forms include nitrogen oxides, ammonia, nitrous oxide and nitrate. Just over half of the reactive nitrogen entering the biosphere now comes from human activity such as fertilizer production. It accumulates, because it is made faster than denitrification removes it. An excess can cause problems such as eutrophication.

  <!-- nature-eco-183 -->

- **The Haber process: feeding billions, at a price**

  Nearly 50% of the nitrogen in human tissues came from the Haber process. Synthetic fertilizer from the process greatly raised farm productivity and population, at the cost of energy use and nitrogen pollution. Vaclav Smil estimated that at 1900 yields, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land. Called the detonator of the population explosion, the process helped world population grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by 2018. Without it, modern agriculture could not support 8 billion people. The costs are large too. Crops use less than 50% of applied nitrogen, so the process is one of the largest sources of reactive nitrogen build-up, and the runoff harms habitats. Making and using nitrogen fertilizer causes around 5% of all global heat-trapping emissions. Cheap synthetic fertilizer also weakens farmers' incentive to rotate in nitrogen-fixing legumes. Haber-process fertilizer is a typical high-carbon import that a Carbon tariff might cover.

  <!-- nature-eco-231 -->

- **How people doubled the nitrogen cycle**

  Human activity now adds more reactive nitrogen to the environment than natural nitrogen fixation does, mainly through synthetic fertilizer and fossil fuel burning. Over the past century these inputs have greatly altered the global nitrogen cycle. They have more than doubled the yearly conversion of nitrogen into biologically available forms and increased the nitrogen falling back onto land and water. One by-product is nitrous oxide. Its level in the air rose from about 270 nmol/mol before industry to about 319 nmol/mol in 2005. It is both a heat-trapping gas and a destroyer of ozone. Nitrous oxide is the third largest contributor to global warming and, mass for mass, nearly 300 times more potent than carbon dioxide. Human activities cause 35% of its global emissions, about 20% from farming sources such as fertilizer and manure. High-temperature combustion has also raised the flow of nitrogen oxides to the air 6- or 7-fold, contributing to smog and acidic rain.

  <!-- nature-eco-232 -->

- **Nitrate in drinking water: fertilizer that slips underground**

  Nitrate dissolves easily and soil holds it poorly, so it readily escapes down to groundwater. Nitrate pollution is the build-up of nitrate from human activities in groundwater and surface water, where it can harm human health. Heavy use of nitrogen fertilizer in farming is a significant source. Other diffuse sources include livestock feeding, contamination from human and animal waste, and municipal and industrial waste.

  <!-- nature-eco-184 -->

- **How overfed waters make people sick**

  Eutrophication harms human health in two main ways. The first is excess nitrate in drinking water. It can cause blue baby syndrome in infants, and it can form disinfection by-products during water treatment. The second is toxic algae. Swimming in or drinking water with toxic algae can cause rashes, stomach or liver illness, and breathing or nerve problems.

  <!-- nature-eco-221 -->

- **Iron fertilization: seeding the sea to bury carbon**

  In about 25 percent of the ocean surface, growth is held back mainly by a lack of iron. Iron fertilization is an idea from Geoengineering. It would speed up the ocean's biological pump so it exports more carbon from the surface to the deep ocean, removing excess carbon dioxide from the air. In practice it is hard to tell whether it works, because the ocean is vast and consumers respond quickly to extra growth. Most scientists do not consider it viable. Its effectiveness and safety remain debated, though no harm has yet been observed in trials.

  <!-- nature-clim-206 -->

- **Four kinds of ocean carbon: DIC, PIC, DOC and POC**

  Ocean scientists sort carbon two ways: organic or inorganic, and dissolved or particulate, meaning in tiny solid bits. That gives four pools: DIC, PIC, DOC and POC. Dissolved inorganic carbon is bicarbonate, carbonate and carbon dioxide, including carbonic acid. Dissolved organic carbon is defined as any organic molecule that passes through a 0.2 μm filter, and what the filter catches is particulate organic carbon. Photosynthesis turns dissolved inorganic carbon into particulate organic carbon. Making calcium carbonate turns it into particulate inorganic carbon.

  <!-- nature-eco-253 -->

- **Seawater carbonate chemistry: carbon dioxide meets the sea**

  Unlike most gases, carbon dioxide does not just dissolve in seawater; it reacts with it. The result is a balance of free carbon dioxide, carbonic acid, bicarbonate and carbonate, together called dissolved inorganic carbon. The balance depends on pH and on alkalinity, seawater's excess of positive ions. The greater the alkalinity, the more carbon dioxide seawater can dissolve. The parts are tightly linked. Measuring any two of total inorganic carbon, total alkalinity, pH and pCO2, the pressure of carbon dioxide, lets scientists work out the rest.

  <!-- nature-eco-272 -->

- **Carbonate saturation: when shells start to dissolve**

  Some seawater helps shells form; some dissolves them. The saturation state, written Ω, measures how readily a mineral such as calcium carbonate will form or dissolve in seawater. It is the product of the calcium and carbonate ion concentrations, divided by the solubility product, their product at equilibrium. Rising dissolved carbon dioxide lowers the carbonate available and so the saturation state, making shells harder to build. Calcium carbonate is supersaturated in most surface waters and undersaturated at depth. So shells tend to dissolve as they sink, and the boundary is called the saturation horizon.

  <!-- nature-eco-249 -->
