- **The Revelle factor: a gauge of the ocean's appetite**

  The ocean's appetite for carbon dioxide is shrinking, and one number tracks it. The Revelle factor is the ratio of the change in carbon dioxide to the change in dissolved inorganic carbon in seawater. It shows how readily seawater absorbs more carbon dioxide: the lower the factor, the more the water can take in. The factor rises as carbon dioxide rises, so the ocean will take up a smaller share of human emissions in future.

  <!-- nature-eco-254 -->

- **Unlocking sulfur: how fuels flood the air with it**

  Mining coal and extracting petroleum mobilizes 150 × 10^12 grams of sulfur a year, more than double the rate of 100 years ago. Burning coal, oil and gas releases sulfur that would otherwise stay locked in rock, greatly increasing sulfur in the air and ocean. Sulfur dioxide forms sulfuric acid in the air, causing acidic rain. Over the most polluted areas, sulfate deposition has risen 30-fold. As pollution controls cut sulfur inputs, sulfur deficiency in crops has become widespread in parts of Europe, raising use of sulfur fertilizers.

  <!-- nature-eco-274 -->

- **Subsea permafrost: frozen ground under the sea**

  Beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves lies frozen ground that was dry land in the last ice age and is now flooded. This subsea permafrost covers about 2 million km2. It holds around 560 GtC, gigatons of carbon, in organic matter and 45 GtC in methane. It responds over millennia, so human-driven warming will affect it mostly hundreds or thousands of years from now. Still, under the high-emissions RCP 8.5 scenario, 43 GtC could be released by 2100 and 190 GtC by 2300.

  <!-- nature-eco-258 -->

- **Net community production: another route to the same number**

  Net community production is net primary production minus the respiration of animals and other heterotrophs, the organisms that eat rather than make their food. It equals net ecosystem production; only the calculation differs. Values vary widely across the ocean. In the tropical South Pacific, annual net community production can be close to zero. Elsewhere in the Pacific it ranges from 2.0 to 2.4 mol C m−2 yr−1, or moles of carbon per square metre per year.

  <!-- nature-eco-242 -->

- **The nitrogen cascade: one atom, many harms**

  The nitrogen cascade is the passing of the same reactive nitrogen from one ecosystem to the next. It moves through air, water and land until it is turned back into nitrogen gas. Pathways that carry nutrients across system boundaries link one nitrogen problem to the next. Some systems store reactive nitrogen along the way, delaying the cascade and intensifying local effects. In the end, nitrogen that people add is either stored or denitrified, but how much goes each way is still poorly known. Some scientists think the cascade may be as big a problem for Earth's ecology as carbon dioxide.

  <!-- nature-eco-234 -->

- **Nitrogen deposition: fertilizer falling from the sky**

  From 1600 to 1990, deposition of reactive nitrogen onto land and sea rose over 200%. Nitrogen deposition is this fall of reactive nitrogen from the air, in rain, as gases or as fine particles. Extra deposition can acidify soils, streams and lakes, and change how productive forests and grasslands are. In grasslands, productivity first rises, then falls once critical thresholds are passed. Nitrogen enrichment also favours fast-growing species and cuts the number of species, as when grasses replace species-rich heathland.

  <!-- nature-eco-233 -->

- **Mycorrhizal fungi: hidden partners in soil carbon**

  Plants are estimated to send 5 to 20% of the carbon they take up to fungi on their roots. These mycorrhizal fungi partner with the roots of almost all plants and may help decide how much carbon soils store. On forested islands in Sweden, mycorrhizal fungi held 50 to 70 percent of the carbon stored in leaf litter and soil. Ectomycorrhizal fungi can compete with free-living decomposers for nutrients, slowing decomposition and raising soil carbon storage. For arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi the evidence is split: studies disagree on whether they and their protein glomalin add soil carbon or cause net losses.

  <!-- nature-eco-239 -->

- **The priming effect: when fungi spur carbon losses**

  Feeding soil microbes an easy meal can make them eat more of the soil's stored carbon. Priming is when fungi or roots release easy-to-use energy compounds that spur free-living decomposers to break down more soil carbon. Lab experiments found that arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi increase soil carbon losses, and more so when carbon dioxide is raised. Evidence for priming by ectomycorrhizal fungi is so far inconclusive.

  <!-- nature-eco-240 -->

### Climate science essentials

Without the gases that trap heat in its air, Earth's surface would average −18 °C instead of about 15 °C. This chapter explains that greenhouse effect, the gases behind it, and how human emissions of those gases, above all carbon dioxide, are strengthening it. It follows the rise in average temperature measured since thermometer records reached global coverage around 1850, along with the extreme weather and wider effects that come with it. Along the way it introduces the yardsticks scientists use to compare causes: radiative forcing, global warming potential, and the feedbacks that amplify or dampen an initial warming.

- **Climate change: a warming world and why it matters**

  2024 was the warmest year on record, at +1.60 °C since regular tracking began in 1850. Present-day climate change is global warming, the ongoing rise in Earth's average temperature, together with its wider effects on the climate system. Human activity drives it. The chief cause is burning coal, oil and gas since the Industrial Revolution, joined by deforestation and some farming and industrial practices that release heat-trapping gases. The atmosphere now holds roughly 50% more carbon dioxide than at the end of the pre-industrial era. The consequences include more flooding, extreme heat, food and water shortages, disease and economic loss. The burden falls unevenly: the poorest communities, who emitted least, are the most vulnerable. Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, nations agreed to keep warming well under 2 °C, yet current pledges would still lead to about 2.8 °C by 2100. Warming can be limited by cutting emissions and by removing carbon dioxide from the air. As of 2019, Carbon pricing: charging for the harm of greenhouse gases covered about 20% of global emissions. The science is old. Joseph Fourier proposed in the 1820s that the air traps heat, the idea explained in The greenhouse effect: Earth's heat-trapping blanket. Climate change reached international public attention in the late 1980s.

  <!-- nature-hist-007 -->

- **The greenhouse effect: Earth's heat-trapping blanket**

  Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's surface would average −18 °C. With it, the average is about 15 °C. The greenhouse effect is the warming of a planet's surface that happens when heat-trapping gases in its atmosphere stop it losing heat to space. It works in two steps. Sunlight passes through these gases and heats Earth's surface. The warm surface then gives off longwave heat radiation, which the gases mostly absorb. Adding more of these gases through human activity strengthens the effect, which is called the enhanced greenhouse effect. That extra heat-trapping has been observed directly, and it is mainly due to more carbon dioxide in the air. The idea is nearly two centuries old. Joseph Fourier proposed the effect as early as 1824, and in 1856 Eunice Newton Foote showed that carbon dioxide strengthens the sun's warming of air. The name is a little misleading, though. Real greenhouses keep heat mainly by blocking moving air, not by absorbing radiation.

  <!-- nature-eco-161 -->

- **Greenhouse gases: the trace gases that warm the world**

  Nitrogen and oxygen make up 99% of dry air, yet they barely absorb heat radiation. Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, under 0.1% of the air, do. A greenhouse gas is a gas in an atmosphere that traps heat and so raises the surface temperature of a planet such as Earth. It absorbs the heat radiation the planet gives off, and that produces the greenhouse effect. Water vapour causes 41–67% of the effect, but human activity does not directly change its global level. Most of the carbon dioxide people add comes from burning fossil fuels, plus cement, fertilizer and land-use change such as deforestation. Emissions reached an all-time high of 53.6±5.2 Gt CO2e per year over 2014–2023. That unit counts every gas by the amount of carbon dioxide that would warm as much, as Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases explains. In 2022 the IPCC warned that emissions must peak before 2025 and fall 43% by 2030 for a good chance of limiting warming to 1.5 °C.

  <!-- nature-eco-162 -->

- **Greenhouse gas emissions: who emits, and how much**

  Global emissions run at about 50 Gt a year, and the estimate for 2024 was 57.7 Gt CO2eq. Greenhouse gas emissions are releases of greenhouse gases from human activities, which strengthen the greenhouse effect and drive climate change. Carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and natural gas is the main cause. By sector, the power sector contributes about 27%, transport 15%, and industrial energy and agriculture 11% each. Emissions began rising with fossil-fuelled industry around 1750 and grew rapidly after about 1950. China emits the most each year, followed by the United States, which emits more per person. Average emissions of 4.9 tonnes per person a year are over twice the 2.3 tonnes consistent with the 1.5 °C goal. There is one hopeful sign: 2015 was the first year with both global economic growth and falling carbon emissions.

  <!-- nature-eco-163 -->

- **Carbon dioxide: the gas at the center of the story**

  In 2026 the air held 432 ppm of carbon dioxide, or 0.0432%. That is a 54% rise from the 280 ppm of the 10,000 years before the mid-18th century. Carbon dioxide is a trace gas in Earth's air, yet it plays a central part in the greenhouse effect, the carbon cycle and photosynthesis. It is one of the three principal greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere, and today's concentration is the highest for 14 million years. The rise is caused by human activity, mainly burning fossil fuels, with cement making, deforestation and biomass burning adding more. Human emissions exceed what natural sinks can absorb, so about half of the carbon dioxide from fossil fuels stays in the air. By 2024 humans had emitted an estimated 2,650 gigatonnes since 1850, at 42 gigatonnes a year, and about 1,050 gigatonnes remain in the air. A projected 20–35% of the fossil carbon released so far will keep levels raised for many thousands of years. The rise is tracked at Mauna Loa, where regular measurements began in 1958, building on Dave Keeling's accurate flask samples of the 1950s.

  <!-- nature-eco-007 -->

- **Observed warming: what the thermometers show**

  The decade from 2016 to 2025 averaged 1.26 °C above the 1850–1900 baseline, and 2024 alone was more than 1.5 °C above it. Observed global warming is this rise in Earth's average surface temperature, measured since thermometer records reached global coverage around 1850. Datasets agree that surface temperature is rising by around 0.2 °C per decade. Scientists measure warming as a 20-year average, because natural variability can make a single year 0.2 °C warmer or colder. The path was not smooth. Up to 1970 there was little net warming, because sulfur dioxide pollution reflected sunlight and offset greenhouse warming. After that, warming sped up. Most of the extra heat is out of sight: over 90% of it since 1970 has gone into the ocean. Land has warmed almost twice as fast as the global average, and the Arctic three to four times faster than the rest of the world. Other signs include retreating glaciers, heavier rain, earlier spring flowering and thousands of species moving to cooler areas.

  <!-- nature-eco-011 -->

- **The effects of climate change, from reefs to economies**

  Damage climbs steeply with temperature: one comparison found total damages at 1.5 °C were 90% lower than at 3.66 °C. The effects of climate change are its well-documented and growing impacts on the natural world and on human societies. They include a warming trend, shifting rainfall and more weather extremes, with fiercer fires, thawing permafrost and spreading deserts. Some changes can become irreversible once tipping points are crossed. Oceans and ice sheets absorb most of the extra heat. That delays some effects, which then continue after surface temperatures settle, and makes Sea level rise a major long-term concern. Mountains, coral reefs and the Arctic are the most immediately threatened ecosystems. At 2 °C, about 10% of land species would become critically endangered. For people, food and water supplies, health, farming, fisheries and forestry are at risk, and heat stress will limit outdoor work in the tropics. The burden is unequal. Poor people, children and Indigenous peoples are especially at risk, while rich industrialised countries, which emitted most carbon dioxide, have more resources to adapt. Wealthy colder countries have felt little economic harm or even gained, while poor hot countries probably grew less than they would have.

  <!-- nature-eco-017 -->

- **Extreme weather: the far ends of the range**

  Since the 1920s, death tolls from natural disasters have fallen over 90 percent, even as population quadrupled. Extreme weather is unexpected, unusual, severe or unseasonal weather at the far ends of the range a place has seen in the past. The main types are heat waves, cold waves, droughts, and heavy rain or storms such as tropical cyclones. The IPCC counts an event as extreme if it is as rare as or rarer than the 10th or 90th percentile of observed weather. Severe weather, which threatens life and property, is one kind. Natural variability, such as El Niño, explains some extremes, but system-wide changes can raise their frequency or intensity. Warmer air holds more moisture, so storms can drop more rain and cause floods and landslides. Paving land and destroying wetlands, which store water naturally, can make floods worse. The toll on food is measurable: drought and extreme heat cut national cereal production by 10% over 1964–2007.

  <!-- nature-eco-001 -->

- **Radiative forcing: the push on Earth's energy balance**

  Radiative forcing is a measure of how much a change, such as more greenhouse gas, shifts the balance of energy flowing into and out of the atmosphere. It is measured in watts per square meter, usually averaged over the whole globe. A planet in radiative equilibrium, with as much energy leaving as arriving, has zero net forcing and a steady temperature. Greenhouse gases, aerosols, which are tiny particles in the air, surface reflectivity and the sun's output all change Earth's energy balance. The IPCC puts human-caused forcing in 2019 at 2.72 W/m2 relative to 1750, within a range of 1.96 to 3.48. Most comes from greenhouse gases, partly offset by aerosols. The 50% rise in carbon dioxide since 1750, as of 2020, corresponds to +2.17 W/m2. Its effect weakens as it accumulates. The forcing is roughly ΔF = 5.35 × ln((C0+ΔC)/C0) W/m2, so each further increase warms less.

  <!-- nature-eco-004 -->

- **Global warming potential: comparing gases with carbon dioxide**

  Over 20 years, methane traps 81.2 times as much heat as the same mass of carbon dioxide; over 100 years, only 27.9 times. Global warming potential, or GWP, measures how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a set period compared with the same mass of carbon dioxide. By definition carbon dioxide has a GWP of 1. A gas's GWP depends on how strongly it absorbs heat radiation, how fast it leaves the air, and the time frame chosen. Methane's two figures differ because it leaves the atmosphere much faster than carbon dioxide. Regulators usually use a 100-year time scale, and international agreements have adopted it as the standard. Since 1997, reporting under the Kyoto Protocol has used fixed IPCC values to convert gases into the common unit described in Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases. Other metrics include the global temperature change potential and GWP*, which treats short-lived pollutants such as methane differently.

  <!-- nature-eco-159 -->

- **Climate feedbacks: how warming amplifies or tames itself**

  Climate change feedbacks are processes set off by an initial warming that either amplify it, called positive feedbacks, or dampen it, called negative feedbacks. The main amplifiers are water vapour, melting ice, which leaves a darker surface behind, and the net effect of clouds. The main balancing mechanism is simple: a warmer surface gives off more heat to space. The Arctic shows the amplifiers at work. Shrinking snow and sea ice make the surface darker, speeding Arctic warming and helping thaw permafrost, which releases methane and carbon dioxide. Carbon sinks respond too. Land and oceans have absorbed about half of human carbon dioxide. That share could rise to about 70% if emissions fall, but drop below 40% if they rise sharply. Feedbacks are expected to become more positive as emissions continue, raising the Climate sensitivity: the warming from doubled carbon dioxide. Uncertainty about feedbacks, especially clouds, is the main reason computer models of the climate disagree on how much warming a given amount of emissions causes.

  <!-- nature-eco-014 -->

- **The main greenhouse gases and how long they linger**

  Water vapour causes about 50% of Earth's natural greenhouse effect and clouds about 25%, yet neither counts as a driver of climate change. The main greenhouse gases are the ones that do most of the heat-trapping in Earth's atmosphere: water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, methane and nitrous oxide, plus clouds. Without this natural effect, Earth's surface would average about −18 °C instead of around 15 °C. Water vapour and clouds change with temperature, so scientists treat them as feedbacks. Carbon dioxide, which causes about 20% of the effect, changes independently of temperature. So do ozone in the lower atmosphere, the industrial chemicals called CFCs, and nitrous oxide. These count as external forcings. Human emissions in 2019 equalled 59 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide: 75% was carbon dioxide, 18% methane, 4% nitrous oxide and 2% fluorinated gases. Methane comes from livestock, wetlands, rice, landfills, coal mining and oil and gas. Nitrous oxide comes mostly from microbes breaking down fertilizer. Lifetimes differ widely. Methane lasts about 12 years in the air on average, while carbon dioxide lasts much longer. In the IPCC table, nitrous oxide lasts 121 years with a 100-year GWP of 265, and some fluorinated gases are far stronger, such as SF6 at 23,500. By 2022, carbon dioxide had risen about 50% and methane 164% since 1750.

  <!-- nature-eco-009 -->

- **Fingerprints: how scientists pin warming on people**

  The sun is not to blame. Its energy reaching Earth has shown no upward trend since 1880, and the upper atmosphere is cooling rather than warming. Scientists identify the causes of recent warming by comparing the fingerprints of each possible cause with observed patterns. Natural cycles such as El Niño cause short-term spikes and dips. Longer changes come from external forcings: greenhouse gases, the sun, volcanoes and Earth's orbit. Volcanic carbon dioxide equals less than 1% of human emissions, and natural forcings have had negligible effect on temperature trends since the Industrial Revolution. That leaves human activity, mainly burning coal, oil and gas, which has raised greenhouse gas levels. Some human effects cool. Aerosols from air pollution have a smaller cooling effect, and changes in land use have so far slightly cooled the planet by making surfaces more reflective. Natural sinks absorb part of each year's emissions: land removes about 29%, and the ocean absorbed 20 to 30% over the last two decades.

  <!-- nature-eco-013 -->

- **Climate models: simulating the planet**

  A climate model represents the physical, chemical and biological processes that shape the climate system, and it is used to project future warming. Models are tested by checking how well they reproduce present and past climates. They are not perfect: past models underestimated how fast Arctic ice would shrink and rainfall would increase. Some models add population, economic growth and energy use to produce emission scenarios, which feed physical and carbon cycle models. Depending on the scenario, they give carbon dioxide concentrations from 380 to 1400 ppm.

  <!-- nature-eco-015 -->

- **Climate sensitivity: the warming from doubled carbon dioxide**

  Double the carbon dioxide in the air, and how much hotter does Earth get? Climate sensitivity is the answer. Doubling carbon dioxide gives a forcing of about 3.7 W/m2, which without feedbacks would cause roughly 1 °C of warming. But warming triggers feedbacks, such as melting ice and more water vapour, whose strength is not known exactly. In 1990 the IPCC put equilibrium sensitivity between 1.5 and 4.5 °C. Observations and physics now give a very likely range of 2.3 to 4.7 °C. The number carries a large price tag. The cost of cutting emissions depends on how fast carbon neutrality is needed, so sensitivity has large economic and policy consequences. One study suggests that halving the uncertainty in the transient climate response, a shorter-term version of the measure, could save trillions of dollars. If sensitivity is high, the Paris goal of well below 2 °C cannot be met, at least temporarily.

  <!-- nature-eco-158 -->

- **Projected warming: what the coming decades may bring**

  The IPCC expects the 20-year average to pass +1.5 °C in the early 2030s. Projected future warming is the estimate of how much hotter Earth will get, and it depends mainly on future greenhouse gas emissions. By 2100 warming is very likely to reach 1.0–1.8 °C with very low emissions, 2.1–3.5 °C with intermediate emissions, or 3.3–5.7 °C with very high emissions. In the intermediate and high scenarios, warming continues past 2100. The remaining carbon dioxide that can still be emitted for a given temperature limit, the Carbon budget, comes from modelling the carbon cycle and climate sensitivity. UNEP says a 50% chance of staying below 2.0 °C allows 900 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide after 2023. That is about 16 years of current emissions.

  <!-- nature-eco-012 -->

- **Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases**

  Two tonnes of a gas with a global warming potential of 100 count as 200 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, or CO2e. That is the arithmetic of the unit: the mass of carbon dioxide that would warm the Earth as much as a given mass of another greenhouse gas. It gives one common scale for the climate effects of different gases. It is calculated as the gas's global warming potential times its mass. Values depend on the time scale chosen, usually 100 or 20 years. The unit matters for money, because carbon markets and Carbon tax schemes price emissions per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.

  <!-- nature-eco-160 -->

- **What extreme weather costs economies**

  A 2023 study put the cost of climate-driven extreme weather at about US$2.86 trillion over 2000–2019, roughly US$143 billion a year. The economic cost of extreme weather is the monetary loss such events cause to economies. In 2011 the IPCC estimated that annual losses since 1980 ranged from a few billion to above US$200 billion, peaking in 2005, the year of Hurricane Katrina. These figures understate the harm. Losses of lives, cultural heritage and ecosystem services are hard to put a price on, so loss estimates reflect them poorly. The risk is widely felt: in the 2023–2024 World Economic Forum risk survey, 66 percent of respondents named extreme weather a top risk.

  <!-- nature-eco-002 -->

- **Water vapour feedback: warming that breeds more warming**

  Water vapour causes 41–67% of the greenhouse effect, yet people do not directly change its global level. It stays in the air only about nine days, so local changes such as irrigation have little global effect. Temperature controls it instead. A law of physics, the Clausius–Clapeyron relation, means warmer air holds more water vapour per unit volume. That creates the water vapour feedback: warming lets the air hold more water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which adds further warming.

  <!-- nature-eco-010 -->

- **Climate change and the world's food supply**

  Disasters from extreme weather caused food production losses estimated at US$123 billion in 2025, 5% of global agricultural GDP. Climate change threatens people's ability to grow, reach and rely on enough food. The causes include higher carbon dioxide, heat, changed rainfall, more extreme events, and shifting pests and diseases. Climate change is projected to weaken the food supply on every front, affecting how much food exists, its price and quality, and how stable the supply is. The sea is affected too. Ocean biomass is expected to fall by about 5% per degree of warming, hitting tropical seas hardest.

  <!-- nature-eco-019 -->

- **The economic sectors most exposed to climate**

  Climate-sensitive sectors are the parts of the economy most exposed to climate change, because they depend directly on weather: farming, fishing, forestry, tourism and energy. Thermal power plants need cooling water and run less efficiently when hot, while hydropower suffers when river flows fall. Heat, lower water flow and changed rainfall could cut total energy production by 7% a year by the end of the century. Insurance premiums are rising, and Munich Re warned in 2019 that home insurance could become unaffordable for average-income households. Above 1.5 °C of warming, tourism and outdoor work may reach the limits of how far they can adapt.

  <!-- nature-eco-020 -->

- **How climate change harms human health**

  Climate change harms health in many ways, from heat illness and worse air to disease spread and extreme weather. Longer exposure to high temperatures can cause heat illness and heat-related deaths. Diseases spread by mosquitoes and ticks, such as dengue fever and malaria, may become more common in some regions, as may waterborne diseases. Lower crop yields can raise food prices and cause undernutrition, and clean water supplies can shrink. Together these can increase poverty, migration, violent conflict and mental health problems.

  <!-- nature-eco-018 -->

- **Melting ice sheets and the long rise of the seas**

  Losing the whole West Antarctic ice sheet would raise sea level by over 5 metres. Ice sheet decline is the melting of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, which will keep raising sea levels over long time-scales. A partial collapse in West Antarctica could be abrupt and irreversible for centuries or longer. Sustained warming between 1 °C and 4 °C would melt the Greenland ice sheet entirely over millennia, adding 7 m to sea levels. The melting feeds itself. As the ice surface melts it gets lower and warmer, a self-reinforcing feedback that can make the loss irreversible.

  <!-- nature-eco-021 -->

- **CO2 fertilization: more carbon, faster photosynthesis**

  Earth's land has greened markedly since the early 1980s. Part of the reason is the CO2 fertilization effect: the speeding-up of plant photosynthesis, with less water lost through leaves, caused by more carbon dioxide in the air. It has been reported to cause 44% of the increase in gross primary productivity since the 2000s. Its strength depends on plant species, temperature and the water and nutrients available. But faster photosynthesis does not always mean more growth or carbon storage, and plants are unlikely to cut carbon dioxide levels much over the next century.

  <!-- nature-eco-008 -->

- **Extreme event attribution: weighing climate's role**

  Was that heat wave caused by climate change? A single extreme event generally cannot be blamed on any one cause. Extreme event attribution instead works out how far causes such as climate change explain trends in extreme weather events. Much of the work relies on climate models, which are vital but only approximations.

  <!-- nature-eco-003 -->

- **The climate sensitivity parameter: turning forcing into degrees**

  The climate sensitivity parameter is a number, in kelvin per W/m2, that links a radiative forcing to the eventual change in surface temperature. A kelvin is the same size as a degree Celsius. The parameter is the inverse of the climate feedback parameter. A value of about 0.8 gives about 1.6 K of warming since 1750 from carbon dioxide rising from 278 to 405 ppm, a forcing of 2.0 W/m2. The same value predicts a further 1.4 K of warming if carbon dioxide doubled from its pre-industrial level.

  <!-- nature-eco-005 -->

- **Earth's albedo: the share of sunlight bounced back**

  Earth reflects about 30% of incoming sunlight back to space, giving Earth's albedo a value of 0.30 on annual average. Clouds, aerosols, oceans, land, snow, ice and vegetation do the reflecting, and Earth absorbs the other 70%. Human changes push both ways. Deforestation typically raises reflectivity, while Arctic ice loss lowers it.

  <!-- nature-eco-006 -->

- **Earth system sensitivity: warming over millennia**

  Earth system sensitivity measures the long-term warming from doubled carbon dioxide, including slow feedbacks, such as melting ice sheets and changing vegetation, that take millennia. These slower feedbacks make it larger than equilibrium climate sensitivity, possibly twice as large. It is estimated from Earth's geological history, so future values are highly uncertain.

  <!-- nature-eco-016 -->

### Biodiversity and its loss

Every change people make to land and water reaches the living things that depend on it. This chapter follows those changes, from forests cleared for farms, ranches and towns to habitats broken into small, isolated patches. It traces how fertile land wears out, how dry regions slide toward desert, and how fish, forests and groundwater are taken faster than they can renew. The end point is loss: species that fade from one area, and species that vanish when their last member dies. Against this stands nature conservation, the movement to save species, restore habitats and protect the variety of life.

- **Cattle outweigh wild mammals: measuring the human footprint**

  Domesticated cattle and pigs now outweigh all the world's wild mammals by 14 to 1. The world's chickens weigh three times as much as all wild birds. Numbers like these measure human impact on the environment: the changes people cause, directly or indirectly, to physical surroundings, ecosystems, biodiversity and natural resources. People have changed their surroundings ever since they first spread across the Earth. The impacts grew sharply after the Industrial Revolution of the 1700s. A 2018 study found 87% of the oceans altered by people, along with 77% of land outside Antarctica. Only 23% of the land was left as wilderness. Global Footprint Network estimates put humanity's demand 70% above what all the planet's ecosystems can regenerate. The damage is linked to growing populations, rapid economic growth, heavy consumption, pollution and forest clearing. It is also linked to harvesting resources faster than they renew, the subject of Overexploitation: taking more than nature can replace. The results include global warming, ocean acidification, the mass loss of species and the collapse of whole ecological systems, a form of Environmental degradation: 70% of the land, already altered. At sea, a 2019 report by the panel described in IPBES blames one driver above all. Catching fish faster than they can breed is the main cause of the mass loss of ocean species.

  <!-- nature-eco-129 -->

- **Habitat destruction, the leading cause of species loss**

  The tropics once held about 16 million square kilometers of rainforest. Less than 9 million remain. That shrinkage is habitat destruction. A natural home for wildlife, explained in Habitat: the place a species can live, becomes unable to support the species that live there, so they move away or die. It is the leading cause worldwide of lost biodiversity and of species dying out. People cause it through resource use, agriculture, industry, urban sprawl, mining, logging and fishing with trawl nets. A habitat need not be bulldozed to fail. Degradation, fragmentation and pollution can collapse it without outright destroying it. When habitat goes, the land can support fewer native animals, and each Population: one species, one place, one time declines, sometimes until it disappears. Endemic species with small ranges suffer most because they live nowhere else. For people, the deepest cost is lost ecosystem services such as regulating climate, pollinating plants and managing water. Poor people suffer most. Wealthier people and countries can pay to keep receiving more than their share of natural resources.

  <!-- nature-eco-041 -->

- **Deforestation: trading forest for farms, ranches and towns**

  Forests cover about 31% of Earth's land. That is one-third less than before agriculture spread, and half of that loss came in the last century. Deforestation is the clearing of a forest or stand of trees so the land can serve a non-forest use, such as farms, ranches or towns. It is one of the main forms of Habitat destruction, the leading cause of species loss. Between 2015 and 2020 it ran at an estimated 10 million hectares a year, down from 16 million a year in the 1990s. Agriculture is by far the main direct cause. In 2025 the spread of cropland and pasture drove nearly 90% of global deforestation. Logging, urbanization, mining and climate-driven wildfires add to it. Clearing destroys habitat, so it brings loss of biodiversity, species dying out, local climate change and the displacement of forest peoples. It also cuts the carbon forests take up, weakening their role in slowing climate change. Cleared regions often suffer soil erosion and the slide toward desert described in Desertification: how dry land turns to desert. The costs can dwarf the gains. In Brazil, economic losses from deforestation could reach around 317 billion dollars a year, about 7 times the value of the commodities it produces.

  <!-- nature-eco-053 -->

- **Extinction: when the last of a species dies**

  More than 99.9% of all the species that have ever lived are gone. The average species lasts 1–10 million years. Extinction is the end of a species, reached when its last member dies. The end can come before that last death, though. A species is functionally extinct once its few survivors can no longer reproduce and recover. The exact moment is hard to pin down over a large range, so extinction is usually declared after the fact. Life on Earth has passed through at least five mass extinctions. Fossil studies confirm that climate change has caused extinctions. A 2003 review predicted that 15–37% of land species would be 'committed to extinction' by 2050 because of climate change. Humans have become an extra cause, both as a new mega-predator and by moving animals and plants around the world. Today the main human cause is habitat degradation, and agriculture is the main cause of habitat degradation worldwide. In 2014 a special edition of the journal Science declared a widespread consensus that humans are driving mass species extinctions.

  <!-- nature-eco-105 -->

- **Biodiversity loss: a decline far faster than nature's pace**

  Between 1970 and 2016, monitored animal populations fell by an average of 68%, the WWF reported. The figure covered 4,400 animal species and nearly 21,000 populations. Biodiversity loss is the decline of living variety. It happens when species vanish from Earth entirely, as Extinction: when the last of a species dies describes, or when they shrink or disappear from a particular area. To measure it at a site, scientists record the number of species present, a count explained in Species richness: counting how many kinds live here, and how it changes over time. The current global rate is estimated at 100 to 1000 times the natural background rate at which species die out, set out in The background extinction rate: nature's normal pace. All of today's loss has been attributed to human activities. Habitat destruction, often for farming, is currently a bigger driver than climate change. The loss is temporary if the damage can be reversed, for example by repairing ecosystems as Ecological restoration describes, and permanent if it cannot. Damaged ecosystems provide poorer ecosystem services, such as pollinating crops, cleaning air and water, decomposing waste and supplying goods from forests. Governments have struggled to respond. Of 20 worldwide targets for biodiversity set in 2010, covered in Aichi Biodiversity Targets, only six were partially achieved by 2020.

  <!-- nature-eco-035 -->

- **Invasive species: newcomers that harm their new home**

  An introduced species usually starts small. It has to persist at low densities first, and sometimes it takes several introductions before it takes hold. An invasive species is one that people have carried to a new place, where it harms the environment it has entered. Invasive species are the subset of established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity. Invasions happen naturally too, but human help has greatly increased their rate, scale and geographic range. Biological invasion is now one of the five top drivers of Biodiversity loss: a decline far faster than nature's pace worldwide, and it is growing with tourism and globalization. Successful invaders share common traits: fast growth, rapid reproduction, association with humans and a record of earlier successful invasions. Scientific consensus holds that their effects on biodiversity are mainly negative. Some can still provide habitat or food for other organisms. The label itself is slippery, since "invasive" is poorly defined and often subjective.

  <!-- nature-eco-026 -->

- **Nature conservation: the movement to save what remains**

  The forester described in Gifford Pinchot coined the term 'conservation' in 1907. Nature conservation is the ethic and movement devoted to saving species from extinction, keeping and restoring habitats, enhancing ecosystem services and protecting biodiversity. Its goals range widely: conserving habitat, preventing deforestation, keeping soil organic matter, halting extinctions, reducing the overharvesting of fish and slowing climate change. Its early choices were shaped by money. The first parks often protected 'worthless lands' of little commercial interest, such as alpine and dry habitats. As of 2018, 15% of land and 7.3% of the oceans were protected. Many environmentalists aim to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030. Money and management still lag behind. Reserves in developing countries, home to perhaps 70–80% of the world's species, get very little effective management. Private fundraising is not enough to pay for managing the more than 10% of the world that is legally protected.

  <!-- nature-eco-140 -->

- **Overexploitation: taking more than nature can replace**

  About 40% of the bird species lost since 1500 were affected by overexploitation. The word means harvesting a resource that renews itself, such as fish, forests, groundwater or wildlife, faster than it can replenish, to the point of diminishing returns. A Population: one species, one place, one time is overexploited when it is harvested faster than its natural births and deaths can make up. That can wipe out populations or whole species. Ecologists count it among the five main activities threatening biodiversity worldwide, and it threatens one-third of endangered vertebrates. Excluding edible fish, the illegal trade in wildlife is valued at $10 billion a year. The same logic applies beyond animals. An underground water store is overexploited when water is pumped out faster than it recharges, and it is then said to be overdrafted. Forests are overexploited when logging outpaces the regrowth of trees. Harvesting can be sustainable if it stays within limits, as well-managed fishing grounds show. Why do people overharvest at all? Hardin's tragedy of the commons explains how people sharing a resource, each acting in self-interest, can overexploit and destroy it.

  <!-- nature-eco-063 -->

- **Habitat fragmentation: when one wild place becomes many islands**

  Keep 10% of a habitat as one unbroken remnant and, as a rough rule, half its biodiversity is lost. Habitat fragmentation is the breaking up of a large, continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches. It splits populations and degrades ecosystems. Five changes come bundled together. There is less total habitat and less interior compared with edge. Fragments are cut off from each other, one patch splits into several, and patches get smaller on average. People cause it by clearing native vegetation for farms, rural development, cities and hydroelectric reservoirs. Dams and water diversions do the same to rivers and lakes. Fragmentation consistently reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75%. It also impairs ecosystem functions such as biomass production and nutrient cycling. Small, isolated populations are fragile. Minor swings in climate or resources that a large population would absorb can wipe them out. The damage is slow to show, and experiments find biodiversity and ecosystem functioning still declining 20 or more years later. Linking fragments with corridors of native vegetation, bridges or underpasses can ease isolation, as Wildlife corridors: reconnecting cut-off populations explains. It does not restore interior habitat.

  <!-- nature-nbs-115 -->

- **Land degradation: when land loses its power to produce**

  Every year around 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded. Land degradation is the process by which land becomes less healthy and productive, through human activity or natural conditions. Unsustainable land management is often the main cause, and over 60% of human-induced degradation occurs on farmland. The UN estimates that about 30% of land is degraded worldwide, with about 3.2 billion people living in degrading areas. A major 2005 global review, The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: a health check for the planet, defined it more narrowly, as the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of dry lands. Its effects spread outward. It lowers crop yields and ecosystem diversity, leaves land more exposed to floods and droughts, and releases greenhouse gases. Degraded land is also less resilient, so further shocks can drive still more degradation. The flip side is hopeful. Reversing 10% of human-induced cropland degradation could feed an additional 154 million people a year.

  <!-- nature-eco-060 -->

- **Desertification: how dry land turns to desert**

  Dry regions cover about 40–41% of Earth's land and are home to more than 2 billion people, at least 90% of them in developing countries. Desertification is the gradual degradation of fertile land in those regions into desert, through natural processes and human activities. It is the harshest form of Land degradation: when land loses its power to produce. The immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation. Drought, climate shifts, tillage, overgrazing and cutting trees for fuel or building all strip it away. Bare dry soil then blows or washes off, leaving infertile layers that bake into unproductive hardpan. Some 10–20% of dry regions are already degraded, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification. Climate change is expected to expand dry regions from 38% of continental land in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by 2100. Remedies exist: shelter belts and woodlots, planted lines and blocks of trees, fix soil and cut erosion. Yet the economics can work against them. Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when they benefit society and the environment.

  <!-- nature-eco-091 -->

- **Genetic diversity: a species' insurance against change**

  Koalas carry little genetic variety, and that weakness is linked to their failure to fight off chlamydia. Genetic diversity is the total variety of inherited characteristics within a species. It lets populations adapt to changing environments, because some individuals are more likely to carry variants suited to new conditions. Lower diversity leaves a population more exposed to changes such as climate change or new diseases. Small populations lose diversity by chance, a process called genetic drift, and through inbreeding. A bottleneck, a sudden crash in numbers, can cut it rapidly. Mutation and gene flow, such as pollen carried by wind or migrating birds, add new variants. A 2007 study found that diversity within species and diversity among species depend on each other. In farm animals, the loss of genetic diversity has been attributed to the spread of markets and economic globalization.

  <!-- nature-eco-118 -->

- **Species richness: counting how many kinds live here**

  The simplest measure of nature's variety is a headcount of kinds. Species richness is the number of different species in a community, landscape or region. It ignores how common each species is. That makes it different from a fuller measure that also weighs how evenly individuals are shared among species, explained in Species diversity: richness and evenness combined. Larger samples tend to contain more species, so richness values can be compared only when sampling effort is standardized. Many groups of organisms have the most species in the tropics, so richness changes with latitude. Conservationists often use it to judge a habitat's value, but it is blind to which species are present. Areas with many endemic or rare species usually count for more. How richness relates to an ecosystem's productivity is unsettled: studies disagree, and no global consensus has emerged.

  <!-- nature-eco-150 -->

- **Wildlife corridors: reconnecting cut-off populations**

  In a South Carolina experiment, butterflies were two to four times more likely to move to a patch linked by a corridor than to unlinked patches. A wildlife corridor is an area that links wildlife populations cut off from each other by farms, cities, roads and other development. It eases the harm of Habitat fragmentation: when one wild place becomes many islands, a major threat to biodiversity. When animals can move between populations, isolated groups avoid inbreeding and the loss of genetic diversity, and pollen and seeds spread. Corridors joining warmer and cooler habitat help species shift their ranges as the climate changes. They can be continuous strips of habitat or 'stepping stones' of small separate patches, and they include river zones and road crossings. Success needs a shared vision among stakeholders, clear rules and incentive programs to bring in private landowners. Corridors can also lead wildlife into settlements, causing conflicts such as crop raiding and attacks on livestock.

  <!-- nature-eco-152 -->

- **Abundance: how common a species is**

  In most ecosystems a few species are common and many are rare. Abundance measures how well represented a species is in a particular ecosystem, usually counted as individuals per sample. Relative species abundance compares one species with the others around it, and both measures feed into biodiversity calculations. Counting methods vary. Large animals are counted with spotlights, tracks and even roadkill, while plants are often measured by the share of a plot they cover. Abundant species tend to be generalists that use many resources, and rare ones specialists with narrow needs. Abundant species also produce more colonizing offspring. That loop yields widespread core species and scarce satellite species.

  <!-- nature-eco-069 -->

- **Endemism: species found in one place only**

  Charles Darwin first used the word "endemic" in 1872, for a species restricted to one place. Endemism is the state of a species being found naturally in only one defined place, such as a single island, country or region. Its opposite is a cosmopolitan distribution, a global or widespread range. Isolation breeds endemics, so remote islands such as Hawaii, the Galápagos and Socotra hold many. Endemic does not mean rare, and rare does not mean endemic. Small ranges do raise the stakes: endemics face greater risk than widespread species from habitat loss and fast climate change. Conservation biology uses endemism to measure a place's biodiversity, judge extinction risk and set priorities, the idea behind Biodiversity hotspots: small areas, most of the species. Some scientists argue it is a poor guide, because high-endemism areas do not consistently match high biodiversity or high threat.

  <!-- nature-eco-103 -->

- **Forests and climate: a feedback loop of loss**

  Standing forests in the tropics help cool the global average temperature by more than 1 °C. Clearing them works the other way. Changing how land is used, mainly through deforestation, is the second largest human source of carbon dioxide after burning fossil fuels. The emissions come from burning the wood and leaves of forests and from decomposing plant material and soil carbon. As of 2019, deforestation caused about 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year. That service is weakening. In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of heat, drought and deforestation. The link runs both ways, as a self-amplifying loop. More tree loss means more warming, which brings more wildfires, pests and storms, and so more tree loss. Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and the collapse of forest ecosystems.

  <!-- nature-eco-066 -->

- **Poaching: illegal hunting and its ripple effects**

  As many as 35,000 African elephants are killed each year for their ivory. Poaching is the illegal hunting or capture of wild animals, and since the 1980s also the illegal harvesting of wild plants. It is an unlawful form of Overexploitation: taking more than nature can replace. In rural Africa the main motives are a lack of jobs and limited farming potential, and selling wild meat to cities brings cash. International markets draw organized gangs, and crime syndicates traffic body parts abroad. Poachers treat the edges of reserves as open-access resources, free for anyone to take. That shrinks the reserves' effective size, and wildlife tourism loses income. Removing large animals also changes how seeds are spread, so large-seeded trees come to dominate and small-seeded plants vanish locally. A UN goal, Sustainable Development Goal 15, calls for action against the poaching and trafficking of protected species. The label is contested: critics argue it has been used to criminalize Indigenous peoples' traditional subsistence hunting.

  <!-- nature-eco-144 -->

- **The 2019 global assessment: a million species at risk**

  Of an estimated 8 million animal and plant species, 1 million are threatened with extinction. That was the headline of the Global Assessment Report, whose summary for policymakers came out on 6 May 2019. It was produced by the panel described in IPBES. It reviews 50 years of change, drawing on over 15,000 scientific publications and Indigenous knowledge. It was the UN's first worldwide assessment of biodiversity since the 2005 review covered in The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: a health check for the planet. The threatened include 40% of amphibians and more than a third of marine mammals. Wild mammal biomass has fallen by 82%, while humans and their farm animals now make up 96% of all mammal biomass. Over the same 50 years the human population doubled and GDP per person quadrupled. The report ranked the drivers: changes in land and sea use, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive alien species. Pollinator loss threatens food worth $235 to $577 billion a year. The report urged countries not to fixate on economic growth and to shift government support away from industries that harm nature.

  <!-- nature-eco-123 -->

- **Diversity indices: boiling variety down to one number**

  Counting species tells only part of the story. A diversity index is a number that measures how many different types, usually species, a dataset or community contains, often weighted by how common each is. Indices summarize parts of biodiversity such as richness, evenness and dominance, so communities or sites are easy to compare. Richness, explained in Species richness: counting how many kinds live here, is a simple count of types. It is popular in ecology because data on abundance are often lacking. Abundance itself can be measured as numbers of individuals, biomass or coverage. The Shannon and Simpson indices also account for each type's share of the total. The same measures work outside ecology, for demographic groups or even letters of the alphabet.

  <!-- nature-eco-093 -->

- **Biodiversity hotspots: small areas, most of the species**

  Biodiversity hotspots cover just 2.4% of the planet's surface, yet they support nearly 60% of the world's plant, bird, mammal, reptile and amphibian species. A hotspot is a region with exceptionally high biodiversity, especially species found nowhere else, that is threatened by human activity. Norman Myers developed the idea in articles in 1988 and 1990, revised in 2000. The test is strict. A region must hold at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species, plants with veins that carry water, which is over 0.5% of the world total. It must also have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation. Globally, 36 zones qualify. Most are tropical, and only a small share of their land is protected. Critics note that the approach ignores the cost of conservation. It also ignores phylogenetic diversity, the variety of evolutionary lineages a place holds.

  <!-- nature-eco-081 -->

- **Bushmeat: wild meat, food security and vanishing species**

  As of 2016, 301 land mammal species were threatened with extinction by bushmeat hunting, including every species of pangolin. Bushmeat is meat from wild animals hunted for people to eat, especially in Africa. For poor rural communities in the humid forests of the tropics, it is a main source of animal protein and income. The trade in West and Central Africa was estimated at 1–5 million tonnes a year around the turn of the 21st century. Hunting for a family's own use in large landscapes can be sustainable. Market hunting is another matter. It threatens large, slow-breeding species, a clear case of Overexploitation: taking more than nature can replace. Logging roads and trucks give hunters access to remote forests and carry the meat to towns. The phrase "bushmeat crisis", coined in 2007, names the double threat of vanishing food supplies and wildlife extinctions. Suggested remedies include affordable alternative protein, giving communities rights over wildlife, and enforcing the protection of reserves.

  <!-- nature-eco-084 -->

- **Why forests are over-cleared: the benefits no one pays for**

  A forest's timber has a price, but many of its other benefits do not. Many important forest functions have no markets, and hence no economic value readily apparent to forest owners or the communities that depend on them. This gap, a case of Missing markets: trades that would help but never happen, is the economic reason forests are over-cleared. Owners see more profit in converting a forest than in keeping it. Yet short-term gains from converting forest or overharvesting wood typically cost long-term income and biological productivity. Studies found poverty and agricultural rent, the income land earns from farming, to be principal factors behind deforestation. Proposed policies would align economic activity in critical forests with their value for ecosystem services and climate mitigation. Their tools include certification, traceability, which tracks where products come from, and the trade charges described in Eco-tariff.

  <!-- nature-eco-056 -->

- **Habitat conservation: protecting the places species live**

  Repairing a damaged ecosystem is thought to cost far more than conserving it in the first place. Habitat conservation is the management of habitats to protect and restore them, and to stop species from going extinct, being fragmented or losing range. It is a central practice of Nature conservation: the movement to save what remains. Natural habitats provide ecosystem services, such as timber from forests and clean water from streams. Conserving them can also pay through tourism and time spent outdoors. Putting a value on conserving different areas is often criticized as too utilitarian, judging nature only by its usefulness. Priority usually goes to Biodiversity hotspots: small areas, most of the species and to the homes of flagship, umbrella or at-risk species. Crops show what is at stake. Wild relatives of crops resist disease better, and the wild corn teosinte resists 4 corn diseases. Seed banks plus habitat conservation are therefore proposed to secure food supplies. Scientific uncertainty is handled by the approach described in Adaptive management, which gathers information and adjusts conservation plans over time.

  <!-- nature-eco-126 -->

- **Indirect drivers: the forces behind the bulldozer**

  A bulldozer clearing forest is the visible end of a long chain. Indirect drivers are the political, economic and social forces that give rise to the human activities that harm the environment. They include population, economic development, urbanization, technology and climate change. Direct drivers, such as mining, agriculture, urban infrastructure and transport, result from them. Together they shape Cattle outweigh wild mammals: measuring the human footprint. Consumption beyond what ecosystems can sustain can be measured with the tool described in Ecological footprint. Impact depends on lifestyle, affluence and pollution as much as on the raw number of people. Cultural values matter too: how a society views nature shapes how hard it works to preserve it. Blaming growing human numbers for environmental problems is controversial. Critics say it can unfairly blame poor people in the Global South.

  <!-- nature-eco-130 -->

- **HIPPO and the Evil Quartet: naming the drivers of loss**

  Edward O. Wilson boiled the problem down to one acronym, HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, human over-Population and Over-harvesting. Jared Diamond's version is an "Evil Quartet" of habitat destruction, overkill, introduced species and secondary extinctions. Both lists name the main human pressures behind Biodiversity loss: a decline far faster than nature's pace. Today's fuller list is habitat loss, land-use intensification, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change. Habitat destruction leads worldwide. At sea, a 2019 report by the panel described in IPBES found catching too many fish to be the main driver of mass extinction. Invasive species can drive natives extinct by outcompeting them, pushing them out of their role in the ecosystem, or interbreeding with them. The pressures also interact. In 2021 the same panel and the UN's climate science panel issued a joint report. It found that biodiversity loss and climate change must be tackled together, because they are inextricably linked.

  <!-- nature-eco-036 -->

- **Farming, the largest driver of biodiversity loss on land**

  As of 2023, about 38% of Earth's land surface was used for agriculture, the dominant use of land. That reach makes farming the largest single cause of biodiversity decline on land. As farmland expands and intensifies, it converts and degrades natural habitat, the process described in Habitat destruction, the leading cause of species loss. The 2019 global assessment described in The 2019 global assessment: a million species at risk found industrial agriculture to be the primary driver of biodiversity collapse. A 2014 UN outlook report estimated that agriculture causes 70% of projected biodiversity loss on land. Animal farming takes the biggest share of space. Livestock systems occupy about 77% of agricultural land but provide less than 20% of the world's calories. The pressure is set to grow. More than 17,000 species risk losing habitat by 2050 as farming expands to meet food needs. Diet is one lever. A global shift toward mostly plant-based diets would free land for restoring ecosystems and biodiversity.

  <!-- nature-eco-037 -->

- **The $423 billion bill for invasive species**

  The economic impact of invasive species was estimated to exceed $423 billion a year as of 2019. That cost has quadrupled every decade since 1970. It covers the money lost to damage from invasive species and the money spent on controlling them, a form of Economic cost: counting what you pass up. The costs split into direct production losses in farming and forestry and the costs of management. In the United States, estimated damage and control costs exceed $138 billion a year. In France, damage costs were nearly eight times higher than spending on management. Even these figures understate the bill. Valuing lost species and ecosystem services would raise it sharply. Some invaders bring benefits, such as invasive trees used in commercial forestry, but their returns are usually far smaller than their costs. Early detection and rapid response is often called the key to management. It helps only when reintroduction is rare and response is affordable.

  <!-- nature-eco-027 -->

- **Wildlife trade: a vast, poorly watched market**

  Global imports of wildlife products were worth US$187 billion in 2012, with fish and other catches from the sea and fresh water making up $113 billion. Wildlife trade is the exchange of products from wild animals or plants, taken from nature or raised in captivity, whether alive, dead or as parts. Legal trade is regulated by the agreement described in CITES, which has 184 member countries, called Parties. Illegal trade is one of the major illegal economic activities, comparable to drug and arms trafficking. Interpol puts it at $10 billion to $20 billion a year. Trade and other use are the second major threat to endangered mammals, and among the top ten threats to birds, amphibians and cycads. Live wildlife markets have been linked to outbreaks of diseases including COVID-19, H5N1 bird flu, SARS and mpox. The trade is poorly monitored, because customs codes record most wildlife imports only under broad categories. Legal trade can also help. Quotas on Florida alligators give an economic incentive to keep habitat.

  <!-- nature-eco-154 -->

- **Island biogeography: why small, remote places hold fewer species**

  Simberloff and Wilson once cleared every arthropod, the group of jointed-legged animals that includes insects, from small Florida islands of salt-tolerant trees, the coastal forests described in Mangroves: trees that live in the sea's edge. Within a year the islands were recolonized, nearer islands fastest. Island biogeography studies what controls the number of species and how they diversify in isolated natural communities. Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson started the field in the 1960s. Its theory holds that an island's species count is set by a balance between new arrivals and extinction. Remote islands receive fewer immigrants. Larger islands have more habitat and a lower chance of species dying out by bad luck. An 'island' can be any patch of suitable habitat surrounded by unsuitable land, such as a mountaintop, a woodland or a park amid development. Seeing reserves as habitat islands raised fears that they would lose species. That fear led to wildlife corridors and to a vigorous debate over how reserves should be laid out, the subject of One big reserve or several small ones? The SLOSS debate.

  <!-- nature-eco-134 -->

- **Defaunation: the quiet emptying of animal life**

  More than 50 percent of all wildlife is estimated to have been lost in the last 40 years. Defaunation is the global, local or functional loss of animal populations or species from ecological communities. Unlike extinction, it counts falling animal numbers as well as disappearing species. Growing human numbers and better harvesting technology have stripped large vertebrates from many communities. Large mammals are especially vulnerable because they need large home ranges. Invasive species matter too: over 50% of extinct animal species with a known cause were affected by them. Tropical regions such as the Brazilian Amazon, the Congo Basin and Indonesia are hit hardest. The losses are old as well as new. Links in the food webs of land mammals have fallen by 53% over the past 130,000 years as humans expanded. Emptier communities work less well. Defaunation can weaken services such as nutrient cycling, decomposition, pollinating crops, controlling pests and keeping water clean.

  <!-- nature-eco-050 -->

- **Conservation status: rating a species' risk of extinction**

  Counting the animals left is not enough to judge a species' danger. Conservation status is a rating of whether a species or other group still exists and how likely it is to go extinct in the near future. Assessments weigh population trends, breeding success and known threats, not just how many individuals remain. Two international systems exist, run by the IUCN and by the trade agreement described in CITES. Others work at regional, national and local levels. The best known is the IUCN's list described in IUCN Red List. It sorts species into nine groups using criteria such as rate of decline, population size, range and fragmentation. Three categories, critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable, together count as "threatened". The rest run from Extinct and Extinct in the Wild to Near Threatened, Least Concern and Data Deficient. The trade agreement, in force since 1975, aims to ensure that trade between countries in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival. Guides that help shoppers choose seafood rate species in a similar way. They also weigh fishing harms such as catching unwanted animals by accident and dragging heavy nets along the seabed.

  <!-- nature-eco-087 -->

- **Endangered species and the bald eagle's comeback**

  In 1963 the United States had just 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles. By 2020 it had 71,400, thanks to habitat protection, legal protection and a ban on the pesticide DDT. An endangered species is one at very high risk of going extinct in the near future, worldwide or in a particular region. On the IUCN's Red List, described in Conservation status: rating a species' risk of extinction, "Endangered" sits between "Vulnerable" and "Critically Endangered". The criteria are specific. One is a population that falls 20% within five years and has fewer than 2,500 mature individuals left. Another is a decline of 50% to 70% over 10 years or three generations, whichever is longer. Species become endangered mainly through habitat loss and loss of genetic variation. In 2026 the Red List named 49,500 species worldwide as threatened with extinction. Many nations respond by banning hunting or harvest, restricting development or setting land aside as reserves.

  <!-- nature-eco-099 -->

- **Threatened species: the red-listed 40 percent**

  About 40% of the 40,177 species assessed under the IUCN's Red List criteria are listed as threatened, a total of 16,119. A threatened species is any animal, plant or fungus species vulnerable to extinction in the near future. The IUCN, the foremost authority, groups three categories as threatened: critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable, as Conservation status: rating a species' risk of extinction explains. Near threatened, least concern, not evaluated and data deficient species are not counted. Threatened species are also called red-listed species, after the IUCN's Red List of Threatened Species. The label reaches below whole species, too. Subspecies, populations and stocks can also be classed as threatened.

  <!-- nature-eco-151 -->

- **The background extinction rate: nature's normal pace**

  At nature's normal pace, one bird species would go extinct about every 400 years. The background extinction rate is the normal rate at which species go extinct through Earth's history, outside mass extinctions. It is roughly one extinction per million species-years. In other words, among a million species watched for a year, about one would vanish. Extinction is a normal part of evolution, and the background rate measures how often it happens naturally. At normal rates species typically last 5–10 million years, and mammal species about 1 million years on average. The rate is not fixed. It has fallen over the Phanerozoic, the current eon of abundant animal life, a decline linked to rising oxygen in the oceans. Its main use is as a yardstick, showing how much faster species are vanishing today.

  <!-- nature-eco-078 -->

- **Mass extinctions: when life's variety collapses**

  The end-Permian 'Great Dying' killed about 81% of marine species and an estimated 70% of land vertebrate species. It was the largest extinction event, or mass extinction: a widespread and rapid fall in the variety of life on Earth. Such events happen when extinctions outpace both the normal The background extinction rate: nature's normal pace and the rate at which new species form. Estimates of how many major ones occurred in the last 540 million years range from five to more than twenty. Large extinctions tend to follow when a biosphere already under long-term stress suffers a short-term shock. Scientists still debate the causes of each one. Afterward, usually only adaptable 'weedy' species survive, and new groups can take over the emptied niches. Research since 1982 concludes that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is under way, with extinctions over 1,000 times the background rate since 1900. It is driven by growing populations, economic growth and the overuse of nature's resources.

  <!-- nature-eco-112 -->

- **The Holocene extinction: the sixth great dying, caused by people**

  Species are now disappearing an estimated 100 to 1,000 times faster than the natural background rate. The Holocene extinction is this ongoing wave of extinctions of plants and animals, on land and at sea, caused by human activity in the current geological epoch. It is sometimes called the sixth extinction, after the five earlier mass extinctions described in Mass extinctions: when life's variety collapses. When the emphasis falls on human causes, it is also called the Anthropocene extinction. A 2023 study counted at least 73 animal genera, groups of closely related species, lost since 1500. It judged that rate 35 times higher than the background rate without human impacts. The 2019 assessment described in The 2019 global assessment: a million species at risk estimated that about one million species are at risk of extinction within decades because of human activities. The drivers include climate change, deforestation, the destruction of swamps and marshes, fishing too hard, ocean acidification, growing populations, economic growth and rising consumption, especially in affluent societies. Scientists broadly agree that habitat destruction, resource consumption and the elimination of species are the main human drivers. Beneath them lie two centuries of growth in population, in economic output and in consumption per person. Proposed remedies include shifting economic activity toward low-impact sectors, plant-based diets, and enlarging the areas protected on land and at sea.

  <!-- nature-eco-022 -->

- **Extinction debt: species doomed by losses already made**

  In the Azores, over 95% of native forest was destroyed in 600 years. More than half of the islands' arthropods are now thought committed to extinction, still alive but doomed. That is extinction debt: the future extinction of species already set in motion by past events such as habitat loss. It arises from time lags. Long-lived trees, for example, may survive for years after new trees can no longer be produced. Habitat fragmentation and habitat destruction are its best-known drivers, because they cut off species' ability to recolonize other patches. The debt is most likely in long-lived species and in specialists with narrow habitat needs. Tilman, May, Lehman and Nowak first used the term in 1994. It is likened to the 'climate commitment' of warming that continues after emissions stop. Modeling suggests that 80–90% of the extinctions due to past Amazon deforestation have yet to happen. Protecting today's habitat may not be enough. Still, the long delay gives time for restoration to prevent losses.

  <!-- nature-eco-110 -->

- **How climate change spreads infectious disease**

  Dengue and Lyme disease now appear at higher latitudes and elevations than before. Warmer, wetter conditions let the mosquitoes and ticks that carry such diseases survive in places once too cold or dry. Climate change is altering how widely and heavily many infectious diseases are transmitted around the world. Warmer water and more flooding spread bacteria such as Vibrio cholerae. Drought and poor water access raise the risk of diarrheal diseases. Damage to nature adds to the danger. Deforestation, habitat fragmentation and biodiversity loss raise the risk of diseases jumping from animals to people, as people encroach on habitats and ecosystems favor efficient disease carriers. Low-income communities with weak healthcare and sanitation are the most vulnerable. Diseases like malaria slow their path to prosperity, worsening global inequality. The UN Environment Programme says the most fundamental protection against diseases from animals is to prevent the destruction of nature. Responses increasingly follow the One Health approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health as one.

  <!-- nature-eco-157 -->

- **Soil biodiversity: the hidden life beneath a football pitch**

  A football pitch is estimated to hold underground organisms equal in mass to 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the variety of life in soil, along with the soil properties that can be managed to support it. Soil is home mainly to microbes such as bacteria and fungi, but also to protozoa, nematodes, microarthropods, earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their main job is breaking down and reusing organic matter from the plant-based food web above ground. Keeping soil fertile has been called one of the most vital ecological services the living world performs. Microbial secretions do most of the work of binding soil particles into crumbs, called aggregates, and they protect soil carbon from breakdown. Erosion, acidification, salinization and chloride from potash fertilizer all threaten soil organisms. Because soils are a dispersed asset, healthy soil is best secured by a broad, consistent and economically appealing approach. Liming is one example, and the plow-free method described in No-till farming is another.

  <!-- nature-eco-146 -->

- **In-situ conservation: saving species where they live**

  Moving a species elsewhere is the fallback; keeping it at home comes first. In-situ conservation protects species and their genetic material on site, in the natural populations where they live. Its methods include nature reserves, parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biodiversity hotspots and gene sanctuaries. Keeping populations in the setting where they developed their traits lets evolution and adaptation carry on. Reserves must be large enough to hold populations with the genetic diversity needed to keep adapting. The opposite approach, Ex situ conservation: seed banks and frozen backups, keeps threatened species or their material elsewhere, as in seed libraries and gene banks. It is a last resort when in situ conservation is too difficult or impossible.

  <!-- nature-eco-131 -->

- **Climate change as a threat of extinction**

  Today 84% of coral-built reefs could withstand marine heatwaves. At 1.5 °C of warming, 2022 estimates suggest, only 0.2% could. Climate change can drive species extinct by pushing temperature and weather outside the conditions each evolved to live in, its niche. A species can adapt where it is or move. So far the IUCN links only 20 of 864 recorded species extinctions to climate, usually on weak evidence. Projections are grimmer. A 2011 review of 74 studies found an average projected loss of 11.2% of species by 2100. For insects, a 2018 study looked at three levels of warming: 1.5 °C, 2 °C and 3.2 °C. It estimated that 6%, 18% and about 49% of species, respectively, would lose over half their climatic range. A 2021 estimate that warming like that of the Big Five would bring a similar mass extinction was disputed the next year. At sea, climate already threatens 45% of at-risk species, though fishing and pollution do more damage for now. Prevention means limiting warming and protecting habitat, as in the 30x30 effort.

  <!-- nature-eco-114 -->

- **Global biodiversity: how many species share the Earth**

  About 1.74 million species had been catalogued by 2018, yet over 80% of species have not been described at all. Global biodiversity is the total variety of life forms on Earth. Nobody knows its size. Estimates of the number of species alive today run from 2 million to 1 trillion. Most are around 11 million or fewer, and the highest figures are disputed. Insects dominate, with about 1,000,000 described and an estimated 5,000,000 in all. The total rises as new species form and falls with extinction, at a background rate of about one extinction per million species-years. Habitat destruction, often to expand farming, is currently a bigger driver of loss than climate change. The world has struggled to slow it. Of 20 global targets set in 2010, described in Aichi Biodiversity Targets, only six were 'partially achieved' by 2020.

  <!-- nature-eco-124 -->

- **Forest genetic resources: the variety inside trees**

  In 2014 the FAO's first State of the World's Forest Genetic Resources found half the regularly used forest species threatened by land conversion, overexploitation and climate change. Forest genetic resources are the genetic material, of present or future value, of forest tree and shrub species. Forest communities depend on them for timber and for products such as fruits, gums and resins, and they underpin plantation wood. Their diversity lets tree species adapt to climate change. Not all can adapt fast enough, so moving seed and other forest reproductive material may be needed.

  <!-- nature-eco-156 -->

- **Gross loss versus net change in forest area**

  A country can lose forest every year and still gain forest overall. The difference lies between gross forest loss and net change, which subtracts new forest gained from forest lost over a period. Deforestation is the conversion of forest to other uses, whether or not people caused it. Net change can be positive or negative, depending on whether gains exceed losses. Replanting and new planting, especially in East Asia, are increasing forest area, which grew in 22 of the 50 most forested nations.

  <!-- nature-eco-054 -->

- **Indigenous land rights as a brake on deforestation**

  In Brazil, forests held under Indigenous tenure are cleared at even lower rates than government parks.
