In these tropical moist forests, waterlogged soil stops dead leaves and wood from fully rotting, building a thick layer of acidic peat. They store far more carbon in their soil than forests on mineral soil. About 62% of tropical peatland lies in the Indomalayan realm, mostly Indonesia, and 36% in the Congo Basin. Drainage, logging and fire speed up decay and release that carbon. Protecting them pays well under REDD+, earning more emission reductions per hectare, at lower opportunity cost, than saving other forests.

  <!-- nature-eco-553 -->

- **Four ways an estuary can form**

  San Francisco Bay was made by the earth moving, not by the sea rising. Estuaries are classed by how they formed into four types. Drowned river valleys, flooded as sea level rose, are the most common type in temperate climates. Bar-built estuaries are shallow and cut off from the sea by sand spits or barrier islands, and they are common in the tropics. Fjord-type estuaries lie in deep valleys carved by glaciers. Tectonic estuaries, formed by faulting, volcanoes or landslides, are few, and San Francisco Bay is one of them.

  <!-- nature-eco-532 -->

- **How fresh and salt water mix in an estuary**

  Fresh water is lighter than seawater, so in a calm estuary the river can float right over the sea. Estuaries are also classed by how their fresh and salt water mix. In a salt wedge estuary river flow dominates, and fresh water rides over a wedge of denser seawater. Stronger tides stir the layers into partial mixing. When tides dominate, the water column becomes well mixed, with no change in saltiness from top to bottom. In dry climates, where evaporation far exceeds the inflow of fresh water, inverse estuaries form. Some estuaries are intermittent, the final class.

  <!-- nature-eco-533 -->

- **Estuaries overloaded with nutrients**

  An algal bloom can briefly boost fish numbers, then drive them down. Eutrophication of estuaries is nutrient overloading, mostly by nitrogen, that fuels blooms of algae and harms plants, animals and fisheries. Feedbacks during the process cut available silica and raise nitrogen and phosphorus, letting harmful blooms persist. As the algae die and decay, oxygen keeps falling, and fish populations decline. The losses reach the economy through lower fishing sales; the US fishing industry employs 1.7 million people yearly.

  <!-- nature-eco-535 -->

- **What people have done to estuaries**

  Chesapeake Bay's oysters once filtered the whole estuary every three or four days. After years of fishing them too hard, the job takes almost a year. Estuaries are degraded by pollution, taking too many fish, development, dams and diversions. Because they sit at the bottom of rivers, they gather pollutants from far upstream, and long-lived toxins can build up in aquatic life. Fertilizer and waste runoff deplete oxygen and can create dead zones, cutting water quality and fish numbers. Dams and diversions have shrunk some great desert-river estuaries. The Colorado River Delta is now essentially a salt flat.

  <!-- nature-eco-534 -->

- **The non-living conditions that shape water life**

  Dissolved oxygen often decides how much life a body of water holds, and what kind. It is one of the abiotic factors in aquatic ecosystems: the non-living conditions, such as bottom material, depth, nutrients, temperature, salinity and flow, that shape what lives there. Nitrogen and phosphorus levels decide which algae dominate. Too much algae can kill fish as it decays, and in places like the Gulf of Mexico decaying overgrowth creates oxygen-starved dead zones. Changes far upstream matter too. Dams can reduce spring floods and sediment, letting salt water push into coastal wetlands.

  <!-- nature-eco-506 -->

- **Lake ecosystems: still waters, deep and shallow**

  Still waters range from a temporary rainwater pool a few inches deep to Lake Baikal, 1642 m at its deepest. A lake ecosystem is a still-water, or lentic, freshwater ecosystem of a lake or pond, with its living things and its physical and chemical conditions. Lakes are the main example of still-water ecosystems, which also include ponds and wetlands, in contrast with flowing waters. Depth sets ponds and lakes apart. A pond has its whole bottom in light. A lake has a dark deep zone, the profundal. Ponds have an open-water zone and a bottom-and-shore zone, called the benthic zone.

  <!-- nature-eco-503 -->

- **Marine coastal ecosystems: where land meets ocean**

  Earth has about 620,000 kilometres (390,000 mi) of coastline. Along it lie marine coastal ecosystems, the parts of the sea where land meets the ocean. Coastal habitats reach out to the edge of the continental shelves, the shallow underwater margins of the continents, covering about 7 percent of the ocean's surface area. That thin band includes many different habitats and stands out for high biodiversity and productivity.

  <!-- nature-eco-500 -->

- **Coral reefs: rainforests of the sea**

  Coral reefs cover less than 0.1% of the ocean, about half the area of France, yet they house at least 25% of all marine species. A coral reef is an underwater ecosystem built by reef-building corals. Each coral is a colony of tiny animals called polyps, held together by calcium carbonate, the mineral in limestone and shells. Shallow reefs, sometimes called rainforests of the sea, are among Earth's most diverse ecosystems. Over 4,000 species of fish live on them. Reefs are estimated to cover 284,300 km2, 91.9% of it in the Indo-Pacific region. They grow best in warm, shallow, clear, sunny and agitated water, even though that water holds few nutrients. Reefs also protect their neighbours. Fringing reefs, which hug the shore, shield nearby mangroves and beds of underwater sea plants from strong currents and waves. Reefs are both ancient and young. They first appeared 485 million years ago, but most living reefs are less than 10,000 years old. And they are vanishing fast: shallow tropical coral reefs have declined by 50% since 1950.

  <!-- nature-eco-453 -->

- **Seagrasses: flowering plants that went back to sea**

  Per hectare, seagrass beds hold twice as much carbon dioxide as rainforests. Seagrasses are the only group of flowering land plants that grows in the sea, usually forming meadows in shallow, sheltered coastal waters. About 60 fully marine species exist. They evolved from land plants that recolonised the ocean 70 to 100 million years ago, and most pollinate and complete their whole life cycle underwater. Seagrass beds hold more than 10% of the ocean's carbon storage. Seagrass is an ecosystem engineer that reshapes its surroundings. Its roots hold sediment in place and its blades damp waves, reducing erosion of the shore and the storm-driven rise in sea level. They feed turtles, manatees and fish, and serve as nurseries for commercially valued fish, scallops and shrimp. They cover only 0.1–0.2% of the ocean surface, and over 20% of global seagrass area has been lost since the late 19th century, at 1.5% a year. About a quarter of species (15 of 72) could be rated Threatened or Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List.

  <!-- nature-eco-558 -->

- **Salt marshes: tidal grasslands of the coast**

  Measured as net productivity, salt marshes are matched only by tropical rainforests. A salt marsh is a coastal wetland between land and sea, regularly flooded by tides and covered with dense salt-tolerant herbs, grasses or low shrubs. Marshes form on sheltered, calm shores of temperate and high latitudes, such as estuaries and the back side of barrier islands. In the tropics and subtropics, mangroves take their place, with salt-tolerant trees instead of soft-stemmed plants. A later study conservatively put global saltmarsh area at 90,800 km2, with the largest marshes outside the tropics. Marsh plants trap and bind sediment, which keeps the marsh stable. Salt marshes feed coastal food webs, deliver nutrients to coastal waters, support land animals and protect coasts. They also serve as sheltered feeding and nursery grounds for migratory fish.

  <!-- nature-eco-428 -->

- **What coral reefs are worth, and why estimates differ**

  About 500 million people benefit from coral reef ecosystem services, chiefly tourism, fisheries and protection of coastlines. Putting a price on them has proved hard. The global economic value of coral reefs has been estimated at between US$29.8 billion and $375 billion per year, and other studies give figures far higher. Estimates of the annual global value differ by orders of magnitude, so any single number should be read with caution. Local figures are firmer. A study in Belize valued reef and mangrove services at $395–559 million a year, and Bermuda's reefs were valued at $722 million a year on average. Fish are a big part of it. About six million tons are taken from reefs each year, and a well-managed reef yields on average 15 tons of seafood per square kilometre a year. Southeast Asia's reef fisheries alone yield about $2.4 billion in seafood annually. Losing reef is costly: destroying one square kilometre was estimated to cost between $137,000 and $1,200,000 over 25 years. To help coastal policy, the World Resources Institute built tools to value reef tourism, shoreline protection and fisheries.

  <!-- nature-eco-456 -->

- **Kelp forests: underwater woods of brown seaweed**

  Kelp forests and coral reefs together cover only 0.1% of Earth's surface, yet they account for 0.9% of global primary productivity. A kelp forest is an underwater area densely grown with kelp, a large brown seaweed; smaller patches are called kelp beds. They are counted among the most productive and dynamic ecosystems on Earth. Kelp forests grow along temperate and polar coasts worldwide, and in 2007 they were also found in tropical waters near Ecuador. Kelp acts as an ecosystem engineer, building the physical habitat for fish, invertebrates, seals, sea otters and seabirds. These forests can shape coastal ocean patterns and provide many ecosystem services. They are also fragile. Taking too many fish, along with climate change, has all but wiped them out in vulnerable places such as Tasmania's east coast and Northern California.

  <!-- nature-eco-422 -->

- **Seagrass meadows: grassland under the sea**

  Seagrass meadows are being destroyed at about 3 square metres per second. A seagrass meadow is an underwater ecosystem made up of seagrasses, flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal and estuary waters. These meadows rank among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, supporting marine life as diverse as coral reefs do. Seagrasses descend from land plants that returned to the sea about 75 to 100 million years ago. They grow on the continental shelves of every continent except Antarctica, down to depths of about 60 metres. They prefer sheltered bays, lagoons and estuaries, where waves are small and light and nutrients plentiful. The meadows shelter endangered species such as seahorses, turtles and dugongs, and they are nurseries for shrimps, scallops and many commercial fish. The threats are pollution from land runoff, dredges and trawls, and taking too many fish.

  <!-- nature-eco-486 -->

- **Coral reefs as natural breakwaters**

  Reefs can cut wave energy by 97%, and many small islands would not exist without them. Coral reefs protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy before it reaches the shore, helping prevent deaths and property damage. They damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters, and in the tropics restoring reefs is much cheaper than building breakwaters. About 197 million people living below 10 m elevation and within 50 km of a reef may get risk reduction from them. The top meter of reef does much of the work. Without it, expected flood damage would double and costs from frequent storms would triple. For 100-year storms, the kind expected about once a century, flood damage would rise by 91% to $US 272 billion.

  <!-- nature-eco-457 -->

- **What is killing coral reefs**

  Coral reefs worldwide declined 14% from 2009 to 2018. They are threatened by nutrient pollution, warming and acidifying oceans, Overfishing and destructive uses of land and sea. Some threats are local: coral mining, dragging nets along the seabed, blast fishing, too much fishing and marine pollution, which persist where regulation is weak. Too much fishing and excess nutrients from land let algae outcompete and kill coral. The global threats are larger. Greenhouse gas emissions warm the sea and raise sea level, causing widespread loss of coral cover as stressed corals turn white. Ocean acidification slows the corals' building of their limestone skeletons and speeds its dissolving, though corals can partly adjust. The outlook is stark: 70–90% of today's warm-water coral reefs will disappear even if warming is kept to 1.5 °C.

  <!-- nature-eco-458 -->

- **Protecting coral reefs: what works**

  Healthier Caribbean reefs have large parrotfish populations, found in countries that protect parrotfish and ban fish trapping and spearfishing. Coral reefs are protected mainly through marine reserves, known as Marine protected area, plus limits on fishing, pollution and coastal development. These reserves aim at responsible management of fishing and habitat protection, and can also serve restoration, biodiversity and economic goals. How well they work is still debated. Some studied sites showed no difference from unprotected areas, and some caused local conflict. Others provide local revenue roughly equal to what people would have earned without controls. The evidence suggests reserves can protect reefs, but only with clear management and enough money. Protecting networks of diverse, healthy reefs also preserves the genetic diversity corals need to adapt to new climates.

  <!-- nature-eco-460 -->

- **Salt marshes under human pressure**

  As of 2002, over half the world's population was estimated to live within 60 km of the coast, putting coastal habitats under heavy pressure. Salt marshes have been hit hard. People long treated them as coastal wastelands to be drained, built on or polluted. Marshes were lost to land reclamation for farming, urban development, salt production and recreation. A 2022 study blamed direct human activity for 22% of saltmarsh loss from 1999 to 2019, while 30% of gains came from deliberate actions such as restoration. Urban development of marshes has slowed since about 1970, as people recognised the services marshes provide. A newer threat comes from the sea itself. Rising seas driven by climate change threaten marshes through erosion and drowning.

  <!-- nature-eco-430 -->

- **Can salt marshes outrun rising seas**

  Mean sea level could rise between 0.6m to 1.1m by 2100. Rising seas threaten to flood and erode salt marshes, but marshes can sometimes build themselves up fast enough to keep pace. The rule is simple. A marsh survives only if its surface rises faster than the sea; otherwise it drowns. Drowning starts from within. Rising water opens pools inside the marsh, and their edges erode until the marsh can break up into open water. Marshes fight back with their plants. The plants slow currents and calm waves so that sediment settles. That sediment helps the plants grow, and bigger plants trap still more, a self-reinforcing loop scientists call a positive bio-geomorphic feedback. Marshes have one more escape route: moving inland. That needs accommodation space, room to retreat, which is often blocked by coastal roads, sea walls and other development. A marsh squeezed between rising water and a fixed wall has nowhere to go.

  <!-- nature-eco-433 -->

- **What kelp forests give people**

  One theory holds that the first people to reach the Americas followed a 'kelp highway' of Pacific kelp forests during the last ice age. Kelp forests have mattered to people for thousands of years, and they still provide food, materials, recreation and other benefits specific to these forests. Modern fisheries for kelp-dwelling species such as lobster and rockfish support local economies. Kelp itself is harvested to feed farmed abalone and to extract alginic acid, used in toothpaste and antacids. Recreation such as scuba diving and kayaking brings two separate benefits: income for the industry and enjoyment for the people who take part.

  <!-- nature-eco-425 -->

- **Otters, urchins and kelp: a trophic cascade**

  In Alaska, the fate of a whole underwater forest hangs on one furry predator. Sea otters there are the keystone species, eating the plant-eating sea urchins and keeping them in check. A kelp forest trophic cascade is what happens when that control breaks. Lose the predators, and urchins multiply and graze away the kelp. When otters are removed, for instance by hunting, urchin numbers soar, kelp is overgrazed, and the species that depend on it are lost. The forest gives way to an 'urchin barren', bare rock covered in urchins. This shift is widespread, and the two conditions are seen as alternative stable states, each able to persist once established. Not every coast is so fragile. In Southern California, several predators, including lobsters and large fish, control urchins, so losing one matters less there than in Alaska. Recovery is possible: kelp can return after big shocks such as urchin disease or large temperature shifts. Control also works from the bottom up. Nutrient-rich water rising from the deep lets kelp grow and feed the grazers and the animals that eat them.

  <!-- nature-eco-424 -->

- **What threatens kelp forests**

  In the 2010s Northern California lost 95% of its kelp ecosystems to marine heatwaves. Kelp forests are threatened mainly by too much fishing, pollution, kelp harvesting, invasive species and climate change. The most pressing threat may be Overfishing, because removing predators lets the forest collapse into an urchin barren. Heat is the rising one. The 2022 IPCC report says kelp and other seaweeds are suffering mass die-offs and range shifts from extreme heat in most regions. Pollution such as sewage, industrial chemicals, heavy metals and farm runoff has damaged kelp forests in southern California. Managers often limit kelp harvesting and fishing, but that does not protect the whole ecosystem. Marine reserves cover the wider web of interactions. Restoration in California mainly removes sea urchins, using divers and sea otters.

  <!-- nature-eco-427 -->

- **Seagrass decline: meadows lost at speed**

  Some 30,000 km2 (12,000 sq mi) of seagrass has been lost in recent decades, mostly because of human activity. The pace has quickened, from 0.9% per year before 1940 to 7% per year in 1990. Some damage is physical. Bottom-dragged fishing nets and boat propellers tear meadows apart. Much of it is chemical. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus feed algae that smother seagrass and block its light, starting a feedback loop that can replace seagrass with algae. Heavy fishing can make this worse indirectly, since removing top predators may cut the small grazers that keep algae down. Low-oxygen water starves seagrass roots and can kill meadows, and the decay of the dead plants uses up more oxygen. Warming, sediment and coastal development add to the decline. Some models predict Posidonia oceanica, a Mediterranean seagrass, will be extinct or nearly so by 2050. The main protection tools are cutting nutrient and other pollution, marine reserves, and transplanting.

  <!-- nature-eco-491 -->

- **What seagrass meadows do for coasts**

  Near small Indonesian islands without sewage treatment, harmful bacteria such as Enterococcus were 50 percent lower where seagrass was present. Seagrass meadows give coastal areas cleaner water, oxygen, food and shelter. They improve water quality by locking up heavy metals and other toxins, removing excess nutrients and lowering acidity. They release large amounts of oxygen into the water, and their roots carry oxygen into the sediment for the animals living there. Turtles, parrotfish, surgeonfish and sea urchins eat the grass, while small invertebrates feed on films on the leaves. People once gathered seagrass to fertilize sandy soils and to stuff mattresses. Conserving the meadows supports 16 of the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals.

  <!-- nature-eco-487 -->

- **Coral farming: gardening a reef back to life**

  Unprecedented reef die-offs worldwide have turned coral restoration into a growing field. Coral farming, also called Coral gardening, grows coral fragments in nurseries and then replants them on damaged reefs. It relies on corals' natural ability to keep growing from broken pieces that anchor to new surfaces. The method skips the early growth stages, when young corals are most likely to die. Nurseries have become the most widespread and arguably most effective restoration method, largely replacing the transplanting of whole colonies.

  <!-- nature-eco-461 -->

- **Corals and their algae: a partnership in sunlight**

  A coral polyp cannot make food from sunlight, yet reefs grow in sunny water for a reason. The polyps live in partnership with tiny algae, called zooxanthellae, inside their tissues. The algae photosynthesize and feed the polyp with sugars and other compounds such as glucose, glycerol and amino acids. The partnership has a breaking point. Stressed corals expel these colourful algae, a response called bleaching.

  <!-- nature-eco-455 -->

- **Coral bleaching: when heat breaks the partnership**

  One study of the Great Barrier Reef found 50% reef mortality after an extreme heatwave with a 3–4 °C rise. Coral bleaching is the stress response in which corals expel the colourful algae living in their tissues. Corals depend on these single-celled algae, zooxanthellae, which feed them through photosynthesis. Lose them and the coral turns white and starts to starve. Most corals tolerate only a 4–5 °C range in temperature, and rising ocean temperatures may be the biggest threat to reefs. Greenhouse gas emissions are warming the seas and causing widespread bleaching. El Niño events, natural warm spells in the Pacific every 4–7 years, also bleach heat-sensitive reefs, with especially widespread bleaching in 1998 and 2010. Reefs can take decades to recover. Yet they are getting less time. A report, Status of Coral Reefs of the World 2025, found the gap between warming events has shrunk to five or six years in many regions. It used to be about a decade. There is some resilience. Corals hosting certain algal types (Clade A or D) resist heat better than those with Clade C, and some reefs become more resistant after a severe event.

  <!-- nature-eco-459 -->

- **Fringing, barrier, atoll: the shapes of coral reefs**

  An atoll is a ring of reef around a lagoon with no island in the middle, and it usually began as a reef around a volcanic island. Coral reefs are classed by shape and setting, classically as fringing reefs, barrier reefs and atolls, with platform reefs often added. A fringing reef is attached to the shore or separated from it by a narrow, shallow channel. A barrier reef is separated from the shore by a deep channel or lagoon. Platform reefs grow wherever the seabed rises near enough to the surface for reef-building corals.

  <!-- nature-eco-454 -->

- **Life on the ocean's skin**

  Some snails spend their lives floating at the very top of the sea. They belong to the neuston, the community of organisms that live at the ocean's surface, along with drifting Sargassum seaweed. This marine surface ecosystem matters more than its thinness suggests. Many ecologically and economically important fish species are part of the neuston or depend on it. The surface is also on the front line of climate change and pollution.

  <!-- nature-eco-501 -->

- **River ecosystems: water that drains the land**

  Fast, turbulent water carries more dissolved oxygen than a slow pool, and it supports more species. A river ecosystem is a flowing-water, or lotic, ecosystem that drains the landscape, with its living things and physical and chemical conditions. Each river is part of a larger watershed, where small headwater streams feed ever larger channels. Food sources change along the way. Streams under a forest canopy get most of their food from trees, while wider, open streams get most from algae. Threats include water loss, dams, chemical pollution and introduced species. Dams cut spring floods and trap sediment, harming wetlands downstream.

  <!-- nature-eco-504 -->

- **Riparian zones: the green strip along a river**

  The name comes from the Latin ripa, meaning river bank. A riparian zone is the strip where land meets a river or stream, with its own water-loving vegetation. Such strips also go by names such as buffer zones and corridors. They work as natural filters, shielding waters from excess sediment, polluted runoff and erosion. Buffer zones can cut nitrate pollution from manure and fertilizer washing off farm fields, and riparian zones that are also wetlands remove nitrate especially well. Riparian plants give shelter and food to many aquatic animals, and their shade limits swings in stream temperature. Because they support so many species, these strips are often protected under national plans for wildlife. Some are natural; others are engineered to hold soil or restore damaged land. Land beside a watercourse that stays waterlogged for a season or more is usually called a wetland instead, because of its hydric soils, soils formed under saturation.

  <!-- nature-eco-482 -->

- **Floodplains: the land a river borrows**

  The Nile and Mississippi basins grew farms and cities on land their rivers regularly reclaim. A floodplain is the land beside a river, from its banks to the edges of the valley, that floods when the river runs high. Regular floods deposit nutrients, so floodplain soils are often very fertile. People have settled there to use that rich soil and fresh water, and the risk of flooding has led to growing efforts to control floods. Floodplains support diverse, productive and often very species-rich ecosystems. Floodplain forests protect waterways from erosion and pollution and soften the impact of floodwaters. Yet the main ways people destroy floodplain ecosystems are flood control itself, reservoirs for hydroelectric power, and conversion to farmland.

  <!-- nature-eco-462 -->

- **How wetlands soak up floods**

  Walling a river in can make its floods worse. Floodplains and other wetlands act as natural storage reservoirs that soak up excess water and so reduce flooding downstream. They work in several ways. River floodplains let floodwater spread over a wide area, which lowers its depth and speed. Headwater wetlands, high in a river's catchment, slow rain runoff and snowmelt so they do not rush straight into rivers, which helps prevent sudden floods. During heavy rain, wetlands hold the extra water, reducing the area, depth and duration of flooding. Remove that storage and the system changes. Draining floodplains or hemming rivers in with levees forces the same rain through a narrower channel. Flood peaks then get higher and arrive faster. A wetland controls floods by giving water room; take the room away and the peaks rise.

  <!-- nature-eco-443 -->

- **Floodplain ecology: life timed to the flood pulse**

  Many river fish spawn just as the flood begins, using the newly flooded river edge, and their young must grow fast before the water falls. Floodplain ecology centres on this flood pulse: the yearly cycle of flooding and drying that brings nutrients and shapes life on the floodplain. Floods bring in nutrient-rich debris and release nutrients from the soil they cover. Floodplain plants and animals grow and die fast, which lets them colonise shifting ground, and floodplain trees are fast-growing. Away from the river, plant zones follow a gradient of soil moisture, oxygen and flood frequency. Floodplain forests covered 1% of Europe in the 1800s, and because they were cleared less than other forests, they are important refuges for biodiversity. Flood control sharpens the boundary between water and land, which reduces habitat diversity.

  <!-- nature-eco-464 -->

- **When water ecosystems are pushed too far**

  The Great Lakes show how pollution, over-harvesting and invasive species can combine. Threats to aquatic ecosystems are the stresses that degrade them once they exceed what the ecosystem can absorb. Stresses can be physical, such as changes in temperature, flow or light. They can be chemical: nutrients, oxygen-consuming materials and toxins. Or they can be biological, like over-harvesting and exotic species. Human-driven climate change disrupts where plants and animals live and has hurt deep-sea biodiversity, coastal fish and coral reefs. Even human-made waters such as ditches and fish-farm ponds trade biodiversity for their intended purpose.

  <!-- nature-eco-507 -->

- **Large marine ecosystems: managing the sea by region**

  There are 66 large marine ecosystems, contributing an estimated $3 trillion a year and 90% of the world's annual marine fish catch. A large marine ecosystem is an ocean region of roughly 200,000 km2 or more, defined by its seabed shape, water movement, productivity and linked food webs. The US agency NOAA developed the concept in 1984. Its aim was to guide conservation and shared management of whole ecosystems across national borders.

  <!-- nature-eco-548 -->

- **Planting trees on grasslands: a contested fix**

  A map by the World Resources Institute and the IUCN, showing 2 billion hectares for restoring forests, was criticised for including 900 million hectares of grasslands. Planting trees on grasslands, often to store carbon, can damage grasslands and the services they provide. Critics say tree-planting campaigns target grasslands and savannas where forests would not naturally grow. Restoration focused on forests risks misclassifying grassland as degraded forest, which helps make grasslands the least protected biome. Grasslands and savannas benefit people too, and they are not meant to be forests.

  <!-- nature-eco-472 -->

- **Fire and grazing: keeping grasslands open**

  Reserves in Brazil that banned fire and grazing were quickly taken over by shrubs. Many grasslands depend on disturbances such as fire and grazing to stay open, so how they are managed can make them persist or vanish. Grazing and fire keep woody plants from invading. In Brazilian highland grasslands, areas without the traditional burning every two years and cattle grazing could disappear within 30 years. Not everyone agrees on how far grasslands depend on fire and grazing, and the question remains controversial.

  <!-- nature-eco-473 -->

- **Semi-natural grasslands: wild meadows kept by people**

  A meadow in Estonia held a European record of 76 plant species in a single square meter. It was a semi-natural grassland: one with wild, unsown plant communities, kept open by human activities such as grazing and mowing. These grasslands can be extremely species-rich. Almost 90% of Europe's semi-natural grasslands disappeared during the 20th century, for political and economic reasons. Fertilizing and re-sowing them for farming usually leaves few wild plants. To save what remains, conservation groups buy these grasslands or pay landowners grants to manage them appropriately.

  <!-- nature-eco-469 -->

- **Prairie, pampas, steppe: kinds of grassland**

  During the Pleistocene ice ages, a cold, dry 'mammoth steppe' grassland covered much of the Northern Hemisphere. Today grasslands are grouped by climate and setting into broad types: tropical, temperate, flooded, montane, tundra and desert grasslands. Tropical and subtropical grasslands and savannas get 90 to 150 centimeters of rain a year and support grazers like wildebeest and zebra. Temperate grasslands include the North American prairie, the Pampas and the European steppes, home to large herbivores such as bison. Flooded grasslands such as the Everglades and the Pantanal are under water seasonally or all year.

  <!-- nature-eco-468 -->

- **What riverside strips do for people**

  A shaded stream stays cool; thin out the trees along its banks and its temperature climbs and swings, sometimes enough to kill fish. Riparian zones provide many such benefits, from slowing floods and filtering runoff to wildlife habitat and recreation. River bends, plants and roots slow the water, which reduces soil erosion and flood damage. Trapped sediment leaves the water clearer and builds the banks. The strips serve as wildlife corridors, letting aquatic and riverside organisms move along rivers instead of living in isolated groups. They also raise nearby property values through views and amenity, and make room for fishing, swimming and boating.

  <!-- nature-eco-483 -->

- **Leaving buffers when forests are logged**

  Logging next to a stream can fill it with sediment, change its species and pollute its water. Riparian buffers in logging mean leaving the riverside strip undisturbed during timber harvesting so it keeps protecting the stream. The untouched soil and vegetation give shade, leaf litter and wood, and hold back soil eroding from the logged area. How well a buffer works depends on soil type, root structure, climate and plant cover.

  <!-- nature-eco-484 -->

- **Repairing damaged riverbanks**

  Clearing land and then flooding can quickly strip a riverbank of grasses and soil. Riparian zone restoration repairs such damage by removing human structures, by active rehabilitation, or simply by giving the bank time. Methods range from erosion control and replanting to log sills, rock placement and short barriers jutting into the stream (Groyne), plus invasive species control. Fast-growing pioneer 'weeds' can kick-start succession, holding soil until trees and grasses return. Conservationists urge that the value of riparian ecosystem services be written into management plans, where it has usually been left out.

  <!-- nature-eco-485 -->

- **Rainforest layers: from dark floor to emergent crowns**

  Only 2% of the sunlight reaches a rainforest floor, so only low-light plants grow there. Rainforests are organised into vertical layers, from forest floor and understory to canopy and emergent layer, each with its own community of plants and animals. The canopy forms a roof over the lower layers and contains most of the largest trees, typically 30–45 m tall. Emergent trees rise above it to 45–55 m, occasionally 70–80 m. Only this top layer is unique to tropical rainforests.

  <!-- nature-eco-564 -->

- **Living with floods on the floodplain**

  River floods, especially on China's Yellow River, have been among the deadliest natural disasters, led by the 1931 China floods. Floodplain flood control covers the rules, maps, insurance and works that limit flood damage to floodplain residents. How far a floodplain floods depends on the size of the flood, expressed as a return period, such as the 100-year flood with a one-in-a-hundred chance each year. In the United States, a national program offers Flood insurance for properties in flood-prone areas drawn on risk maps. Yet upstream development such as a large car park can raise flood levels, and the maps are rarely updated. Some towns have been moved off floodplains. Elsewhere annual floods are part of the rural economy, supporting recessional agriculture: planting as the water recedes.

  <!-- nature-eco-465 -->

- **How rivers build their floodplains**

  A meandering river eats away the outside of each bend and builds a sandbar, a point bar, on the inside, slowly laying down a level floodplain. Most floodplains are built this way, by rivers depositing sediment both inside their bends and when floods spill over the banks. Water spilling over the banks drops a thin layer of sediment, thickest and coarsest near the channel. Over time this forms natural levees, low ridges along the river's edge. In undisturbed rivers, overbank flow typically happens every one to two years.

  <!-- nature-eco-463 -->

- **Floodplains as phosphorus traps**

  Much of the phosphorus in fresh water comes from wastewater treatment plants and farm runoff, and too much of it is a problem. Floodplains can store phosphorus in their soils and plants, keeping it from overloading rivers downstream. Floodplain forests act as phosphorus sinks. Cutting rivers off from their floodplains removes that sink and worsens the overload.

  <!-- nature-eco-466 -->

- **Mosquito ditching: a cure that bred more mosquitoes**

  In the early 20th century people dug straight ditches through salt marshes, believing that draining them would reduce mosquitoes. It backfired. The ditches destroyed habitat for killifish, small fish that eat mosquitoes, so mosquito numbers actually rose and wading birds lost food. The ditches are still visible despite efforts to refill them.

  <!-- nature-eco-434 -->

- **Too much nitrogen in salt marshes**

  Salt marsh plants are normally short of nitrogen, so adding more reshuffles which species win. Nitrogen loading is the extra nitrogen from sewage, urban runoff and farm and industrial waste that flows into salt marshes and changes their plant life. Disturbed marshes can be invaded by the aggressive reed Phragmites australis, which crowds out native plants and harms insects and birds too.

  <!-- nature-eco-432 -->

- **How a mudflat becomes a salt marsh**

  A salt marsh begins as bare tidal mud. It forms when that mud builds up with sediment until tides flood them less often, letting plants take root. Rivers slow down as they reach the flat tidal zone and drop their sediment, helped by the rising tide. Pioneer plants, the first to arrive, catch more sediment around their stems, forming mounds that join into raised terraces bound by roots. As the surface rises, flooding gets shorter and shallower, and a succession of plant communities moves in.

  <!-- nature-eco-429 -->

- **Reclaiming salt marsh for farmland**

  In one English estuary, abandoned reclaimed land saw little vegetation return in 60–75 years, because the ground was too low and compacted. Land reclamation turned salt marsh into dry farmland, often by building dikes that kept the tide out. It changed vegetation, sediment, salinity and water flow, caused biodiversity loss and added nutrients. Once done, the damage can last for decades.

  <!-- nature-eco-431 -->

- **Salt marsh restoration: bringing back the tide**

  Once seen as wasteland, salt marshes are now recognised as among the most productive habitats on Earth, rivalling tropical rainforests. Salt marsh restoration brings damaged or reclaimed marshes back toward their natural state, a practice that has grown since the 1980s. Many countries now protect marshes by law; the US Clean Water Act and the EU Habitats Directive give them strong protection. Restoration can use Managed retreat, letting the sea back onto reclaimed land, or reclaim land for marsh, either leaving a site to recover naturally or actively rebuilding the habitat. Natural recovery can take 2–10 years or longer. Replanting native vegetation speeds it up and usually works better. Effective restoration takes considerable time and effort and needs careful long-term monitoring. Not everywhere has changed course. Fast-growing coastal populations in parts of Asia still tend to ignore marsh value and keep reclaiming the land.

  <!-- nature-eco-435 -->

- **The microbes that run a salt marsh**

  In salt marsh mud, bacteria that breathe sulfate instead of oxygen can account for up to 50% of the breakdown of organic matter. Microbes do most of the nutrient cycling and chemical processing in salt marshes, thriving in the salty, low-oxygen mud. These sulfate-reducing bacteria help recycle nutrients and reduce nitrate pollution. Cyanobacteria are important nitrogen fixers, turning nitrogen from the air into a usable form and supplying it to diatoms and other microalgae.

  <!-- nature-eco-436 -->

- **How a forest stand grows old**

  A forest stand, a patch of trees growing together, ages in stages. After a disturbance that replaces it, it passes through stand initiation, stem exclusion and understory reinitiation before reaching old growth. In stem exclusion, trees compete for light: slow growers die and canopies close, so only very shade-tolerant plants survive beneath. In understory reinitiation, scattered tree deaths open gaps that let shade-tolerant species establish below. In old growth, canopy trees die at different times, so trees beneath grow at different stages and rates, giving a mixed-age stand. Such stands are more stable, because a uniformly aged climax stand degrades fairly quickly into a new cycle of succession.

  <!-- nature-eco-551 -->

- **Old growth through a logger's eyes**

  To a logging company, an old-growth stand is one past the economic best age for harvesting, usually 80 to 150 years depending on species. Old-growth forests were often logged first. They held the most valuable timber, were thought at risk of rot or pests, and occupied land wanted for faster-growing second growth. Their large trees have been aggressively logged worldwide, causing many conflicts between logging companies and environmental groups. Old growth is not always the most profitable timber, though. Coastal British Columbia is shifting harvests to younger second-growth stands.

  <!-- nature-eco-552 -->

- **Fire as the boreal forest's renewal**

  Boreal fires often burn more than 10,000 ha, and sometimes more than 400,000 ha. Fire is the main disturbance that renews boreal forest stands, and an area's fire regime describes the type, size and frequency of its fires. The boreal regime is dominated by intense crown fires, which race through the treetops, or by severe fires along the ground. Fire rotation is the average time it takes for fires to burn an area equal to the whole ecosystem; individual sites may be skipped or burn more often. In lichen woodland, large damaging fires recur roughly every 70 to 100 years.

  <!-- nature-eco-560 -->

- **Mire, bog and fen: sorting the peatlands**

  Ecologists call any land with at least 30 cm of peat a peatland, even if it has been drained. A mire is a peatland still forming peat. It comes in two types. A bog sits higher than its surroundings and gets all its water from rain and snow. A fen lies on a slope, flat or hollow and gets most of its water from surrounding soil or water underground. In both, water passing through peat loses nutrients and becomes more acidic, so mires are usually nutrient-poor.

  <!-- nature-eco-476 -->

- **Palm oil on peat: profit against carbon and fire**

  Palm oil needs only 0.26 hectares of land to produce 1 ton of oil, and it has given income to smallholders in countries such as Indonesia and Malaysia. In Southeast Asia, that profit has a cost. Large areas of peatland forest have been drained and cleared for palm oil, trading economic gains against losses of carbon, biodiversity and safety from fire. About 12.9 Mha, about 47% of Southeast Asian peatlands, had been deforested by 2006. Emissions from palm oil on peatland are estimated at 12.4 to 76.6 t CO2/ha, and converted land can stay a carbon source after 12 years. Drained peat dries into a flammable layer, and its fires cause thousands of deaths each year.

  <!-- nature-eco-479 -->

- **Tropical peat fires: smoke across borders**

  Southeast Asian tropical peatlands cover only 0.2% of land but emit an estimated 2 Gt CO2 a year, equal to 7% of global fossil fuel emissions. Once drained and cleared, these peatlands burn increasingly often, releasing huge amounts of carbon dioxide. A severe fire can release up to 4,000 t of CO2/ha, and such fires usually burn for 1–3 months. More than 2 million hectares burned in Southeast Asia in the past ten years. The smoke does not stay home: peat fires send it across international borders almost every year.

  <!-- nature-eco-480 -->

- **Kelp as a carbon sink**

  Macroalgae, the large seaweeds such as kelp, take up 200 million tons of carbon dioxide every year. Kelp absorbs carbon as it grows. When it sinks to the deep ocean floor, that carbon can stay stored, far from human disturbance. Around Australia, kelp forests were estimated to store 1.3-2.8 teragrams of carbon per year, 27–34% of the carbon the continent's coastal habitats store each year, its Blue carbon.

  <!-- nature-eco-426 -->

- **The layers of a kelp forest**

  Giant kelp grows tall enough to form floating canopies at the ocean surface. A kelp forest is built in layers, from these canopy kelps down to kelps and algae on the sea floor, and its structure decides which species live there. Below the canopy, stipitate kelps stand a few meters above the sea floor, and prostrate kelps lie along it; together they form the understory. Beneath them lies a bottom layer of other algae and attached animals.

  <!-- nature-eco-423 -->

- **Cutting peat for fuel and gardens**

  Peat supplies more than 20% of home heat in Ireland, and it is burned for fuel in Finland, Scotland, Germany and Russia. Peat extraction means cutting peat from bogs to burn as fuel or to sell as a garden soil improver. Russia is the leading exporter of fuel peat, at more than 90 million metric tons per year. Peat builds up so slowly that a bog is hard to restore once the peat is gone. More than 90% of England's bogs have been damaged or destroyed, and in 2011 the UK announced plans to remove peat from gardening products.

  <!-- nature-eco-510 -->

- **Bogs drying, draining and warming**

  Many Arctic and sub-Arctic bogs are warming at 0.6 °C per decade, twice the global average, and releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases. Bogs take thousands of years to form and are very hard to recover, yet drying, drainage and warming are degrading them. Northern European sphagnum bogs were often cleared and drained for farming. European peatlands have dried quickly in recent centuries from drainage, peat cutting and burning. These changes have caused severe declines in peatland biodiversity across Northern Europe. Many agencies now treat bogs as priority habitats, including the UK's national plan for wildlife (Biodiversity action plan).

  <!-- nature-eco-512 -->

- **Raised, blanket, quaking: kinds of bog**

  A quaking bog is a floating mat of moss and sedge, about half a meter thick, that moves when someone walks on it. Bogs are classed by landscape position, water source and nutrient supply. Valley bogs form in gently sloping hollows; because they rely on ground or surface water, they occur only on acidic ground. Raised bogs grow over centuries from a lake, through marsh and fen, until a rain-fed peat dome a few meters high forms. Blanket bogs cover hilltops and slopes in cool places with rain on more than c. 235 days a year.

  <!-- nature-eco-509 -->

- **How seagrass shields the shore**

  Without seagrass, currents carry seafloor sediment away and erode the bottom. Seagrass leaves and roots calm waves and hold sediment, protecting coasts from erosion and storm-driven high water. Seagrass is an ecosystem engineer that reshapes their surroundings physically and chemically. Their leaves slow currents so sediment settles and builds up the seafloor. By reducing wave energy and building sediment, they protect houses and cities from the sea and from rising sea levels.

  <!-- nature-eco-489 -->

- **Seagrass: where fisheries begin**

  About half of global fisheries are estimated to get their start in seagrass habitats. Lose the seagrass, and the fisheries go too. Seagrass meadows are sheltered nurseries for young fish and shellfish that later support fishing. They give young fish a home in over 1/5th of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species. Gleaning shellfish by hand in seagrass exposed at low tide feeds hundreds of millions of people, and small-scale seagrass fishing acts as a safety net for the poor. Yet a 2019 study found this role is poorly reflected in the decisions of the authorities who manage seagrass.

  <!-- nature-eco-490 -->

- **Replanting lost seagrass**

  In Chesapeake Bay, several million eelgrass seeds are gathered each year with a mechanical harvester. Seagrass restoration re-establishes lost beds by transplanting plants or sowing seeds and other propagules, the plant parts that can grow into new plants. Communities in Virginia, Florida, Hawaii and the United Kingdom are restoring beds lost to human activity, and reintroductions improve ecosystem services. Most projects use cuttings, rhizome fragments or cores taken from donor meadows; few use seeds. Seed-based restoration has had low and variable results, with more than 90% of propagules failing to survive.

  <!-- nature-eco-493 -->

- **Wasting disease: a slime mold that kills eelgrass**

  After the 2015–2016 northeast Pacific heatwave, the share of eelgrass infected by wasting disease rose from 5–70% in 2013 to 60–90% by 2017. Over the same period eelgrass shoot density fell by 60%. Seagrass wasting disease attacks eelgrass, the most widespread seagrass, and is caused by the marine slime mold Labyrinthula zosterae. The pathogen enters leaf tissue, impairs photosynthesis and breaks down cells, leaving dark spots and streaks. Warmer seas fuel outbreaks. Meadows with little disease may mark refuges that can withstand climate change, worth putting first for protection and restoration.

  <!-- nature-eco-492 -->

- **The intertidal zone: between high and low tide**

  Some shore animals spend part of every day out of the water. The intertidal zone is the shore area exposed to air at low tide and covered by seawater at high tide. It is divided into the spray zone and the high, middle and low intertidal zones, each with its own conditions and wildlife. The high zone's changing conditions favour hardy animals such as barnacles, snails, mussels and hermit crabs. The low zone is almost always under water, and life is more abundant there.

  <!-- nature-eco-544 -->

- **Mangrove forests: carbon-rich nurseries of the tropics**

  The world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans, covers 10,000 km2 in the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta. Mangrove forests are productive wetlands of salt-tolerant trees growing in tropical and subtropical intertidal zones. About 80 mangrove species exist. They cannot survive freezing, which keeps them in warm climates. Their stilt-like roots slow tidal water so sediment settles, forming a barrier that reduces erosion of the shore by waves and storm-driven high water. The roots shelter many species and act as nurseries for young fish, including commercially important ones. Mangroves are among the most productive ecosystems, with net primary productivity of about 208 Tg C per year, and they generally take up more carbon than they release. They sequester over 25 million tons of carbon each year, so losing them reduces carbon storage. Losses are heavy. Where data exist, about 35% of mangroves have been destroyed, and around 2% of mangrove area has been lost each year since the 1980s. Shrimp farming causes about a quarter of the destruction, and fish farming, oil and timber production have also driven losses.

  <!-- nature-eco-542 -->

- **Mudflats: the shorebirds' refuelling stations**

  Tens of millions of migratory shorebirds depend on mudflats as stopovers between their breeding and non-breeding areas. Mudflats, or tidal flats, are coastal wetlands formed in intertidal areas where tides or rivers have deposited sediment. A 2019 global analysis found they are as extensive as mangroves, covering at least 127,921 km2, with 44% in Asia. Once seen as economically unimportant, they were often dredged or converted to farmland. Up to 16% of the world's tidal flats have disappeared since the mid-1980s. Around the Yellow Sea, more than 65% of the mudflats present in the early 1950s had been destroyed by the late 2000s.

  <!-- nature-eco-549 -->

- **Vegetated coasts: seagrass, mangrove and marsh together**

  Seagrass beds, mangrove forests and tidal marshes together cover about 50 million hectares. These plant-dominated shore habitats are known as vegetated coastal ecosystems. They provide fish production, coastline protection, pollution buffering and high carbon storage. Their secret lies below. They sit on organic-rich sediments, sometimes metres deep, whose carbon stocks can be several times those of forests. When they are degraded or converted, that sediment is exposed to oxygen, and microbes release large amounts of greenhouse gases. They are being lost to fish farming, agriculture, dams, dredging, eutrophication, urban development and rising seas.

  <!-- nature-eco-545 -->

- **Seagrass blue carbon: burying carbon in the seabed**

  Seagrass meadows cover only 0.1% of the ocean floor yet account for 10–18% of all carbon buried in the ocean. Seagrass blue carbon is the carbon dioxide these meadows pull from the air and bury in seabed sediment, part of the coastal carbon store called Blue carbon. Per hectare, seagrass holds twice as much carbon dioxide as rain forests, and meadows can take up about 27 million tons of CO2 a year. Global meadows are estimated to store up to 19.9 Pg (billion tons) of organic carbon. The trick is in the mud. Carbon builds up in low-oxygen seabed sediments, where slow decomposition preserves it for decades to millennia. Land habitats lose carbon to decay, fire or deforestation; marine sinks can keep it far longer. Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 140 g C m−2 yr−1. Restoration works on a human timescale too. Restored seagrass meadows began storing carbon in sediment within about four years.

  <!-- nature-eco-488 -->

- **The outwelling hypothesis: mangroves feeding the coast**

  A mature mangrove forest reaches its maximum biomass after about 20–30 years. After that, the carbon it keeps fixing must be stored in sediment, exported or lost to the air. The outwelling hypothesis holds that much of it is exported as organic matter that feeds detritus-based food webs, which run on dead material, in nearby coastal habitats. Mass-balance studies, which add up carbon going in and out, support the idea. Mangroves usually fix far more carbon than they store, though the amount exported varies a lot between forests.

  <!-- nature-eco-543 -->

- **Reefs, seagrass and mangroves as one system**

  Protecting fish in a mangrove can raise fish numbers on a nearby reef. Coral reefs, seagrasses and mangroves are linked systems that shield one another and exchange fish and invertebrates. Mangroves and seagrasses regulate the sediment, freshwater and nutrients that reach coral reefs. Their ecosystem services reinforce each other: protecting fisheries in one raises fish biomass in the others, and tourism gains from both.

  <!-- nature-eco-547 -->

- **Five depth zones of the open ocean**

  The open ocean is divided by depth into five layers: epipelagic, mesopelagic, bathypelagic, abyssopelagic and hadopelagic. The sunlit epipelagic zone is the only layer with enough light for photosynthesis. Nearly all ocean primary production and about 90% of marine life are found there. The twilight mesopelagic zone gets only trace sunlight; many of its animals make their own light or rise to the surface at night to feed. In the pitch-black bathypelagic zone most animals live on 'marine snow', detritus falling from above. The hadal zone, below 6,000 m in trenches, reaches 10,935 m at Challenger Deep, with pressures of 1,100 atm.

  <!-- nature-eco-555 -->

- **Permafrost thaw: warming that feeds itself**

  The IPCC estimates permafrost emissions at 14–175 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent per 1 °C of warming, against about 40 billion tonnes of human CO2 emissions in 2019. Permafrost is ground that stays frozen year-round. As warming thaws it, stored carbon escapes as greenhouse gases that cause more warming and more thaw, a positive feedback. A 2018 article suggested that at about 2 °C of warming, permafrost thaw would add a further 0.09 °C (range 0.04–0.16 °C) by 2100. Thaw also threatens roads, pipelines and other infrastructure built on frozen ground.

  <!-- nature-eco-566 -->

- **From bog to rich fen: a gradient of species**

  Calcium-rich water can turn a peatland from a species-poor bog into a species-rich fen. The bog–rich-fen gradient arranges peatlands from species-poor bogs, through poor fens, to species-rich fens. Where a site falls depends strongly on its pH and on calcium and bicarbonate levels. Rich fens get much of their water from mineral-rich sources, and their near-neutral water supports high biodiversity. Poor fens are more acidic, with a pH of about 5.5 to 4, and their thicker peat cuts plants off from the mineral soil below.

  <!-- nature-eco-537 -->

- **Is the Sahel really turning to desert**

  The Sahel, in Africa, has greened over recent decades. That fact sits awkwardly with a familiar story of spreading deserts, and the dispute over whether that story is accurate is the desertification narrative debate. Desertification is a real and major threat to ecosystems and people, worst in Western Asia and South America. Critics say the Sahel is wrongly seen as drying faster than elsewhere, a view they trace to colonial readings of how local people used the land. Researchers remain divided, and the dominant narrative for the Sahel is contested rather than settled.

  <!-- nature-eco-527 -->

- **What drylands give the world**

  Millions of people in developing countries rely on dryland ecosystems for a secure food supply and a good life. Drylands provide food, livelihoods, carbon storage and biodiversity, both to local people and to the world. Dryland ways of life help slow climate change by locking away carbon, and they conserve species. Drylands provide significant global economic value through their ecosystem services and biodiversity. The Rio+20 conference in June 2012 also stressed that dryland biodiversity is worth protecting for its own sake.

  <!-- nature-eco-523 -->

- **From sub-humid to hyper-arid: grading drylands**

  Arid lands cover about 10% of the world's land and hold 20% of its people. Drylands are graded into four classes by aridity: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid. Dry sub-humid lands produce a large share of the world's crops and livestock. By one rainfall-based measure, semi-arid lands get between 500 and 800mm a year. Arid lands have an aridity index of ~0.05-0.20 under the UNCCD, the UN treaty on desertification. Hyper-arid lands cover ~8% of the world and get barely more than 100 mm of rain; the UNCCD leaves them out of its dryland definition.

  <!-- nature-eco-521 -->

- **Drylands in a warming world**

  From 1982 to 2015, 12.6% of the world's drylands degraded because of human-caused climate change. Climate change and human activity are degrading drylands, bringing more drought, desertification and erosion. About 7.6% of global land has recently turned drier, an area larger than Canada. Dryland degradation and desertification affect 213 million people, mostly in the Global South, and threaten people's food supply. People are adapting. Herders move their herds earlier, keep smaller herds, change how they manage water and vary their migration routes. Mobile herding and other sustainable land management, restoration and climate-smart farming can soften the impacts.

  <!-- nature-eco-522 -->

- **Restoring drylands: hard ground, patchy hope**

  Restoring a dryland is hard. Rain is rare and variable, heat is high, soils are poor and invasive species spread. Dryland restoration is deliberate work to help degraded drylands recover, either by restoring their former function or by preventing further decline. The IUCN and IPCC stress ecosystem restoration as a tool for slowing climate change and adapting to it. The IUCN also counts restoration as one of the three pillars of Nature-based solutions. Techniques target the patchy vegetation typical of drylands. Some plant small patches meant to spread (Restoration islands: small patches that spread) or encourage soil animals. Others plant trees, fence out grazing animals, combine trees with livestock, or build semicircular bunds, low earth banks that catch runoff. The FAO offers 10 practice principles to guide ecosystem restoration.

  <!-- nature-eco-524 -->

- **Local knowledge in restoring drylands**

  Dryland communities have combined trees, crops and livestock successfully for centuries. Restoration builds on that experience when it uses local and indigenous knowledge and community involvement. Case studies find that involving indigenous knowledge and local communities makes restoration more successful. Indigenous fire practices, for example, can lower fuel loads and help prevent large, devastating fires.

  <!-- nature-eco-529 -->

- **Restoration islands: small patches that spread**

  Instead of planting a whole hillside, some restorers plant a few well-placed patches and let nature do the rest. Restoration islands are small planted patches that then spread into the land around them. They suit the patchy vegetation of drylands and need fewer resources than large plantations. The benefits include lower fire risk, less erosion, weed control, seed sources and wildlife habitat. Patience is required. In drylands, patches spread more slowly than in humid ecosystems.

  <!-- nature-eco-525 -->

- **Managing rangelands for grass, carbon and herders**

  Rangelands, the open lands grazed by livestock, cover about 25% of drylands globally. Sustainable rangeland management means managing and restoring these grazing lands so they keep producing while storing carbon and resisting desertification. Because of its potential to lock away carbon, rangeland restoration counts as a way to slow climate change, and it can improve herders' livelihoods. Whether a practice is adopted depends heavily on local context, including ecological, economic, political and cultural factors.

  <!-- nature-eco-526 -->

- **Intact forest landscapes: the last big wild woods**

  Protecting the world's wildest forests is often cheap, because the remoteness and low economic value that kept them undeveloped also keep protection costs down. An intact forest landscape is a large, unbroken natural forest area with no sign of significant human activity or fragmentation. Technically it must cover at least 500 km2 (50,000 ha), be at least 10 km wide, and show minimal influence from economic activity. Such landscapes cover about 23 percent of forest ecosystems (13.1 million km2), almost all in tropical and subtropical forests (45 percent) and boreal forests (44 percent). Only 10 percent of their global area is strictly protected, and about seven percent was lost after 2000.

  <!-- nature-eco-539 -->

- **The river continuum: a river's diet from source to sea**

  A river's diet changes along its length. The river continuum concept is a framework describing how temperate river ecosystems change in function from small headwaters to large rivers. It uses stream order, a ranking of streams by size, to mark position along that gradient. Small shaded headwaters depend on leaf litter from land. Mid-sized rivers get enough light for algae. Large rivers rely again mainly on outside inputs. Animal communities track the food: shredders, which tear up leaves, thrive in small streams, and grazers at mid-sized sites. The idea has critics. Junk and colleagues argue it rests on small temperate streams and has been wrongly applied to all rivers, including those that switch between flowing and still states. They prefer a rival framework for such rivers, the Flood pulse concept.

  <!-- nature-eco-557 -->

- **Coarse woody debris: the value of dead wood**

  A fallen trunk can lie on the forest floor for a very long time. Coarse woody debris is dead wood such as fallen trunks and branches, which decays slowly. Its chemistry, especially lignin, the tough compound that stiffens wood, makes it rot slowly compared with most organic matter. It decays even more slowly in dry or cold places. Lying for long periods, it shapes wildlife habitat, fire behaviour and how trees regenerate.

  <!-- nature-eco-421 -->

- **Bathyal, abyssal, hadal: the deep-sea zones**

  The deepest band of the ocean runs from 6 to 11 km down. Scientists divide the deep ocean into three depth bands: the bathyal, abyssal and hadal zones. The bathyal zone, or continental slope, runs from 200 to 3,000 meters and mixes features of the shelf above and the abyss below. The abyssal zone lies between 3–6 km deep, and the hadal zone between 6–11 km.

  <!-- nature-eco-518 -->

- **Forest biomass: the weight of the woods**

  The world's forests hold about 606 gigatonnes of living biomass above and below ground, plus 59 gigatonnes of dead wood. Forests build up large amounts of living plant material, and many do so quickly, which makes them highly productive. That store is not permanent. Fires and falling trees can release it suddenly, reshaping the forest's structure.

  <!-- nature-eco-420 -->

- **Hydrothermal vents: life without the sun**

  Water leaving 'black smoker' chimneys on the seafloor can reach 400 °C (752 °F), kept from boiling by the enormous pressure. Around these hydrothermal vents live communities powered by chemosynthetic bacteria, microbes that make food from chemical energy rather than sunlight. They are among the few ecosystems on the planet that do not depend on sunlight at all. Tube worms such as Riftia live in partnership with these bacteria.

  <!-- nature-eco-519 -->

- **Mycorrhizal networks: fungi that feed the forest**

  Some conifers cannot survive without their fungal partners. A mycorrhizal network is a partnership in which fungi and plants share resources through connections in the soil. Fungal threads reach farther into the soil than roots, helping plants get phosphorus and water. Many conifers trade sugars to the fungi in return for nutrients. The network can move water and nutrients between plants and can help them resist drought. The benefit is not universal: it varies by plant species and shrinks where soil nutrients are plentiful.

  <!-- nature-eco-419 -->

- **Shore, open water, depths: the zones of a lake**

  At the bottom of a deep lake, no sunlight reaches, and the food web runs on detritus drifting down from above. Lakes are commonly divided into three zones. The littoral zone is the shallow shoreline, where rooted wetland plants grow. The open, sunlit zone feeds algae. The deep zone is dark. The same zones are also called the pelagic, limnetic and profundal zones.

  <!-- nature-eco-540 -->

- **Lake layers and the autumn turnover**

  Water is densest at about 4 °C, and that quirk splits big lakes in two each summer. As the surface warms, it forms a warm upper layer, the epilimnion, floating over a cold bottom layer, the hypolimnion. Between them lies the thermocline, a band of rapid temperature change. The layers stay apart until autumn cooling mixes the lake to a uniform temperature, a process called lake turnover. In winter the layers form again in reverse beneath the ice. This layering also affects how much oxygen each zone holds.

  <!-- nature-eco-541 -->

- **What sets how much methane a wetland releases**

  Big bursts of methane have followed droughts that lowered a wetland's water table, because gas moves more easily through soil than through water. Many factors set how much methane a wetland releases, such as water table, temperature, soil and plants. The key balance is between two groups of microbes. Methanogens make methane; methanotrophs eat it. Net release depends mainly on how much methane escapes before it is oxidized. Plentiful cellulose and a soil pH of about 6.0 give optimum conditions for making methane. Scientists measure emissions with eddy covariance, gradient or chamber flux methods.

  <!-- nature-eco-496 -->

- **Draining wetlands: less methane, or more**

  Draining a wetland can cut its methane, or not. Drainage for development, housing and farming lowers the water table, which lets soil bacteria consume more methane. But the drainage ditches themselves stay waterlogged and warm, and they can emit large amounts of methane. Lowered far enough, the water table can turn a wetland from a methane source into a methane sink.

  <!-- nature-eco-497 -->

- **Three routes for methane to escape a wetland**

  Wetland methane is made by archaea, single-celled microbes that ferment acetate or combine hydrogen with carbon dioxide. It reaches the air by three main routes: diffusion, transport through plant tissue, and bubbling, or ebullition. When the water table is low, methane rising through the soil passes a layer of methane-eating bacteria, which reduces emissions. Plants with aerenchyma, porous air-carrying tissue, act as a shunt that lets methane skip that layer. In ebullition, pockets of methane build in the soil until a bubble bursts, moving gas up too fast for microbes to consume it.

  <!-- nature-eco-495 -->

- **What boreal ecosystems provide**

  Canada's boreal ecosystem is one of the world's largest carbon reservoirs, and it has high potential for hydroelectric power. Boreal ecosystems provide many services, led by timber and a steadier climate through the carbon cycle. Boreal forests supply lumber and regulate water, soil and air quality. These services compete. Managing an ecosystem to maximize one tends to reduce the supply of the others.

  <!-- nature-eco-515 -->

- **Climate change in the boreal north**

  Permafrost stores double the carbon now in the atmosphere, and thawing can release it as greenhouse gases. Warming is changing boreal ecosystems, and their changes feed back on the climate. Thawing ground, milder winters and hotter summers displace cold-adapted species, increase forest fires and can turn boreal areas into other ecosystem types. Plants and animals are already shifting northward, though plants may lag the warming by decades to a century. Thaw, fire and insect outbreaks have led some models to suggest boreal forests are now a net carbon source rather than a sink.

  <!-- nature-eco-514 -->

- **The environmental troubles of growing cities**

  Pockets of extra warmth in cities (Urban heat island) make extreme heat more frequent, hitting the elderly and people without cooling hardest. Growing cities face pollution, loss of green space, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, heat and disease. Air pollution from vehicles, factories and power plants exceeds safe limits in many cities and causes respiratory and heart disease. Development replaces forests, wetlands and grasslands, and losing green space lowers air and water quality, health and biodiversity. Heavily urbanized areas also have more invasive species than rural ones.

  <!-- nature-eco-439 -->

- **Green and blue infrastructure: building nature into cities**

  Buildings certified under LEED, a green building rating system, report using 30% less energy and gaining economic and mental benefits from natural light. Green and blue infrastructure means building in ways that weave natural systems such as vegetation and water into human-made structures. The green side includes nature preserves and added vegetation such as vertical gardens. The blue side includes ways of managing rainwater, such as planted channels that soak up runoff (Bioswale).

  <!-- nature-eco-440 -->

- **Studying city nature: a young and lopsided field**

  A review of 217 papers found most studies of urban ecosystem services were done in Europe, North America and China, at the scale of a single city. The ecology of cities, including the study of what urban nature provides, is a young field whose research is still limited and unevenly spread. Another review found a strong bias toward the northern hemisphere, with case studies mostly in the United States and China. Assessments use biophysical models, digital mapping and valuation, but few findings have been turned into policy on how land is used. Researchers are building better tools to map services such as water regulation, air cooling and the cleaning of water.

  <!-- nature-eco-438 -->

## Ecosystem services

In 1997 Gretchen Daily's edited book Nature's Services laid out a framework for something people had long taken for granted: the economic benefits that flow from the natural workings of ecosystems. In 2005 a United Nations-backed study, the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, carried that idea around the world. This part follows ecosystem services from their roots to their hardest questions. What is nature's work worth, who gains from it, and what happens when boosting one service drains another? Along the way it meets nature's own recycling system, the cycles that keep matter moving back into new life.

### The ecosystem services idea

The notion that ecosystems serve people began as ancient observation and became a standard scientific term. Gretchen Daily's 1997 book gave it a framework, and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, launched in 2001, made it famous. This chapter asks what the idea means and who benefits, whether they live beside an ecosystem or feel its effects from far away. It follows economists trying to express services in money so they can be weighed in decisions. It also meets the hard parts: services that rise only at another's expense, land-use choices that juggle ecology and economics, and a newer name from IPBES, {{ref:nature-es-123}}.

- **The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: a health check for the planet**

  More than 1300 authors from 95 countries spent four years on one question: what are people doing to the ecosystems that keep them alive? Their answer was the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, a United Nations-backed study called for in 2000, launched in 2001 and published in 2005. An earlier book, Nature's Services: the 1997 book that framed a field, was described as a catalyst for it. The assessment popularized the term ecosystem services, meaning the benefits people gain from ecosystems. It sorted them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting, with supporting services underpinning the other three. Its findings were sobering. In the past 50 years humans had changed ecosystems faster and more widely than ever before, mainly to meet demand for food, fresh water, timber, fiber and fuel. Those changes made many lives better and fueled development. They also degraded many ecosystem services and made some groups poorer. The bottom line was blunt. Human actions were depleting Earth's natural capital so much that ecosystems' ability to sustain future generations could no longer be taken for granted. The next UN report on the state of biodiversity did not come until the global assessment of IPBES in 2019.

  <!-- nature-es-001 -->

- **Putting a price on nature's work**

  What is clean water worth to a fisher? The economics of ecosystem services tries to answer questions like that, expressing services in economic terms so their value can be weighed in decisions. It translates scientific knowledge into comparable units of impact on people's lives. People decide for many reasons, but overall trends reveal what a society prefers, and value can be inferred from them. There are six main ways to value services in money, from avoided cost and Replacement cost to travel cost, hedonic pricing and Contingent valuation. One of them, factor income, counts how a service raises incomes, as when cleaner water increases the fish catch and fishers' earnings. Scale is a stubborn problem, because ecological data gathered at one place and time may not hold at another. Some reject the whole exercise. Salles (2011) argued that biodiversity's total value is infinite, since no one can live without it. As of 2012 many companies still did not grasp how much they depend on ecosystems.

  <!-- nature-es-006 -->

- **From Plato's springs to a scientific term**

  Around 400 BC Plato understood that cutting down forests could cause soil erosion and dry up springs. The idea took a very long time to get a name. Modern thinking probably began in 1864, when Marsh challenged the belief that Earth's resources are unlimited by pointing to changing soil fertility around the Mediterranean. In the late 1940s Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr, William Vogt and Aldo Leopold argued that people depend on the environment. In 1956 Paul Sears stressed ecosystems' role in processing wastes and reusing nutrients. By 1970 the warnings were starker: Paul Ehrlich and Rosa Weigert said human activity could destroy the ecological systems our species depends on. That year a report spoke of 'environmental services', listing insects that carry pollen, fisheries, regulating climate and flood control. E. F. Schumacher coined 'natural capital' in his 1973 book, Small Is Beautiful. In the 1990s two works became seminal: Daily's Nature's Services: the 1997 book that framed a field and Costanza and colleagues' first attempt to put a money value on ecosystem services. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment then popularized the idea, and 'ecosystem services' became the standard term.

  <!-- nature-es-005 -->

- **Protecting services when a price tag is not enough**

  Ecosystem services are estimated to add $125 trillion to $140 trillion to the economy each year. Even so, protecting them is hard. Decision-makers must balance present and future needs, often with valid but incomplete information. Existing laws are often seen as inadequate because they rest on human-health standards, which do not match what healthy ecosystems require. As of 2005, local to regional collective management was considered suitable for services such as pollinating crops and for resources like water. Since the 1990s, markets have grown that sell credits for protecting services, such as guarding carbon sinks or restoring service providers. These schemes need clearly defined rights to land, often missing in developing countries, and they raise worries about inconsistent compensation. Because protecting services often overlaps with protecting biodiversity, some suggest merging the two goals. Law lags behind. As of 2018 the concept was not properly built into international and regional law, though Sustainable Development Goal 15 targets conserving, restoring and sustainably using ecosystem services. The stakes keep rising: climate-driven shifts in biomes may cut services by 9% globally by 2100.

  <!-- nature-es-009 -->

- **Tracing a product's footprint on nature's services**

  Every product leaves a trail of environmental pressures, from the land cleared to make it to the nutrients that wash into rivers. Life-cycle assessment tracks those pressures. Its impact methods now link them, such as land-use change and eutrophication, to changes in ecological functions and ecosystem services. A 2026 review found three main kinds of model: land-use impact models, extended ecosystem quality models and inventory-based models. They differ in the services, ecosystems and indicators they cover, and in whether they count supply, demand or both. That makes comparison hard. Freshwater and marine services remain poorly represented, so the field needs more consistent guidance.

  <!-- nature-es-011 -->

- **Nature's contributions to people: a broader name, or a new label?**

  In 2017 the 5th plenary meeting of IPBES made a decision about words. Its assessments would now speak of nature's contributions to people: all the ways nature benefits people. The phrase replaced 'nature's benefits to people' from then on. The aim was to bring diverse worldviews, including indigenous and local knowledge, into biodiversity assessments. Not everyone was persuaded. Some scientists objected that the term was confusing and not significantly different from ecosystem services.
