Fencerows, forest-to-marsh transitions and riparian zones along rivers are classic examples. An edge is the part of an ecosystem near its border, where neighboring patches make conditions differ from the interior, often changing which species live there.

  <!-- nature-es-048 -->

- **Patches, corridors and matrix: the parts of a landscape**

  Landscape ecologists read land as a mosaic. A patch is a fairly uniform area that differs from its surroundings. Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides. The matrix is the well-connected background system that holds them. Connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is: a forest with fewer open gaps is better connected. Patches change and fluctuate over time, a process called patch dynamics.

  <!-- nature-es-047 -->

- **Fragmentation: when the landscape breaks apart**

  Landscape fragmentation is the breaking up of a habitat, ecosystem or land-use type into smaller, separate pieces. Repeated random clearing, natural or human, can splinter continuous cover into isolated patches. The change is not gradual. Once cleared area passes a critical level, a landscape flips from connected to disconnected. Metapopulation models, which treat scattered groups as linked populations, gave conservation biologists a tool to judge whether populations can survive this.

  <!-- nature-es-049 -->

- **Lotka and Volterra: the dance of predator and prey**

  After fishing in the Adriatic was cut back during the First World War, fish and shark numbers swung in puzzling ways. Vito Volterra built a model to explain them in 1926, a year after Alfred Lotka developed the same idea. The Lotka–Volterra model is a pair of equations, one for prey and one for its predator, describing how their numbers rise and fall together. Its parameters are the prey's growth rate, the predation rate, the predator's assimilation efficiency and the predator's death rate. It is not unchallenged: supporters of the rival Arditi–Ginzburg model argue the field data reject it.

  <!-- nature-es-064 -->

- **i-Tree: putting a value on every tree**

  How much is a city's tree canopy worth? A suite of US Forest Service software called i-Tree tries to answer. It measures and values the services trees provide in cities and the countryside. It quantifies services such as pollution removal, carbon storage and rainwater runoff avoided. Some tools work up from ground inventories of trees, others down from remote sensing data. Urban foresters use it to turn a forest's structure into ecosystem services and economic value. It began in 2002 as a sample survey that simulated a full urban tree inventory.

  <!-- nature-es-065 -->

- **Participatory GIS: maps made by the people who live there**

  Participatory GIS puts mapping tools in the hands of local people, so their own knowledge shapes planning decisions. It combines sketch maps, 3D models, aerial photos, satellite images and GPS to turn what people know about places into maps for discussion. Its aim is to empower marginalized groups and protect traditional knowledge by leaving control of sensitive maps with their makers. Uses range from neighborhood planning to managing forests, water and wildlife. Practitioners still debate top-down against bottom-up approaches, and critics ask who really gets access to the technology.

  <!-- nature-es-070 -->

- **InVEST: free software for mapping nature's value**

  InVEST is used in more than 185 countries to map valuable ecological resources and weigh trade-offs in land and water use. The name stands for Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs. It is free, open-source software from the Natural Capital Project for mapping and valuing ecosystem services, with 20+ models covering land, freshwater, marine, coastal and urban settings. Users steer investments toward both conservation and development. Alongside the ARIES project and the Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, it is one of several tools that help businesses value services. Its developer works with governments, banks, companies and communities to bring nature's values into decisions.

  <!-- nature-es-080 -->

- **The modifiable areal unit problem: same data, different answers**

  Draw a population density map using state boundaries, then redraw it using county boundaries, and the results differ radically. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, a source of statistical bias. Results change depending on how point data are grouped into areas such as districts or regions. Totals, rates and densities all depend on both the shape and the size of the units chosen.

  <!-- nature-es-075 -->

- **Spatial autocorrelation: near things are related**

  Values at nearby locations tend to be related, positively or negatively. This spatial autocorrelation breaks the independence that standard statistics assume. Regressions that ignore it can give unstable estimates and unreliable significance tests. Spatial regression models capture it, and it can also be read as useful information rather than a nuisance. Classic measures include Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G.

  <!-- nature-es-074 -->

- **Testing a land change model against reality**

  A model can look brilliant by cheating. Calibrating it with data from after its first time period can make it seem far more accurate than it really is. Land change model validation guards against this by comparing a model's processes or predicted maps with what really happened. Pattern validation often uses three maps: the real maps at two dates and the simulated second map. Pixels are sorted into hits, misses, false alarms and similar classes. The Figure of Merit turns these into one percentage for the overlap between real and simulated change.

  <!-- nature-es-067 -->

- **Runoff curve numbers: how much rain runs off**

  A paved parking lot has a curve number of 98; open space in good condition on sandy soil has 39. The runoff curve number is an empirical figure used in hydrology to predict how much rainfall runs straight off the land rather than soaking in. It ranges from 30 to 100; higher numbers mean more runoff. It depends on the soil and on how land is used and treated. Soils fall into four groups, from A, deep sands that soak water up fast, to D, clays and shallow soils that absorb it very slowly.

  <!-- nature-es-071 -->

## Valuing nature

Water keeps people alive, yet diamonds cost far more. That old puzzle opens this part of the course, which asks what it means to say nature has value. Economists separate a thing's usefulness from the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Philosophers ask a different question: is nature good only as a means to human ends, or good in itself? Between the belief that humans are the most important beings on the planet and the view that every living thing has equal worth lies a wide range of positions, and societies turn out to value the non-human world in several ways at once.

### Kinds of value

Some things are very useful and trade for little; others are nearly useless and trade for a fortune. This chapter starts with that gap between usefulness and exchange. It then turns to philosophy, which separates what is good as a means from what is good as an end in itself. From there come rival views of humanity's place: one centered on people, one on all living things, one on nature as a whole, and one that trusts technology to solve environmental problems. Along the way the chapter sorts the ways societies see importance in the non-human world, as useful, as valuable in itself, and through relationships with it.

- **Use value: what a thing is good for**

  Gold can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor. Each of those is a use, and together they make up its use value: the features that let a thing satisfy a human want or need. The idea comes from classical and Marxist economics. Adam Smith noticed that use and price can part company. Diamonds have little use but fetch a great deal in trade, while water is very useful yet cheap. For Marx, every commodity, a good made to be traded, is both a use value and an Exchange value: what a thing trades for: the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Not every useful thing can become a commodity. It must be tradable, its ownership must pass securely from one person to another, and there must be real demand. Later, marginalist economics traced use value to the Marginal utility: the value of the next piece consumers find in a good. Critics of turning nature into commodities still draw on Marx's double idea.

  <!-- nature-val-058 -->

- **Exchange value: what a thing trades for**

  Marx gave every commodity four attributes: use value, exchange value, value and price. Exchange value is the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods. It is not the same as the money price, which only roughly matches it. Behind both, Marx held, lies value itself, set by the socially necessary labor time needed to produce a good: the work it typically takes. Modern neoclassical economics, the mainstream school, no longer treats exchange value as a separate idea. For it, exchange value is simply the market price, the subject of Price: where buyers and sellers agree. Before anything can be traded at all, certain conditions must hold: secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand. Critics of turning nature into commodities see a danger here. Expressing every kind of worth through a single exchange value puts very different things on one scale.

  <!-- nature-val-068 -->

- **Environmental philosophy: do rivers have rights?**

  Do rivers have rights? Questions like that belong to environmental philosophy, the branch of philosophy concerned with the natural environment and humans' place in it. It emerged as a branch of its own in the 1970s. Its early figures include Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Richard Routley, Arne Næss and J. Baird Callicott. A major debate of the 1970s and 80s asked whether nature has value in itself or only as a means to human ends. On one side stood nature-centered views, including Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness; on the other stood human-centered ones. Another debate asks whether wilderness really exists, or whether, as William Cronon suggested, it is a cultural construct with colonial overtones. Today the field also takes up environmental activism, environmental justice, climate change and the depletion of finite resources.

  <!-- nature-val-065 -->

- **The paradox of value: why diamonds outprice water**

  Nothing is more useful than water, Adam Smith observed, yet it will buy scarcely anything. Diamonds are far less useful and cost much more. This is the paradox of value, also called the diamond–water paradox. Smith is its classic presenter, though the puzzle appears as early as Plato's Euthydemus. Smith split 'value in use' from 'value in exchange', the ideas now called use value and exchange value, and noted that the most useful things often have little exchange value. Supporters of the labor theory of value had one answer: price reflects the toil of acquiring a good. Marginalists had another. They separated total utility from Marginal utility: the value of the next piece. Water is so plentiful that one more unit adds little, while scarce diamonds add more. Böhm-Bawerk's farmer with five sacks of grain shows the logic: he values the last sack by its least important use, feeding pigeons. Change the setting and the paradox flips. A person dying of thirst in a desert would pay more for water than for diamonds.

  <!-- nature-val-070 -->

- **Good as a means, or good in itself**

  A hammer and a washing machine are valuable for what they do. Their value is instrumental: they are good as a means to an end. Happiness and pleasure are different. They are usually thought valuable for their own sake, the kind of worth explored in Intrinsic value: worth for its own sake. The sociologist Max Weber coined the terms. Not everyone accepts the split. John Dewey thought belief in value for its own sake was a mistake, and treated instrumental judgment as the only way to coordinate behavior well. J. Fagg Foster treated sustainability as a synonym for instrumental value, since success must never be short term.

  <!-- nature-val-057 -->

- **Anthropocentrism: putting humans at the center**

  In 1906 J. Howard Moore argued that Darwin's theory of common descent had 'sealed the doom' of anthropocentrism. The idea has proved hard to kill. Anthropocentrism is the belief that human beings are the central or most important beings on the planet. In this view humans stand apart from nature and above it, and animals, plants and minerals are resources for human use. Nature's value becomes instrumental: it matters as a means to human ends. Environmental ethics often treats this outlook as the root cause of human-made problems in the ecosphere, the living envelope of the planet. Val Plumwood compared its role in green theory to that of androcentrism, the male-centered outlook, in feminist theory. Its defenders answer that the real problem is only shallow anthropocentrism. A sound long-term view, they argue, would keep the environment suitable for humans. William Grey called for an enriched idea of human interest to replace short-term, self-regarding views. Environmental philosophers still dispute who is right: whether human-centered thinking itself causes ecological harm, or only its shallow, short-term form. Religion enters the argument too. The word 'dominion' in Genesis has been used to justify the view, though some now see it as a possible mistranslation. Pope Francis's 2023 Laudate Deum speaks instead of a preferable 'situated anthropocentrism'.

  <!-- nature-val-059 -->

- **Intrinsic value: worth for its own sake**

  The Zoological Society of London warns that insect decline means a double loss. Species lose their instrumental value, and their intrinsic value as well. Intrinsic value, in ethics, is the value something has in itself, for its own sake, rather than as a means to something else. Instrumental value, by contrast, comes from a thing's relation to some other valued thing. Every major ethical theory treats something as intrinsically valuable. Virtue ethics points to flourishing; consequentialists, who judge acts by their results, point to pleasure. Some conservation biologists argue that nature has intrinsic value independent of its usefulness to people. Arne Næss's Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness, coined in 1972, gave all non-human beings this kind of worth. Whether absolute intrinsic value exists at all is debated. John Dewey accepted only value relative to a situation.

  <!-- nature-val-056 -->

- **Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness**

  Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, published in 1962, is often seen as the start of the movement. The Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss gave it a name, coining 'deep ecology' in 1972 and first using the phrase in a 1973 article. Deep ecology holds that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match. Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish. Næss set it against 'shallow ecology', which he criticized as utilitarian, human-centered and consumer-oriented. Deep ecology rejects nature as a resource to exploit. The materialist outlook, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced. Critics push back. Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores overconsumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic. Others call it Eurocentric or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge. Its ideas also feed arguments for valuing ecosystems outside markets.

  <!-- nature-val-062 -->

- **Ecocentrism: valuing nature as a whole**

  Where anthropocentrism puts humans at the center, ecocentrism puts nature there. It denies any division between humans and the rest of nature that would make humans the only, or the greater, bearers of intrinsic value. It values the biotic community, all the living things of a place, as a whole. Its aim is to keep the composition and processes of ecosystems intact, covering living and non-living systems rather than organisms alone. Aldo Leopold conceived the ethic, and his Land ethic is central to it. Supporters argue that a human-centered ethic always makes protecting nature depend on human welfare, while an ecocentric ethic gives protection a firmer basis. Critics reply that it risks sacrificing human wellbeing for an ill-defined greater good.

  <!-- nature-val-063 -->

- **Biocentrism: equal worth for every living thing**

  The US Endangered Species Act has been described as unusually biocentric, because it puts non-human species first. Biocentrism is the environmental ethic that gives equal inherent value to all living things. It sits among close neighbors. Anthropocentrism is centered on humans. Sentientism values only beings that can feel pleasure or pain. Ecocentrism extends value to the whole of nature. Biocentrism rests on four pillars: humans and other species share Earth's community; all species depend on one another; each organism pursues its own good; and humans are not inherently superior. The family includes Albert Schweitzer's 'reverence for life', Peter Singer's animal liberation and Paul W. Taylor's biocentric egalitarianism. Its advocates often promote biodiversity preservation, rights for animals and environmental protection. Critics call it anti-human, and say it focuses too much on individual lives while neglecting wholes such as ecosystems.

  <!-- nature-val-060 -->

- **Three ways societies value nature**

  Timber, clean water and air, carbon storage, pollination: these are the familiar ways nature serves people. They are only one of three kinds of value that societies see in the non-human world. The first kind is extrinsic, or instrumental, value: nature's usefulness to people, often called ecosystem services. Many extrinsic values can be given an economic value. That lets them enter impact assessments, Cost–benefit analysis studies and national accounts. The second kind is intrinsic value. It holds that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans. The third kind, Relational values: ties between people and nature, covers the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature. IPBES, building on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, promotes this broad account of nature's values to guide policy and restoration.

  <!-- nature-val-066 -->

- **Technocentrism: trusting science to fix nature**

  Not everyone who worries about the environment wants to shrink industry. Technocentrism is a set of values centered on technology. It holds that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science. Technocentrics accept that environmental problems exist, but they do not see cutting industry as the solution. Ecocentrics, by contrast, see themselves as subject to nature. They prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance.

  <!-- nature-val-064 -->

- **Social ecology: how people treat nature and each other**

  'The ecological crisis is a social crisis,' Murray Bookchin argued. His 1982 philosophy of social ecology links how humans treat nature to how they treat each other. Practices such as monocropping, growing a single crop over and over, and overfishing mirror social tendencies to dominate people. Bookchin defined nature itself as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom. Social ecology calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

  <!-- nature-val-067 -->

- **Rights of nature: writing nature's rights into law**

  In 2008 Ecuador became the first country to put rights of nature in its constitution. Its Article 71 gives nature the right to respect for its existence and for the regeneration of its life cycles, structure, functions and evolution. Rights of nature are the legal recognition that nature has rights of its own, an application of biocentric values in law. The idea rejects treating nature as a 'resource' to own, use and degrade, as most twentieth-century laws did. Cities in Maine, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire and Virginia have adopted such laws, aimed especially at corporate exploitation and toxic dumping.

  <!-- nature-val-061 -->

- **Non-market goods: valuable but never sold**

  Clean air, clean water, landscapes, parks, rivers and forests share an awkward trait for economists. They are non-market goods, things that are not bought and sold in markets. Most environmental goods fall into this group. Without prices, putting a value on them is inherently uncertain. That difficulty is one reason environmental assets are usually left out of measures of wealth. In 1947 S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed a way around it: surveys asking people what such a good is worth to them, the approach later called Contingent valuation.

  <!-- nature-val-073 -->

- **Non-use value: caring about what you never use**

  People can value a resource they have never used and never will. Economists call this non-use value. It is often attached to natural resources, and it stands apart from use value, which comes from using a good directly. Non-use value has several strands. It can include Option value: paying to keep choices open, Bequest value: saving nature for future generations, Existence value: the worth of knowing it is there and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it. All these categories grew from the first of them, introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964. Measuring them is hard. Market prices and other methods that read value from what people buy generally cannot capture it, because nobody is buying anything. Economists instead ask people directly in surveys, such as Contingent valuation. Attempts to value ecosystems sort the value of their services into use and non-use categories.

  <!-- nature-val-069 -->

- **Total economic value: adding up nature's worth**

  Most people will never see a tiger in the wild, yet knowing tigers live there is worth something to many of them. Total economic value tries to count that, along with everything else. It is the full value people get from a natural resource, heritage site or piece of infrastructure, compared with not having it. In environmental economics it adds up the values an ecosystem provides. It is built in layers. Use value comes first, split into direct and indirect. Direct use covers removable products such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use covers non-removable things such as a sunset or a waterfall. Non-use value comes next. It covers simply knowing that a resource exists, as with those tigers. Two more strands look ahead. One, Option value: paying to keep choices open, is placed on keeping the possibility of using a resource in future, even when that use is unlikely. Another, Bequest value: saving nature for future generations, comes from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Adding the layers gives a single figure. Cost–benefit analysis uses a similar approach.

  <!-- nature-val-052 -->

- **Existence value: the worth of knowing it is there**

  A wilderness can be worth money even if nobody ever walks into it. That was John V. Krutilla's argument in his essay 'Conservation Reconsidered', which introduced the idea of existence value. It is the benefit people get simply from knowing that something exists, whether Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species. Because no direct use is needed, it is a leading example of non-use value. It is usually measured with Contingent valuation surveys. The idea has legal force. Since the case Ohio v. Department of the Interior, existence values can be recovered as damages in US law. After the Exxon Valdez oil spill, damages included an estimate of the existence value of a pristine Prince William Sound.

  <!-- nature-val-054 -->

- **Option value: paying to keep choices open**

  Why fund a rail service or a wildlife refuge that most taxpayers will rarely use? Option value is one answer. It is what people are willing to pay to keep a public asset or service available, even if they are unlikely ever to use it. Policy assessments use it to justify investing in parks, wildlife refuges, land conservation and rail services. In environmental research it means the value of preserving threatened natural resources so they might be used in future. Burton Weisbrod developed the idea in 1964. He rested it on three conditions: future need is uncertain, loss would be irreversible or costly, and the asset cannot be stored. Later economists proposed refinements such as 'option price' and 'quasi option value', which stresses irreversibility. Option value in finance is a different idea, though both can be read as ways of valuing risk.

  <!-- nature-val-055 -->

- **Bequest value: saving nature for future generations**

  Part of what people value in nature is what they can hand on. Bequest value is the satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Together with existence value, it makes up non-use value. It is often used when estimating the value of an environmental good or service. Attempts to value ecosystems count it as the welfare an ecosystem may give future generations. In some optimization models, mathematical models that search for the best plan, it goes by another name: the 'salvage value' of the system.

  <!-- nature-val-053 -->

- **Direct and indirect use: taking versus enjoying**

  Catching a fish and watching a waterfall both use nature, but only one takes something away. Direct use value comes from goods removed from nature, such as timber, fish and water. Indirect use value comes from benefits nature provides without anything being removed, such as a sunset or a waterfall. When ecosystems are valued, indirect use value arrives through the positive externalities ecosystems provide, benefits that reach people without a price. For livestock breeds, direct use is milk or meat. Indirect use includes regulating services such as nutrient cycling, seed dispersal and fire control. These values can often be inferred from behavior, such as recreational trip costs or house prices.

  <!-- nature-val-071 -->

- **Relational values: ties between people and nature**

  Some ties to nature are neither about usefulness nor about worth in itself. Relational values arise from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature. In one framing of nature's values they sit alongside intrinsic values, held for their own sake, and extrinsic values, held as means. Ignoring them has costs. Western regenerative agriculture has been criticized for overlooking the relational values of Indigenous systems, causing epistemic injustice: a wrong done to people in their capacity as knowers.

  <!-- nature-val-072 -->

## Environmental policy instruments

Some of the costliest things an economy makes are never sold. Microscopic particles drift through city air, acidic rain falls on forests and lakes, and everyday rubbish needs somewhere to go. Breathing fine particles is linked to disease throughout the body and to large numbers of early deaths. This part of the course follows those unwanted by-products and the tools societies use to limit them. It begins with the harm itself, and with the ways economists try to put a money value on the damage an environmental change causes.

### Pollution economics and environmental health

Pollution is what happens when the costs of making and using things spill onto people who never agreed to bear them. Particles too small to see drift through the air, and rain turns unusually acidic. Waste piles up as household rubbish, as dangerous chemical leftovers, and as old factory land left behind. Some contamination has no single source at all, gathering in small amounts from whole landscapes. This chapter looks at each of these harms in turn, what they do to health and ecosystems, and what has worked to reduce them.

- **Particulate matter: the most dangerous thing in the air**

  No level of exposure is safe. Particulate matter is the name for microscopic solid or liquid particles suspended in the air, and it is considered the most dangerous form of Air pollution: 7 to 8 million deaths a year. A mix of particles and air is called an aerosol. The particles come from both natural and human sources. Some are wind-blown mineral dust and sea salt. Others are organic matter, or form in the air from gases such as sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ammonia. The danger lies in how far they travel inside the body. Particles reach deep into the lungs and then ride the blood to organs such as the brain. Airborne particulate matter is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen, a substance known to cause cancer. Fine particles, called PM2.5 (PM10 and PM2.5: sizing up deadly dust), are the leading environmental risk factor for early death worldwide. Yet this is also a hopeful story. Because so many sources are human, the risk is one that policy can reduce, and many countries now set standards for it. After the United States passed its Clean Air Act (United States) of 1970, combined emissions of the main regulated pollutants and the gases that form them fell 79% between 1970 and 2024.

  <!-- nature-pol-068 -->

- **Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky**

  In 1852, in industrial Manchester, Robert Angus Smith first linked acid rain to air pollution. Acid rain is rain, snow or other precipitation that is unusually acidic. Acidity is measured on the pH scale, where lower numbers mean more acid. Most water sits between 6.5 and 8.5, while acid rain averages about 4–5; one definition draws the line below 5. The acid starts as gas. Burning fuels and smelting ores release sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which reactions in the air turn into sulfuric and nitric acid. Humans now dominate the supply, upsetting the natural The sulfur cycle: an element that trades electrons. Fossil fuels and industry emit 70 Tg (teragrams) of sulfur a year as SO2, far more than wildfires (2.8 Tg) and volcanoes (7–8 Tg) combined. Power plants alone produce two-thirds of the sulfur dioxide in the air and a quarter of the nitrogen oxides. Coal-fired stations, animal farming, fertilizers, steel mills and vehicles all contribute. The worst-hit regions run from eastern Europe into Scandinavia, across the eastern third of the United States and into southeastern Canada.

  <!-- nature-pol-046 -->

- **Municipal solid waste: what a city throws away**

  What a city throws away says a lot about it. Municipal solid waste is everyday rubbish: the trash or garbage of items thrown out by the public. Most definitions leave out industrial, agricultural, medical and radioactive waste, and sewage sludge. Its make-up varies greatly between places and over time. Typical Chinese municipal waste is 55.9% food residue, 11.2% plastics and 8.5% paper. Where recycling is well developed, what is left is mainly plastic film and packaging that cannot be recycled. The industry that handles it has four parts: recycling, composting, disposal and burning waste to make energy. Waste hierarchies rank these methods from most to least preferred. Reducing and reusing come first, then recycling or composting, then recovering energy, and only last treatment and disposal. The ranking matters for the climate too. Municipal waste produces large amounts of methane, and nearly 90% of it could be avoided with existing technologies.

  <!-- nature-pol-064 -->

- **Landfill: burying the rubbish, and the costs**

  Burying rubbish is the oldest and most common way to get rid of it. A landfill is a site for disposing of waste, including household rubbish (Municipal solid waste: what a city throws away). Yet systematic burial, with daily and final covers over the waste, only began in the 1940s. The modern sanitary landfill followed. It is an engineered facility that separates and confines waste, and it was widely adopted in the 1960s and 1970s to end open dumps. Landfills still carry costs. They take up much land and can contaminate groundwater and soil. Neighbors put up with dust, odor, noise, and disease-carrying rats and flies, and local property values fall. Permitting a new US landfill generally takes five to seven years and costs millions of dollars. When a site closes, it often gets a second life as a park, a bike course or a solar farm.

  <!-- nature-pol-058 -->

- **Hazardous waste: rubbish that stays dangerous**

  Some rubbish stays dangerous long after it is thrown away. Hazardous waste is waste that can damage human health or the environment. It earns that label in one of four ways: it is toxic, reactive, corrosive or ignitable. As of 2022, humanity produced 300–500 million metric tons of it a year. The sources are surprisingly ordinary. Solvents, batteries and the by-products of metal refining are common ones. So are dry cleaners, car repair shops, hospitals and photo labs. Handled badly, this waste becomes Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill of the worst kind. It fouls the air, raising illness and death, and contaminates groundwater and soil. That is why it is regulated at local, national and international levels.

  <!-- nature-pol-054 -->

- **Nonpoint source pollution: contamination with no address**

  A single factory pipe is easy to find. A thousand fertilized fields are not. Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse contamination of water or air that does not come from one identifiable source. It is often the combined effect of small amounts of pollutants gathered from a large area. It contrasts with Point source pollution, which comes from a single source. Nonpoint pollution travels by Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in, rain, deposition from the air, drainage and seepage, which makes it hard to trace back. Paved city surfaces and farms that spread fertilizer and manure are major sources. Even a smokestack, a single source where it stands, acts as nonpoint where its pollution lands after being carried far and mixed with others. In the United States it is the leading cause of water pollution, mainly from farm runoff and altered waterways.

  <!-- nature-pol-075 -->

- **Brownfield land: the polluted leftovers of industry**

  The word was first used on June 28, 1992, at a US congressional field hearing. Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may be polluted from past industrial use. Countries define it differently, mainly over whether contamination must actually be present. Examples include abandoned factories, ash ponds, old landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations. Their ground may hold spilled hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead. The United States alone is estimated to have over 500,000 brownfield sites contaminated below the level that triggers Superfund. Not all of this land is dead ground. Industrial brownfields can be valuable ecosystems that support rare plants, animals and invertebrates. Redeveloping them has become a key part of large urban greening projects.

  <!-- nature-pol-050 -->

- **How breathing particles shortens lives**

  In 2023, fine particles in the air contributed to 7.9 million deaths worldwide. Of these, 4.9 million were linked to outdoor air pollution and 2.8 million to household air pollution. Breathing Particulate matter: the most dangerous thing in the air is linked to disease throughout the body. It contributes to stroke, heart disease, respiratory disease, many cancers, preterm birth and cognitive impairment. Both short bursts and long years of exposure cause harm. Scientists first showed the link to premature deaths in the early 1970s, and the 1993 Harvard Six Cities study established it firmly for cities. Policy can bend these numbers. In the EU, deaths from PM2.5 fell 57% between 2005 and 2023, as policies cut primary emissions, the particles released directly, by 38%. China's 2013 air pollution action plan cut average PM2.5 by a third by 2017, and fewer people died.

  <!-- nature-pol-070 -->

- **What acid rain does to lakes, forests and stone**

  Below a pH of 5, most fish eggs will not hatch. Below 4, adult fish die. Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky harms forests, fresh waters and soils, kills plants and animals, damages buildings and affects human health. In lakes and streams, lower pH comes with more aluminum in the water, which harms fish, other aquatic animals, microbes and plants. In soil, acid kills sensitive microbes and disables their enzymes, so functions such as decomposition collapse. High-altitude forests suffer most, because the clouds and fog around them are more acidic than rain. Cities feel it too. Acids react with limestone and marble in buildings and statues to form gypsum, which flakes off. And breathing the pollutants linked to acid rain, such as nitrogen dioxide, can damage the airways.

  <!-- nature-pol-048 -->

- **Damage functions: pricing each degree of warming**

  How much does one more degree of warming cost? A damage function is the economist's answer: a relationship, used in Cost–benefit analysis, that estimates the economic damage caused by an environmental change such as warming. Researchers have built them for rising seas, farm productivity and the effect of heat on how much work people get done. A common base form makes damages grow with the square of warming. So 2 °C causes 4 times the damage of 1 °C, and 3 °C causes 9 times. Some versions add tipping points, so damages speed up, or jump, once warming passes 2-3 °C. Estimates of the Social cost of carbon, the money value of harm from each extra unit of emissions, are highly sensitive to the damage function chosen, along with the discount rate. A 2020 paper using an updated function found that around 2 °C of warming would be 'optimal' in one leading climate-economy model, DICE. Critics such as Nicholas Stern argue that standard damage functions miss many of society's most important risks. The argument is far from settled.

  <!-- nature-clim-234 -->

- **How airborne particles cool and cloud the planet**

  Particles in the air do not only harm lungs; they also change the climate. Aerosols alter how much incoming sunlight and outgoing heat Earth keeps. They act directly, by scattering and absorbing radiation, and indirectly, by changing clouds, since cloud droplets form on particles. Not all particles behave alike. Soot absorbs radiation strongly, while sea-salt particles only scatter it. Overall, the direct effect is a negative Radiative forcing: the push on Earth's energy balance, which means cooling. Aerosol effects remain the biggest source of uncertainty in climate predictions.

  <!-- nature-pol-073 -->

- **Coarse, fine and ultrafine: sorting particles by size**

  Size decides how deep a particle gets, and so how much harm it can do. Scientists group particles by diameter. Coarse PM10 particles measure 10 micrometers or less, and fine PM2.5 particles 2.5 micrometers or less. Ultrafine particles are smaller still. A micrometer is a thousandth of a millimeter. Coarse particles lodge in the nose, throat and upper airways. Fine ones penetrate deep into the lungs, reaching the smallest airways and air sacs. That is why, across all causes of death, PM2.5 has more severe effects than PM10.

  <!-- nature-pol-069 -->

- **Filters, scrubbers and charged plates that catch dust**

  Much of the dust a factory makes never leaves the building. In most industrialized countries particle emissions are highly regulated, and industries meet the rules with dust collection systems. These include cyclones, fabric filters, wet scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators, all forms of Pollution control: better to prevent than to clean up. Fabric filters, also called baghouses, are the most common in general industry. Electrostatic precipitators work differently. They give particles an electric charge and collect them on large charged plates.

  <!-- nature-pol-074 -->

- **Who breathes the dirtiest air**

  Particle pollution does not fall evenly. Its burden lands more heavily on non-White people and on those living in poverty. Living near facilities that emit particles raises PM2.5 exposure and rates of illness and death. About 1.6 billion people live near sources of PM2.5 and other toxins, and 900 million of them live near super-emitting facilities. In the United States, the gap for Black people is larger than income alone explains, and scholars link it to housing segregation. The pattern repeats the wider story of Who breathes the dirtiest air.

  <!-- nature-pol-072 -->

- **The WHO's limits for safe air**

  By the World Health Organization's yardstick, 97% of the world's population breathes unsafe air. The WHO sets guideline limits for particle exposure, above which health risks rise. For PM2.5, the yearly average should not exceed 5 μg/m3, and the 24-hour average 15 μg/m3. For PM10, the limits are 15 μg/m3 a year and 45 μg/m3 over 24 hours. The unit means micrograms of particles in each cubic meter of air. The 97% figure comes from the 2021 guideline for PM2.5.

  <!-- nature-pol-071 -->

- **Acid deposition: wet and dry routes to the ground**

  Acid does not need rain to fall. Acid deposition is the delivery of acids from the air to the ground, by two routes. Wet deposition happens when rain, snow or fog carries acids down to the surface. Dry deposition happens when particles and gases simply stick to the ground, plants or other surfaces. That quieter route matters. Dry deposition can make up 20 to 60% of total acid deposition, so Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky tells only part of the story.

  <!-- nature-pol-047 -->

- **How scrubbers, treaties and trading tamed acid rain**

  Acid rain has been cut back in three ways. The first is technical. Scrubbing sulfur from power-station exhaust, called flue-gas desulfurization, removes 95% or more of the SO2 from a typical coal-fired station. The second is diplomatic. Under the 1979 Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, sulfur and particle emissions have fallen 30-80% in Europe and 30-40% in North America since 1990. The third is economic: Emissions trading: a cap on pollution, a market in permits. Each polluter holds allowances, permits for its emissions, and can sell the ones it no longer needs after installing controls. The first such market came with the 1990 amendments to the US Clean Air Act (United States), to cut SO2 at the lowest cost to society.

  <!-- nature-pol-049 -->

- **Alternatives to burying waste**

  Burying waste is not the only option, and not always the cheapest. Alternatives to Landfill: burying the rubbish, and the costs include cutting waste and recycling, burning it to make energy, composting, and anaerobic digestion, in which microbes break waste down without oxygen. Depending on local economics and incentives, these can be made cheaper than landfilling. Some governments push hard. Germany, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland have banned landfilling untreated waste. The UK taxes biodegradable waste sent to landfill, and England set up a scheme for councils to trade landfill quotas. The idea of Zero waste aims to shrink landfill volume as far as possible.

  <!-- nature-pol-063 -->

- **Landfill gas: methane from buried rubbish**

  Landfills are the third largest emitter of methane worldwide. Landfill gas is the mix produced when microbes digest buried organic waste without oxygen. On average it is about half methane and slightly less than half carbon dioxide, which links landfills to Methane: a small gas with a big warming punch. Well-managed landfills collect the gas, then either burn it off in a flare or use it to generate electricity. More than 850 US landfills recover it. Capturing landfill methane is also a common kind of project for carbon offsets, schemes in which one party pays to cut emissions to make up for its own.

  <!-- nature-pol-061 -->

- **Leachate: the poisoned liquid under a landfill**

  Rain that falls on a landfill does not stay clean. Leachate is the contaminated liquid formed when water seeps through the waste, picking up organic matter, heavy metals and other pollutants. If it escapes, it can contaminate groundwater. Modern landfills fight back with impermeable liners several meters thick, stable sites and systems that collect the liquid. When a landfill is full, it is sealed to keep rain out, so no new leachate forms.

  <!-- nature-pol-060 -->

- **Landfill aftercare: a cost that may never end**

  A landfill's costs do not stop when it closes. Aftercare is the long period after a site is full and capped, when liners, gas capture (Landfill gas: methane from buried rubbish) and treatment of leachate (Leachate: the poisoned liquid under a landfill) keep limiting harm. It may last several decades, or forever. Sealed waste keeps its power to pollute, so replacing liners and treating leachate is an indefinite requirement. In the Netherlands, aftercare can cost more than 20 million euros per landfill.

  <!-- nature-pol-062 -->

- **Inside a landfill: the slow life of buried waste**

  A sealed landfill is less a tomb than a slow digester. A sanitary landfill works as a biological reactor, in which microbes break organic waste into simpler, less toxic compounds over several phases. First, oxygen trapped in the waste feeds aerobic breakdown until the microbes use it up. The rest of the work happens without oxygen (Anaerobic respiration: breathing without oxygen). In the acid phase, fatty acids build up and the leachate's pH falls from about 7.5 to 5.6. In the longest phase, methane-making microbes turn the acids into methane and carbon dioxide. Finally methane production almost stops, as nutrients run short and oxygen seeps back in.

  <!-- nature-pol-059 -->

- **Reuse: keeping things in service**

  The greenest item is often the one already made. Reuse means using things again, by repairing, gifting, refurbishing or lending them, instead of throwing them away. It lengthens product life and reduces the need for fresh raw materials. Unlike recycling, it does not break items down into raw materials, which saves time, money, energy and resources. That makes extending an item's use the least energy-intensive option, preferable to recycling or disposal. Online networks such as Freecycle list unwanted items for others to take, keeping them out of landfills.

  <!-- nature-pol-066 -->

- **Source separation: sorting waste where it starts**

  Sorting rubbish at home makes everything downstream easier. Source separation means sorting waste into types, such as biodegradable, recyclable, residual and hazardous, where it is produced. It improves recycling, prevents contamination, allows composting and ensures hazardous waste is properly treated. Separated and mixed wastes then go to materials recovery facilities, which sort them by hand and with screens, magnets and optical sorting. Separating, composting and recycling together can also cut methane emissions from municipal waste.

  <!-- nature-pol-065 -->

- **Waste-to-energy: power from rubbish**

  Rubbish can keep the lights on. Waste-to-energy is generating power from municipal waste, by burning it, by capturing landfill gas, or through pyrolysis or gasification, which break waste down with heat. Older incinerators emitted many pollutants. New rules and technology changed that. US rules in 1995 and 2000 cut dioxin emissions from such plants by over 99% below 1990 levels, and mercury by over 90%. Because waste contains food, wood and paper, burning it can partly count as bioenergy, energy made from living material.

  <!-- nature-pol-067 -->

- **Disposing of hazardous waste: bury, burn or recycle**

  Dangerous waste has three main exits: secure landfills, fire and recycling. For landfilling, it is first treated and stabilized, and the landfill needs barriers along its foundations to stop groundwater contamination. Incinerators burn it at 870–1400 °C, greatly shrinking it, but the leftover ash and gases can be hazardous too. Some materials, such as lead–acid batteries and circuit boards, can be recycled into new products. At the extreme, plasma treatment above 3000 °C turns waste into inert, rock-like slag. It is very expensive, but it suits persistent pollutants such as PCBs.

  <!-- nature-pol-055 -->

- **Exporting poison: the trade in hazardous waste**

  When disposal got expensive at home, the waste went abroad. As laws such as the US RCRA raised disposal costs in developed nations in the 1970s, shipments of Hazardous waste: rubbish that stays dangerous to poorer countries with weaker rules grew fast. In 1990, OECD countries, a club of mostly rich nations, exported around 1.8 million tons of it. The 1992 Basel Convention, signed by 199 countries, set out to stop this flow. The aim lives on in the UN's global goals, where Goal 12 includes sound management of chemicals and wastes throughout their life cycle.

  <!-- nature-pol-057 -->

- **Who lives next to hazardous waste**

  Hazardous waste does not land at random. Poorer people and social minorities face a higher risk of exposure to it and its pollution. An Austrian study found that people living near industrial sites are more often unemployed and less educated, and twice as likely to be immigrants. Groups who rely on local land and streams for food and water, including Native Americans, face multiplied risk.

  <!-- nature-pol-056 -->

- **Slowing the runoff: controlling diffuse pollution**

  Stopping diffuse pollution mostly means slowing water down. Nonpoint source pollution: contamination with no address is controlled by land practices that slow runoff and trap pollutants before they reach water. Grass buffer strips between paved areas and streams let soil absorb pollutants first. Retention ponds hold storm runoff so contaminants settle out and stay trapped. Farmers use contour plowing, mulching, rotating crops, perennial crops and plowing less. They also leave strips of vegetation along waterways (Riparian buffer). Mixing trees with farming (Agroforestry) can also clean the air by absorbing pollutants such as particulate matter.

  <!-- nature-pol-077 -->

- **Why diffuse pollution escapes the regulators**

  A permit needs a pipe to attach to. Nonpoint pollution has no single discharge point, so it is hard to regulate, and US federal law leaves it largely to states and voluntary programs. For that reason, diffuse sources were excluded from the permit program of the Clean Water Act. State programs rely instead on best management practices, seeking the least costly way to cut the most pollution. Since 1987, federal grants under section 319 of that law have funded these state programs. The results are weak. A 2015 article found the law effective for single-source discharges but not for diffuse ones.

  <!-- nature-pol-078 -->

- **Sediment, nutrients, toxins and germs in runoff**

  Four kinds of pollutant dominate runoff: sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and disease-causing pathogens. Sediment clouds water, cutting light for underwater plants and for the fish and shellfish that depend on them. Of the nutrients, phosphorus and nitrogen cause the most concern. The toxic chemicals include heavy metals and compounds such as PCBs and DDT, which resist breakdown and persist in the environment. For pathogens, coliform bacteria in runoff serve as an indicator of water pollution rather than as a cause of disease.

  <!-- nature-pol-076 -->

- **Why polluted land sits empty for decades**

  Some contaminated land sits unused for decades for a simple reason: cleaning it would cost more than the land would then be worth. Brownfields also carry an environmental stigma that can delay redevelopment. The US Superfund law has been criticized for pushing investment to greenfields, undeveloped land, through severe no-fault liability, which makes owners pay whether or not they caused the pollution. Redevelopment grew in the 2000s as developable land became scarcer in crowded areas. Governments help too. The federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) awarded nearly 1,000 cleanup grants worth almost $190 million from 2002 through 2013, and cleanup costs are fully tax-deductible.

  <!-- nature-pol-052 -->

- **Cleaning up brownfields**

  Poisoned ground can be healed, though rarely by one method alone. Brownfield remediation is cleaning contaminated former industrial land so it can be reused. Techniques include heating soil in place, bioremediation, which uses living organisms to break pollutants down, oxidizing contaminants in place, and soil vapor extraction, which draws out polluting gases. They are often combined. Binders can be mixed into soil to stop chemicals leaching out. In phytoremediation, deep-rooted plants draw heavy metals out of the soil.

  <!-- nature-pol-053 -->

- **What is a polluted plot worth?**

  Contamination scrambles the usual sums of property. Valuing a brownfield needs specialized appraisal, because pollution changes a site's best use and its value both before and after cleanup. The value should allow for lingering stigma and possible liability to third parties. Normal appraisal often fails, so appraisers turn to Contingent valuation, case studies or statistical analysis. The payoff from cleanup can be large. A 2014 study looked at EPA cleanup grants from 2002 through 2008. It found an average benefit of almost $4 million per site, and a median, or middle value, of $2.1 million. Some environmental firms team up with insurers to guarantee cleanup costs.

  <!-- nature-pol-051 -->
