### Tradable permits and carbon markets

Since 2005, every ton of carbon dioxide released by a covered European power plant or factory has needed a permit. That rule is the heart of {{ref:nature-pol-253}}: a government caps total emissions, issues permits, and lets polluters buy and sell them. Trading is meant to make cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost. This chapter follows the idea from theory to working markets in Europe and China, and weighs it against a {{ref:nature-pol-081}}, which fixes the price instead of the amount. It also hears the critics, who call carbon trading ineffective, unfair or open to abuse, and who warn that cuts in one country can raise emissions in another.

- **Emissions trading: a cap on pollution, a market in permits**

  What if the right to pollute were something a firm had to buy? Emissions trading, also called cap and trade, rests on that idea. A government caps the total amount of a pollutant that may be released and issues permits up to that cap. Each polluter must hold permits equal to its emissions. One that wants to emit more must buy permits from others willing to sell. In effect the buyer pays a charge for polluting, while the seller is rewarded for cutting its emissions. A Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else, a cost dumped on others, so acquires a price. The goal is to meet a set emissions target at the lowest cost. Unlike Command and control regulation, which tells each firm what to do, trading lets firms decide how to meet the target. Some schemes let participants bank allowances for later periods, so they can cut emissions when it is most efficient. Usually the government lowers the overall limit over time towards a national reduction target. The approach is used for carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, and for sulfur dioxide and other pollutants. Does it work? A 2024 meta-analysis pooled 80 evaluations across 21 carbon-pricing systems. It found average emission cuts of about 5–21%, or around 4–15% after correcting for Publication bias: the missing studies that skew the record.

  <!-- nature-pol-253 -->

- **Carbon pricing: charging for the harm of greenhouse gases**

  Burning coal, oil or gas releases greenhouse gases, and no market charges for the harm they do. That makes the emissions a negative Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else, and carbon pricing is the standard remedy. It is a government policy that puts a money cost on Greenhouse gas emissions: who emits, and how much, so that polluters burn less fossil fuel. The price usually takes one of two forms: a Carbon tax, or an emissions trading scheme in which firms must buy allowances to emit. Many economists consider it the most economically efficient way to cut emissions, because it fixes the unpriced external cost at its source, in the spirit of a Pigouvian tax. In 2025 carbon pricing covered 28% of global greenhouse gas emissions, and in 2020 it raised $53B in revenue. Of 21 schemes evaluated, at least 17 reduced emissions, by between 5% and 21%. A 2020 study found that carbon prices have not harmed economic growth in wealthy industrialized democracies. The weak point is the level of the price. About one third of schemes charge less than $10 per tonne of carbon dioxide ($10/tCO2), and most less than $40. Only Sweden and Switzerland exceed $100/tCO2. The IPCC says prices of $135–$5500 per tonne in 2030 and $245–$13,000 in 2050 would be needed to stay below the 1.5°C limit.

  <!-- nature-pol-239 -->

- **Carbon markets: trading the right to emit greenhouse gases**

  In 2023 carbon trading worldwide was worth a record 881 billion euros, and about 87% of it sat in the European Union's scheme. Carbon emission trading is Emissions trading: a cap on pollution, a market in permits applied to carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. A total limit on all participants' emissions sets the price. A polluter emitting more than its quota must buy the right from emitters with fewer emissions. In economic terms, the scheme creates property rights to the atmosphere, a global Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few, to deal with an externality that crosses borders. Compliance is checked by comparing each emitter's actual emissions with the permits it surrenders. Countries use these markets to meet their pledges under the Paris Agreement, with schemes running in China, the European Union and elsewhere. Prices vary widely. In September 2021 allowances cost €7 per tonne in China's national scheme and €63 per tonne in the EU's. The markets share two weaknesses. Their caps are usually not matched to the total emissions allowed if warming is to stay within 1.5 °C or 2 °C. And oversupply can push allowance prices too low to matter.

  <!-- nature-pol-244 -->

- **Carbon leakage: cuts at home, emissions abroad**

  Regulating emissions in one place can push them to places with less regulation. This is carbon leakage. It happens when climate policy raises local costs, so production moves to countries with laxer rules while demand stays the same. It can also run through fuel markets: lower demand cuts fuel prices, and countries without a carbon price use more. The leakage rate divides the rise in emissions outside the acting countries by the cut inside them. A rate above 100% would mean domestic action actually increased global emissions. Estimates for action under the Kyoto Protocol ranged from 5 to 20%, but were seen as very uncertain. There is no consensus on how large leakage is in the long run. The EU gives free allowances to sectors at high risk, such as aluminum, ranked by trade intensity times emission intensity. Yet firm-level evidence found its trading scheme cut regulated manufacturers' CO₂ emissions by 14–16% with no observed leakage.

  <!-- nature-pol-252 -->

- **China's national carbon market: the largest of its kind**

  China proposed a carbon tax in 2010 but never passed it. Instead it set up an emissions trading scheme in February 2021, which began operating that year. Seven pilot markets came first, starting in Shenzhen on June 18, 2013, with compliance rates over 96%. The national scheme began with power plants and covers 40% of China's emissions, which is 15% of world emissions. No scheme of its kind is larger. Unusually, it caps Emission intensity, the emissions per unit of output, rather than the total. In July 2021 permits were handed out free and traded at around RMB 50 per tonne, roughly half the EU price. Studies find it cut carbon emissions by up to 18.2% and power sector emissions by 13% in 2013-2020. It also delivered about a third of China's air pollution health benefits. Some researchers found it can reduce GDP or hold back innovation. By 2027 it is expected to cover all major industrial emitters and move to an absolute cap for stable sectors.

  <!-- nature-pol-270 -->

- **Why permit trading puts the cheapest cuts first**

  Trading permits makes pollution cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost. The logic runs through each firm's books. A polluter compares the permit price with its Marginal abatement cost: the extra cost of cutting one more unit of pollution, a kind of Marginal cost: the price of one more unit. Then it chooses to buy or sell permits, install cleaner technology or cut output. In theory this spreads reductions efficiently among polluters and lowers compliance costs compared with command-and-control rules. It is a version of the equi-marginal principle, which economists use to find the most efficient decision. In the mathematics of the least-cost target, the Lagrange multipliers: pricing the constraints plays the role of the market permit price. The idea has a famous ancestor. Coase (1960) argued that social costs could be handled by negotiating property rights, assuming perfect markets and equal bargaining power (The Coase theorem: bargaining your way out of harm).

  <!-- nature-pol-254 -->

- **Free or auctioned: how permits are handed out**

  Once a government decides how many permits to issue, it must decide who gets them. There are two routes. Under free allocation, existing emitters receive permits and the government earns no carbon revenue. Under auctioning, it sells them and receives their full value on average. Either way the permits are equally scarce, so they sell at the same market price. The difference lies in who keeps the money. Emitters generally profit from permits given to them free, while paying for permits reduces their profits. Advance notice or a gradual introduction keeps the one-time cost of a new carbon price small.

  <!-- nature-pol-245 -->

- **The EU Emissions Trading System: Europe's carbon market**

  The European Union Emissions Trading System began in 2005 as the world's first large greenhouse gas trading scheme. Each allowance lets its holder emit 1 ton of CO2. It operates in 30 countries: the 27 EU states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. As of 2026 it covers around 40% of the EU's emissions, and its cap should reach zero by 2039. Phase I issued too many permits, and this over-allocation drove the carbon price to zero in 2007. Between 2005 and 2023, emissions from covered power plants and factories fell by 47%. A 2023 study found it cut emissions by 10% between 2005 and 2012, with no significant effect on profits or employment. Fraud has struck too: hackers stole 28 to 30 million euros of allowances in 2011, and VAT fraud cost Germany about €850 million. Critics say over-allocation, windfall profits and price volatility mean it has failed its goals. Proponents call Phase I a learning phase and point to measured cuts.

  <!-- nature-pol-272 -->

- **The case against carbon trading**

  Supporters see carbon trading as an efficient climate tool. Critics call it ineffective, unjust and open to manipulation, and the argument is far from settled. The first objection is scale. Climate change, critics argue, needs more radical, systemic cuts in fossil fuel use than pollution trading can deliver. The second is direction. The market picks the easiest short-term carbon savings, which may differ from the steps needed to reduce climate change. The third is fairness. Carbon trading has been called a form of colonialism that lets rich countries keep consuming while claiming savings abroad. Then there is abuse. Some companies in China and India produced greenhouse gases artificially in order to earn credits for destroying them. Schemes have also been criticized for creating speculative markets through financial derivatives (The derivative: how fast things change right now), and for changes linked to money laundering.

  <!-- nature-pol-249 -->

- **Tax or cap: two ways to price carbon**

  A Carbon tax fixes the price of each tonne emitted and lets the amount adjust. Emissions trading does the reverse: it fixes the total amount emitted and lets the price move. Economists disagree over which is better. A tax is generally favored for its simplicity and price stability. It is also easier to enforce broadly: British Columbia enacted and implemented its carbon tax in five months. A cap can in principle hold emissions to a fixed remaining total. Most cap-and-trade programs lower the cap by a fixed percentage each year, guaranteeing that emissions decline. Permits therefore suit cases where certainty about emissions is needed. Prices under a cap are more volatile, though. That makes them riskier for investors, consumers and governments that auction permits. Both tools can be bent by politics. Industries may lobby their way out of a tax, while freely handed-out permits can invite corrupt behavior. On paper the two are close cousins. Both are efficient, and if permits are auctioned they have the same social cost and effect on profits. A last dispute concerns other climate policies. Some economists say a cap stops measures such as renewable energy support from cutting emissions further; others say only an enforced cap guarantees cuts (Why renewable energy support adds nothing under a binding cap).

  <!-- nature-pol-240 -->

- **Internal carbon pricing: companies that charge themselves**

  As of 2024, 1,753 companies in 56 countries reported through the Carbon Disclosure Project that they put a price on their own greenhouse gas emissions. Internal carbon pricing is voluntary and comes on top of any price a government imposes. It works like a Pigouvian tax inside the firm, making fossil fuel use more expensive. Tools include internal emissions trading, proxy prices, carbon fees, implicit prices and hybrids of these. Proxy pricing, used by about two-thirds of reporting companies, writes a set carbon price into investment decisions without any actual payment. Companies often base their price on the Social cost of carbon or on the cost of the last cut needed to reach a target. An analysis of 500 firms reporting from 2011 to 2018 linked adoption to a significant fall in emissions per unit of revenue and per employee. Some researchers worry it can serve as Greenwashing, deterring governments from stricter carbon rules.

  <!-- nature-pol-243 -->

- **Kyoto's flexible mechanisms: cutting emissions where it costs least**

  Cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, but it benefits the atmosphere equally wherever it happens. That idea underlies the three flexible mechanisms of the Kyoto Protocol: emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation: emission projects between rich countries. Each lets countries meet emission targets more cheaply by acting in other countries. The protocol required Annex I countries, the developed nations with targets, to cut emissions on average 5.2% below 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012. International emissions trading let parties buy Kyoto units from other countries to help meet their targets. The main argument for flexibility is cost-effectiveness, which keeps fairness separate from the efficiency of cutting emissions cheaply. Negotiators disagreed over whether that was wise. Critics feared rich countries would avoid domestic cuts and take up all the cheap reductions in developing countries. Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement are their successor.

  <!-- nature-pol-275 -->

- **The Acid Rain Program: America's first cap and trade**

  A US power plant that emitted a ton of sulfur dioxide beyond its allowances paid a fine of $2,000. That rule enforced the Acid Rain Program, the first cap-and-trade emissions program in the United States. Run by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), it cut sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides, the gases that cause Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky. Title IV of the 1990 amendments to the Clean Air Act (United States) set a falling cap on SO2, aiming to bring emissions to 50% of 1980 levels. In 2007 total SO2 emissions were 8.9 million tons, reaching the long-term goal ahead of the 2010 deadline. Its expected yearly cost by 2010, $1 billion to $2 billion, was only one fourth of the first prediction. A 2021 study found lasting air quality gains, cutting mortality risk by 5% over 10 years. The EPA, industry and economists call it a success, and it became a model for later greenhouse gas schemes. Skeptical environmentalists argue the cuts came from broader trends and other regulation. They note it cut SO2 by 40%, while conventional regulation in the European Union achieved more than 70%.

  <!-- nature-pol-262 -->

- **Europe's carbon charge at the border**

  Since 2026, firms bringing steel or cement into the European Union have had to pay for the carbon released in making it. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, or CBAM, is a Carbon tariff on carbon-intensive imports. Its main aim is to stop Carbon leakage: cuts at home, emissions abroad by charging imports the same carbon price that EU producers pay under the EU ETS. Importers must buy CBAM certificates, priced in line with ETS allowances, to cover the emissions embedded in their goods. It covers aluminum, cement, electricity, fertilizers, hydrogen and iron and steel, with reporting from October 2023. Free ETS allowances in these sectors will be phased out by 2034. It may push other countries to price carbon: Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Serbia are doing so partly because of it. Some see it as the start of a Climate club of the kind proposed by William Nordhaus. Critics are less impressed. An Asian Development Bank report says it will cut emissions only a little while harming imports to the EU. Questions also remain over its fit with World Trade Organization rules and its effect on least developed countries.

  <!-- nature-pol-261 -->

- **Joint Implementation: emission projects between rich countries**

  Joint Implementation is a mechanism of the Kyoto Protocol. Under it, one developed (Annex I) country invests in an emission-cutting project in another and counts the cuts towards its own target. Projects earn credits (Emission reduction units: credits from Joint Implementation), each equal to one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. These come out of the host country's own pool of units, so the total among Annex I parties does not change. Because hosts also have emission commitments, it raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the Clean Development Mechanism. Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, expected to total around 300 million units by 2012.

  <!-- nature-pol-277 -->

- **Baseline and credit: rewards for beating your own past**

  Not every trading scheme starts with a cap. In a baseline-and-credit scheme, polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their own historical emissions. Polluters that face a regulatory limit can then buy those credits. Programs usually require Additionality: would it have happened anyway?: the cuts must go beyond what existing rules already demand. That test is hard to define and monitor. Some companies deliberately raised their emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

  <!-- nature-pol-258 -->

- **From computer models to carbon markets**

  Emissions trading began as a computer result. Simulation studies of air pollution costs between 1967 and 1970 found that a least-cost solution was dramatically cheaper than conventional ways of cutting pollution. The 1977 Clean Air Act took up an offset mechanism: a firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant. The first cap-and-trade system was the US The Acid Rain Program: America's first cap and trade under the 1990 Clean Air Act, announced as a paradigm shift in Environmental policy. From US clean air policy, the approach then spread to the European Union and to global climate policy.

  <!-- nature-pol-255 -->

- **Linking carbon markets across borders**

  California and Québec linked their cap-and-trade systems in 2014, and the EU's scheme has linked with Switzerland's. Linking means each system recognizes the other's allowances for compliance. The result is a larger carbon market, which can lower compliance costs, raise liquidity, the ease of finding a buyer or seller, and stabilize prices. Some scholars see linking as a bottom-up starting point for international climate policy, built from existing national and regional schemes.

  <!-- nature-pol-259 -->

- **Measure, report, verify: keeping a carbon market honest**

  A permit market is only as good as its numbers. Monitoring, reporting and verification are the checks that make it credible: emissions are measured or calculated, reported, then verified by government or third-party auditors. Some emissions are measured by sensors in chimneys, but many activities rely on calculations instead. Acid Rain Program plants had to monitor SO2 and NOx continuously and send data to the EPA daily. Polluters exceeding their allowances face fines and sanctions. The worries are the cost of checking and the risk of facilities lying. For voluntary credits, robust independent third-party validation and verification is one of the Core Carbon Principles.

  <!-- nature-pol-281 -->

- **The safety valve: a cap with a price limit**

  A safety valve is a hybrid of a cap and a tax. Emitters can buy permits on the market, or from the government at a set trigger price, which holds the permit price below a maximum. Some designs instead hold it above a minimum. A trigger price set high enough, or a permit supply small enough, lets the system mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument (Prices versus quantities). Each limit has a cost. A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit. A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.

  <!-- nature-pol-257 -->

- **Auctioning permits: making polluters pay up front**

  Businesses tend to oppose auctioning emission permits. Economists almost uniformly recommend it. Under auctioning, firms buy their permits at auction and the government receives their value. That revenue can fund low-carbon investment and cuts in distortionary taxes, the kind that discourage useful work and investment. Auctioning can also be more efficient and fairer than free allocation. And it removes the perverse incentive created by Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters.

  <!-- nature-pol-247 -->

- **Carbon trading and the neighbors of polluters**

  Carbon trading can move money from richer, higher-emitting countries to poorer, lower-emitting ones for climate action. That is its promise as a tool of Climate justice. The problem starts at the factory gate. Schemes cap only greenhouse gases, so a factory can buy permits instead of cutting its local air pollution. Low-income and minority communities living near emitters therefore keep facing an exposure gap. The sources record both sides: trading can advance that cause, yet it has also been linked to environmental injustice near emitters.

  <!-- nature-pol-250 -->

- **Toward a single global carbon market**

  In 2023 carbon markets worldwide were worth $948.75 billion, a figure expected to reach 2.68 trillion dollars by 2028. A truly worldwide market in emission allowances is still a proposal, though the Paris Agreement provides a legal basis for one. At COP 30, the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets formed with a plan for a global cap near current emissions, falling to net zero by 2050. Such a market could speed emission cuts seven-fold in participating countries, while raising $200 billion per year for clean energy and social programs.

  <!-- nature-pol-251 -->

- **Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters**

  Grandfathering gives out emission permits for free, according to how much each firm emitted in the past. It can create perverse incentives. A firm that cuts its emissions sharply may receive fewer permits later. Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits. The EU's trading scheme gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition. Free allocation is complex, and it encourages lobbying and Rent-seeking, the pursuit of favors from government.

  <!-- nature-pol-246 -->

- **Too many permits: how a carbon price collapses**

  A permit market lives or dies by the number of permits. Issue too many and the price sinks so low that firms have little reason to cut emissions. Issue too few and the risk flips to an excessively high price. Europe's trading scheme showed the first danger. Its price was fairly strong from 2005 to 2009 but was later undermined by oversupply and the Great Recession. Under the Kyoto Protocol, Russia held surplus allowances after its economic collapse. Buying them would not have reduced emissions.

  <!-- nature-pol-248 -->

- **Certified emission reductions: credits from developing countries**

  Between 2001 and 7 September 2012, the Clean Development Mechanism issued 1 billion certified emission reductions, or CERs. Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of Carbon dioxide equivalent: one scale for many gases (CO2e), measured against a baseline. Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their Kyoto targets. By 2013, 57% came from destroying just two gases, HFC-23 or N2O. Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012, amid recession and over-allocation in Europe's trading scheme.

  <!-- nature-pol-269 -->

- **Carbon revenue: what to do with the money**

  A carbon tax or a permit auction raises money, and governments must decide how to spend it. One standard proposal returns it to the public per person. Richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, so poorer people can come out ahead. Per-person refunds would not, however, cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses. Other proposals fund renewable energy support, research, public transport and car sharing. Revenue could also pay for negative emissions, which remove carbon dioxide and cost about $150–165 per ton depending on the technology.

  <!-- nature-pol-241 -->

- **Why renewable energy support adds nothing under a binding cap**

  Under a carbon tax, public support for renewable energy adds to the emission cuts. Under a binding cap, it does not. While the cap applies, renewable support brings no further emission cuts, because the cap has already fixed the total amount emitted. So the choice between a tax and a cap (Tax or cap: two ways to price carbon) also decides what other climate policies can achieve.

  <!-- nature-pol-242 -->

- **Assigned amount units: Kyoto's national allowances**

  Under the Kyoto Protocol, each Annex 1 country received assigned amount units up to its emission target for the 2008–2012 commitment period. Each unit allowed it to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. Under Article 17, countries below their targets could sell spare units to countries above theirs. Such trading had to be supplemental to domestic action: a top-up to cuts at home, not a replacement.

  <!-- nature-pol-266 -->

- **Emission reduction units: credits from Joint Implementation**

  A landfill releases methane, a gas with a 100-year Global warming potential: comparing gases with carbon dioxide of 25 compared with carbon dioxide. Capture and burn one tonne of it, and it yields nearly 3 tonnes of CO2, a saving of 22 emission reduction units. Each unit is a Kyoto credit for one tonne of CO2 equivalent cut by a Joint Implementation project. The market for them later collapsed. ERU prices declined 89 percent in 2012, falling to 15 euro cents in December.

  <!-- nature-pol-271 -->

- **EU ETS2: a carbon market for buildings and road transport**

  EU ETS2 is a second European trading system for carbon dioxide from buildings, road transport and other sectors outside the original scheme. It covers emissions upstream: fuel suppliers, not end consumers, must report and pay for them. Its cap aims for a 42% cut by 2030 compared with 2005. Part of the revenue funds a Social Climate Fund for vulnerable groups. Together the two systems will cover 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions. In 2025, under pressure from member states worried about inflation and energy affordability, its start was delayed to 2028.

  <!-- nature-pol-274 -->

- **The Market Stability Reserve: soaking up surplus permits**

  The Market Stability Reserve changes how many EU permits are auctioned each year, according to how many surplus permits are in circulation. It runs on predefined rules, with no discretion for the Commission or member states. It did not work at first. Back-loading and the reserve law failed to cut the surplus or lift prices in 2014–2017, when prices stayed below €10/tCO2. Since 2023, allowances in the reserve above a threshold are permanently invalidated. About 2.5 billion were invalidated on 1 January 2023.

  <!-- nature-pol-273 -->

- **Water trading: markets for the right to use water**

  Chile's 1981 Water Code made water rights freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial. Water trading is the buying and selling of water access entitlements, often called water rights, between willing sellers and buyers. A seller holds rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more. Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more productive uses: urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers. The older first-in-time system of prior appropriation led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology. Water is a Common-pool resources: hard to fence, easy to deplete, but once rights make its use rival and excludable, it behaves like a private good. It is still no standard commodity. Supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin. Trades can also harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller. Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.

  <!-- nature-pol-264 -->

- **CORSIA: offsetting the growth of international flights**

  In October 2016 the International Civil Aviation Organization adopted CORSIA, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation. It makes airlines buy credits (Carbon credit) to offset growth in emissions from international flights, aiming for carbon-neutral growth from 2020. It is voluntary from 2021 until 2027, when it becomes compulsory, though least developed and small island states are not required to join. Domestic flights are not included, and it will regulate 25% of aviation's international emissions. Supporters call it a compromise step forward. Critics say it won't reduce jet fuel demand, and one hundred organizations rejected it as letting warming pass 1.5 °C.

  <!-- nature-pol-267 -->

- **Personal carbon trading: an allowance for every adult**

  Personal carbon trading would give each adult an equal share of emission credits within a national limit on emissions. People would surrender credits when buying fuel or electricity. Those who emit more than their allowance would buy credits from those who use less, who would profit. Research finds it would be progressive, moving money from rich to poor, unlike a carbon tax before its revenue is redistributed. Norfolk Island trialed the world's first program starting in 2011. Proponents call it fair and effective. Critics point to complexity, high costs and possible political unacceptability, and a 2008 UK study found it ahead of its time.

  <!-- nature-pol-279 -->

- **Market design: engineering the rules of exchange**

  Some markets are built on purpose. Market design is the branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange, who gets what and by what procedure, to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes. It is closely related to Mechanism design: game theory run in reverse and auction theory. Alvin Roth pioneered applications in labor-market matching, organ transplantation and school choice. He and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel prize for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design. Auction theory supplies results such as the Revenue equivalence: when the auction format does not matter: with independent private values, sealed first-price and second-price auctions bring the same expected revenue.

  <!-- nature-pol-278 -->

- **Voluntary emission reductions: offsets bought by choice**

  Not every carbon offset is bought to meet a legal target. A Voluntary Emission Reduction, also called a Verified Emission Reduction or VER, is traded in the voluntary market. Companies and individuals buy them to compensate voluntarily for their emissions. They are usually certified outside the Kyoto Protocol. One VER equals 1 tonne of CO2 emissions. Standards set how reductions are measured, and every VER should at least be verified by an independent third party.

  <!-- nature-pol-283 -->

- **Windfall gains: income that drops from the sky**

  A windfall gain is a sudden, usually unexpected addition to Income: what you gain over a period well above the norm. It comes from luck or circumstance rather than planning. A windfall profit is the business version, caused for example by unexpected demand or by government regulation. Europe's carbon market supplied a case: fossil fuel generators priced freely allocated permits into electricity and reaped a massive windfall gain. Some legislators favor a windfall profits tax, since taxing unforeseen profits should not hurt the company.

  <!-- nature-pol-285 -->

- **Cap and dividend: sell the permits, pay the citizens**

  Who owns the sky? Peter Barnes asked in the title of his 2001 book, Who Owns the Sky?, where he first proposed the idea as 'Skytrust'. Cap and dividend is a cap-and-trade system in which all permits are sold and the money is paid back to citizens to offset higher energy prices. The cap often falls on upstream sources such as fossil fuel suppliers, which must buy permits for their emissions. Unlike ordinary cap and trade, no permits are given away free. The pollution rents, the value of the scarce permits, are captured publicly rather than becoming private assets. Households that emit least receive a bigger dividend than they pay in higher prices, which rewards those who conserve. A 2009 US bill would have auctioned 100 percent of permits and returned all proceeds as a monthly dividend, but it did not pass. The policy was vigorously debated: one critic called it 'fatally incomplete', while Time magazine hailed it.

  <!-- nature-pol-263 -->

- **Green certificates: trading proof of renewable power**

  A green certificate proves that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, came from renewable sources. It represents the environmental value of that power and can be traded separately from the electricity itself. Poland, Sweden, the UK, Italy and Belgium use such certificates as a more market-like alternative to Feed-in tariff. There is a catch. Buying a certificate only shifts the claim to renewable power; it does not change how much renewable energy is generated.

  <!-- nature-pol-276 -->

- **Pollution hot spots: when location matters**

  Carbon dioxide has a similar effect wherever it is released, so for trading its location does not matter. Regional pollutants such as SO2, NOx and mercury are different. The same amount does far more harm in some places than in others, so under a cap it can pile up in hot spots. Carbon trading has a related blind spot. Because it limits only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits without cutting local air pollution, leaving nearby low-income communities exposed. One answer is markets in location-based pollution licenses, which cap the rise in pollution at each monitoring point (Ambient permits: trading the right to raise local pollution).

  <!-- nature-pol-286 -->

- **Ambient permits: trading the right to raise local pollution**

  An ordinary permit grants the right to emit a set amount. An ambient permit grants the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount. Pollution at each monitoring point is modeled as a weighted sum of all emissions, written q=H⋅e, where the diffusion matrix H records how each source's output spreads. A polluter that affects several points must hold a portfolio of licenses covering all of them. Montgomery showed that both kinds of market allocate licenses efficiently, but pollution-license markets apply more widely.

  <!-- nature-pol-260 -->

- **Water quality trading: cleaner rivers at the lowest cost**

  Different polluters in one watershed, the land draining to a river or lake, face very different costs to control the same pollutant. Water quality trading puts that gap to work. Sources that can cut water pollution cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly. Most programs trade nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen (Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing). The US EPA issued its Water Quality Trading Policy in 2003, and all programs must meet the Clean Water Act. Funders include watershed beneficiaries, polluters compensating for their impacts and public good payers.

  <!-- nature-pol-287 -->

- **White certificates: trading proof of saved energy**

  In some countries, suppliers of electricity, gas and oil must deliver efficiency measures equal to a set percentage of their annual sales, or pay a penalty. White certificates are tradable proof that a certain amount of energy saving has been achieved. They are cousins of green certificates. As with emissions trading, tradability in theory meets the overall saving target at least cost. Great Britain started a scheme in 2002, Italy in 2005, and France and Denmark a year later.

  <!-- nature-pol-284 -->

- **Carbon retirement: taking permits off the market for good**

  A record 164 million credits (Carbon credit) were retired in voluntary markets in 2023. Retirement means permanently removing emission allowances or credits from circulation, so they can never be sold or used again. Under a cap, retiring allowances shrinks supply, which raises their scarcity and price. The EU's Market Stability Reserve invalidated about 2.5 billion allowances on 1 January 2023, and more than 3 billion by 2026. In voluntary markets, companies retire credits to offset emissions they cannot yet eliminate. Citizen groups have even bought and retired sulfur dioxide allowances in US EPA auctions, to cut the supply available to polluters.

  <!-- nature-pol-268 -->

- **Transferable development rights: paying land to stay open**

  Land carries a bundle of Property rights: the rules of who owns what, including the right to develop it. Transferable development rights let that one right be sold on its own. Developers buy the building rights of land in a protected sending area: farmland, wilderness or historic sites at risk of development. They use those rights to build more densely in a receiving area, an urban place suited to higher density. Landowners get paid for conserving environmental, heritage or farming values, and sprawl is curbed by concentrating development. Such programs operate in over 200 U.S. communities.

  <!-- nature-pol-280 -->

## Paying for nature

In 1997 Costa Rica became the first country to run a national program that pays landowners for the services their land provides. This part of the course follows that idea: paying farmers and landowners to manage land so that it delivers clean water, stored carbon or thriving wildlife. China, the United States and the mineral-water brand Vittel have all tried versions of it, and Uganda tested one as a randomized controlled trial. Every scheme meets the same hard question. Did the payment cause an outcome that would not have happened anyway, judged against a prediction of what would have happened without it?

### Payments for ecosystem services

A payment for ecosystem services offers farmers or landowners money to manage their land so that it keeps providing a service from nature. The US Conservation Reserve Program pays farmers to plant grass, trees or buffer strips on cropland. China's Grain for Green, launched in 1999, pays them to turn eroding farmland back into vegetation. This chapter looks at how such schemes are designed, from auctions in which sellers underbid one another to the rule that money flows only when the service is delivered. It also asks how anyone can tell whether a payment made a difference at all.

- **Paying landowners for the services their land provides**

  Climate change mitigation, watershed services and biodiversity conservation draw most of the money. They are the 'big three' of payment for ecosystem services, or PES. The idea is simple: farmers or landowners are paid to manage their land so that it keeps providing an ecosystem service. One definition calls PES a transparent system for securing additional environmental services through conditional payments to voluntary providers. The provider usually holds the property rights over the land and is compensated by those who benefit from its services. For a deal to make sense to both sides, beneficiaries should pay less than the service is worth to them. Providers, in turn, should accept more than it costs them to supply it. In practice, few deals are direct contracts between a buyer and a seller. Most programs are funded by governments and run through intermediaries such as NGOs, groups that sit outside government. PES is often promoted as a tool for rural development, though most programs are not designed mainly to reduce poverty. National programs that pay farmers to set land aside exist in Canada, the EU, Japan and Switzerland, as well as the US and China.

  <!-- nature-mkt-136 -->

- **Additionality: would it have happened anyway?**

  Paying someone to do what they were going to do anyway buys nothing. Additionality is the test for that trap. It asks whether an intervention, such as a payment or a credit, actually causes an outcome that would not have happened otherwise. The answer depends on a baseline, a prediction of what people would do without the policy, with everything else held constant. Strictly, additionality is the intervention's impact minus the impact of that reference case. It must also be counted net of side effects such as deadweight, paying for what would happen anyway, and leakage, harm pushed somewhere else. Displacement and substitution can shrink the gain in similar ways. A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead without the credit revenue, for instance because it was profitable anyway. That scenario is called business as usual. Additionality can be checked after the fact, as in program evaluation, or beforehand, as a screen for which projects may issue environmental credits. The stakes are high. Large markets for Biodiversity offsetting have shown serious shortcomings on it. Problems with additionality and double counting can also undermine trust in the offsets described in Carbon credit. One industry watchdog, the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market, cited additionality concerns when it excluded several renewable energy crediting methods. Every payment scheme in this chapter rises or falls on this question.

  <!-- nature-mkt-144 -->

- **Watershed management: sharing the water a landscape gathers**

  One group's actions upstream can harm everyone downstream, and that is why watersheds need managing. A watershed is the land that drains into one river, lake or stream. Watershed management plans and runs programs that keep a watershed working and share its resources sustainably among its plants, animals and people. It covers water supply, water quality, drainage, stormwater runoff and water rights. On farms the tools include buffer strips, grassed waterways, restored wetlands, conservation tillage and crop rotation. In towns, retention ponds, filters and wetlands let stormwater soak in, so soil and plants clean it before it reaches streams. People are the hard part. Groups sharing a watershed often have unequal and divergent interests. Even the basic framing is disputed: donors backed by the World Bank argue freshwater should be priced as an economic good, while NGOs see it as a social good. States sharing the Rhine, Nile and Lake Chad basins have tried network governance, in which stakeholders form voluntary partnerships.

  <!-- nature-mkt-145 -->

- **The Conservation Reserve Program: paying US farmers not to plow**

  More than 9 billion tons of soil had been kept from eroding by December 1, 2015, thanks to one American program. The Conservation Reserve Program, run by the US Department of Agriculture, pays farmers to take cropland out of production and plant protective cover such as grass, trees or buffer strips. It is a payment for ecosystem services on a national scale. Its aims are to reduce soil erosion, improve water quality and benefit wildlife. It grew out of the Soil Bank of the 1950s and was formally set up by the 1985 Farm Bill, with contracts of 10 to 15 years. Farmers receive rental payments, up to 50% of the cost of establishing cover, and extra incentives. Money is limited, so only the most qualified land is enrolled. The benefits reach beyond the fields. In 2007 it was estimated to have kept 278 million pounds of nitrogen and 59 million pounds of phosphorus from leaving farmland. Ducks in the Prairie Pothole Region rose 30 percent after 1992 with its help.

  <!-- nature-mkt-141 -->

- **Three ways of seeing payments for nature**

  Is paying a farmer to keep a forest a sensible trade, an imperfect tool, or a moral mistake? Thinkers give three broad answers, and they still disagree. Environmental economics sees a payment for ecosystem services as a voluntary, conditional deal between a buyer and a seller of a service, rooted in the The Coase theorem: bargaining your way out of harm. Reality is messier than the theory. Transaction costs, the costs of making and policing a deal, are almost always present. Promises of future payments are not time consistent, meaning a payer may later prefer to break them. Financing often runs short. Ecological economics treats natural and manufactured capital as complements: one cannot simply stand in for the other. It judges a scheme by the weight of its incentive, how directly the money reaches providers, and how far the service is turned into a commodity. Some services, such as tons of carbon stored, are easy to measure; others are hard. The third view rejects the idea of ecosystem services altogether. These critics argue that nature should be valued for its own sake, and that a market framing protects nature only when it is useful to people. Pragmatists accept the problems of putting a value on nature. Still, they argue, in a commodified society 'something is better than nothing'. The split between the first two schools is traced in Two schools: environmental and ecological economics.

  <!-- nature-mkt-137 -->

- **Reverse auctions: letting sellers bid the price down**

  In an ordinary, or forward, auction, buyers bid prices up. A reverse auction flips the roles. One buyer faces many sellers, and the sellers compete by underbidding each other, so prices typically fall. Government procurement through public tenders is a common example. For conservation the format has a special use. A landowner knows the Opportunity cost: the price of the road not taken of setting land aside, while the program paying for it does not. Bids in a reverse auction reveal those private costs, which helps design incentive programs for public goods, shared resources and ecosystem services. Each seller should first work out the lowest price it will accept, which requires knowing its true marginal cost, the cost of supplying one more unit. In a scoring auction, the buyer announces in advance how it will score the price and other features of each offer.

  <!-- nature-mkt-148 -->

- **Grain for Green: China trades fields for forest**

  Some 124 million people in 1,897 counties across 25 provinces have taken part in Grain for Green. China launched the program in 1999 to pay farmers for turning erosion-prone farmland back into vegetation, curbing flooding and soil erosion. It is a payment for ecosystem services in a very literal form: farmers receive grain for not farming forested slopes. By 2010 around 15 million hectares of farmland and 17 million hectares of barren land had returned to natural vegetation. The bill is large and uncertain. One account puts the cost at $43 billion, while some sources cite $95 billion for the whole program. On the whole it has paid off economically and reduced erosion and flooding. Its weak spot is wildlife. Many plantings were cheap single-species stands that did little for biodiversity, though mixed forests could help at little extra cost.

  <!-- nature-mkt-143 -->

- **Costa Rica's pioneering national payment scheme**

  In 1997 Costa Rica set up Pagos por servicios ambientales, the first program of payments for ecosystem services run on a national scale. It pays for four services: greenhouse gas mitigation, water services, biodiversity protection and scenic beauty. A fuel tax paid for it at first, and a water tariff was added in 2006. By the end of 2005 its contracts covered 10% of the country. It is estimated to have prevented 11 million tons of carbon emissions from 1999 to 2005. Its flat payment has a flaw. Many high-value areas stay out, because their opportunity costs are higher than the payment.

  <!-- nature-mkt-138 -->

- **Uganda's forest payment experiment**

  Between 2010 and 2013, forest owners in Hoima and Kibaale, Uganda, took part in the first payment scheme set up as a Randomized controlled trials: the gold-standard experiment to measure its effect on deforestation. Owners were paid $28 per hectare per year for two years to keep their forest intact, about 5% of typical annual income. Deforestation ran at 2 to 5% in participating villages, against 7 to 10% in control villages. The scheme ended once the evaluation was done. Old forest practices are assumed to resume once payments stop.

  <!-- nature-mkt-140 -->

- **Vittel pays farmers to protect its spring water**

  From the 1970s, more intensive farming raised nitrate levels in the aquifer, the underground water store, behind Vittel mineral water. The brand itself was under threat. The pollution came from many scattered sources, so no single farmer's share could be measured. The company negotiated instead. It bought some land and gave nearby farmers technical support and time-limited payments to change their practices. The deal is perhaps the world's best-known payment for ecosystem services built on direct negotiation. It is often cited as a case of the private bargaining described by the The Coase theorem: bargaining your way out of harm. Community grievances and possible overuse of water remain controversial.

  <!-- nature-mkt-139 -->

- **Baselines: measuring against a world that never happened**

  Knowing what a payment achieved means knowing what would have happened without it, and that world can never be observed. The baseline, or counterfactual, is that predicted outcome without the payment or project, against which its real effect is measured. Establishing it is a key challenge for any claim that payments for ecosystem services work. Carbon markets show why. Under the Clean Development Mechanism, credits are issued for the monitored gap between baseline and actual emissions. Because the baseline cannot be seen, it is built from hypothetical scenarios, similar activities elsewhere, or emissions before the project. That invites gaming. Project partners may gain from a high baseline, risking spurious credits, and offsets can even reward emitting more to inflate it. How much leakage gets counted also depends partly on how the baseline is drawn. It is the hidden half of every judgment about additionality.

  <!-- nature-mkt-150 -->

- **No service, no payment: the rule of conditionality**

  No service, no money. Conditionality is the rule that a payment for ecosystem services is made only if the service is delivered or the agreed land use is kept up. It sits inside one well-known definition of PES: additional environmental services secured through conditional payments to voluntary providers. Most design debates turn on how conditions are set and enforced through monitoring and verification. The idea also runs through social policy. The programs described in Conditional cash transfers: paying families to choose school pay families for schooling and health care, and in Mexico the conditions raised secondary-school attendance most. Conditions are not welcome everywhere. Supporters of a rights-based approach to development argue strongly against attaching them to social cash transfers.

  <!-- nature-mkt-149 -->

- **Paying for results, not promises**

  Most payment programs pay for management practices, and only less commonly for measured outcomes. Results-based payments reverse that. Money flows only for measured, verified environmental results, such as emission reductions, rather than for planned actions. Forests are the biggest test. REDD+ uses such payments to put a financial value on carbon stored in forests, as the last of four stages after readiness, a finance agreement and verification. To qualify, a country needs a national system for monitoring its forests, documented methods and data, and reporting under the Warsaw Framework. It also needs an assessed benchmark of its past forest emissions and a report on how agreed social and environmental safeguards are respected. The Carbon Fund of the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility pays only after independent verification of reported cuts. The Green Climate Fund ran a pilot from 2017 to 2022 and made it a permanent window in 2024. Farming has a version too. The European Commission defines results-based schemes as paying for outcomes such as breeding birds, leaving the methods to the farmer.

  <!-- nature-mkt-152 -->

- **How New York City keeps its water clean by guarding its watersheds**

  Only 10% of New York City's water is filtered, though all of it is disinfected. The rest stays clean because the city protects the upstate watersheds that supply it. Its three systems, Croton, Catskill and Delaware, reach up to 125 miles (201 km) north of the city. Together they deliver over 1.2 billion US gallons a day to more than eight million residents. Since 1997 the city has bought, or protected through legal limits on development, over 130,000 acres (53,000 ha) of watershed land. The Department of Environmental Protection runs a $1.5 billion Watershed Protection Program. The payoff is a partial exemption from filtration rules. That spares the city more than $10 billion for a filtration plant and at least $100 million a year to run it. In 2018 the city announced a further US$1 billion investment to keep its unfiltered supply pure, partly against cloudier water driven by climate change. Here a protected landscape does the work of a machine.

  <!-- nature-mkt-147 -->

- **Conditional cash transfers: paying families to choose school**

  Few development programs have been evaluated as rigorously as conditional cash transfers. These programs fight poverty by paying cash only to people who meet conditions, such as sending children to school or getting them vaccinated. By 2011 they had spread to 18 Latin American countries, covering up to 129 million people. Brazil's Bolsa Família, for example, pays poor households if school-age children are enrolled and younger children vaccinated. The conditions seem to matter. Evidence from Mexico and Malawi found they raised school enrollment compared with unconditional payments.

  <!-- nature-mkt-146 -->

- **Putting conservation money where it counts most**

  A flat payment treats every hectare alike, but land is not alike. Spatial targeting means directing conservation payments to the places where they buy the most environmental benefit for the money. Costa Rica shows the cost of skipping it. Its flat-rate payments leave many high-value areas unenrolled, because landowners there face higher opportunity costs. Its water tariff, tied to particular watersheds, was criticized for concentrating money in areas of relatively low ecological importance. Two tools help. Reverse auctions can reveal what each landowner really needs to be paid. The Conservation Reserve Program, with limited money, admits only the most qualified land.

  <!-- nature-mkt-151 -->

- **Farm stewardship schemes in England and Switzerland**

  An environmental management scheme gives landowners and land managers incentives to look after the environment. England runs such schemes under Environmental Stewardship, administered by Natural England. After leaving the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, the British government started its Environmental Land Management scheme in 2024. Switzerland ties the money directly to practice. Since 1998 it has made farm subsidies depend on good environmental care, such as keeping at least 7% of farmland as ecological compensation areas.
